sceneCredit.creator: Rohitjahnavi

lessons.title: Conservation of Forest and Wildlife in India

activities.prompt: What happens to us if India's forests and wild animals keep disappearing?
activities.explanation: Now read on to find out.

activities.title: Why do we conserve forests and wildlife?
activities.body: Wildlife and forests were declining fast, so conservation became essential. It protects ecological diversity and the systems that keep life going. It also saves the genetic variety of plants and animals, which helps them grow and breed well. In the 1960s and 1970s, conservationists asked for a national wildlife protection programme.
keyPoints: Conservation became essential because wildlife and forests declined rapidly.
It preserves ecological diversity and life support systems.
It protects genetic diversity for better growth and breeding.
activities.explanation: Protecting nature keeps life on Earth healthy for everyone.

activities.prompt: A village pond has many kinds of fish and water plants. One year, the water plants die. Soon the fish catch becomes very small. Why did this happen?
steps: The fish in the pond depend on the water plants for food and shelter.
When the plants die, the fish lose their life support in the pond.
So fewer fish survive, and the fishermen catch much less.
This shows that fisheries depend on the many kinds of living things in water.
activities.explanation: Think it through with Hooty.

activities.prompt: Why did conservation become essential in India?
options: Because wildlife and forests declined rapidly
Because forests grew too quickly
Because there were too many parks
activities.explanation: Well done! Wildlife and forestry fell fast, so saving them became vital.

activities.prompt: In the 1960s and 1970s, conservationists demanded a national wildlife ______ programme.
activities.hint: It is the word for keeping something safe from harm.
activities.explanation: Great! Conservationists asked for a national wildlife protection programme.

activities.prompt: Match each need with what it depends on.
pairs: Genetic diversity of plants and animals
activities.explanation: Super! Farms, fisheries and breeding all depend on different kinds of diversity.

activities.prompt: What did the wildlife protection programme do to save endangered species?
options: Banned hunting and restricted trade
Encouraged hunting in forests
Sold endangered animals abroad
activities.explanation: Correct! Banning hunting and restricting trade helped protect endangered species.

activities.prompt: An all-India list of ______ species was published.
activities.hint: These are the species the programme keeps safe.
activities.explanation: Well done! The list told everyone which species were protected.

activities.prompt: Put these steps of the protection programme in order.
items: Conservationists demanded a national wildlife protection programme
An all-India list of protected species was published
Central and state governments set up national parks and wildlife sanctuaries
activities.explanation: Great thinking! First came the demand, then the list, then the parks and sanctuaries.

activities.prompt: A pond has many kinds of water plants and fish. The plants die. Then the fish catch gets smaller. Why did the fish catch get smaller?
options: The fish lost their food and homes when the plants died.
The fish all swam away to another pond far off.
The pond water became too deep for fish to swim.
The fishermen became lazy and stopped going to the pond.

why.The fish all swam away to another pond f: This blames a random escape, not the loss of the fish's life support.
why.The pond water became too deep for fish: This blames a change in water depth, which the story never says.
why.The fishermen became lazy and stopped go: This blames the people instead of the broken web of water life.

activities.explanation: Right. Water life depends on many living things staying healthy together.

activities.prompt: India has one list of protected animals for the whole country. A man sees a rare bird from this list in his field. He wants to shoot it. Why can he not shoot it?
options: Hunting protected animals is banned so rare ones can survive.
The bird is too small, so a gun cannot hit it well.
The bird belongs to his neighbour, so it is not his.
Shooting birds is allowed only on some days of the year.

why.The bird is too small, so a gun cannot h: This thinks size matters, but the rule is about protection, not size.
why.The bird belongs to his neighbour, so it: This thinks ownership is the reason, not the protection law.
why.Shooting birds is allowed only on some d: This thinks the ban is only for some days, not a full ban.

activities.explanation: Right. The ban on hunting protects endangered listed species.

activities.prompt: A farmer grows his family's old rice seeds. He also grows new rice seeds. Why does he keep the old seeds too?
options: Old seeds keep many plant types for better breeding later.
Old seeds always grow faster than any new seed can.
Old seeds need no water, so they save him much work.
Old seeds look pretty, so shops pay him more money.

why.Old seeds always grow faster than any ne: This thinks old seeds are simply better growers, which is not the reason.
why.Old seeds need no water, so they save hi: This adds a magic power the old seeds do not really have.
why.Old seeds look pretty, so shops pay him: This thinks the reason is money from looks, not saving plant variety.

activities.explanation: Right. Farming still needs old varieties, and their genes help better breeding.

activities.prompt: A big forest stands near a village. The forest is cut down. After some years, the village springs give less water. Why did the springs give less water?
options: The forest was a life support system that kept water flowing.
The villagers used the spring water to wash too many clothes.
The springs moved underground because they did not like the village.
The sun drank all the spring water in that one year.

why.The villagers used the spring water to w: This blames the villagers' washing, not the loss of the forest.
why.The springs moved underground because th: This gives springs feelings and a choice, which they do not have.
why.The sun drank all the spring water in th: This blames one hot year, but the change came after the forest fell.

activities.explanation: Right. Forests are life support systems, so losing them harms water too.

lessons.sceneCaption: A female Bengal tiger in Kanha National Park, India.

lessons.title: Project Tiger

activities.prompt: How did India bring its tigers back from the edge of disappearing?
activities.explanation: Now read on to find out.

activities.title: Why we save the tiger
activities.body: The tiger is a key species in the faunal web, the web of animal life in a forest. Long ago there were about 55,000 tigers, but by 1973 only 1,827 were left. Poaching, shrinking habitat and loss of prey hurt them. So India started Project Tiger in 1973 to protect tigers and the large wild places they live in.
keyPoints: The tiger is a key species in the faunal web.
Tiger numbers fell from 55,000 to 1,827 by 1973.
Project Tiger began in 1973 to protect tigers and their homes.
activities.explanation: Saving the tiger also saves the whole forest it lives in.

activities.prompt: A tiger skin is sold in a market far away. Why does that one sale hurt a whole forest?
steps: The tiger sits at the top of the faunal web, so it holds many links together.
Buyers pay well for skins and bones, so poaching gives quick money.
Every tiger killed weakens the web and pushes the species near extinction.
So one sale in a market can damage a whole living system.
activities.explanation: Think it through with Hooty.

activities.prompt: At the turn of the century, the tiger population was estimated at 55,000.
activities.explanation: Yes, there were about 55,000 tigers at the turn of the century.

activities.prompt: In 1973, authorities realised the tiger population had dwindled to ______.
activities.hint: It is a four-digit number, just over 1,800.
activities.explanation: The count in 1973 was only 1,827 tigers. That shocked the country.

activities.prompt: Match each tiger reserve with its first letter.
activities.explanation: Corbett, Sunderbans, Bandhavgarh, Sariska, Manas and Periyar are tiger reserves.

activities.prompt: Which of these is a major threat to tigers, according to your book?
options: Heavy rain in forests
Poaching and shrinking habitat
Too many tourists
Cold winters
activities.explanation: Poaching, shrinking habitat and depletion of prey are the major threats.

activities.prompt: India and Nepal became prime targets for poaching and illegal trading because they hold about two-thirds of surviving tigers.
activities.explanation: True. With so many tigers, these two nations drew poachers and traders.

activities.prompt: Put these events in the correct time order.
items: About 55,000 tigers at the turn of the century
activities.explanation: First tigers were many, then the count fell, then Project Tiger began.

activities.prompt: India and Nepal together have about two-thirds of the world's surviving tigers. Poachers and illegal traders focus their work there. Why did poachers choose these two countries?
options: Because most surviving tigers live in these two countries
Because these two countries have the largest forests in Asia
Because tigers in these countries are weaker and easier to catch
Because these countries pay no punishment for catching tigers

why.Because these two countries have the lar: Wrong: this confuses big forests with having the most tigers.
why.Because tigers in these countries are we: Wrong: this invents a reason; the fact says nothing about weak tigers.
why.Because these countries pay no punishmen: Wrong: this confuses poaching with a lack of punishment.

activities.explanation: Right: poachers go where the tigers are, and most tigers live there.

activities.prompt: At the turn of the century, India had about 55,000 tigers. By 1973, only 1,827 were left. What does this big drop tell us about those years?
options: Tigers were counted more carefully in 1973 than before
Tigers were disappearing fast and needed urgent saving
Tigers had moved from India to other countries
Tigers had always been few in number in India

why.Tigers were counted more carefully in 19: Wrong: a better count cannot explain such a huge fall in numbers.
why.Tigers had moved from India to other cou: Wrong: the fact says the population dwindled, not that tigers moved away.
why.Tigers had always been few in number in: Wrong: 55,000 at the turn of the century shows tigers were once many.

activities.explanation: Right: a fall from 55,000 to 1,827 shows tigers were vanishing fast.

activities.prompt: In 1973, authorities realised the tiger population had dwindled to 1,827. In the same year, Project Tiger was launched. Why did the project start in that exact year?
options: Because 1973 was a good year for starting new projects
Because the low tiger count made leaders act at once
Because tiger reserves were ready many years earlier
Because people had stopped buying tiger skins by then

why.Because 1973 was a good year for startin: Wrong: a year being 'good' is not a real reason for a government plan.
why.Because tiger reserves were ready many y: Wrong: reserves came with the project, not before it.
why.Because people had stopped buying tiger: Wrong: trade in skins and bones was still a threat at that time.

activities.explanation: Right: the shocking count of 1,827 pushed authorities to launch the project.

activities.prompt: Project Tiger did not only count and protect tigers. It also aimed to preserve biotypes of sizeable magnitude. Why did saving tigers mean saving large wild areas too?
options: Because tigers need big living spaces with their prey
Because tigers like to live close to big cities
Because large areas are cheaper for the government to buy
Because tigers can only be counted inside huge parks

why.Because tigers like to live close to big: Wrong: tigers live in wild habitats, not near cities.
why.Because large areas are cheaper for the: Wrong: cost is not the reason given in the facts.
why.Because tigers can only be counted insid: Wrong: counting is not why large biotypes were preserved.

activities.explanation: Right: a big animal at the top of the web needs a big habitat with prey.

activities.prompt: A trader sells tiger bones for use in traditional medicines. A trader sells deer meat in the same market. Which sale pushes tigers closer to extinction, and why?
options: The deer meat, because deer are bigger than tigers
The deer meat, because tigers eat deer as their prey
The tiger bones, because tiger trade left tigers near extinction
Both equally, because any animal product harms all animals

why.The deer meat, because deer are bigger t: Wrong: size is not the reason deer meat matters here.
why.The deer meat, because tigers eat deer a: Wrong: deer meat hurts prey numbers, but the fact links extinction to tiger trade.
why.Both equally, because any animal product: Wrong: the facts name tiger trade, not all trade, as the near-extinction cause.

activities.explanation: Right: trade in skins and bones is the trade that left tigers near extinction.

activities.prompt: In a forest, poachers keep catching the deer and wild animals that tigers eat. The tigers themselves are not shot. What will happen to the tigers in this forest over time?
options: They will grow in number because no tiger is shot
They will move to cities to find new food
They will dwindle because their prey is being depleted
They will stay the same because deer are not tigers

why.They will grow in number because no tige: Wrong: no shooting alone cannot save tigers if their food disappears.
why.They will move to cities to find new foo: Wrong: tigers live in wild habitats, not in cities.
why.They will stay the same because deer are: Wrong: tigers depend on prey, so losing prey hurts them too.

activities.explanation: Right: depletion of prey is named as a major threat to tigers.

lessons.sceneCaption: A Bengal tiger in Sanjay Dubri Tiger Reserve, Madhya Pradesh, India, a habitat protected for tigers.

lessons.title: Types and Distribution of Forest and Wildlife Resources

activities.prompt: Who really owns India's forests, and how are they sorted?
activities.explanation: Now read on to find out.

activities.title: Three Kinds of Forests
activities.body: Forests and wildlife are hard to manage and look after. Much of them is owned or managed by the government. To make this easier, forests are sorted into categories. Reserved forests are the biggest group and are most valuable for conservation. Protected forests are kept safe from further loss. Unclassed forests are other forests and wastelands.
keyPoints: Forest and wildlife resources are hard to manage and control.
Much forest land is owned or managed by the government.
Forests are grouped as reserved, protected and unclassified.
activities.explanation: Sorting forests into groups helps the government look after them better.

activities.prompt: A state wood, a family grove, and village trees sit nearby. Why does the government sort them into different groups?
steps: Trees and animals are useful, so losing them hurts everyone.
No one can watch every tree, so control is very hard.
The government owns much forest, so it sorts land into groups.
So grouping helps manage land that no one can fully control.
activities.explanation: Think it through with Hooty.

activities.prompt: Which category covers more than half of the total forest land?
options: Reserved forests
Protected forests
Unclassed forests
activities.explanation: Well done! Reserved forests take up more than half of all forest land.

activities.prompt: The state with the largest area under permanent forests is ______.
activities.hint: A large state in the middle of India.
activities.explanation: Great! Madhya Pradesh has the largest area under permanent forests.

activities.prompt: Match each forest category with what it means.
pairs: More than half of forest land
activities.explanation: Each category covers a different share and kind of forest land.

activities.prompt: Why are reserved forests so special?
options: They are most valuable for conservation
They are wastelands of private people
They are the newest forests in India
activities.explanation: Reserved forests are the most valuable ones for conservation of nature.

activities.prompt: Put these categories in order, from the most carefully guarded to the least.
activities.explanation: Reserved forests are most valuable for conservation, then protected forests, then unclassified ones.

activities.prompt: What does it mean when protected forest land is saved from further depletion?
options: It will not be used up and lost any more
It will be given to private people to own
It will be counted as unclassified forest
activities.explanation: Depletion means loss. Protected forests are kept safe so they are not used up further.

activities.prompt: In one district, trees are being cut very fast. The government wants to stop this depletion. Which type should this forest be?
options: Reserved forest
Protected forest
Unclassed forest
Any type works

why.Reserved forest: Thinks the most valuable type must fit every problem.
why.Unclassed forest: Thinks the weakest type gets the strongest protection.
why.Any type works: Thinks categories do not matter, but each type has its own rule.

activities.explanation: Protected forest is protected from further depletion, so it fits.

activities.prompt: State A keeps most of its forest as reserved forest. State B keeps most as unclassed forest. Which state's forests are safer for conservation?
options: State A
State B
Both the same
Cannot be said

why.State B: Thinks open unclassed land means well cared for.
why.Both the same: Thinks a label never changes how land is treated.
why.Cannot be said: Thinks forest types tell us nothing about safety.

activities.explanation: Reserved forests are the most valuable for conservation.

activities.prompt: A forest lies between two villages. Both villages cut wood there. Quarrels grow every year. The government takes over managing this forest. Why did it do so?
options: Forest resources are hard to manage and control
The government wants to sell all the wood
Villages are not allowed to own any land
Whoever cuts first owns the forest

why.The government wants to sell all the woo: Thinks takeover is about money, not better control.
why.Villages are not allowed to own any land: Blames a false ownership ban instead of hard control.
why.Whoever cuts first owns the forest: Thinks might makes ownership; rules do not work that way.

activities.explanation: Such resources are difficult to manage, control and regulate.

activities.prompt: Reserved and protected forests are permanent forest estates. A report says Madhya Pradesh has the largest area under them. What does the report tell us?
options: Its reserved and protected forests cover the largest area
Its unclassed forests cover the largest area
Its forests can never be cut or used
Its wastelands are larger than its forests

why.Its unclassed forests cover the largest: Swaps categories; unclassed land is not a permanent estate.
why.Its forests can never be cut or used: Thinks permanent means no use; estates also give timber.
why.Its wastelands are larger than its fores: Mixes wastelands with estates; wastelands are unclassed land.

activities.explanation: Permanent estates mean reserved plus protected, and MP tops there.

activities.prompt: More than half of forest land is reserved forest. Almost one-third is protected forest. A student says most forest land lies in these two types. Is she thinking correctly?
options: Yes, the two types together cover most forest land
No, unclassed forests are the biggest part
Yes, because unclassed land is not real forest
No, half and one-third make a small part

why.No, unclassed forests are the biggest pa: Reverses the sizes; unclassed is the small leftover.
why.Yes, because unclassed land is not real: Right guess, wrong reason; unclassed forests are still forests.
why.No, half and one-third make a small part: Adds the shares wrongly; together they cover most land.

activities.explanation: More than half plus almost one-third leaves only a small rest.

activities.prompt: A village looks after a small wood. It calls the wood 'our protected grove'. No government order covers this wood. Which forest type is it, by the rule?
options: Unclassed forest
Protected forest
Reserved forest
Permanent forest

why.Protected forest: Trusts the name on the sign, not the rule.
why.Reserved forest: Thinks saving wood for village use makes it reserved.
why.Permanent forest: Thinks any cared-for wood is an estate; estates are reserved and protected.

activities.explanation: Community and private woods without government orders are unclassed.

lessons.sceneCaption: A map showing how much of each Indian state is covered by forest.

lessons.title: Community and Conservation

activities.prompt: Can ordinary villagers really protect forests better than anyone else?
activities.explanation: Now read on to find out.

activities.title: People Who Protect Nature
activities.body: Saving forests is not new in India. Some traditional communities live in forests and know them well. When their homes and livelihoods are at risk, local people fight to protect them. They struggle with officials so that habitats stay safe for the long term.
keyPoints: Conservation strategies are not new in India.
Forests are home to some traditional communities.
Local communities work to conserve habitats for their long-term livelihood.
activities.explanation: People who live closest to nature often care for it the most.

activities.prompt: A village sits next to a forest. The people collect fruits and firewood from it. One day, a company wants to dig mines there. Why do the villagers fight to stop the mine?
steps: The forest gives the villagers food, wood and other things every day, so it is their livelihood.
If the mine destroys the forest, the villagers lose these things for many years, not just one day.
Officials may see only short-term gain, but the villagers think about their children's future too.
So the villagers fight to conserve the forest because their long-term life depends on it.
activities.explanation: Think it through with Hooty.

activities.title: Villagers Take Charge
activities.body: In many areas, villagers protect habitats on their own and say no to government help. The Chipko movement resisted deforestation and proved that communities can grow forests too. When people plant and guard trees together, this is called community afforestation, and it can succeed.
keyPoints: In many areas, villagers protect habitats and reject government involvement.
The Chipko movement resisted deforestation.
Community afforestation can succeed.
activities.explanation: Trust in local people can work as well as big official plans.

activities.title: The Villagers of Sariska
activities.prompt: In Sariska Tiger Reserve, what did villagers use to fight against mining?
options: The Wildlife Protection Act
A new village school
A court order from another country
A ban on all farming
activities.explanation: The villagers of Sariska used the Wildlife Protection Act to fight mining. Good thinking!

activities.title: Rules of the Forest
activities.prompt: The villagers of Sonchuri made rules that do not allow ______ and protect wildlife from encroachments.
activities.hint: What activity with animals did the villagers stop?
activities.explanation: The rules ban hunting so that wildlife stays safe. Well done!

activities.title: Sonchuri Check
activities.prompt: Five villages in Alwar declared 1,200 hectares of land as Bhairodev Dakav 'Sonchuri'.
activities.explanation: Yes! Five villages set aside 1,200 hectares and called it Sonchuri.

activities.title: Who Did What?
activities.prompt: Match each place or group with what they did.
pairs: Fought mining with the Wildlife Protection Act
Showed crop growing without synthetic chemicals works
activities.explanation: Each group found its own way to protect nature. You matched them all!

activities.title: The Chipko Lesson
activities.prompt: What did the Chipko movement show can succeed?
options: Community afforestation
Mining in forests
Hunting of wildlife
Building of factories
activities.explanation: Chipko resisted deforestation and showed that communities can grow forests successfully.

activities.title: Farming Without Chemicals
activities.prompt: Farmers and citizen's groups showed that growing many crops without synthetic chemicals is what?
options: Viable
Illegal
Impossible
Harmful
activities.explanation: They proved that diversified crop production without synthetic chemicals is viable, meaning it can work well.

activities.prompt: A forest village gets fruits, firewood and fodder from the forest. Officials want to cut part of it. The villagers protest for many years. Why do the villagers keep fighting?
options: They want to sell the forest land to another company
The forest is their livelihood for the long term
They want officials to plant new trees for them
They enjoy fighting with officials every year

why.They want to sell the forest land to ano: This mixes up villagers with miners, who are the ones harming the forest.
why.They want officials to plant new trees f: This thinks villagers depend fully on government, but they often act on their own.
why.They enjoy fighting with officials every: This sees protest as a hobby, not as a serious need to protect their life.

activities.explanation: Right. Local communities struggle to conserve habitats because their long-term livelihood depends on them.

activities.prompt: In Sariska, villagers went to court using the Wildlife Protection Act. In Alwar, five villages made their own rules called Sonchuri. What is the main difference between the two ways?
options: Sariska used a government law, Alwar made their own rules
Sariska wanted mining, Alwar wanted hunting
Sariska protected animals, Alwar protected only trees
Sariska failed, Alwar succeeded in saving wildlife

why.Sariska wanted mining, Alwar wanted hunt: This confuses the two sides; villagers in both places were against mining and hunting.
why.Sariska protected animals, Alwar protect: Both places protected wildlife and habitats, not just one thing.
why.Sariska failed, Alwar succeeded in savin: The facts do not say one failed; both are examples of communities acting.

activities.explanation: Right. Sariska used the Wildlife Protection Act, while Alwar villages declared their own Sonchuri rules.

activities.prompt: A village near a forest sees hunters coming at night. The villagers declare their own protected area, like Sonchuri. Which rule would fit their plan?
options: Nobody may hunt animals or encroach on the forest
Only government officers may enter the forest area
Hunting is allowed on weekends for all villagers
The forest is open to mining companies for money

why.Only government officers may enter the f: This is the opposite; many villagers reject government involvement and guard habitats themselves.
why.Hunting is allowed on weekends for all v: This allows the very harm the village wants to stop.
why.The forest is open to mining companies f: Mining destroys habitats, so villagers would never invite it.

activities.explanation: Right. Sonchuri rules did not allow hunting and protected wildlife from encroachments.

lessons.title: Sacred Groves and Nature Worship

activities.prompt: Why would people leave a whole forest completely untouched for centuries?
activities.explanation: Now read on to find out.

activities.title: Forests Kept Safe by Faith
activities.body: Long ago, tribal people believed that every part of nature must be protected. This belief is called nature worship. Because of it, some forest patches were left untouched by local people. These green patches stayed wild and pure. They are called Sacred Groves, the forests of God and Goddesses. Nobody is allowed to harm them.
keyPoints: Nature worship says all creations of nature must be protected.
Sacred Groves are virgin forests kept in pristine form.
Local people left these forest patches untouched.
Any interference with Sacred Groves is banned.
activities.explanation: Faith helped keep whole forests safe and wild.

activities.prompt: Two forests grow next to a village. After many years, one forest is still thick and full of trees. The other forest has become small and empty. Why did one forest survive?
steps: The village believes all creations of nature must be protected, so this belief guides what people do.
One forest is a sacred grove, which means it is seen as the forest of gods and goddesses.
Because the grove belongs to the gods, any interference with it is banned by the local people.
So the sacred grove is left untouched and stays pristine, while the other forest is used and shrinks.
activities.explanation: Think it through with Hooty.

activities.prompt: What is a Sacred Grove?
options: A garden made by a king
A forest patch left untouched by local people
A farm where trees are planted in rows
A park with swings and slides
activities.explanation: Sacred Groves are forest patches people left untouched out of belief. Well done!

activities.prompt: The Mundas and Santhal worship the ______ tree and the kadamba tree.
activities.hint: It rhymes with 'bahuva' and starts with 'ma'.
activities.explanation: The mahua and kadamba trees are worshipped by the Mundas and Santhal.

activities.prompt: Which pair of trees is considered sacred?
options: Tamarind and mango
Mahua and kadamba
Peepal and banyan
Kadamba and mango
activities.explanation: Peepal and banyan trees are considered sacred by many people.

activities.prompt: Match each group or place with the trees it worships.
activities.explanation: Different people hold different trees sacred. You matched them all!

activities.prompt: Put these steps in order to show how a Sacred Grove is formed.
items: People believe all creations of nature must be protected
Local people leave a forest patch untouched
The forest stays virgin and pristine
It is honoured as a Sacred Grove
activities.explanation: Belief comes first, then care, then a pristine forest. Lovely thinking!

activities.prompt: Macaques and langurs live around temples and are fed every day. Why?
options: They are treated as devotees
They guard the temple gate
They carry offerings for priests
They perform tricks for visitors
activities.explanation: These monkeys are treated as devotees, so they are fed daily. Nature worship respects animals too!

activities.prompt: A company wants to cut trees in a sacred grove. The local people stop the company. Why do the people stop it?
options: The grove belongs to gods and no one may touch it.
The trees there are too old to be cut down.
The company did not pay the village any money.
The wood there is too weak for building shops.

why.The trees there are too old to be cut do: Wrong: this thinks the rule is about the age of trees, not about belief.
why.The company did not pay the village any: Wrong: this thinks the reason is money, but the ban is not about payment.
why.The wood there is too weak for building: Wrong: this thinks the reason is wood quality, but the ban is about belief.

activities.explanation: Right: a sacred grove is a forest of gods and goddesses, and any interference with it is banned.

activities.prompt: Two forests grow near a village. One is a sacred grove. One is a normal forest. After fifty years, which forest still looks the same?
options: The sacred grove, because people left it untouched.
The normal forest, because people left it untouched.
The sacred grove, because people planted new trees there.
Both forests, because nobody ever uses any forest.

why.The normal forest, because people left i: Wrong: this mixes up the two forests; normal forests are used by people.
why.The sacred grove, because people planted: Wrong: the grove survived because it was untouched, not because of new planting.
why.Both forests, because nobody ever uses a: Wrong: this thinks no one uses forests, but people do use normal forests.

activities.explanation: Right: local people leave sacred groves untouched, so they stay in pristine form.

activities.prompt: A new road must pass a big peepal tree. The builders curve the road around the tree instead of cutting it. Why do they curve the road?
options: People consider the peepal tree sacred.
The tree roots make the road stronger there.
Cutting the big tree costs too much money.
The tree gives cool shade to road workers.

why.The tree roots make the road stronger th: Wrong: this thinks roots help roads, but the reason is belief.
why.Cutting the big tree costs too much mone: Wrong: this thinks the reason is money, but the reason is reverence.
why.The tree gives cool shade to road worker: Wrong: this thinks shade matters, but the reason is that the tree is sacred.

activities.explanation: Right: peepal trees are considered sacred, so people protect them.

activities.context: A village depends on a nearby forest for grazing and firewood. Last year, part of the forest was cleared to build a road. Since then, the stream that waters the fields carries more mud, the soil on the slopes looks poorer, and the birds and insects the farmers used to see have become fewer. Worried, the village head calls a meeting to discuss what has changed and what should be done next.
activities.prompt: Why did the quality of the village's soil and stream begin to decline after the forest was cleared?
options: Removing the vegetation broke the natural processes that kept renewing the soil and the water
The road made the stream flow faster and carry more water than before
The farmers started drawing far more water from the stream for their fields
The birds and insects left because the stream became too noisy near the road

why.The road made the stream flow faster and: Wrong: the passage gives no reason to think the stream's flow or speed changed because of the road
why.The farmers started drawing far more wat: Wrong: nothing in the case says the farmers changed how much water they use
why.The birds and insects left because the s: Wrong: the birds and insects are described as a result of the change, not its cause

activities.explanation: Correct: plants, animals and micro-organisms are what keep re-creating the quality of soil and water, so clearing them harms both

activities.context: A village depends on a nearby forest for grazing and firewood. Last year, part of the forest was cleared to build a road. Since then, the stream that waters the fields carries more mud, the soil on the slopes looks poorer, and the birds and insects the farmers used to see have become fewer. Worried, the village head calls a meeting to discuss what has changed and what should be done next.
activities.prompt: If the clearing of the forest continues, what is the most likely consequence for the village and its surroundings?
options: Only the remaining trees will be affected, while the fields, stream and animals stay unchanged
The stream will gradually become cleaner as the loose mud settles on the fields
More and more living things around the village will suffer, since they all rest on the plants at the base
The soil on the slopes will repair itself within a few weeks without any help

why.Only the remaining trees will be affecte: Wrong: living beings form one connected system, so the effects cannot stay limited to the trees
why.The stream will gradually become cleaner: Wrong: with the vegetation gone, there is less to renew water and soil quality, so things would worsen, not improve
why.The soil on the slopes will repair itsel: Wrong: the soil's quality is maintained by living organisms, so it cannot simply recover on its own once they are reduced

activities.explanation: Correct: all other living beings depend on the primary producers, so losing more of them weakens the whole system

activities.context: A village depends on a nearby forest for grazing and firewood. Last year, part of the forest was cleared to build a road. Since then, the stream that waters the fields carries more mud, the soil on the slopes looks poorer, and the birds and insects the farmers used to see have become fewer. Worried, the village head calls a meeting to discuss what has changed and what should be done next.
activities.prompt: What should the village head most sensibly propose at the meeting?
options: Ask villagers to protect the remaining forest, because the whole living community around the village rests on it
Suggest digging deeper wells so the village needs less water from the muddy stream
Advise farmers to stop grazing animals altogether until the forest grows back by itself
Recommend waiting for good rainfall, which will wash the mud out of the stream

why.Suggest digging deeper wells so the vill: Wrong: deeper wells treat the symptom, not the cause, and do nothing about the damaged soil and declining wildlife
why.Advise farmers to stop grazing animals a: Wrong: stopping grazing alone does not restore the living processes that renew soil and water, and the forest will not regrow by itself
why.Recommend waiting for good rainfall, whi: Wrong: rainfall may move the mud along but cannot bring back the lost vegetation and the benefits it provided

activities.explanation: Correct: since every other living being depends on the primary producers, safeguarding the remaining forest protects the entire system the village relies on

activities.prompt:
Assertion (A): India is counted among the countries of the world richest in the variety of living forms.
Reason (R): The species found in India differ widely in form and function yet remain closely integrated with one another.
options: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true but R is false.
A is false but R is true.
activities.explanation: Both statements are true, but the close integration of species does not by itself explain why India ranks among the richest countries in biological diversity.

activities.prompt:
Assertion (A): Humans can survive comfortably even if the ecological system around them is damaged.
Reason (R): Humans are just one small part of a complex web that links all living organisms.
options: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true but R is false.
A is false but R is true.
activities.explanation: The assertion is false because humans are very much dependent on the system, while the reason is a true statement about our place in the web.

activities.prompt: Explain why forests are described as playing a key role in the ecological system.
activities.answer: Forests are called primary producers in the ecological system. This means they produce the basic material on which the rest of the system is built. All other living beings depend on these primary producers for their survival, so if forests are harmed, the effect spreads through the whole web of life. Forests also support the plants, animals and micro-organisms that re-create the quality of air, water and soil. This is why forests are not just one part of nature but hold a key position on which the entire ecological system rests.
points: States that forests are primary producers
Explains that all other living beings depend on primary producers
Links forests to the re-creation of the quality of air, water and soil
Concludes that this dependence makes the forest's role a key one in the system
activities.explanation: Compare your answer with the points a marker looks for.

activities.context: In a district beside a large river, fish catches had been falling and forest cover had shrunk, so wildlife populations declined rapidly. After conservationists demanded a national wildlife protection programme in the 1960s and 1970s, the government published an all-India list of protected species, banned hunting of endangered animals, restricted their trade, and set up national parks and wildlife sanctuaries. Farmers in the district still grow traditional crop varieties, and fishing remains the main livelihood of many families.
activities.prompt: What would most likely happen to the district's fish families if the river's aquatic biodiversity declined much further?
options: Their traditional crop varieties would improve
Their main livelihood would come under threat
Hunting of endangered animals would resume
The protected species list would become longer

why.Their traditional crop varieties would i: Wrong: crops are a separate livelihood; river change does not improve them.
why.Hunting of endangered animals would resu: Wrong: hunting bans apply to land animals, not river fish.
why.The protected species list would become: Wrong: the list covers protected species; a decline would not lengthen it.

activities.explanation: Correct: fisheries depend heavily on aquatic biodiversity, so losing it hits fishing livelihoods.

activities.context: In a district beside a large river, fish catches had been falling and forest cover had shrunk, so wildlife populations declined rapidly. After conservationists demanded a national wildlife protection programme in the 1960s and 1970s, the government published an all-India list of protected species, banned hunting of endangered animals, restricted their trade, and set up national parks and wildlife sanctuaries. Farmers in the district still grow traditional crop varieties, and fishing remains the main livelihood of many families.
activities.prompt: A trader offers to buy skins of an animal named on the all-India protected list. What should the seller decide, and why?
options: Sell, because trade restrictions only apply outside the district
Sell, because hunting is banned but selling is not
Refuse, because trade in protected species is restricted by the programme
Refuse, because only state governments can punish traders

why.Sell, because trade restrictions only ap: Wrong: the restriction is an all-India rule, not limited to one district.
why.Sell, because hunting is banned but sell: Wrong: the programme restricted trade as well as banning hunting.
why.Refuse, because only state governments c: Wrong: the reason to refuse is the trade restriction, not who enforces it.

activities.explanation: Correct: the programme aimed to protect endangered species by restricting trade.

activities.prompt:
Assertion (A): Conservation preserves the genetic diversity of plants and animals.
Reason (R): Genetic diversity is needed for the better growth and breeding of plants and animals.
options: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true but R is false.
A is false but R is true.
activities.explanation: Both statements are true, and the reason directly explains why genetic diversity is preserved.

activities.prompt:
Assertion (A): National parks and wildlife sanctuaries can be established by both central and state governments.
Reason (R): An all-India list of protected species was published under the wildlife protection programme.
options: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true but R is false.
A is false but R is true.
activities.explanation: Both statements are true, but publishing the list does not explain who establishes parks and sanctuaries.

activities.prompt: Explain why conservation of forests and wildlife became essential in India.
activities.answer: Conservation became essential because the population of wildlife and the extent of forests declined rapidly. This loss threatened ecological diversity and the life support systems that all living things depend on. It also put at risk the genetic diversity of plants and animals, which is needed for their better growth and breeding. Since agriculture still depends on traditional crop varieties and fisheries depend heavily on aquatic biodiversity, losing biodiversity would harm food and livelihoods. Hence protecting forests and wildlife became necessary for nature and for people.
points: Rapid decline in wildlife population and forests
Preserves ecological diversity and life support systems
Preserves genetic diversity for better growth and breeding
Agriculture and fisheries depend on this biodiversity
activities.explanation: Compare your answer with the points a marker looks for.

activities.context: Ranger Meera works in a tiger reserve not far from the Nepal border. Her region, along with India, shelters about two-thirds of the world's surviving tigers, which makes it a magnet for poachers and illegal traders. Since Project Tiger was launched in 1973, patrols have protected tigers in reserves like Corbett, Manas and Periyar. But lately Meera notices deer, the tigers' main prey, becoming scarce, and she has heard rumours of tiger bones being sold to medicine makers.
activities.prompt: If the deer population in Meera's reserve keeps falling, what is the most likely consequence for the tigers there?
options: They will wander out of the reserve in search of food, making them easier targets for poachers
They will start hunting each other to survive the shortage
They will migrate permanently to Nepal, emptying the reserve completely
They will breed faster to replace the lost prey species

why.They will start hunting each other to su: Tigers do not prey on other tigers; the threat listed is depletion of prey, not tiger-on-tiger hunting.
why.They will migrate permanently to Nepal,: Nothing in the case suggests tigers move to another country; this invents an outcome not supported by the facts.
why.They will breed faster to replace the lo: A shrinking food supply would reduce breeding success, not increase it; this reverses the logic.

activities.explanation: Correct: depletion of prey is a major threat, and hungry tigers leaving the protected area face greater danger.

activities.context: Ranger Meera works in a tiger reserve not far from the Nepal border. Her region, along with India, shelters about two-thirds of the world's surviving tigers, which makes it a magnet for poachers and illegal traders. Since Project Tiger was launched in 1973, patrols have protected tigers in reserves like Corbett, Manas and Periyar. But lately Meera notices deer, the tigers' main prey, becoming scarce, and she has heard rumours of tiger bones being sold to medicine makers.
activities.prompt: Meera hears that tiger bones are being sold locally for use in traditional medicines. What should she and her team do first?
options: Ignore it, since bones are less valuable than live tigers and the trade will stop on its own
Investigate and report the trade, because the skin and bone trade is what pushed tigers near extinction
Buy the bones herself so poachers lose their profit and the matter ends quietly
Wait for the next tiger census before acting, since numbers must be confirmed first

why.Ignore it, since bones are less valuable: The facts show the bone trade contributed to near extinction, so ignoring it would repeat the mistake of the past.
why.Buy the bones herself so poachers lose t: Purchasing bones would itself feed the illegal trade and is not a lawful or effective response.
why.Wait for the next tiger census before ac: A census counts tigers but does nothing to stop the trade; action on poaching cannot wait for paperwork.

activities.explanation: Correct: trade in skins and bones for traditional medicines is a documented cause of the tiger's decline, so it demands immediate action.

activities.prompt:
Assertion (A): Project Tiger was launched in 1973.
Reason (R): By 1973, authorities had realised that the tiger population had dwindled to 1,827.
options: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true but R is false.
A is false but R is true.
activities.explanation: The alarming fall in tiger numbers is exactly why the project was launched that year.

activities.prompt:
Assertion (A): Sariska and Periyar are included among India's tiger reserves.
Reason (R): Tiger conservation also aimed to preserve biotypes of sizeable magnitude.
options: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true but R is false.
A is false but R is true.
activities.explanation: Both statements are true, but the conservation aim does not explain why these particular places are reserves.

activities.prompt: Explain why Project Tiger was launched in 1973, referring to what had happened to the tiger population over the previous decades.
activities.answer: At the turn of the century, the tiger population was estimated at about 55,000, but by 1973 it had dwindled to just 1,827. This drastic fall happened because of poaching, shrinking habitat and depletion of prey, while trade in tiger skins and bones for traditional medicines pushed tigers near extinction. Seeing the tiger, a key species in the faunal web, heading towards disappearance, the authorities launched Project Tiger in 1973 to save it and its habitat.
points: Mentions the fall from about 55,000 to 1,827
Links decline to poaching, habitat loss and prey depletion
Refers to the skin and bone trade pushing tigers near extinction
Connects the tiger's importance in the faunal web to the launch of the project
activities.explanation: Compare your answer with the points a marker looks for.

activities.context: A district officer is preparing a report on the forests of her region. She finds that most of the forest land is directly under the government, which finds it hard to manage, control and regulate it all. The land has been sorted into categories: reserved, protected, and unclassed forests, the last being wastelands belonging to the government, private people and communities.
activities.prompt: The officer notices that more than half of the district's forest land is reserved. If a proposal suggests shifting some of this reserved land to the unclassed category, what is the most likely consequence for conservation?
options: Conservation would weaken, because reserved forests are the most valuable category for conservation
Conservation would improve, because unclassed forests are managed more strictly
Conservation would stay the same, since all categories are equally valuable
Conservation would improve, because private people manage land better than government

why.Conservation would improve, because uncl: Wrong: unclassed forests are not the strictly managed category
why.Conservation would stay the same, since: Wrong: the categories differ in value for conservation
why.Conservation would improve, because priv: Wrong: the case says much forest is government-owned or managed, not that private control is better

activities.explanation: Correct: reserved forests are the most valuable for conservation, so moving land out of this category weakens it

activities.context: A district officer is preparing a report on the forests of her region. She finds that most of the forest land is directly under the government, which finds it hard to manage, control and regulate it all. The land has been sorted into categories: reserved, protected, and unclassed forests, the last being wastelands belonging to the government, private people and communities.
activities.prompt: A villager argues that since the government finds it difficult to manage, control and regulate these resources, all forests should simply be left unclassed. What is the flaw in this argument?
options: Unclassed forests are wastelands of government, private people and communities, so they are not a managed solution
Unclassed forests receive the strongest protection, so the problem would remain
The government owns no forest land, so nothing would change
Unclassed forests cannot exist alongside reserved or protected forests

why.Unclassed forests receive the strongest: Wrong: unclassed forests are not the strongly protected category
why.The government owns no forest land, so n: Wrong: much forest and wildlife is owned or managed by government
why.Unclassed forests cannot exist alongside: Wrong: the categories exist together in classification

activities.explanation: Correct: unclassed forests are simply other forests and wastelands held by government, private people and communities, not a remedy for management difficulty

boss.title: Chapter challenge: Natural Vegetation and Wildlife

activities.prompt: In the web of life, forests are called primary producers. What does that mean for other living beings?
options: They depend on forests for their survival
They can live without forests quite easily
They produce more food than forests do
They replace forests when forests disappear
activities.explanation: Forests are primary producers, and all other living beings depend on them. Well done if you spotted the link!

activities.prompt: Humans are separate from the ecological system, so they do not depend on it.
activities.explanation: Humans are only one part of the system, and they depend on it very much. Every living thing is connected in the web of life.

activities.prompt: Project Tiger was launched in the year ______ .
activities.hint: It was the same year people realised how few tigers were left.
activities.explanation: In 1973, the tiger count had fallen to 1,827, so Project Tiger was launched. You remembered a key year!

activities.prompt: Match each type of forest land with what you know about it.
pairs: More than half of total forest land
Almost one-third of total forest area
Wastelands of government, private people and communities
activities.explanation: Reserved, protected and unclassed forests are the three categories, and reserved and protected form the permanent estates. Great matching!

activities.prompt: Why did conservation of wildlife and forests become essential in India?
options: Wildlife population and forestry had declined rapidly
Forests had grown too large to walk through
Villagers wanted to sell more forest land
Tigers had moved into new countries
activities.explanation: A rapid fall in wildlife numbers and forests made conservation essential. You understood the main reason!

activities.prompt: Put these tiger events in the correct time order, earliest first.
items: Tiger population estimated at 55,000 at the turn of the century
Authorities realise the tiger population has dwindled to 1,827
activities.explanation: First there were 55,000 tigers, then only 1,827 were counted in 1973, and Project Tiger began that year. A sad fall, but a strong rescue plan!

activities.prompt: Local people may cut trees in Sacred Groves whenever they need timber.
activities.explanation: Sacred Groves are forests of God and Goddesses, left untouched by local people. Any interference with them is banned.

activities.prompt: The largest area under permanent forests is in the state of ______ .
activities.hint: Think of the big state right in the middle of India.
activities.explanation: Madhya Pradesh has the largest area under permanent forests. A handy fact for your exam!

activities.prompt: What did the Chipko movement show about ordinary people and forests?
options: Community afforestation with local effort can succeed
Only officials can ever plant new trees
Deforestation helps villages grow richer
Forests should be left with no protection at all
activities.explanation: The Chipko movement resisted deforestation and showed that community afforestation can succeed. People power works!

activities.prompt: Match each sacred tree belief with the people who follow it.
pairs: Worshipped by the Mundas and Santhal
Worshipped at weddings by tribals of Odisha and Bihar
Fed daily and treated as devotees
activities.explanation: Nature worship is an old tribal belief that all creations of nature must be protected. You connected each belief beautifully!

chapters.title: Water Resources
chapters.summary: In this chapter: water availability and scarcity; conservation and management of water; dams and multi-purpose river projects; impacts of large water projects.

lessons.title: Water Availability and Scarcity

activities.prompt: Why can water be everywhere while some people still lack it?
activities.explanation: Now read on to find out.

activities.title: Water Is Available, but Limited
activities.body: Three-fourths of Earth’s surface is covered with water. However, only a small part is usable freshwater. Freshwater mainly comes from surface run-off and ground water. Water moves through the hydrological cycle, so it is renewable. Yet water can become scarce through over-exploitation, excessive use, unequal access, and rising demand.
keyPoints: Three-fourths of Earth is covered with water.
Only a small part is usable freshwater.
Water moves through the hydrological cycle.
activities.explanation: Water is plentiful overall, but safe supplies are limited.

activities.prompt: A town has water all around, but little usable freshwater. Should it expand irrigated farms?
steps: Earth is mostly water, but only a little is usable freshwater.
Expanding irrigated farms can over-exploit water because dry-season farming needs irrigation.
This can worsen scarcity because irrigated agriculture uses the most water.
So farmers should try drought-resistant crops and dry farming to modernise agriculture.
activities.explanation: Think it through with Hooty.

activities.title: Why Water Becomes Scarce
activities.body: Water scarcity often happens when water is over-used or over-exploited. Different social groups may not have equal access to water. A large and growing population increases demand. People need water for homes and for producing food. Irrigated agriculture is the largest consumer of water.
keyPoints: Excessive use and over-exploitation cause scarcity.
Different groups may have unequal water access.
Irrigated agriculture uses the most water.
activities.explanation: Scarcity can affect people and farming in different ways.

activities.title: Freshwater Sources
activities.prompt: Which pair mainly supplies freshwater?
options: Over-exploitation and excessive use
Surface run-off and ground water
Different social groups and dry farming
Surface run-off and unequal access
activities.explanation: Freshwater mainly comes from surface run-off and ground water. Great choice!

activities.title: The Biggest Water User
activities.prompt: Irrigated ______ uses the largest amount of water.
activities.hint: Name the farming method that needs water.
activities.explanation: Irrigated agriculture is the largest consumer of water. Good try!

activities.title: Water Clues
activities.prompt: Match each water clue with its lesson answer.
activities.explanation: You matched each clue with the matching water idea. Well done!

activities.title: Growing Water Needs
activities.prompt: What two needs increase when more people need more water?
options: Homes and producing food
Over-exploitation and excessive use
Different groups and water access
Dry farming and irrigated areas
activities.explanation: More people need more water for homes and for producing food. Nice thinking!

activities.title: Reasons for Over-Exploitation
activities.prompt: Why are water resources over-exploited?
options: To reduce irrigated areas for dry-season farming
To limit dry-season farming and water use
To expand irrigated areas for dry-season farming
To protect ground water from farm use
activities.explanation: Water resources are over-exploited to expand irrigated areas for dry-season farming. Good choice!

activities.title: Modernising Agriculture
activities.prompt: A farmer wants to modernise agriculture. Which pair should the farmer consider?
options: Over-exploitation and dry farming areas
Surface run-off and ground water
Different groups and excessive use
Drought-resistant crops and dry farming
activities.explanation: Drought-resistant crops and dry farming can help modernise agriculture. That is a smart choice.

activities.prompt: A town's population is growing. More people need more water for homes and food. What is likely?
options: Water scarcity may rise because demand keeps growing.
Water scarcity may fall because more people bring more water.
Water demand stays equal because each person drinks less.
Water scarcity may rise only if rainfall also falls.

why.Water scarcity may fall because more peo: More people do not bring more water into the town.
why.Water demand stays equal because each pe: A growing population still needs more water for homes and food.
why.Water scarcity may rise only if rainfall: Water scarcity can grow through excessive use, even without less rainfall.

activities.explanation: A growing population increases demand, which can cause water scarcity.

activities.prompt: Place A gets fresh water from runoff and groundwater. Place B relies on only one source. What happens if B's source fails?
options: Place B may have much less usable freshwater.
Place A will also lose both of its sources.
Place B may gain water from groundwater.
Place B will use the same runoff again.

why.Place A will also lose both of its sourc: This wrongly assumes one place's loss affects both places.
This wrongly assumes another source can replace the failed source.
This wrongly assumes the failed source returns immediately.

activities.explanation: B depends on one source, so losing it can reduce its freshwater supply.

activities.prompt: A survey says one group's homes have water only sometimes. Another group's homes have water all day. What can we infer?
options: The two groups have unequal access to water.
The first group must use less water each day.
The second group owns every nearby water source.
The first group lives where no farms exist.

why.The first group must use less water each: Less access does not prove that the first group uses less water.
why.The second group owns every nearby water: The survey gives no information about who owns water sources.
why.The first group lives where no farms exi: The survey gives no information about where farms exist.

activities.explanation: Different water access times show that the groups do not have equal access.

activities.prompt: Farmers expand irrigated land for dry-season farming. Water keeps moving through its cycle. What may happen to water resources?
options: They may be over-exploited as more water is used.
They may increase because farms create new water.
They stay equal because water always moves in a cycle.
They improve because farms return clean water.

why.They may increase because farms create n: This wrongly assumes farms create usable new water sources.
why.They stay equal because water always mov: A renewable resource can still become over-exploited through excessive use.
why.They improve because farms return clean: This wrongly assumes irrigation automatically improves water quality.

activities.explanation: Expanding irrigation can over-exploit water resources during the dry season.

lessons.sceneCaption: A woman walks for drinking water in a remote Jaisalmer village, showing unequal access to water.

lessons.title: Conservation and Management of Water

activities.prompt: How can we keep every sip safe and available for everyone?
activities.explanation: Now read on to find out.

activities.title: Why Water Needs Careful Management
activities.body: Industrialisation means factory growth. Urbanisation means city growth. They created opportunities but raised water and energy needs. Hydroelectric power uses flowing water for electricity. Groundwater means water below ground. Too much groundwater use lowers water levels. Conservation means using water carefully. Atal Bhujal Yojana seeks change from consumption to conservation. Atal Jal includes smart management. Potable means safe to drink. Jal Jeevan Mission seeks piped water for rural households.
keyPoints: Industry and city growth raise water needs.
Too much groundwater use lowers water levels.
Atal Bhujal Yojana seeks changes towards conservation.
activities.explanation: Growth can harm water, so conservation and smart management matter.

activities.prompt: A town adds factories and pumps. What may happen to its water?
steps: More factories can strain freshwater because industry growth creates pressure.
More pumping can lower water levels because groundwater use becomes too high.
Lower water levels can harm food security and create a water risk.
Atal schemes promote conservation and smart management, so water habits should change.
activities.explanation: Think it through with Hooty.

activities.title: Groundwater and Water Levels
activities.prompt: What can happen when people use too much groundwater?
options: Water levels can fall
Water levels can rise
Food security can improve
Water needs can shrink
activities.explanation: Too much groundwater use can lower water levels and harm food security.

activities.title: Power for Industries
activities.prompt: What provides much of the electricity needed by industries?
options: Animal power
Wind power
Hydroelectric power
Human power
activities.explanation: Much of the electricity needed by industries comes from hydroelectric power.

activities.title: A Change in Behaviour
activities.prompt: Atal Bhujal Yojana seeks change from ______ to conservation.
activities.hint: Think about using more resources.
activities.explanation: The programme seeks to change consumption habits towards conservation.

activities.title: Causes and Effects
activities.prompt: Match each cause with its effect.
activities.explanation: Water use and pollution can damage water supplies and harm people.

activities.title: The Jal Jeevan Mission
activities.prompt: What does Jal Jeevan Mission aim to provide to every rural household?
options: Rainwater for farms
Power for factories
Water for cities
Potable piped water
activities.explanation: Jal Jeevan Mission aims to provide every rural household with potable piped water.

activities.title: More Urban Pumping
activities.prompt: A city adds more pumping devices. What may happen to fragile water resources?
options: They can stay unchanged
They can become depleted
They can become cleaner
They can become safer
activities.explanation: Urban pumping devices can cause fragile water resources to become depleted.

activities.prompt: Using more groundwater can lower water levels. What may happen to food security?
options: Water levels may fall, and food security may be harmed.
Water levels may rise, and food security may improve.
Water levels may fall, but food security always stays safe.
Water levels may rise, but food security may be harmed.

why.Water levels may rise, and food security: This wrongly links more pumping with higher water levels.
why.Water levels may fall, but food security: Falling water levels can still harm food security.
why.Water levels may rise, but food security: Rising levels do not show the stated harm from too much use.

activities.explanation: Too much groundwater use can lower levels and harm food security.

activities.prompt: Earlier, a town had few industries. Many industries now need electricity. What change is most likely?
options: Freshwater pressure grows, and hydroelectric power demand also grows.
Freshwater pressure falls, and hydroelectric power demand also falls.
Freshwater pressure grows, but hydroelectric power demand disappears.
Freshwater pressure disappears, but hydroelectric power demand also grows.

why.Freshwater pressure falls, and hydroelec: This wrongly suggests industry growth lowers both water and power needs.
why.Freshwater pressure grows, but hydroelec: Industrial electricity demand does not disappear when industries grow.
why.Freshwater pressure disappears, but hydr: Growing industries do not remove pressure on freshwater resources.

activities.explanation: More industries pressure freshwater and need much electricity from hydroelectric power.

activities.prompt: A map shows dense homes and urban pumps. Both are near a fragile source. What does this suggest?
options: City water needs may deplete the fragile water resource.
City water needs may help the fragile water resource recover.
Urban pumping may leave the fragile water resource unchanged.
Dense homes may reduce the need for urban pumping.

why.City water needs may help the fragile wa: More urban water use does not help fragile resources recover.
why.Urban pumping may leave the fragile wate: Urban pumping can deplete fragile resources instead of leaving them unchanged.
why.Dense homes may reduce the need for urba: Dense cities increase water needs rather than reducing pumping.

activities.explanation: Dense cities raise water needs, and urban pumps can deplete fragile resources.

activities.prompt: Homes and factories release waste. Farms use chemicals, pesticides and fertilisers. What happens to nearby water?
options: The water may become polluted and unsafe for people.
The water may become cleaner and safer for people.
Only factory waste may affect the water, not farm chemicals.
The water may become safer because chemicals remove pollution.

why.The water may become cleaner and safer f: This wrongly treats waste and farm chemicals as water cleaners.
why.Only factory waste may affect the water,: Farm chemicals also affect safety, so the effect is not only industrial.
why.The water may become safer because chemi: Chemicals, pesticides and fertilisers do not make polluted water safer.

activities.explanation: Household and factory wastes can pollute, while farm chemicals make water unsafe.

activities.prompt: Atal Bhujal Yojana seeks changes from consumption to conservation. Which action best fits this aim?
options: Use smart water management and encourage conservation habits.
Use smart energy management and keep wasteful water habits.
Manage industries only and ignore household conservation.
Increase daily consumption and avoid smart water management.

why.Use smart energy management and keep was: Smart energy management does not replace water conservation and smart water management.
why.Manage industries only and ignore househ: Household habits also matter, so managing only industries misses the aim.
why.Increase daily consumption and avoid sma: More consumption and less smart management go against conservation.

activities.explanation: It seeks conservation habits, and smart management is part of Atal Jal.

lessons.title: Dams and Multi-Purpose River Projects

activities.prompt: How can one river help farms, homes, and factories all at once?
activities.explanation: Now read on to find out.

activities.title: How Dams Help Us
activities.body: People have built water structures since ancient times. Ancient examples included dams, reservoirs, embankments and canals. A dam blocks, directs or slows flowing water. It often creates a reservoir, also called a lake or impoundment. Dams store river water and rainwater for fields. Today, they provide electricity, household water and industrial water. They can support flood control, recreation, navigation and fish breeding. Projects combining many water uses are multi-purpose projects.
keyPoints: A dam blocks, directs or slows flowing water.
Stored water can irrigate fields and provide other services.
Multi-purpose projects combine many water uses.
activities.explanation: One barrier can store water and support many useful purposes.

activities.prompt: Your village river has very little water in summer. A dam is proposed. Why can that one dam help farms and also give electricity?
steps: A dam is a barrier that obstructs, directs or slows flowing water, because it holds water back.
The water held back forms a reservoir, so it is kept there for later use.
That stored water can irrigate fields, and dams can also make electricity.
So one dam can serve many needs at once, like a multi-purpose project.
activities.explanation: Think it through with Hooty.

activities.title: What Does a Dam Do?
activities.prompt: What does a dam do to flowing water?
options: It stores water underground.
It blocks, directs or slows it.
It turns water into electricity.
It dries nearby fields.
activities.explanation: A dam is a barrier that obstructs, directs or slows flowing water.

activities.title: Structures in Ancient Times
activities.prompt: Ancient hydraulic structures included dams, reservoirs, embankments and canals.
activities.explanation: This matches the ancient structures listed in your lesson.

activities.title: Match Projects With Their Uses
activities.prompt: Match each item with its correct link.
pairs: Obstructs, directs or slows flowing water
Combines many uses of impounded water
activities.explanation: Each item has the use or purpose shown in your lesson.

activities.title: Uses of Bhakra–Nangal Water
activities.prompt: Bhakra–Nangal water is used for hydroelectric power and ______.
activities.hint: Name the other use of this water.
activities.explanation: Bhakra–Nangal water supports hydroelectric power and irrigation.

activities.title: From Barrier to Irrigation
activities.prompt: Put these steps in order.
items: A dam obstructs, directs or slows flowing water.
A reservoir, lake or impoundment often forms.
Stored rainwater can later irrigate agricultural land.
activities.explanation: The barrier comes first, then water collects. Stored water can later irrigate land.

activities.title: Identify the Project
activities.prompt: A project combines electricity, irrigation and flood control from impounded water. What is it?
options: An ancient hydraulic structure
A single-use water store
A multi-purpose project
A modern river basin
activities.explanation: Using impounded water for several needs makes the project multi-purpose.

activities.prompt: A dam is built across a river. What happens to the flowing water?
options: It is blocked or slowed so it collects behind.
It flows through faster because of the new wall.
It stops completely and never moves again.
It rushes away from the river into nearby fields.

why.It flows through faster because of the n: This mistake thinks a wall makes the water move faster.
why.It stops completely and never moves agai: This mistake thinks blocking water means it never moves.
why.It rushes away from the river into nearb: This mistake thinks the dam sends water out into fields.

activities.explanation: This is right: a dam obstructs, directs or slows the flowing water.

activities.prompt: An old book shows a dam and a canal built long ago. What does this tell us?
options: People long ago could plan and use water well.
People long ago had no use for water at all.
People long ago built these only in modern times.
People long ago made water structures without any plan.

why.People long ago had no use for water at: This mistake thinks old people did not care about water.
why.People long ago built these only in mode: This mistake mixes up ancient times with modern times.
why.People long ago made water structures wi: This mistake thinks old structures were made without thought.

activities.explanation: This is right: people have built sophisticated water structures since ancient times.

activities.prompt: How do the Bhakra–Nangal and Hirakud water projects differ?
options: Bhakra–Nangal gives power and irrigation; Hirakud saves water and controls floods.
Bhakra–Nangal controls floods; Hirakud only works by making electricity for homes.
Bhakra–Nangal has no water; Hirakud has no dam or reservoir at all.
Both projects do exactly the same set of works for the same needs.

why.Bhakra–Nangal controls floods; Hirakud o: This mistake swaps the two projects and misses Hirakud's flood control work.
why.Bhakra–Nangal has no water; Hirakud has: This mistake thinks both projects are without any stored water.
why.Both projects do exactly the same set of: This mistake thinks all water projects serve the same purposes.

activities.explanation: This is right: Bhakra–Nangal serves power and irrigation, while Hirakud joins saving water and flood control.

activities.prompt: A map shows a dam and a big blue area behind it. What is the blue area?
options: The reservoir of water held back by the dam.
The old river path where the water used to flow.
The canal that carries water away from the river.
The fields that the stored water will later irrigate.

why.The old river path where the water used: This mistake reads the blue area as the river's old route.
why.The canal that carries water away from t: This mistake thinks the blue area is a canal for moving water away.
why.The fields that the stored water will la: This mistake reads the blue area as fields, not as stored water.

activities.explanation: This is right: the barrier often creates a reservoir, lake or impoundment.

activities.prompt: The government wants one dam to give power and water for farms. What should it build?
options: A multi-purpose project using impounded water for many needs.
A project that stores rain water only for irrigating fields.
A project that makes power but gives no water to anyone.
A project used only for recreation, fishing and boating.

why.A project that stores rain water only fo: This mistake picks only one use, so it is not a multi-purpose project.
why.A project that makes power but gives no: This mistake also picks one use and leaves out the other need.
why.A project used only for recreation, fish: This mistake chooses only fun uses and leaves out power and farms.

activities.explanation: This is right: projects combining many uses of impounded water are multi-purpose.

activities.prompt: Why did modern India keep building dams in most river basins?
options: Because dams give water and power, and help control floods.
Because ancient people had stopped making dams altogether.
Because most rivers of India carry no water in any season.
Because canals can be made easier without any stored water.

why.Because ancient people had stopped makin: This mistake thinks building started again after a long gap.
why.Because most rivers of India carry no wa: This mistake thinks the rivers have no water to store.
why.Because canals can be made easier withou: This mistake thinks canals need no water at all.

activities.explanation: This is right: modern dams give electricity and water, and also help with floods.
