lessons.title: Impacts of Large Water Projects

activities.prompt: How do large dams change rivers and the lives of nearby communities?
activities.explanation: Now read on to find out.

activities.title: Large projects can change rivers and land
activities.body: Large water projects can provide irrigation for land. They can also disturb rivers and floodplains. Regulating or damming rivers may reduce natural flow and sediment flow. Reservoirs can submerge vegetation and soil. They may also make migration difficult for aquatic animals. Other possible effects include sedimentation, floods, soil erosion, earthquakes, diseases, pests and pollution. Salinisation means soil becomes salty. Water-intensive crops need much water.
keyPoints: Regulating and damming rivers can disturb their natural flow.
Reservoirs can submerge vegetation and soil.
Irrigation changes can encourage water-intensive crops and cause soil salinisation.
activities.explanation: Large projects can provide irrigation, but they can also cause many impacts.

activities.prompt: A dam's reservoir has heavy silt. Why can the dam cause floods?
steps: Damming a river reduces its natural flow, including the movement of sediment.
Therefore, excess sediment can settle and build up inside the reservoir.
As sediment gathers, the dam can trigger floods instead of controlling them.
So sediment build-up can turn flood control into flood creation.
activities.explanation: Think it through with Hooty.

activities.title: What happens to regulated rivers?
activities.prompt: What can happen when rivers are regulated and dammed?
options: Increase the natural flow of rivers
Their natural flow can be disturbed
Make aquatic migration easier
Protect vegetation from reservoir flooding
activities.explanation: Good choice! Regulating and damming rivers can disturb their natural flow.

activities.title: Reservoirs and floodplains
activities.prompt: Floodplain reservoirs can submerge existing vegetation and soil.
activities.explanation: Correct! Reservoirs can cover vegetation and soil in floodplains.

activities.title: The Narmada project
activities.prompt: Sardar Sarovar Dam has been built over the ______ River in Gujarat.
activities.hint: Think of the river named in your lesson.
activities.explanation: Excellent! Sardar Sarovar Dam was built over the Narmada River in Gujarat.

activities.title: How sedimentation can develop
activities.prompt: Put these stages in order.
activities.explanation: Well done! Dam regulation can disturb flow and reduce sediment flow. This can cause sedimentation.

activities.title: Sedimentation and floods
activities.prompt: Sedimentation can make dams control floods instead of triggering them.
activities.explanation: Not quite. Sedimentation can make dams trigger floods instead of controlling them.

activities.title: Effects of irrigation changes
activities.prompt: You see irrigation changes after a large project. Which result can follow?
options: Reduce river sediment and block aquatic migration
Submerge vegetation and remove natural silt from floodplains
Encourage aquatic migration and protect floodplain soil
Encourage thirsty crops and cause salinisation
activities.explanation: Good choice! Irrigation changes can encourage water-intensive crops. They can also cause soil salinisation.

activities.prompt: A new dam changes how a river carries silt. Much silt now collects in its reservoir. Why?
options: Damming reduces sediment flow, so extra silt settles in the reservoir.
The dam sends all silt downstream, so the reservoir stays clear.
The dam makes fish drop their silt inside the reservoir.
The dam increases sediment flow, so less silt settles in the reservoir.

why.The dam sends all silt downstream, so th: This wrongly believes the dam sends sediment away from the reservoir.
why.The dam makes fish drop their silt insid: This wrongly blames fish for sediment carried by the river.
why.The dam increases sediment flow, so less: This wrongly treats more sediment flow as the cause of extra settling.

activities.explanation: This follows the link between reduced sediment flow and reservoir sedimentation.

activities.prompt: A farmer changes how fields are watered after a water project. What may encourage soil salinisation?
options: Growing more water-intensive crops under the changed irrigation system.
Growing fewer crops after the irrigation system changes.
Keeping the same crops and the same watering pattern.
Stopping crop growth on all fields near the reservoir.

why.Growing fewer crops after the irrigation: This wrongly treats fewer crops as the stated cause.
why.Keeping the same crops and the same wate: This wrongly treats unchanged farming as the irrigation change described.
why.Stopping crop growth on all fields near: This wrongly assumes stopping crops encourages more water-intensive crops.

activities.explanation: This is right because changed irrigation can encourage water-intensive crops and salinisation.

lessons.sceneCaption: Sardar Sarovar Dam stands on the Narmada River in Gujarat.

lessons.title: Traditional Rainwater Harvesting

activities.prompt: How did ancient communities turn rainfall into a lasting lifeline?
activities.explanation: Now read on to find out.

activities.title: How ancient India used rainwater
activities.body: Ancient India had an extraordinary tradition of harvesting rainwater. People knew about different rainfall patterns and soil types. They developed methods for harvesting rainwater, groundwater, river water and flood water. Rooftop rainwater harvesting was common for storing drinking water in Rajasthan. Underground tankas also stored drinking water in dry parts of Rajasthan. In Bengal floodplains, inundation channels irrigated fields. In dry regions, rain-fed structures kept the soil moist. The first spell of rain was usually left to clean roofs and pipes.
keyPoints: Rooftops and tankas stored drinking water in Rajasthan.
Inundation channels irrigated fields in Bengal floodplains.
The first rain cleaned roofs and pipes before collection.
activities.explanation: These traditions helped people store water and support farming.

activities.prompt: Why did families in Rajasthan leave the first rain uncollected?
steps: Rooftop rainwater was common for drinking water in Rajasthan.
The first rain was left because it cleaned the roofs and pipes.
Later rain could be collected for household drinking water.
This stored water could last until the next rainfall.
activities.explanation: Think it through with Hooty.

activities.title: Rooftop rainwater harvesting
activities.prompt: Where was rooftop rainwater harvesting common for storing drinking water?
options: Rajasthan
Bengal floodplains
Outside Rajasthan
Only in Bengal
activities.explanation: Rooftop rainwater harvesting was common in Rajasthan for storing drinking water.

activities.title: Underground storage
activities.prompt: Houses in dry parts of Rajasthan had underground tanks called tankas.
activities.explanation: These tankas stored drinking water below ground.

activities.title: Traditional water structures
activities.prompt: Match each structure with its place or purpose.
activities.explanation: Khadins and Johads stored water in Rajasthan, while tankas stored water underground.

activities.title: The first rain
activities.prompt: Usually, the ______ spell of rain was left uncollected.
activities.hint: This rain cleaned the roofs and pipes.
activities.explanation: The first spell of rain was usually left uncollected because it cleaned the roofs and pipes.

activities.title: Why leave the first rain?
activities.prompt: Why did people usually leave the first spell of rain uncollected?
options: It cleaned the roofs and pipes.
It filled the inundation channels.
It stored water in tankas.
It kept the soil moist.
activities.explanation: The first rain cleaned the roofs and pipes, so people usually left it uncollected.

activities.title: The first spell of rain
activities.prompt: Put these events in the correct order.
items: The first spell of rain arrives.
The rain cleans the roofs and pipes.
The first spell is left uncollected.
activities.explanation: The first rain arrived, cleaned the roofs and pipes, and was then left uncollected.

activities.title: Keeping soil moist
activities.prompt: A farmer in a dry region wants to keep field soil moist. Which method fits the lesson?
options: Rain-fed storage structures
Underground tankas
Inundation channels
Rooftop rainwater harvesting
activities.explanation: Rain-fed storage structures kept the soil moist in dry regions.

activities.title: Rajasthan drinking water
activities.prompt: Which pair correctly matches two methods with their use?
options: Tankas and rooftops store drinking water
Tankas and rooftops irrigate fields
Khadins and Johads dry the soil
Inundation channels store drinking water
activities.explanation: Both tankas and rooftop harvesting stored drinking water in Rajasthan.

activities.prompt: A map shows rainwater harvesting methods. It marks channels in Bengal and tankas in Rajasthan. What does this suggest?
options: People adapted water methods to local needs.
People used one method in every place.
People stored only drinking water everywhere.
People ignored rivers and floods completely.

This wrongly assumes one method was used everywhere.
why.People stored only drinking water everyw: This wrongly assumes drinking-water storage was the only need.
why.People ignored rivers and floods complet: This wrongly assumes rivers and floods were never used.

activities.explanation: This is right because the map shows different methods in different places.

lessons.sceneAlt: A johad, a traditional village pond in Thathawata, Rajasthan, stores water and supports irrigation.
lessons.sceneCaption: A traditional johad stores water in a Rajasthani village for irrigation.

lessons.title: Modern Rainwater Harvesting and Bamboo Drip Irrigation

activities.prompt: How can rain and bamboo gently water a thirsty garden?
activities.explanation: Now read on to find out.

activities.title: Two ways to use water
activities.body: Rooftop rainwater harvesting collects rain for household use. It is common in Shillong, where nearly every household has a structure. It supplies 15–25 per cent of household water needs. Meghalaya also uses an old bamboo pipe system. Gravity pulls spring water downhill. The final section drops water near plant roots.
keyPoints: Rooftop harvesting is common in Shillong.
It supplies 15–25 per cent of household water needs.
Bamboo pipes carry spring water downhill.
activities.explanation: These systems show two ways of collecting and carrying water.

activities.prompt: How do bamboo pipes cross roads and still reach plant roots?
steps: Water moves downhill because gravity carries perennial springs through bamboo pipes.
The pipe rises above ground so a road can pass below it.
Water continues for hundreds of metres and reaches plants as drops.
Thus, bamboo drip irrigation delivers spring water to plant roots.
activities.explanation: Think it through with Hooty.

activities.prompt: Which practice is most common in Shillong?
options: Bamboo pipe system
Rooftop rainwater harvesting
Raised road crossing
Final root drip
activities.explanation: Rooftop rainwater harvesting is the most common practice in Shillong.

activities.prompt: Nearly every household in Shillong has a rooftop rainwater harvesting structure.
activities.explanation: Nearly every Shillong household has this kind of structure.

activities.prompt: A house in Gendathur can collect about ______ litres of rainwater each year.
activities.hint: The amount is a large number of litres.
activities.explanation: A Gendathur house can collect about 50,000 litres each year.

activities.prompt: Why do bamboo pipes carry spring water downhill?
options: Roof tops push water downhill
Road crossings lift the water
Gravity pulls the water downhill
Bamboo sections push it uphill
activities.explanation: The bamboo pipes carry spring water downhill by gravity.

activities.prompt: Put the bamboo drip irrigation steps in order.
items: Water enters the bamboo pipe system.
Water travels downhill for hundreds of metres.
The final section drops water near plant roots.
activities.explanation: Water enters first, travels through the system, and reaches plant roots last.

activities.prompt: What happens at the final bamboo section?
options: Drops water near plant roots
Raises pipes above roads
Carries springs uphill
Stores water on rooftops
activities.explanation: The final bamboo section drops water near the roots of each plant.

activities.prompt: Tamil Nadu makes rooftop harvesting compulsory. Shillong has nearly every household with it. What is the key difference?
options: Tamil Nadu uses a rule; Shillong has a common practice.
Both places use a rule; Shillong has less practice.
Shillong uses a rule; Tamil Nadu has a common practice.
Both places use only custom; neither has a rule.

why.Both places use a rule; Shillong has les: This wrongly treats Shillong's common practice as a rule.
why.Shillong uses a rule; Tamil Nadu has a c: This swaps the rule and common practice between the places.
why.Both places use only custom; neither has: This wrongly says both places rely only on custom.

activities.explanation: Compulsory means a rule, while Shillong's practice is described as common.

activities.prompt: Shillong rooftop harvesting supplies 15–25 per cent of household needs. Why can households still need other water?
options: Rooftop harvesting supplies only part of their water needs.
Rooftop harvesting supplies all of their water needs.
The bamboo system supplies more water than the rooftop.
Nearly every household uses no other water source.

why.Rooftop harvesting supplies all of their: The stated share is only part, not all, of household needs.
why.The bamboo system supplies more water th: The facts do not compare bamboo supply with rooftop supply.
why.Nearly every household uses no other wat: Having a rooftop structure does not mean other water is unused.

activities.explanation: A 15–25 per cent share leaves most household needs outside rooftop water.

activities.prompt: Tamil Nadu makes rooftop harvesting compulsory for all houses. A family builds a new house there. Must it include the structure?
options: Yes. It is compulsory for all houses in Tamil Nadu.
No. Only Shillong makes it compulsory for every house.
No. It is optional, but common in most Shillong households.
Yes. It is compulsory only when bamboo pipes cross roads.

why.No. Only Shillong makes it compulsory fo: This confuses Shillong's common practice with Tamil Nadu's rule.
why.No. It is optional, but common in most S: This confuses Shillong's common practice with a legal rule.
why.Yes. It is compulsory only when bamboo p: This wrongly connects the house rule to bamboo road crossings.

activities.explanation: Tamil Nadu applies the compulsory rule to every house, including new ones.

activities.prompt: Bamboo drip irrigation carries spring water downhill. One pipe crosses a road. What should the pipe and its final section do?
options: Rise over the road, then drop water near plant roots.
Stay below the road, then drop water on each road.
Rise above the road, then send water back uphill.
Stay on the road, then drop water near the bamboo source.

why.Stay below the road, then drop water on: The pipe must rise at roads, and the last section waters roots.
why.Rise above the road, then send water bac: Raising the pipe is correct, but water does not flow uphill.
why.Stay on the road, then drop water near t: The pipe is raised, but the final water reaches plant roots.

activities.explanation: The pipe rises at roads, and the last section drops water near roots.

activities.context: In a farming community, farms use large quantities of water to expand irrigated areas for dry-season farming. Meanwhile, a growing population needs more water for homes and food production. Over-exploitation of water resources is increasing, and some social groups have better access to water than others. The farmers must decide whether to continue expanding irrigation or adopt drought-resistant crops and dry farming.
activities.prompt: What should the farmers do to modernise agriculture while reducing pressure on water resources?
options: Try drought-resistant crops and dry farming instead of enlarging irrigated areas.
Expand irrigated areas further to increase dry-season farming.
Use more water for irrigation because farming is the largest consumer of water.
Improve household water use and leave agricultural water demand unchanged.

why.Expand irrigated areas further to increa: Further expansion can increase over-exploitation of water resources.
why.Use more water for irrigation because fa: Being the largest consumer does not mean that using still more water is sustainable.
why.Improve household water use and leave ag: Households alone are not the largest consumer, so this would ignore major agricultural demand.

activities.explanation: These methods can modernise agriculture while reducing pressure on water resources.

activities.context: In a farming community, farms use large quantities of water to expand irrigated areas for dry-season farming. Meanwhile, a growing population needs more water for homes and food production. Over-exploitation of water resources is increasing, and some social groups have better access to water than others. The farmers must decide whether to continue expanding irrigation or adopt drought-resistant crops and dry farming.
activities.prompt: If over-exploitation continues while the population grows, what is likely to happen next?
options: Water demand will rise, increasing the risk of water scarcity.
Water scarcity will ease because water moves in the hydrological cycle.
Irrigated areas will need less water as the population grows.
Water demand will remain unchanged because freshwater is renewable.

why.Water scarcity will ease because water m: Renewability does not prevent over-exploitation from causing scarcity.
why.Irrigated areas will need less water as: Population growth increases rather than reduces demand for water.
why.Water demand will remain unchanged becau: A renewable resource can still face rising demand and excessive use.

activities.explanation: More people will need more water for homes and producing food.

activities.prompt:
Assertion (A): Water is a renewable resource because it moves through the hydrological cycle.
Reason (R): All of the earth's water is usable freshwater.
options: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true but R is false.
A is false but R is true.
activities.explanation: The assertion is true, but the reason is false because only a small part of the earth's water is usable freshwater.

activities.prompt:
Assertion (A): A growing population can cause water scarcity.
Reason (R): More people need more water for homes and producing food.
options: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true but R is false.
A is false but R is true.
activities.explanation: The rising demand for water explained by the reason can intensify water scarcity.

activities.prompt: Explain how water can be renewable yet still scarce.
activities.answer: Water is renewable because it moves continually through the hydrological cycle. However, only a small part of the water covering three-fourths of the earth's surface is usable freshwater. Freshwater is mainly obtained from surface run off and ground water, but it can be over-exploited or used excessively. A growing population can also cause scarcity because more people need more water for homes and producing food. Different social groups may face unequal access, so the movement of water does not ensure that everyone has enough.
points: Water moves through the hydrological cycle.
Only a small part of the earth's water is usable freshwater.
Over-exploitation and excessive use can cause scarcity.
Population growth and unequal access can intensify the problem.
activities.explanation: Compare your answer with the points a marker looks for.

activities.context: A fast-growing town has several industries and dense neighbourhoods. Industrial growth is putting pressure on freshwater, while urban lifestyles have increased water and energy needs. Pumping devices are also depleting fragile water resources. Domestic and industrial wastes, chemicals, pesticides and fertilisers are affecting water safety. The town is considering smart water management under Atal Jal and examining Atal Bhujal Yojana, which seeks a change from consumption to conservation.
activities.prompt: If the town continues pumping groundwater at the present rate, what is most likely to happen next?
options: Groundwater levels will fall, and food security could be harmed.
Groundwater levels will rise because extra pumping releases stored water.
Fragile water resources will recover as industrial water use increases.
Food security will improve because industries create more opportunities.

why.Groundwater levels will rise because ext: Pumping removes groundwater rather than causing water levels to rise.
why.Fragile water resources will recover as: Greater industrial use puts more pressure on freshwater resources.
why.Food security will improve because indus: Industrial opportunities do not remove the possible harm to food security.

activities.explanation: Excessive groundwater use can lower water levels and harm food security.

activities.context: A fast-growing town has several industries and dense neighbourhoods. Industrial growth is putting pressure on freshwater, while urban lifestyles have increased water and energy needs. Pumping devices are also depleting fragile water resources. Domestic and industrial wastes, chemicals, pesticides and fertilisers are affecting water safety. The town is considering smart water management under Atal Jal and examining Atal Bhujal Yojana, which seeks a change from consumption to conservation.
activities.prompt: What should the town prioritise to address both its water shortages and water pollution?
options: Use smart water management, encourage conservation and keep harmful wastes and chemicals out of water.
Increase groundwater pumping to meet all the town's water and energy needs.
Encourage greater water consumption so that industries can expand more rapidly.
Continue industrial growth while allowing domestic and industrial wastes to enter water sources.

why.Increase groundwater pumping to meet all: More groundwater pumping can lower water levels and harm food security.
why.Encourage greater water consumption so t: Atal Bhujal Yojana seeks the opposite of greater consumption.
why.Continue industrial growth while allowin: Allowing wastes to enter water sources can make the water unsafe for people.

activities.explanation: This combines conservation, smart management and action against the stated causes of pollution.

activities.prompt:
Assertion (A): Domestic and industrial wastes can pollute water.
Reason (R): Smart water management is an important part of Atal Jal.
options: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true but R is false.
A is false but R is true.
activities.explanation: Smart water management is important under Atal Jal, but this fact does not explain why domestic and industrial wastes can pollute water.

activities.prompt:
Assertion (A): Atal Bhujal Yojana seeks to increase water consumption in rural households.
Reason (R): Atal Bhujal Yojana seeks behavioural changes from consumption to conservation.
options: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true but R is false.
A is false but R is true.
activities.explanation: The reason is true, but the assertion reverses the Yojana's conservation goal.

activities.prompt: Explain why using too much groundwater can threaten food security.
activities.answer: Excessive use of groundwater can lower water levels. Lower water levels can harm food security because they reduce the amount of water available. This risk is greater when industrial growth is already putting pressure on freshwater resources and urban lifestyles are increasing water needs. Urban pumping devices can also deplete fragile water resources. Therefore, excessive groundwater use can worsen both water-scarcity and food-security risks. Conservation is important because it can reduce the pressure to extract more groundwater.
points: Too much groundwater use can lower water levels.
Lower water levels can harm food security.
Industries and urban lifestyles increase pressure on water resources.
Urban pumping can deplete fragile water resources.
activities.explanation: Compare your answer with the points a marker looks for.

activities.context: Modern India has continued building dams in most river basins. At the Bhakra–Nangal project, stored water is used for hydroelectric power and irrigation. Elsewhere, the Hirakud project combines water conservation with flood control. Together, these examples show how dams can serve several purposes: they store water, supply homes and industries, and support activities such as flood control, recreation, navigation and fish breeding.
activities.prompt: Heavy rainfall causes the river to rise near the Hirakud project. Which result would most closely match the purpose of this project during the situation?
options: Reducing the impact of high river water
Increasing hydroelectric power production
Improving navigation along the river
Supporting more fish breeding

why.Increasing hydroelectric power productio: Option 2 confuses flood control with electricity production.
why.Improving navigation along the river: Option 3 confuses flood control with navigation.
why.Supporting more fish breeding: Option 4 confuses flood control with fish breeding.

activities.explanation: Option 1 directly matches the project's flood-control purpose.

activities.context: Modern India has continued building dams in most river basins. At the Bhakra–Nangal project, stored water is used for hydroelectric power and irrigation. Elsewhere, the Hirakud project combines water conservation with flood control. Together, these examples show how dams can serve several purposes: they store water, supply homes and industries, and support activities such as flood control, recreation, navigation and fish breeding.
activities.prompt: Planners want one dam project to provide hydroelectric power, irrigate fields and control floods. How should they describe the project?
options: A project serving several purposes at once
A project serving only agriculture
A project serving only electricity generation
A project serving only water supply

why.A project serving only agriculture: Option 2 ignores the power and flood-control purposes.
why.A project serving only electricity gener: Option 3 ignores the irrigation and flood-control purposes.
why.A project serving only water supply: Option 4 ignores the power and irrigation purposes.

activities.explanation: Option 1 correctly identifies the combination of several uses.

activities.prompt:
Assertion (A): A dam can create a reservoir, lake or impoundment.
Reason (R): The barrier obstructs, directs or slows flowing water, allowing an impoundment to form.
options: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true but R is false.
A is false but R is true.
activities.explanation: Both statements are true, and the barrier's effect on flowing water explains why an impoundment forms.

activities.prompt:
Assertion (A): Bhakra–Nangal water is used only for hydroelectric power.
Reason (R): Bhakra–Nangal water is also used for irrigation.
options: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true but R is false.
A is false but R is true.
activities.explanation: The assertion is false because the water also supports irrigation, while the reason is true.

activities.prompt: Explain the difference between the traditional and modern uses of dams.
activities.answer: Traditionally, dams stored river water and rainwater so that it could later irrigate fields. In modern times, their uses have expanded: dams provide electricity and water for homes and industries. They can also support flood control, recreation, navigation and fish breeding. Therefore, the main difference is that traditional dams focused on storing water for irrigation, whereas modern dams serve several additional purposes and can be planned as multi-purpose projects.
points: Traditional dams stored river water and rainwater.
Stored water was later used to irrigate fields.
Modern dams provide electricity and water for homes and industries.
Modern dams can also support flood control, recreation, navigation and fish breeding.
activities.explanation: Compare your answer with the points a marker looks for.

activities.context: Students studying Sardar Sarovar Dam in Gujarat visit a reservoir built over the Narmada River. The project is one of India’s largest water resource projects, will provide irrigation for 18.45 lakh hectares, and covers 3,112 villages in 15 districts of Gujarat. Fine material has collected behind the dam, while aquatic animals struggle to reach spawning areas. In newly irrigated fields, farmers are growing water-intensive crops.
activities.prompt: If more fine material accumulates in this reservoir, what is a possible next effect?
options: The dam could worsen flooding rather than prevent it.
The river would carry more natural silt back to its floodplain.
Aquatic animals would face fewer barriers to migration.
Existing vegetation would reappear beneath the reservoir.

why.The river would carry more natural silt: This is incorrect because reduced sediment flow, rather than increased silt, is a possible effect of damming.
why.Aquatic animals would face fewer barrier: This is incorrect because dams can make migration more difficult.
why.Existing vegetation would reappear benea: This is incorrect because floodplain reservoirs can submerge vegetation.

activities.explanation: This is correct because sedimentation can make dams trigger floods.

activities.context: Students studying Sardar Sarovar Dam in Gujarat visit a reservoir built over the Narmada River. The project is one of India’s largest water resource projects, will provide irrigation for 18.45 lakh hectares, and covers 3,112 villages in 15 districts of Gujarat. Fine material has collected behind the dam, while aquatic animals struggle to reach spawning areas. In newly irrigated fields, farmers are growing water-intensive crops.
activities.prompt: Which change would reduce the risk of soil salinisation in the newly irrigated fields?
options: Choose crops that require less water and avoid excessive irrigation.
Choose crops requiring much more water than the present ones.
Keep the present water-intensive crops and increase the water supplied to them.
Grow less water-demanding crops but apply even more water to every field.

why.Choose crops requiring much more water t: This is incorrect because choosing more water-demanding crops can increase the risk.
why.Keep the present water-intensive crops a: This is incorrect because increasing water-intensive cropping and watering can worsen salinisation.
why.Grow less water-demanding crops but appl: This is incorrect because applying excessive water can contribute to soil salinisation.

activities.explanation: This is correct because water-intensive crops and irrigation changes can encourage soil salinisation.

activities.prompt:
Assertion (A): Damming and regulating a river can disturb its natural flow and reduce downstream sediment.
Reason (R): Sediment that would have moved farther along the river is retained when a dam interrupts the flow.
options: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true but R is false.
A is false but R is true.
activities.explanation: Both statements are true, and sediment being retained behind the dam explains the reduction in downstream sediment.

activities.prompt: What often causes water scarcity?
options: Over-exploitation and excessive use
More renewable water in the cycle
Equal access for all groups
Fewer people needing water
activities.explanation: Over-exploitation and excessive use often cause water scarcity.

activities.prompt: Using too much groundwater can lower water levels.
activities.explanation: Lower water levels can harm food security.

activities.prompt: A ______ is a barrier that obstructs, directs or slows flowing water.
activities.hint: Look at the lesson's water structures.
activities.explanation: Dams control or guide flowing water.

activities.prompt: Put the water's journey in order.
activities.explanation: Gravity carries water through bamboo pipes towards plant roots.

activities.prompt: Which project combines water conservation with flood control?
options: Hirakud project
Bhakra–Nangal water
Sardar Sarovar Dam
Atal Jal scheme
activities.explanation: The Hirakud project combines water conservation with flood control.

activities.prompt: Sedimentation can make dams trigger floods instead of controlling them.
activities.explanation: Excessive sedimentation can reduce a dam's flood-control ability.

activities.prompt: The Jal Jeevan Mission targets a regular supply of ______ litres per person each day.
activities.hint: This target is stated in your book.
activities.explanation: Its target is 55 litres per person each day.

options: Bamboo pipes
Rooftop drains
Underground tankas

activities.explanation: Bamboo pipes carry spring water downhill and release drops near plant roots.

chapters.title: Agriculture
chapters.summary: In this chapter: agriculture and the main farming types; intensive, plantation and commercial farming; cropping seasons; major food and grain crops.

lessons.title: Agriculture and the Main Farming Types

activities.prompt: How do different farms feed people and shape life in India?
activities.explanation: Now read on to find out.

activities.title: Farming in India
activities.body: India is an agriculturally important country. Agriculture is a primary activity. It produces most food people consume and raw materials for industries. Farming ranges from subsistence farming to commercial farming. Primitive subsistence farming means farming on small patches with simple tools. It is also called slash and burn agriculture. Farmers move to a fresh patch when soil fertility falls. Two-thirds of India's population is engaged in agriculture.
keyPoints: Agriculture provides food and raw materials for industries
Primitive farming uses small patches and simple tools
Two-thirds of India's population is engaged in agriculture
activities.explanation: This card introduces India's farming range and primitive subsistence farming.

activities.prompt: A family grows food on a small patch. The soil becomes less fertile. What should they do, and why?
steps: Simple tools and a small patch match primitive subsistence farming.
This type of farming is also called slash and burn agriculture.
When soil fertility falls, the family moves because the soil is less fertile.
Thus, they should move to and clear a fresh patch of land.
activities.explanation: Think it through with Hooty.

activities.prompt: What does agriculture produce for industries?
options: Raw materials
Small patches
Simple tools
Fresh patches
activities.explanation: Agriculture produces raw materials for industries.

activities.prompt: Which agricultural products does India export?
options: Hoes, daos and digging sticks
Tea, coffee and spices
Small patches of land
Raw materials for industries
activities.explanation: Tea, coffee and spices are among the agricultural products that India exports.

activities.prompt: Primitive subsistence farming is practised on ______ patches of land.
activities.hint: These patches are not large.
activities.explanation: Primitive subsistence farming is practised on small patches of land.

activities.prompt: Match each description with the correct detail.
pairs: Another name for primitive subsistence farming
Reason farmers move to fresh land
activities.explanation: Primitive farming is also called slash and burn. Farmers use simple tools and move when soil fertility falls.

activities.prompt: What makes farmers move to and clear a fresh patch of land?
options: When food consumption falls
When soil fertility falls
When agriculture becomes newer
When industries stop needing raw materials
activities.explanation: Farmers move to and clear a fresh patch when soil fertility falls.

activities.prompt: Put these events in the order described in the lesson.
items: Farmers move to a fresh patch
activities.explanation: The lesson says farmers move to and clear a fresh patch when soil fertility falls.

activities.prompt: A family's small patch loses soil fertility. They use simple tools. What will they most likely do?
options: Move to and clear a fresh patch of land.
Keep farming the same patch for many years.
Start using large machines on that patch.
Leave farming entirely and buy food elsewhere.

why.Keep farming the same patch for many yea: This ignores the stated move when soil fertility falls.
why.Start using large machines on that patch: The facts give simple tools, not a change to large machines.
why.Leave farming entirely and buy food else: The rule says to move to fresh land, not leave farming.

activities.explanation: The facts say they move when soil fertility falls.

activities.prompt: Two-thirds of India's people work in agriculture. What does this show about the sector?
options: It involves a very large share of people.
It involves only a few city workers.
It supplies all industrial raw materials.
It exports only tea, coffee and spices.

This mistakes two-thirds for only a small group.
why.It supplies all industrial raw materials: The facts do not say agriculture supplies every industrial material.
The word among shows these are not the only exports.

activities.explanation: Two-thirds of India's population is engaged in agriculture.

activities.prompt: Long ago, farming was already an economic activity. Today, two-thirds work in it. What does this show?
options: Agriculture is old and remains important now.
Agriculture began only in modern times.
Agriculture was important only in old times.
Agriculture matters now but has no exports.

This treats an old activity as a new one.
why.Agriculture was important only in old ti: This wrongly makes its importance belong only to the past.
why.Agriculture matters now but has no expor: This ignores the listed agricultural exports.

activities.explanation: Agriculture is old and two-thirds still work in it.

activities.prompt: A map marks a few areas of primitive subsistence farming. Commercial farming also exists. What does this show?
options: Indian farming ranges from subsistence to commercial farming.
Only the marked areas practise farming in India.
All Indian farming is primitive subsistence farming.
Commercial farming is the same as primitive farming.

why.Only the marked areas practise farming i: This mistakes a few pockets for the whole country.
why.All Indian farming is primitive subsiste: This overlooks the stated range of farming types.
why.Commercial farming is the same as primit: This confuses two different types of farming.

activities.explanation: Farming in India ranges from subsistence to commercial farming.

lessons.title: Intensive, Plantation and Commercial Farming

activities.prompt: How do farming methods shape the way people grow, work, and trade?
activities.explanation: Now read on to find out.

activities.title: Three ways of farming
activities.body: Intensive subsistence farming happens where land pressure is high. It uses large amounts of farm inputs and irrigation. Plantation farming grows one crop over a large area. It links agriculture with industry. Plantations use inputs needing much money and migrant labourers. All plantation produce is used as raw material in industries. Commercial farming uses modern inputs like HYV seeds and chemical fertilisers. Inheritance can divide land and make holdings uneconomical.
keyPoints: High land pressure and heavy input use
One crop grown over a large area
Higher doses of modern inputs
activities.explanation: These farming types differ in land use, inputs and links with industry.

activities.prompt: A tea plantation sends its produce to industries. Why do good transport and communication links matter?
steps: Tea is an important plantation crop.
Plantation produce becomes industrial raw material, so farming and industry connect.
Good transport and communication links support plantation development.
Therefore, these links help plantations strengthen their connection with industries.
activities.explanation: Think it through with Hooty.

activities.title: One crop or many?
activities.prompt: Plantation farming grows several crops over a small area.
activities.explanation: Plantation farming grows one crop over a large area.

activities.title: Fill the gap
activities.prompt: Plantation farming grows ______ crop over a large area.
activities.hint: This is the number of crops grown on a plantation.
activities.explanation: A plantation grows one crop over a large area.

activities.title: Match each farming type
activities.prompt: Match each farming type with its main feature.
pairs: One crop over a large area
activities.explanation: Each pair links a farming type with its main feature.

activities.title: Plantation produce
activities.prompt: Which statement about plantation produce is correct?
options: All produce becomes raw material for industries.
Some produce becomes raw material for industries.
All produce is eaten by farm workers.
All produce is sold in local markets.
activities.explanation: All plantation produce is used as raw material in industries.

activities.title: Effects of inheritance
activities.prompt: Inheritance never makes land holdings uneconomical.
activities.explanation: Inheritance can divide land and make holdings uneconomical.

activities.title: Effects of inheritance
activities.prompt: Put the effects of inheritance in order.
activities.explanation: Inheritance can divide land among generations and make holdings uneconomical.

activities.prompt: Many families depend on a small amount of farmland. Which farming fits best?
options: Intensive subsistence farming, because land pressure is high.
Plantation farming, because one crop covers a large area.
Commercial farming, because it can use modern inputs.
Commercial farming, because inheritance always keeps holdings large.

why.Plantation farming, because one crop cov: One large crop describes plantation farming, not the small-land situation.
why.Commercial farming, because it can use m: Modern inputs are associated with commercial farming, but land pressure gives the clue.
why.Commercial farming, because inheritance: Inheritance can divide holdings rather than keep them large.

activities.explanation: High pressure on land is the main clue for intensive subsistence farming.

activities.prompt: This farm uses higher doses of modern inputs. These include HYV seeds and chemical fertilisers. Which type fits?
options: Commercial farming, because it uses higher doses of modern inputs.
Intensive subsistence farming, because it uses biochemical inputs.
Plantation farming, because one crop covers a large area.
Commercial farming, because inheritance keeps land holdings large.

why.Intensive subsistence farming, because i: Intensive farming also uses biochemical inputs, but no high land pressure is given.
why.Plantation farming, because one crop cov: A large one-crop area describes plantation farming, not the modern-input clue.
why.Commercial farming, because inheritance: Inheritance can make holdings uneconomical; it does not keep them large.

activities.explanation: Commercial farming uses higher doses of modern inputs, exactly as described.

lessons.title: Cropping Seasons

activities.prompt: Why does India’s weather shape when and where farmers grow their crops?
activities.explanation: Now read on to find out.

activities.title: India’s Three Cropping Seasons
activities.body: India’s cropping patterns reflect its physical diversity and cultural variety. India has three main cropping seasons. Rabi crops are sown (planted) from October to December. Examples are wheat, barley, peas, gram and mustard. Kharif crops grow when the monsoon begins. They include paddy, maize, jowar, cotton and jute. The zaid season comes during summer. Zaid crops include water melon, muskmelon, cucumber, vegetables and fodder crops.
keyPoints: India has three main cropping seasons.
Rabi crops are sown from October to December.
Kharif crops grow when the monsoon begins.
activities.explanation: This card shows when each season happens and gives useful crop examples.

activities.prompt: A northern farmer sows wheat in October. Another farmer waits for the monsoon before sowing. Why do they farm differently?
steps: Northern and north-western states produce rabi crops, so wheat fits there.
Rabi sowing runs from October to December, so the farmer starts then.
Kharif farming begins with the monsoon, so the farmer waits for rain.
India's physical and cultural variety allows different cropping patterns.
activities.explanation: Think it through with Hooty.

activities.prompt: Which season comes during the summer months?
options: Rabi season
Kharif season
Zaid season
Monsoon season
activities.explanation: The lesson says the zaid season comes during summer. You found the correct season.

activities.prompt: ______ crops are sown from October to December.
activities.hint: Think of the October-to-December season.
activities.explanation: Rabi crops are sown from October to December.

activities.prompt: Match each season with one important crop.
activities.explanation: Mustard belongs to rabi, jute to kharif, and cucumber to zaid.

activities.prompt: Why do rabi crops succeed in northern and north-western states?
options: Winter precipitation from western temperate cyclones helps them succeed.
Summer precipitation from western temperate cyclones helps them succeed.
Monsoon rainfall from western temperate cyclones helps them succeed.
Zaid irrigation from western temperate cyclones helps them succeed.
activities.explanation: Those states are important for rabi crops. Winter precipitation from western temperate cyclones helps them succeed.

activities.prompt: Match each item with its correct detail.
pairs: Paddy in Assam, West Bengal and Odisha
Three crops are grown in a year
activities.explanation: Each detail identifies the right season or paddy-growing area.

activities.prompt: Where are three crops of paddy grown in a year?
options: Assam, West Bengal and Odisha
Assam and West Bengal only
West Bengal and Odisha only
Assam and Odisha only
activities.explanation: Three crops of paddy are grown in Assam, West Bengal and Odisha.

activities.prompt: Western temperate cyclones bring winter rain to a northern farm. What is the rain most likely to help?
options: The rabi crops on that farm.
The kharif crops on that farm.
The zaid crops on that farm.
The paddy crops on that farm.

This mistake links winter rain to monsoon crops.
This mistake links winter rain to summer crops.
This mistake treats paddy as a winter crop.

activities.explanation: Winter precipitation helps rabi crops succeed.

activities.prompt: A northern farmer sows wheat from October. An Assam farmer grows paddy after the monsoon. Why can their timing differ?
options: India's physical and cultural variety shapes crop patterns.
India has one crop calendar for every place.
Only the monsoon decides every crop pattern.
Only winter rain decides every crop pattern.

why.India has one crop calendar for every pl: This mistake ignores India's physical and cultural variety.
why.Only the monsoon decides every crop patt: This mistake thinks monsoon timing alone explains all patterns.
why.Only winter rain decides every crop patt: This mistake thinks winter rain alone explains all patterns.

activities.explanation: India's physical and cultural variety is reflected in its cropping patterns.

activities.prompt: A map marks wheat and mustard in northern and north-western states. What does the map suggest?
options: These states are important rabi producers.
These states are important kharif producers.
These states are important zaid producers.
These states are important paddy producers.

why.These states are important kharif produc: This mistake treats rabi map signs as signs of kharif crops.
why.These states are important zaid producer: This mistake treats rabi map signs as signs of summer crops.
why.These states are important paddy produce: This mistake treats rabi map signs as signs of paddy farming.

activities.explanation: Wheat and mustard are rabi crops in important rabi-producing states.

activities.prompt: After Green Revolution help, a new area starts growing wheat and barley. What does this show?
options: Rabi farming spread to more Indian areas.
Kharif farming spread to more Indian areas.
Zaid farming spread to more Indian areas.
Paddy farming spread to more Indian areas.

why.Kharif farming spread to more Indian are: This mistake mistakes a rabi change for kharif farming.
why.Zaid farming spread to more Indian areas: This mistake mistakes a rabi change for summer farming.
why.Paddy farming spread to more Indian area: This mistake mistakes a rabi change for paddy farming.

activities.explanation: The Green Revolution helped rabi crops grow in several Indian areas.

activities.prompt: A farmer wants a crop during summer. They choose water melon instead of wheat. What best explains this choice?
options: Water melon is a summer zaid crop.
Wheat is a summer zaid crop.
Water melon is a winter rabi crop.
Wheat is a monsoon kharif crop.

This mistake treats wheat as a summer crop.
This mistake treats the summer zaid season as winter.
This mistake treats wheat as a monsoon kharif crop.

activities.explanation: Water melon belongs to the summer zaid season.

activities.prompt: A crop calendar shows winter sowing from October to December. A farmer plans wheat then. Why is this plan sensible?
options: Wheat is a rabi crop sown during that time.
Paddy is a rabi crop sown during that time.
Cotton is a rabi crop sown during that time.
Jute is a rabi crop sown during that time.

why.Paddy is a rabi crop sown during that ti: This mistake treats paddy as a rabi crop.
why.Cotton is a rabi crop sown during that t: This mistake treats cotton as a rabi crop.
why.Jute is a rabi crop sown during that tim: This mistake treats jute as a rabi crop.

activities.explanation: Wheat is an important rabi crop, and rabi sowing runs then.

lessons.title: Major Food and Grain Crops

activities.prompt: What helps rice, wheat, and millets thrive in different parts of India?
activities.explanation: Now read on to find out.

activities.title: Our Major Food Crops
activities.body: Rice is the staple food crop of most people in India. India is the second largest rice producer. Rice needs high temperature and humidity. Wheat is a cereal, meaning a grain crop. Wheat matters in northern and north-western India. Jowar, bajra and ragi are millets. These are grain crops. Ragi has iron and calcium. Fodder means animal food, so maize can feed people and animals. Pulses provide protein.
keyPoints: Rice is the staple food crop of most people in India.
Wheat, millets, maize and pulses have important uses.
Pulses are a major protein source in vegetarian diets.
activities.explanation: These crops give people food, nutrients and protein.

activities.prompt: A farmer has a hot, humid field. Which crop is the best match?
steps: Rice needs high temperature and humidity, so the field's conditions suit rice.
Most people in India depend on rice as food, so it is useful to grow.
India is the second largest rice producer, so rice is an important crop here.
Therefore, the farmer should choose rice for this hot, humid field.
activities.explanation: Think it through with Hooty.

activities.prompt: Which crop is the staple food of most people in India?
options: Rice
Wheat
Jowar
Pulses
activities.explanation: Rice is the staple food crop of most people in India.

activities.prompt: ______ is very rich in iron, calcium and other nutrients.
activities.hint: Choose one of the important millets.
activities.explanation: Ragi is very rich in iron, calcium and other nutrients.

activities.prompt: Match each crop with its importance or use.
pairs: Staple food crop for most people in India
Major protein source in vegetarian diets
activities.explanation: Each pair links a crop with its importance or use.

activities.prompt: What can maize be used as?
options: Only food
Food and fodder
Only fodder
Neither food nor fodder
activities.explanation: Maize can be used as both food and fodder.

activities.prompt: Which crop is the third most important food crop by area and production?
options: Rice
Maize
Jowar
Wheat
activities.explanation: Jowar is the third most important food crop by area and production.

activities.prompt: Which crop is a major source of protein in a vegetarian diet?
options: Rice
Pulses
Jowar
Ragi
activities.explanation: Pulses are a major source of protein in a vegetarian diet.

activities.prompt: A farm has high temperature and humidity. Which crop's stated needs fit best?
options: Wheat, because it needs high heat and humidity.
Rice, because it needs high heat and humidity.
Maize, because it needs high heat and humidity.
Pulses, because they need high heat and humidity.

why.Wheat, because it needs high heat and hu: This mistake assumes wheat has the same climate needs as rice.
why.Maize, because it needs high heat and hu: This mistake assumes maize has the same climate needs as rice.
why.Pulses, because they need high heat and: This mistake treats pulses like a rice crop with the same needs.

activities.explanation: This is right because rice needs high temperature and humidity.

activities.prompt: A map shows India is the second largest rice producer. A child says it shows what most Indians eat. Is that reading right?
options: The map gives production rank, not eating habits.
The map gives eating habits, not production rank.
The map proves both production rank and eating habits.
The map proves neither production rank nor eating habits.

why.The map gives eating habits, not product: This mistake swaps the map's production rank with eating habits.
why.The map proves both production rank and: This mistake assumes production rank proves what people eat.
why.The map proves neither production rank n: This mistake denies even the production rank shown by the map.

activities.explanation: This is right because the map shows rank, not eating habits.

activities.prompt: Jowar ranks third by area and production. Does this mean two crops rank above it?
options: No, three crops rank above it in both measures.
No, only one crop ranks above it in both measures.
No, rank third means every other crop is below it.
Yes, two crops rank above it in both measures.

why.No, three crops rank above it in both me: This mistake counts one rank too many above jowar.
why.No, only one crop ranks above it in both: This mistake misreads third place as having only one crop above.
why.No, rank third means every other crop is: This mistake reverses the meaning of a ranking.

activities.explanation: This is right because two crops rank above third place.

activities.prompt: One family wants one crop for food and fodder. Another wants a major protein source. Which pair fits?
options: Rice for food and fodder; ragi for protein.
Maize for food and fodder; pulses for protein.
Wheat for food and fodder; maize for protein.
Pulses for food and fodder; wheat for protein.

why.Rice for food and fodder; ragi for prote: This mistake assigns maize's fodder use to rice and calls ragi protein.
why.Wheat for food and fodder; maize for pro: This mistake gives wheat maize's uses and maize a protein role.
why.Pulses for food and fodder; wheat for pr: This mistake treats pulses as fodder and wheat as a protein source.

activities.explanation: This is right because maize has both uses and pulses give protein.

lessons.title: Food Crops, Plantation Crops and Non-food Crops

activities.prompt: Which crops do we use for food, drinks, clothes, and everyday things?
activities.explanation: Now read on to find out.

activities.title: Crops and Their Uses
activities.body: Climate is a place’s usual weather. Sugarcane grows well where it is hot and humid. It gives sugar, gur, khandsari and molasses. Groundnut and mustard are oil seeds. Some oil seeds make soap, cosmetics and ointments. Tea is a plantation crop. It grows well in tropical and sub-tropical climates. Rubber is an industrial raw material. Jute is called the golden fibre. Cotton, jute, hemp and natural silk are major fibre crops.
keyPoints: Sugarcane needs a hot and humid climate.
Oil seeds include groundnut and mustard.
India’s major fibre crops include cotton, jute, hemp and natural silk.
activities.explanation: These crops give us food, oils, industrial materials and fibres.

activities.prompt: A farmer wants a crop that fits a hot, humid place. Which crop gives sugar products?
steps: Sugarcane fits because it grows well in a hot, humid climate.
It fits the need because it gives sugar, gur, khandsari and molasses.
Both clues agree, so sugarcane is the clear choice.
activities.explanation: Think it through with Hooty.

activities.prompt: Where does sugarcane grow well?
options: cold and wet climate
hot and humid climate
cool and dry climate
cold and dry climate
activities.explanation: Sugarcane grows well in a hot and humid climate.

activities.prompt: Jute is called the ______ fibre.
activities.hint: Jute has a special nickname.
activities.explanation: Jute is known as the golden fibre.

activities.prompt: Tea cultivation is an example of plantation agriculture.
activities.explanation: Yes. Tea cultivation is a well-known example of plantation agriculture.

activities.prompt: Match each crop with its use or special feature.
activities.explanation: Each crop has a special use or feature shown in the lesson.

activities.prompt: Which items can some oil seeds be used to make?
options: Soap, cosmetics and ointments
Tea, sugar and molasses
Rubber, jute and cotton
Tea, jute and silk
activities.explanation: Some oil seeds are used to make soap, cosmetics and ointments.

activities.prompt: Which crop is not one of India’s four major fibre crops?
options: Jute
Groundnut
Hemp
Cotton
activities.explanation: Groundnut is an oil seed. The four major fibre crops are cotton, jute, hemp and natural silk.

activities.prompt: A farm in a hot, humid place needs a good crop. Which crop fits best?
options: Sugarcane, because it grows well in hot, humid weather.
Tea, because it grows well in tropical climates.
Groundnut, because it is a kharif oil seed.
Jute, because it is the golden fibre.

why.Tea, because it grows well in tropical c: This confuses tea's tropical climate with sugarcane's hot, humid climate.
why.Groundnut, because it is a kharif oil se: Groundnut is a kharif oil seed, but no climate fit is given.
Jute is a fibre crop, but no climate fit is given.

activities.explanation: Right: sugarcane grows well in hot, humid climates.

activities.prompt: Tea grows on a plantation in a tropical place. Which choice matches both facts?
options: It shows plantation agriculture in a tropical climate.
It shows food-crop farming in a cold, dry climate.
It shows fibre-crop farming in a snowy climate.
It shows oil-seed farming in a dry, windy climate.

why.It shows food-crop farming in a cold, dr: This confuses plantation farming with food-crop farming.
why.It shows fibre-crop farming in a snowy c: This confuses tea with the four major fibre crops.
why.It shows oil-seed farming in a dry, wind: This confuses tea with groundnut and mustard, which are oil seeds.

activities.explanation: Right: tea shows plantation agriculture and grows in tropical climates.

activities.prompt: A farmer needs a kharif oil seed with a large production share. Which crop fits?
options: Groundnut, because it is kharif and gives about half.
Mustard, because it is a main oil seed.
Tea, because it is a plantation crop.
Jute, because it is the golden fibre.

Mustard is an oil seed, but no fact makes it kharif.
Tea is a plantation crop, not the needed oil-seed choice.
Jute is a fibre crop, not the needed oil-seed choice.

activities.explanation: Right: groundnut is kharif and gives about half of oil-seed production.

lessons.title: Agricultural Reforms and Bhoodan-Gramdan

activities.prompt: How did India’s farmers begin to find new paths toward better harvests?
activities.explanation: Now read on to find out.

activities.title: Changes in Indian Agriculture
activities.body: After Independence, agricultural reforms included collectivisation, consolidation and cooperation. Collectivisation and cooperation mean working together. Consolidation means joining land holdings. Land reform led the First Five Year Plan. Many farmers depend on the monsoon and natural soil fertility. Reforms began in the 1960s and 1970s. A land development programme began in the 1980s and 1990s. Crop insurance, Grameen banks and support prices helped farmers. Vinoba Bhave initiated the Bhoodan-Gramdan movement.
keyPoints: Collectivisation, consolidation and cooperation were important reforms.
Land reform was the main focus of the First Five Year Plan.
Many farmers depend on the monsoon and natural soil fertility.
Vinoba Bhave initiated the Bhoodan-Gramdan movement.
activities.explanation: Agricultural change continued through reforms, support measures and the Bhoodan-Gramdan movement.

activities.prompt: A farmer hears about new land laws, but little changes. Why?
steps: India's farming tradition lasted thousands of years, relying on rain and soil.
Farmers depend on monsoon rain and fertile soil, so harvests stay uncertain.
Progress was hindered because suitable technological and institutional changes were missing.
First Plan land reform was weak, so proper implementation matters for progress.
activities.explanation: Think it through with Hooty.

activities.prompt: For how long has agriculture been practised in India?
options: Since the First Five Year Plan
For thousands of years
Since the 1960s and 1970s
Since the 1980s and 1990s
activities.explanation: Agriculture has been practised in India for thousands of years.

activities.prompt: Operation Flood was the ______ Revolution strategy for improving agriculture.
activities.hint: Choose the colour used in its name.
activities.explanation: Operation Flood was the White Revolution strategy for improving agriculture.

activities.prompt: Using land without suitable technological and institutional changes hindered agricultural development.
activities.explanation: This is true. Such use of land hindered agricultural development.

activities.prompt: Match each measure with its role in the lesson.
pairs: Main focus of the First Five Year Plan
activities.explanation: Land reform was the main focus of the First Five Year Plan. Crop insurance and Grameen banks helped farmers, while support and procurement prices protected them.

activities.prompt: Who initiated the Bhoodan-Gramdan movement?
options: Operation Flood
The First Five Year Plan
Vinoba Bhave
Grameen banks
activities.explanation: Vinoba Bhave initiated the Bhoodan-Gramdan movement.

activities.prompt: One village changes methods and institutions. Another does not. Which develops faster?
options: The first village, because suitable technology and institutions support development.
The second village, because old methods always guarantee better results.
The first village, because rain and fertile soil will protect every crop.
The second village, because technological change can never help farming.

why.The second village, because old methods: This mistake assumes old methods always produce better results.
why.The first village, because rain and fert: This mistake assumes natural conditions guarantee good results.
why.The second village, because technologica: This mistake believes technological change cannot help farming.

activities.explanation: This is right because suitable technological and institutional changes support development.

activities.prompt: A class makes a reform timeline. Which order is correct?
options: Post-Independence changes and First Plan reform, then 1960s-1970s reforms, then 1980s-1990s programme.
Post-Independence changes and 1960s-1970s reforms, then First Plan reform, then 1980s-1990s programme.
Post-Independence changes and 1980s-1990s programme, then First Plan reform, then 1960s-1970s reforms.
Post-Independence changes and 1960s-1970s reforms, then 1980s-1990s programme, then First Plan reform.

why.Post-Independence changes and 1960s-1970: This places the 1960s-1970s reforms before First Plan land reform.
why.Post-Independence changes and 1980s-1990: This places the 1980s-1990s programme before First Plan land reform.
why.Post-Independence changes and 1960s-1970: This places the 1980s-1990s programme before the 1960s-1970s reforms.

activities.explanation: This is right because post-Independence and First Plan reforms came before later programmes.

activities.prompt: A farmer faces crop loss and needs money. Which measures can help?
options: Crop insurance and Grameen banks could help with both needs.
Crop insurance and government support prices could meet both needs.
Collectivisation, consolidation and cooperation could meet both needs.
Operation Flood and Bhoodan-Gramdan could meet these two needs.

why.Crop insurance and government support pr: This uses price protection where a banking measure is needed for money.
why.Collectivisation, consolidation and coop: This chooses broad land-system changes instead of the two support measures.
why.Operation Flood and Bhoodan-Gramdan coul: This names broad programmes rather than measures aimed at both needs.

activities.explanation: This is right because crop insurance and Grameen banks were introduced to help farmers.

lessons.sceneCaption: An Indian farmer works in a cauliflower field in Maharashtra.
