lessons.title: Communication

activities.prompt: How do people and media share messages across India?
activities.explanation: Now read on to find out.

activities.title: Ways of communicating
activities.body: Communication in India has two main forms: personal communication and mass communication. India has the world’s largest postal network. Cards and envelopes travel by air as first-class mail. Other postal items travel over land and water as second-class mail. Radio, newspapers, periodicals and films provide mass communication. They give entertainment and create awareness about national programmes and policies. Digital India is a government programme to change the country using knowledge.
keyPoints: Personal and mass communication are the main forms.
Radio broadcasts in national, regional and local languages.
Newspapers are published in about 100 Indian languages and dialects.
India is the world’s largest producer of feature films.
More than two-thirds of India’s villages have Subscriber Trunk Dialling telephone facilities.
Digital India is a government programme for knowledge-based transformation.
activities.explanation: These ideas introduce the main ways of communicating.

activities.prompt: A card is sent by air between post offices. A book packet travels over land and water. Which mail class is each?
steps: Cards and envelopes are first-class mail, because they travel by air.
Book packets are second-class mail, because they travel over land and water.
The travel route helps us classify the mail, because each class has its stated route.
Therefore, the card is first-class mail and the book packet is second-class mail.
activities.explanation: Think it through with Hooty.

activities.prompt: Which are the two main forms of communication in India?
options: Postal and film communication
Personal and mass communication
Radio and newspaper communication
Digital and telephone communication
activities.explanation: Personal communication and mass communication are the main forms in India.

activities.prompt: How are cards and envelopes sent?
options: By air as first-class mail
Over land as second-class mail
Over water as second-class mail
By air as second-class mail
activities.explanation: Cards and envelopes are first-class mail. They travel by air between post offices.

activities.prompt: Book packets, registered newspapers and periodicals are sent as ______-class mail.
activities.hint: This mail travels over land and water.
activities.explanation: Book packets, registered newspapers and periodicals travel as second-class mail.

activities.prompt: Match each item with its correct detail.
pairs: Book packets, registered newspapers and periodicals
More than two-thirds of India’s villages
activities.explanation: Each item is paired with the detail given in your lesson.

activities.prompt: Newspapers are published in about ______ Indian languages and dialects.
activities.hint: Use the number given for newspaper languages.
activities.explanation: Newspapers are published in about 100 Indian languages and dialects.

activities.prompt: Put the language levels in order, from national to local.
activities.explanation: All India Radio broadcasts in national, regional and local languages.

activities.prompt: A neighbour talks with one child. A radio broadcasts to many listeners. Which pair shows the two main forms of communication?
options: The neighbour's talk is personal communication, while the radio is mass communication.
The neighbour's talk is mass communication, while the radio is personal communication.
Both talks are personal communication, because they reach only nearby people.
Both talks are mass communication, because they use spoken words.

why.The neighbour's talk is mass communicati: This swaps the meanings of personal communication and mass communication.
why.Both talks are personal communication, b: This wrongly treats a broadcast to many listeners as communication between a few people.
why.Both talks are mass communication, becau: This wrongly thinks that spoken words always make communication mass communication.

activities.explanation: This is right because one talk is between people and one broadcast reaches many people.

activities.prompt: India's postal network sends cards by air between post offices. It sends book packets over land and water. How should the office classify each item?
options: Cards are first-class mail, and book packets are second-class mail.
Cards are second-class mail, and book packets are first-class mail.
Cards and book packets are both first-class mail.
Cards and book packets are both second-class mail.

why.Cards are second-class mail, and book pa: This reverses the travel rules for the two classes of mail.
why.Cards and book packets are both first-cl: This wrongly puts book packets with cards, despite their different route.
why.Cards and book packets are both second-c: This wrongly puts cards with book packets, despite their different route.

activities.explanation: This is right because cards travel by air and book packets travel over land and water.

activities.prompt: A registered newspaper travels over land and water. What does this route show about the newspaper?
options: It is second-class mail, because second-class mail uses land and water.
It is first-class mail, because first-class mail uses land and water.
It is mass communication, because newspapers can travel far.
It is personal communication, because a newspaper reaches one reader.

why.It is first-class mail, because first-cl: This gives the wrong travel rule for first-class mail.
why.It is mass communication, because newspa: This confuses the type of communication with the mail class.
why.It is personal communication, because a: This confuses mass communication with communication between two people.

activities.explanation: This is right because registered newspapers travel over land and water as second-class mail.

activities.prompt: A radio programme tells people about a government programme for a knowledge-based change. What does this show?
options: Mass communication can create awareness about national programmes and policies.
Mass communication only entertains people and never creates awareness.
A radio programme changes the country by itself, without listeners.
Personal letters are the best way to explain national programmes.

why.Mass communication only entertains peopl: This wrongly thinks mass communication has no awareness role.
why.A radio programme changes the country by: This wrongly assumes that a broadcast causes change without people listening.
why.Personal letters are the best way to exp: This confuses personal communication with mass communication.

activities.explanation: This is right because mass communication creates awareness about programmes and policies.

activities.prompt: India publishes many newspapers and periodicals each year. One newspaper uses a local dialect. A radio station broadcasts in a regional language. Why are both useful to people?
options: They use different languages, so more people can understand the message.
They use the same language, so every person hears the same words.
They reach no readers, because local languages are not broadcast.
They show that only newspapers can provide local news.

why.They use the same language, so every per: This wrongly treats different regional and local uses as one identical language.
why.They reach no readers, because local lan: This wrongly says local languages are not used in broadcasts or newspapers.
why.They show that only newspapers can provi: This ignores radio, which also broadcasts in regional and local languages.

activities.explanation: This is right because newspapers and radio use many Indian languages and dialects.

lessons.sceneCaption: Offset printers at Sambad Press produce newspapers in Bhubaneswar, Odisha.

lessons.title: International Trade and Tourism

activities.prompt: How do countries connect through trade and tourism?
activities.explanation: Now read on to find out.

activities.title: Understanding Trade
activities.body: Trade is the exchange of goods among people, states and countries. A market is where buying and selling happen. Local trade stays within cities, towns and villages. State-level trade links states. International trade links countries and shows a country's economic prosperity. It is called an economic barometer. The balance of trade compares exports with imports. Tourism supports national integration, local handicrafts and cultural pursuits.
keyPoints: Trade exchanges goods
Markets enable buying and selling
International trade shows economic prosperity
activities.explanation: These ideas help you understand trade, markets and tourism.

activities.prompt: Tourists buy village crafts. Why can this help Indian culture?
steps: The village earns support because tourism supports local handicrafts and cultural pursuits.
The makers gain because visitors buy their handmade items.
The country gains unity because tourism promotes national integration.
Thus, the visit helps both village culture and national integration.
activities.explanation: Think it through with Hooty.

activities.title: India's Trade and Tourism
activities.body: India exports gems, jewellery, chemicals, agricultural products and software. International trade shows a country's economic prosperity, so it acts as an economic barometer. The balance of trade is the difference between exports and imports. A favourable balance means exports are worth more than imports. Tourism has grown greatly and supports national integration. It supports local handicrafts and cultural pursuits.
keyPoints: India exports goods and software
Exports above imports mean a favourable balance
Tourism supports integration and local culture
activities.explanation: Trade shows prosperity, while tourism supports India's communities and culture.

activities.prompt: Where does buying and selling take place according to the lesson?
options: At a market
Within a city
Between two countries
Between two states
activities.explanation: A market is a place where buying and selling take place.

activities.prompt: Trade between two countries is called ______ trade.
activities.hint: This trade links different countries.
activities.explanation: Trade between two countries is called international trade.

activities.prompt: Match each trading term with its meaning.
activities.explanation: Each pair connects a trading term with its correct meaning.

activities.prompt: Put these trade types in order by the area they cover.
activities.explanation: Local trade covers local places. State-level trade covers states. International trade covers countries.

activities.prompt: A country's exports are worth more than its imports. What does this show?
options: More imports than exports
It has a favourable balance of trade
No difference between exports and imports
Only local trade
activities.explanation: A country has a favourable balance when exports are worth more than imports.

activities.prompt: One shop buys goods inside its town. Another buys goods from a seller in another country. Which comparison is correct?
options: The first is local trade, while the second is international trade.
Both are local trade, because buying and selling always stay nearby.
Both are international trade, because the goods move between sellers.
The first is international trade, while the second is local trade.

why.Both are local trade, because buying and: This mistake thinks all buying and selling must happen nearby.
why.Both are international trade, because th: This mistake thinks separate sellers always mean countries are involved.
why.The first is international trade, while: This mistake swaps local trade with international trade.

activities.explanation: This is right because one trade stays local and one crosses countries.

activities.prompt: A map shows trade between two countries. The source says trade shows prosperity. What can we learn?
options: The map shows international trade, which can act as an economic barometer.
The map shows local trade, which can act as an economic barometer.
The map shows tourism, which can act as an economic barometer.
The map shows state trade, which can act as an economic barometer.

why.The map shows local trade, which can act: This mistake treats trade between countries as trade within one area.
why.The map shows tourism, which can act as: This mistake thinks the map shows visitors rather than buying and selling.
why.The map shows state trade, which can act: This mistake treats trade between countries as trade between states.

activities.explanation: This is right because the map shows international trade, which shows prosperity.

activities.prompt: Exports are worth more than imports. What happens to the trade balance?
options: It has a favourable balance of trade because exports exceed imports.
It has no balance of trade because exports and imports are different.
Its balance is equal because the country trades goods in both directions.
It has a favourable balance because imports are worth more than exports.

why.It has no balance of trade because expor: This mistake thinks different exports and imports mean there is no balance.
why.Its balance is equal because the country: This mistake thinks trading in both directions always makes a balance equal.
why.It has a favourable balance because impo: This mistake reverses the rule by saying imports exceed exports.

activities.explanation: This is right because exports exceed imports, which gives a favourable balance.

activities.prompt: An Indian company sells software abroad. An Indian trader also sells gems abroad. What do both sales show?
options: Both are exports because India sells software and goods to other countries.
Both are imports because India sells software and goods to other countries.
Both are local because India sells software and goods to other countries.
Both are tourism because India sells software and goods to other countries.

why.Both are imports because India sells sof: This mistake reverses the meaning of exports and imports.
why.Both are local because India sells softw: This mistake thinks selling goods abroad is still trade within India.
why.Both are tourism because India sells sof: This mistake thinks selling goods abroad is the same as receiving visitors.

activities.explanation: This is right because both sales send software or Indian goods abroad.

activities.prompt: Tourism in India has grown greatly over the past two decades. How can this affect local handicrafts?
options: It can support them because tourism supports local handicrafts and cultural pursuits.
It can stop them because tourism supports local handicrafts and cultural pursuits.
It can move them abroad because tourism supports local handicrafts and cultural pursuits.
It can reduce them because tourism supports local handicrafts and cultural pursuits.

why.It can stop them because tourism support: This mistake thinks tourism stops local handicrafts from growing.
why.It can move them abroad because tourism: This mistake thinks tourism always moves local crafts out of the country.
why.It can reduce them because tourism suppo: This mistake thinks tourism reduces support for local handicrafts.

activities.explanation: This is right because tourism supports local handicrafts and cultural pursuits.

activities.prompt: Tourists from different states visit India together. What effect can tourism have?
options: It can promote national integration among people from different states.
It can divide states because visitors should stay apart from each other.
It can stop local culture because visitors dislike local traditions.
It can shrink trade because tourists avoid buying local goods.

why.It can divide states because visitors sh: This mistake thinks tourism keeps people from different states apart.
why.It can stop local culture because visito: This mistake thinks visitors coming together can stop local culture.
why.It can shrink trade because tourists avo: This mistake thinks tourism reduces trade instead of promoting integration.

activities.explanation: This is right because tourism promotes national integration.

activities.context: After a motorable road linked a village to a major town, a small trader began carrying goods between them. The trader chose road transport because it provided door-to-door service, and the village’s new road also gave access to a nearby railway station. Meanwhile, a State Highway connected the state capital with district headquarters. Traders hoped that better transport links would make it easier for goods to reach places where they were needed.
activities.prompt: Goods arrive at the railway station near the village. What should the trader arrange next, and why?
options: Arrange a road trip from the station to the village because road transport can reduce loading and unloading costs.
Leave the goods at the station until a railway line reaches the village.
Send the goods by water transport to a seaport linked with the station.
Ask the Border Roads Organisation to carry the goods directly to the village.

why.Leave the goods at the station until a r: Incorrect: the case requires a link to an existing railway station, not a new railway line.
why.Send the goods by water transport to a s: Incorrect: water transport does not provide the final journey to the village in this case.
why.Ask the Border Roads Organisation to car: Incorrect: the Border Roads Organisation builds and maintains roads; it does not carry goods.

activities.explanation: Correct: a final road journey can provide door-to-door service and reduce loading and unloading costs.

activities.context: After a motorable road linked a village to a major town, a small trader began carrying goods between them. The trader chose road transport because it provided door-to-door service, and the village’s new road also gave access to a nearby railway station. Meanwhile, a State Highway connected the state capital with district headquarters. Traders hoped that better transport links would make it easier for goods to reach places where they were needed.
activities.prompt: The village still cannot be reached by a motorable road. Which step best follows the rural road scheme’s aim?
options: Provide a motorable link from the village to a major town.
Build a State Highway only between the state capital and a district headquarters.
Use the Super Highways project instead of linking the village to a town.
Construct railway lines through the Border Roads Organisation.

why.Build a State Highway only between the s: Incorrect: a State Highway connects a state capital with district headquarters, not the village directly.
why.Use the Super Highways project instead o: Incorrect: the Super Highways project does not replace the rural scheme’s village connections.
why.Construct railway lines through the Bord: Incorrect: the Border Roads Organisation works on roads in border areas, not railway construction.

activities.explanation: Correct: the rural road scheme seeks a motorable connection between every village and a major town.

activities.prompt:
Assertion (A): Roads may be preferred over railway lines when the main aim is to reduce construction costs.
Reason (R): Building roads costs much less than building railway lines.
options: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true but R is false.
A is false but R is true.
activities.explanation: The reason directly explains why roads may cost less than railway lines.

activities.prompt:
Assertion (A): The Border Roads Organisation has a road-building role in India’s border areas.
Reason (R): The National Highway Authority of India implements the Super Highways project.
options: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true but R is false.
A is false but R is true.
activities.explanation: Both statements are true, but the Super Highways project does not explain the organisation’s border-road role.

activities.prompt: Explain how roads can improve the movement of goods while also supporting other transport systems.
activities.answer: Goods and services cannot reach the places where they are needed without transport. Roads provide door-to-door service, so they can reduce loading and unloading costs. They also feed other transport systems by linking railway stations, airports and seaports. This allows goods to travel by one system and then continue by road. Since building roads costs much less than building railway lines, road links can also be provided more economically. Together, these features help efficient transport support faster national development.
points: Transport is necessary for goods and services to reach where they are needed.
Road transport gives door-to-door service.
Roads reduce loading and unloading costs.
Roads link railway stations, airports and seaports.
activities.explanation: Compare your answer with the points a marker looks for.

activities.prompt:
Assertion (A): The Konkan railway has improved passenger and goods movement along India's west coast.
Reason (R): Its location along India's west coast has helped passenger and goods movement.
options: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true but R is false.
A is false but R is true.
activities.explanation: The reason directly explains the improvement stated in the assertion.

activities.prompt:
Assertion (A): Pipelines are cheap to lay at first.
Reason (R): They are cheap to run after the high cost of laying them.
options: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true but R is false.
A is false but R is true.
activities.explanation: Pipelines are costly to lay initially, although they are cheap to run later.

activities.prompt: Explain the difference between railways and pipelines as means of transport, including what they carry, their costs and their transfer benefits.
activities.answer: Railways carry both passengers and freight, and they are the main way of transporting both in India. Railway building is easier on the flat northern plains, while lines in hilly areas pass through low hills, gaps and tunnels. Pipelines carry crude oil, petroleum products and natural gas. They are costly to lay initially but cheap to run later. They also avoid cargo loss, trans-shipment losses and delays during transfer, making them useful for carrying energy cargo efficiently.
points: Railways carry passengers and freight.
Northern plains provide good railway-building conditions; hilly areas need special routes.
Pipelines carry crude oil, petroleum products and natural gas.
Pipelines have high initial costs but low running costs and avoid trans-shipment losses and delays.
activities.explanation: Compare your answer with the points a marker looks for.

activities.context: Suppose a merchant in Goa needs to export a large consignment of iron ore and wants the cheapest practical way to move heavy and bulky goods. A student learns that about 95 per cent of India’s trade volume moves by sea and that Mormugao is Goa’s main iron ore exporting port. The student also studies India’s 14,500 km of inland navigation waterways and compares Mumbai, Chennai, and Vishakhapatnam while planning the journey.
activities.prompt: The merchant wants to export iron ore from Goa. Which port should the student recommend, and why?
options: The merchant should choose Mormugao, since it is the principal port used for sending iron ore out of the country.
The merchant should choose Mumbai, since it is the country’s largest port and has a roomy natural harbour.
The merchant should choose Chennai, since it is among India’s oldest artificial ports.
The merchant should choose Vishakhapatnam, since it is India’s deepest landlocked and well-protected port.

why.The merchant should choose Mumbai, since: Being the biggest port does not make Mumbai the main iron ore exporting port.
why.The merchant should choose Chennai, sinc: Being an old artificial port does not identify the main iron ore exporting port.
why.The merchant should choose Vishakhapatna: Being deep, landlocked and protected does not identify the main iron ore exporting port.

activities.explanation: Mormugao has the main role in exporting iron ore.

activities.context: Suppose a merchant in Goa needs to export a large consignment of iron ore and wants the cheapest practical way to move heavy and bulky goods. A student learns that about 95 per cent of India’s trade volume moves by sea and that Mormugao is Goa’s main iron ore exporting port. The student also studies India’s 14,500 km of inland navigation waterways and compares Mumbai, Chennai, and Vishakhapatnam while planning the journey.
activities.prompt: The merchant also needs to move suitable heavy and bulky goods inland while keeping transport costs down. What should the student recommend?
options: Recommend inland waterways for the suitable heavy and bulky goods, because they are the least expensive transport method.
Recommend sea transport for the inland leg, because about 95 per cent of India’s trade volume moves by sea.
Recommend Mumbai harbour for the inland leg, because it is spacious and the country’s biggest port.
Recommend Chennai port for the inland leg, because it is one of India’s oldest artificial ports.

why.Recommend sea transport for the inland l: The share of trade moving by sea does not apply to an inland journey.
why.Recommend Mumbai harbour for the inland: A spacious harbour is a feature of a port, not a reason to choose sea transport inland.
why.Recommend Chennai port for the inland le: Being an old artificial port does not identify the most economical inland transport.

activities.explanation: Waterways are both economical and suitable for heavy and bulky goods.

activities.prompt:
Assertion (A): Mumbai is India’s main iron ore exporting port.
Reason (R): Mumbai is India’s biggest port and has a spacious natural harbour.
options: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true but R is false.
A is false but R is true.
activities.explanation: The assertion is false because Mormugao is the main iron ore exporting port, while the reason is true.

activities.prompt: How does the case show the difference between moving goods by sea and using inland waterways?
activities.answer: The case uses sea transport for the overseas iron ore export: about 95 per cent of India’s trade volume moves by sea, and Mormugao is the main iron ore exporting port. Inland waterways serve a different role. They are the cheapest form of transport and are especially suitable for heavy and bulky goods, with India having 14,500 km of inland navigation waterways. The National Waterways were declared under the National Waterways Act, 2016. Thus, the sea route is relevant to trade, while waterways provide an economical way to carry heavy and bulky goods.
points: About 95 per cent of India’s trade volume moves by sea.
Mormugao is the main iron ore exporting port.
Waterways are the cheapest form of transport and suit heavy and bulky goods.
India has 14,500 km of inland navigation waterways.
activities.explanation: Compare your answer with the points a marker looks for.

activities.context: Floods make land travel difficult in a northern district, and a remote settlement there is not well connected. A regional airline plans to use the UDAN scheme to offer a new route so that ordinary people can travel more affordably. At the same time, an oil and natural gas operation in another inaccessible area needs helicopter support.
activities.prompt: What is the most likely result after the regional airline begins serving the remote settlement under UDAN?
options: The settlement may gain a practical air link that ordinary residents can afford to use.
Every resident will be entitled to travel by air without paying.
Only passengers seeking prestige value will have any use for the route.
Helicopter services will replace the need for the airline's regional route.

why.Every resident will be entitled to trave: UDAN does not promise free travel for every resident.
why.Only passengers seeking prestige value w: The scheme aims to widen access rather than serve only prestige-seeking passengers.
why.Helicopter services will replace the nee: Helicopters serve specialised needs in inaccessible areas rather than replacing regional routes.

activities.explanation: Affordability for ordinary citizens is a central aim of UDAN.

activities.context: Floods make land travel difficult in a northern district, and a remote settlement there is not well connected. A regional airline plans to use the UDAN scheme to offer a new route so that ordinary people can travel more affordably. At the same time, an oil and natural gas operation in another inaccessible area needs helicopter support.
activities.prompt: If the regional airline no longer receives the useful policies and incentives offered under UDAN, what may happen?
options: The airline may find it harder to maintain an affordable service on a regional or remote route.
The scheme will guarantee affordable flights even without encouraging airlines to participate.
Helicopter support will become more common in inaccessible oil and natural gas areas.
The regional aviation market will become more attractive because route difficulties will disappear.

why.The scheme will guarantee affordable fli: Removing them does not create a guarantee of affordable flights.
why.Helicopter support will become more comm: Helicopter support for oil and natural gas operations is separate from UDAN.
why.The regional aviation market will become: With less encouragement, the market may become harder to develop rather than easier.

activities.explanation: Policies and incentives encourage airlines to serve regional and remote routes.

activities.prompt:
Assertion (A): Air travel is especially useful in northern and eastern regions where land travel is difficult.
Reason (R): Rivers, forests and floods make land travel difficult in these regions.
options: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true but R is false.
A is false but R is true.
activities.explanation: The reason directly explains why air travel is especially useful in these regions.

activities.prompt:
Assertion (A): Helicopters are the main way that UDAN makes regional flights affordable for ordinary citizens.
Reason (R): Helicopters can reach difficult terrain and support oil and natural gas operations in inaccessible areas.
options: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true but R is false.
A is false but R is true.
activities.explanation: The statement misidentifies the role of UDAN, while the reason is true but does not explain it.

activities.prompt: Explain how the UDAN scheme and helicopters serve different purposes in improving air travel.
activities.answer: UDAN, the Regional Connectivity Scheme, was designed to start the regional aviation market and aims to make flying affordable for ordinary citizens. It encourages airlines to serve regional and remote routes through useful policies and incentives. Helicopters have a different role. They can reach difficult terrain in the north-east and the interior parts of Jammu and Kashmir, Himachal Pradesh and Uttarakhand. They also support oil and natural gas operations in inaccessible areas. Thus, UDAN promotes affordable regional passenger services, while helicopters provide access to difficult and inaccessible places.
points: UDAN is the Regional Connectivity Scheme.
It aims to make flying affordable for ordinary citizens.
Policies and incentives encourage airlines to serve regional and remote routes.
Helicopters reach difficult terrain and support oil and natural gas operations.
activities.explanation: Compare your answer with the points a marker looks for.

activities.context: A student in a village reads a newspaper published in an Indian language and hears a regional programme on All India Radio. The student also wants information about a national programme and sends a card to a friend through the postal network. The village has Subscriber Trunk Dialling facilities, while Digital India seeks a knowledge-based transformation of the country. The student plans to use mass communication to understand policies and share the news.
activities.prompt: If the student wants reliable information about a national programme, which action would be most suitable?
options: Listen to All India Radio for information about the programme.
Send a card to a friend and rely on the postal network.
Send a book packet and expect it to follow the second-class route.
Use Subscriber Trunk Dialling facilities to broadcast programmes in regional and local languages.

why.Send a card to a friend and rely on the: A card carries personal communication but does not itself provide awareness about the programme.
why.Send a book packet and expect it to foll: A book packet is postal material and its route does not provide information about the programme.
why.Use Subscriber Trunk Dialling facilities: Subscriber Trunk Dialling facilities support telephone communication, not broadcasting.

activities.explanation: All India Radio is a mass communication medium that creates awareness about national programmes and policies.

chapters.title: Chapter 1: Development
chapters.summary: In this chapter: what development promises; national development and choosing criteria; average income and its distribution; income and other development criteria.

lessons.title: What development promises

activities.prompt: What do people hope development will make possible for their lives?
activities.explanation: Now read on to find out.

activities.title: Understanding development
activities.body: Development means thinking about basic needs and ways to help everyone have a better life. People hope for change, and democratic politics can help make those hopes real. Different people may want different results. They choose goals that matter most to them, such as regular work, better wages, fair prices, equal treatment, freedom, security and respect. Material goods alone are not enough for a good life.
keyPoints: Development starts with basic needs and better lives.
Democratic politics can help hopes become real.
People want different goals for a good life.
activities.explanation: Development is about helping people have a better life in many ways.

activities.prompt: A village gets more money, but people still lack a good life. Why can more money not solve everything?
steps: Development seeks a better life, so basic needs matter for everyone.
Material goods alone are not enough, because a good life needs more.
Work and prices fulfil hopes, as do equality, freedom, security, and respect.
Development has many goals because valuable things cannot always be measured easily.
activities.explanation: Think it through with Hooty.

activities.title: Different goals for a good life
activities.body: People often want regular work, better wages and fair prices for what they produce. They also value equal treatment, freedom, security and respect. These goals show that development is not only about earning more money. Some valuable parts of life cannot be measured easily. A job may even pay less while giving regular employment, so people may value other benefits too.
keyPoints: People want work, fair pay and fair prices.
Equal treatment and respect matter too.
Development is not only about earning more money.
activities.explanation: A good life includes many goals beyond money.

activities.prompt: What does development involve?
options: Thinking about basic needs
Only buying more goods
Only earning more money
Changing one person's life
activities.explanation: Development involves thinking about basic needs and ways to achieve a better life for everyone.

activities.prompt: Different people may want different things from development.
activities.explanation: Different people can want different things from development.

activities.prompt: Many people want regular work, better wages and ______ for their produce.
activities.hint: This means a suitable amount for what farmers sell.
activities.explanation: Many people want fair prices for the produce they sell.

activities.prompt: Match each idea with its meaning.
activities.explanation: These pairs show needs, hopes and goals connected with development.

activities.prompt: Which situation matches the lesson?
options: Helping one person always helps everyone
Development affects only one person
Helping one person can harm another
All changes help everyone equally
activities.explanation: Something that helps one person may harm another person.

activities.prompt: Which choice best shows developmental goals?
options: Only earning more money
Regular work and fair treatment
Only collecting material goods
Having no developmental goals
activities.explanation: Development goals include regular work, better wages and fair treatment, not only more money.

activities.prompt: A town wants public changes for a better life. People discuss the changes and choose a plan together. Why can this plan make their hopes real?
options: It uses a democratic political process.
It keeps all choices with one leader.
It leaves the people outside the decision.
It depends only on each person's private wish.

This wrongly puts the choice with one person, not people.
why.It leaves the people outside the decisio: This wrongly leaves the people outside the process.
why.It depends only on each person's private: A private wish cannot turn hope into reality.

activities.explanation: A democratic political process can turn hopes for change into reality.

activities.prompt: One family wants regular work and fair prices for its produce. Another family wants equal treatment, freedom, and respect. Which plan should the government follow?
options: Plan around each family's most important hopes.
Plan only material goods for the first family.
Plan only more money for the second family.
Plan one common material goal for both families.

why.Plan only material goods for the first f: This ignores what the second family values.
why.Plan only more money for the second fami: This ignores what the first family values.
why.Plan one common material goal for both f: This wrongly assumes both families want the same material goal.

activities.explanation: Different people can want different things from development.

activities.prompt: A village list names regular work, fair prices, and equal treatment. What does this show about its development goals?
options: It includes both money goals and non-money goals.
It focuses only on earning more money.
It leaves out equal treatment and freedom.
It says material goods alone make life good.

This wrongly treats money goals as all development goals.
why.It leaves out equal treatment and freedo: The list names equal treatment, and freedom is also a goal.
why.It says material goods alone make life g: This wrongly treats material goods as a complete good life.

activities.explanation: The list includes work, prices, fairness, and other important aims.

activities.prompt: A new shop gives families cheap goods. The shop also takes business from a local seller. What does this situation show?
options: One change can help some people and harm others.
One change can help every person in the same way.
Development can improve every person's life equally.
Material goods alone can make every life good.

why.One change can help every person in the: This wrongly overlooks the seller who loses business.
why.Development can improve every person's l: This wrongly assumes development has the same effect on everyone.
why.Material goods alone can make every life: This wrongly treats material goods as a complete good life.

activities.explanation: Helping one person can harm another person at the same time.

activities.prompt: Before, a worker had no regular job. Then, the worker took a job with less money but regular work. Why might the worker still accept this job?
options: Regular work can matter even when the pay is lower.
More money must matter more than regular work.
Regular work matters only after prices become fair.
Material goods alone make the new job better.

why.More money must matter more than regular: This wrongly makes money more important than regular work.
why.Regular work matters only after prices b: This wrongly makes fair prices a condition for regular work.
why.Material goods alone make the new job be: This wrongly treats material goods as the only goal.

activities.explanation: A job may give less money but still offer regular employment.

activities.prompt: A person has enough money for basic needs. The person also wants freedom, security, and respect. Why is more money not the whole development goal?
options: Because freedom, security, and respect also fulfil hopes.
Because money cannot support anyone's basic needs.
Because regular work matters only when its pay rises.
Because fair prices matter only after people earn more.

why.Because money cannot support anyone's ba: This wrongly says money cannot meet basic needs.
why.Because regular work matters only when i: This wrongly makes higher pay the condition for regular work.
why.Because fair prices matter only after pe: This wrongly makes more earnings the condition for fair prices.

activities.explanation: Development goals include more than earning more money.

lessons.title: National development and choosing criteria

activities.prompt: How can we choose a fair way to compare national development?
activities.explanation: Now read on to find out.

activities.title: Making fair choices
activities.body: National development can involve different and conflicting ideas. Making a choice means deciding how to handle those ideas. A fair path should consider what is right for everyone. It should benefit many people, not only a small group. When comparing countries, the criterion depends on the purpose. Income matters, but total income is less useful when populations differ. Average income, also called per capita income, helps compare what people may earn.
keyPoints: National development can involve conflicting ideas.
Fair paths benefit many and consider everyone.
The comparison criterion depends on its purpose.
activities.explanation: Fair choices and suitable criteria help comparisons benefit many people.

activities.prompt: A town can build one project. Some residents want a park for many. Others want a club for a few. How should the town choose fairly?
steps: People can have different ideas because they understand national development in different ways.
Those ideas can conflict, so the town must make a difficult choice.
A fair choice should consider what is right for everyone, because fairness includes all residents.
Therefore, the town should choose a project that benefits many people rather than only a small group.
activities.explanation: Think it through with Hooty.

activities.prompt: What should a fair path consider?
options: What is right for everyone
What is right for one small group
Which ideas are conflicting
What total income shows
activities.explanation: A fair path considers what is right for everyone, not only a small group.

activities.prompt: Average income is another name for ______ income.
activities.hint: The lesson gives another name for average income.
activities.explanation: Average income is also called per capita income.

activities.prompt: Match each income idea with its correct meaning.
pairs: Used to compare people’s incomes across countries
Often linked to obtaining more of what people need
activities.explanation: Total income is less useful when populations differ. Average income supports comparisons between countries.

activities.prompt: Put the comparison process in order.
items: Set the purpose of the comparison
Choose the criterion for that purpose
Compare countries using the chosen criterion
activities.explanation: The purpose guides the criterion. The chosen criterion then guides the comparison.

activities.prompt: Why can total income be a poor comparison when populations differ?
options: It does not show how the comparison criterion was chosen.
It does not show what an average person may earn.
It does not show which national development ideas conflict.
It does not show what is fair for everyone.
activities.explanation: Comparing total incomes does not show what an average person may earn.

activities.prompt: What is higher income often linked with?
options: Obtaining more of what people need
Comparing more countries by their income
Resolving more conflicting ideas about national development
Benefiting only one small group
activities.explanation: Higher income is often linked to obtaining more of what people need.

activities.prompt: Country A has higher income than Country B. Higher income often links to more ability to obtain needs. What may happen to people in Country A?
options: They may obtain more of what people need.
They may have fewer conflicts about development.
They may have a smaller total population.
They may all share one idea about development.

why.They may have fewer conflicts about deve: This confuses income with agreement about development.
why.They may have a smaller total population: This confuses income with population size.
why.They may all share one idea about develo: This wrongly assumes that higher income removes different ideas.

activities.explanation: Higher income often helps people obtain more of what they need.

activities.prompt: Two countries have the same total income. One country has more people than the other. Which measure is more useful for comparing average earnings?
options: Use average income for each country.
Use total income for each country again.
Use the population of the larger country.
Use the income of one person.

Total income does not show average earnings when populations differ.
why.Use the population of the larger country: Population size alone does not show what people earn.
One person's income does not represent a country's average.

activities.explanation: Average income compares what an average person may earn.

activities.prompt: A source gives the total income of two countries. It does not give their populations. What can this source tell us about an average person?
options: It cannot show what an average person may earn.
It can show what an average person may earn.
It can show what every person in each country earns.
It can show what people need in each country.

why.It can show what an average person may e: This treats total income as if it were average income.
why.It can show what every person in each co: This mistakes an average for what each person must earn.
why.It can show what people need in each cou: This confuses total income with what people need.

activities.explanation: Total income alone does not show what an average person may earn.

activities.prompt: A fair path considers what is right for everyone. A government can fund one development project. Which project fits this rule?
options: Choose the project that helps many people.
Choose the project that helps a small group.
Choose whichever project one person prefers.
Choose no project until all people agree.

why.Choose the project that helps a small gr: This favors a small group instead of many people.
why.Choose whichever project one person pref: This lets one person's preference decide what is fair.
why.Choose no project until all people agree: This treats disagreement as a reason to avoid choosing fairly.

activities.explanation: Development should benefit many people rather than only a small group.

lessons.title: Average income and its distribution

activities.prompt: How can we understand what an average income hides inside a country?
activities.explanation: Now read on to find out.

activities.title: Understanding average income
activities.body: In 2024, US$ 66,500 or more meant high income. About US$ 2,300 or less meant low income. India was low middle income, at about US$ 11,000 per person each year. Rich countries are generally called developed countries. Averages can hide differences within a country. Country A was preferred because its income was distributed more equally.
keyPoints: High income starts at US$ 66,500 per person.
India was low middle income in 2024.
Averages can hide unequal income distribution.
activities.explanation: Income groups show averages, but averages may hide differences among people.

activities.prompt: Two villages have the same average income. Which village has fairer income sharing?
steps: Two villages can have the same average income.
An average can hide differences among people inside each village.
Country A was preferred because its income was shared more equally.
Therefore, we must check income sharing, not only the average.
activities.explanation: Think it through with Hooty.

activities.prompt: Which income matches the high income classification in 2024?
options: US$ 66,500 or more per person
About US$ 11,000 per person
About US$ 2,300 or less per person
India's low middle income status
activities.explanation: US$ 66,500 or more meets the high income limit.

activities.prompt: India's per capita income in 2024 was about US$ ______ per annum.
activities.hint: Use the amount given for India.

activities.prompt: Match each item with its correct description.
activities.explanation: Each pair matches an income group with its given description.

activities.prompt: What can a useful average hide?
options: Differences in income within a population
Whether two countries have equal averages
Whether an average is useful for comparison
Whether a country belongs to an income group
activities.explanation: An average can hide differences within a population.

activities.prompt: Why was Country A preferred over a country with the same average?
options: Income was distributed more equally.
Average income was much higher.
Everyone had exactly the same income.
The country had more people.

activities.prompt: Put these per capita incomes from highest to lowest.
activities.explanation: These amounts show the order from highest to lowest.

activities.prompt: India's 2024 per capita income was about US$ 11,000. Why was India not high income?
options: Because US$ 11,000 is below US$ 66,500.
Because US$ 11,000 is above US$ 2,300.
Because US$ 11,000 equals US$ 66,500.
Because US$ 11,000 is not per capita income.

This only shows that India was above the low-income limit.
This makes the two amounts equal, but they are not.
why.Because US$ 11,000 is not per capita inc: This denies the stated per capita income figure.

activities.explanation: This is right because US$ 11,000 is below the US$ 66,500 high-income limit.

activities.prompt: A map shows each country's average income, but no details about people. What can it show?
options: Country averages, but not how income is shared.
Country averages, and every person's exact income.
Country averages, but only for very rich countries.
Country averages, and whether income is equal.

why.Country averages, and every person's exa: This mistakes an average for every person's exact income.
why.Country averages, but only for very rich: This assumes only rich countries can have average incomes.
why.Country averages, and whether income is: This assumes an average proves equal sharing.

activities.explanation: This is right because an average does not show income sharing.

activities.prompt: India's 2024 average is about US$ 11,000 per person. Another country has about US$ 2,300. What can we compare?
options: India has the higher average, but not every person's income.
India has the lower average, but not every person's income.
Both have the same average, but not every person's income.
India has the higher average, so every person earns more.

why.India has the lower average, but not eve: This reverses the two income figures.
why.Both have the same average, but not ever: This treats different averages as the same average.
why.India has the higher average, so every p: This wrongly assumes a higher average proves every person earns more.

activities.explanation: This is right because US$ 11,000 is higher, but averages hide sharing details.

lessons.title: Income and other development criteria

activities.prompt: How can we understand development beyond income?
activities.explanation: Now read on to find out.

activities.title: Looking beyond income
activities.body: Per capita income means income for each person. Haryana had the highest per capita income among the three states, while Bihar had the lowest. But income alone cannot show how developed a place is. Money cannot buy a pollution-free environment. Health, education, nutrition, and public services also matter.
keyPoints: Haryana had the highest per capita income.
Bihar had the lowest per capita income.
Income alone cannot show every part of development.
activities.explanation: A developed place needs more than high income.

steps: Haryana has higher per capita income, so it looks richer.
Income alone cannot fully show development because other needs matter.
Money cannot buy a pollution-free environment, so clean surroundings also matter.
Therefore, Haryana is not automatically more developed in every way.

activities.prompt: Which state had the highest per capita income among the three states?
options: Haryana
Bihar
Kerala

activities.prompt: Match each item to its correct statement.

Lowest per capita income among the three states
Can function well in some states
Collective provision of goods and services

activities.prompt: Why can income by itself not fully show how developed a place is?
options: It cannot show every part of development.
It shows every part of a place's development.

activities.prompt: What is linked to Kerala's low infant mortality rate?

A pollution-free environment alone
Adequate health and educational facilities
The Public Distribution System alone

activities.prompt: Kerala has adequate health and education facilities. What happens to infant deaths?
options: They may fall because good services help children.
They may rise because more children now need care.
They stay the same because services help only adults.
They fall to zero because every child gets care.

why.They may rise because more children now: It wrongly treats more children needing care as causing more deaths.
why.They stay the same because services help: It wrongly thinks health services cannot help babies.
why.They fall to zero because every child ge: It wrongly turns a lower death rate into no deaths.

activities.prompt: A state makes its Public Distribution System work well. Why might health and nutrition improve there?
options: Higher income alone guarantees better health and nutrition.
Poor public services can make children healthier.
Good public services often support better health and nutrition.
More private shops always remove the need for public services.

why.Higher income alone guarantees better he: This wrongly assumes income alone can guarantee good health.
why.Poor public services can make children h: This wrongly treats weak public services as a cause of better health.
why.More private shops always remove the nee: This wrongly assumes private shops can replace working public services.

activities.explanation: Public services work well where health and nutrition are likely better.

activities.prompt: A state has more money but polluted surroundings. Why is income alone not enough to judge its development?
options: Money cannot buy a pollution-free environment by itself.
More money always removes every kind of pollution.
Pollution does not matter when income is high.
A rich state is fully developed if its income rises.

why.More money always removes every kind of: This wrongly assumes more money always gives a clean environment.
why.Pollution does not matter when income is: This wrongly ignores the environment as part of development.
why.A rich state is fully developed if its i: This wrongly treats income as the only measure of development.

activities.explanation: A pollution-free environment also matters, and money cannot buy it.

lessons.title: Nutrition and human development

activities.prompt: What can BMI and the Human Development Report tell us about people’s well-being?
activities.explanation: Now read on to find out.

activities.title: Checking nourishment and development
activities.body: Body Mass Index, or BMI, checks nourishment. Measure weight in kilograms. Divide weight by the square of height to find BMI. A BMI below the normal range can show underweight. Human development also depends on health, education and income. Income cannot fully measure development. The Human Development Report compares countries using education levels, health status and per capita income.
keyPoints: BMI helps check nourishment.
BMI uses weight and height.
Development depends on health, education and income.
activities.explanation: These ideas help you understand nutrition and human development.

activities.prompt: A country has high income, but poor health and weak education. Can income alone show full development?
steps: Income is important, but it cannot fully measure development.
Health and education matter because they also indicate development.
Citizens matter because human development focuses on what happens to them.
So, high income alone cannot prove full development.
activities.explanation: Think it through with Hooty.

activities.prompt: A student's weight should be measured in kilograms for calculating BMI.
activities.explanation: Kilograms are used to measure weight for BMI.

activities.prompt: What does BMI help to check?
options: A student's nourishment
A student's height
A student's income
A country's progress
activities.explanation: BMI is a measure for checking nourishment.

activities.prompt: A BMI below the normal range can show that a student is ______.
activities.hint: This means having less weight than the normal range suggests.
activities.explanation: A BMI below the normal range can indicate underweight.

activities.prompt: Match each item with its correct connection.
pairs: Ahead of India in the comparison
activities.explanation: Each pair shows an important connection in this lesson.

activities.prompt: Which three things does the Human Development Report use?
options: Education levels, health status and income
Height, weight and age
Income, marks and attendance
Weight, height and distance
activities.explanation: The report uses education levels, health status and per capita income.

activities.prompt: Human development gives special importance to what happens to a country's citizens.
activities.explanation: Human development focuses on what happens to a country's citizens.

activities.prompt: Two students have the same height. One weighs more. What happens to the heavier student's BMI?
options: The heavier student's BMI is higher than the lighter student's.
The heavier student's BMI is lower than the lighter student's.
The heavier student's BMI is equal to the lighter student's.
The two students' BMI cannot be compared with each other.

why.The heavier student's BMI is lower than: This mistakes more weight for a smaller BMI result.
why.The heavier student's BMI is equal to th: This wrongly thinks BMI depends only on height.
why.The two students' BMI cannot be compared: This wrongly believes BMI results cannot be compared.

activities.explanation: With the same height, more weight gives a larger BMI.

activities.prompt: A student checks BMI. The result is below normal. What might this show?
options: The student may be underweight because the BMI is low.
The student may be overweight because the BMI is low.
The student must have normal weight because BMI is low.
Nothing can be suggested because BMI shows no weight clue.

why.The student may be overweight because th: This confuses below normal with being overweight.
why.The student must have normal weight beca: This wrongly treats below normal as normal weight.
why.Nothing can be suggested because BMI sho: This wrongly believes BMI cannot give a weight clue.

activities.explanation: A BMI below normal can indicate that a student is underweight.

activities.prompt: Two countries have the same per capita income. The report also checks education and health. Can their places still differ?
options: Yes, because education levels and health status may differ.
Yes, because equal income must give equal results.
No, because equal income gives equal report results.
No, because the report ignores education and health.

why.Yes, because equal income must give equa: This says yes but gives a reason for equal results.
why.No, because equal income gives equal rep: This wrongly thinks income alone fixes the report result.
why.No, because the report ignores education: The report uses education levels and health status too.

activities.explanation: Different education or health can lead to different places.

lessons.title: Sustainability of development

activities.prompt: How can we meet today’s needs without harming tomorrow’s chances?
activities.explanation: Now read on to find out.

activities.title: Development for the future
activities.body: Sustainable development means maintaining today’s level of development for future generations. The present level of development may not be sustainable. A renewable resource becomes overused when taken faster than nature replaces it. Non-renewable resources have a fixed stock and will run out. Environmental harm can cross boundaries. Places share the environment, so their futures are connected.
keyPoints: Maintain development for future generations.
Use renewable resources no faster than nature replaces them.
Non-renewable resources have a fixed, unreplaceable stock.
Environmental harm links different places.
activities.explanation: Thinking about future generations helps us choose development that can last.

activities.prompt: A village uses groundwater faster than nature replaces it. Should it keep doing this to support today's needs?
steps: Groundwater is taken faster than nature replaces it.
The reserve becomes overused because replacement cannot keep up.
If this continues, groundwater levels can decline.
Development should therefore continue without reducing future generations' chances.
activities.explanation: Think it through with Hooty.

activities.title: The main aim
activities.prompt: What is the main aim of sustainable development?
options: Keep development for future generations
Use every resource without limits
Remove future generations from decisions
Keep environmental harm inside one place
activities.explanation: Sustainable development keeps today’s development available for future generations.

activities.title: Using renewable resources
activities.prompt: A renewable resource becomes overused when it is taken ______ than nature replaces it.
activities.hint: Think about the speed of taking and replacing.
activities.explanation: Taking it faster than nature replaces it causes overuse.

activities.title: Reported groundwater changes
activities.prompt: Which change was reported in about 300 districts?
options: A groundwater decline over four metres
A groundwater rise over four metres
A steady groundwater rise in reserves
activities.explanation: About 300 districts reported a groundwater decline of more than four metres.

activities.title: Resources and limits
activities.prompt: Match each resource with its description.
pairs: Becomes overused when taken faster than nature replaces it
Has a fixed stock that cannot be replaced
Depends on imports because reserves are not enough
activities.explanation: Each pair matches a resource with the limit described in the lesson.

activities.title: The life of a non-renewable resource
activities.prompt: Put the stages of a non-renewable resource in order.
items: Start with a fixed stock that cannot be replaced
Use this stock for a period
activities.explanation: A fixed stock supports use for a period, then becomes exhausted.

activities.title: Why India imports oil
activities.prompt: Why does India depend on importing oil?
options: It does not have enough oil reserves
It has more oil reserves than needed
Its groundwater is rising everywhere
India does not import any oil
activities.explanation: India's oil reserves are not enough, so imports are needed.

activities.prompt: Groundwater use is faster than nature's replacement. What happens to the reserve?
options: The reserve becomes overused and may decline.
The reserve is replaced at the same speed.
The reserve stays unchanged because use is faster.
The reserve changes only after it is exhausted.

why.The reserve is replaced at the same spee: This confuses faster use with equal replacement.
why.The reserve stays unchanged because use: This wrongly assumes that faster use prevents change.
why.The reserve changes only after it is exh: This confuses depletion with the start of overuse.

activities.explanation: This is right because use is faster than replacement.

activities.prompt: One district uses groundwater faster than nature replaces it. Another uses it more slowly. Which faces greater risk of decline?
options: The faster district, because its use outpaces replacement.
The slower district, because it saves more groundwater.
Both districts, because any groundwater use causes decline.
Neither district, because groundwater cannot be overused.

why.The slower district, because it saves mo: This confuses lower use with greater groundwater damage.
why.Both districts, because any groundwater: This wrongly treats all groundwater use as overuse.
why.Neither district, because groundwater ca: This denies that renewable resources can become overused.

activities.explanation: This is right because faster use outpaces natural replacement.

activities.prompt: A map shows groundwater decline in many districts. What can a reader conclude?
options: Many places are using groundwater unsustainably.
Only one place has a groundwater problem.
Groundwater decline is limited to one state.
The map shows all future groundwater levels.

why.Only one place has a groundwater problem: This mistakes many reported districts for only one.
why.Groundwater decline is limited to one st: This assumes environmental harm cannot cross boundaries.
why.The map shows all future groundwater lev: This treats a present map as a picture of the future.

activities.explanation: This is right because widespread decline shows overuse.

activities.prompt: A plan helps today's needs but uses groundwater too quickly. Should the government approve it?
options: Yes, because today's needs come first.
No, because development must last for future generations.
Yes, because groundwater can always be replaced.
No, because groundwater use never affects development.

This is right because present development must remain possible for future generations.
why.Yes, because groundwater can always be r: This confuses slower replacement with unlimited replacement.
why.No, because groundwater use never affect: This ignores how groundwater overuse can harm development.

activities.explanation: This wrongly puts today's needs above future generations.
