activities.context: A community is considering two development plans. One would provide regular work but lower wages, while another promises higher earnings but no assurance of steady employment. Some residents want regular income to meet basic needs, while others want better wages and fair prices for their produce. Equal treatment, freedom, security, and respect also matter. The community must choose through a democratic political process, because hopes for change can become real through that process.
activities.prompt: What should the community do before choosing a development plan?
options: Compare how each plan meets different residents' hopes and check who may be helped or harmed.
Choose the plan offering the most money because earning more is the only developmental goal.
Give priority to the plan preferred by one group because everyone wants exactly the same outcomes.
Avoid making a choice because hopes for change cannot become real through a democratic political process.

why.Choose the plan offering the most money: This wrongly treats income as development's only goal.
why.Give priority to the plan preferred by o: This wrongly assumes that people have identical goals.
why.Avoid making a choice because hopes for: This wrongly denies the value of a democratic political process.

activities.explanation: This considers different hopes and possible harm to others.

activities.context: A community is considering two development plans. One would provide regular work but lower wages, while another promises higher earnings but no assurance of steady employment. Some residents want regular income to meet basic needs, while others want better wages and fair prices for their produce. Equal treatment, freedom, security, and respect also matter. The community must choose through a democratic political process, because hopes for change can become real through that process.
activities.prompt: Why might residents still choose the lower-paying plan?
options: Steady employment can help fulfil an important hope even when earnings are smaller.
They believe more money is always better than regular work.
They think fair prices for produce do not matter to anyone.
They expect material goods alone to provide a good life.

why.They believe more money is always better: This ignores the importance of dependable work.
why.They think fair prices for produce do no: This wrongly dismisses fair prices as a developmental goal.
why.They expect material goods alone to prov: This confuses material goods with the wider requirements of a good life.

activities.explanation: Regular employment can be more important than receiving less money.

activities.context: Two classmates are preparing a report comparing two countries and deciding what counts as national development. One country has the higher total income, while their populations differ, so the classmates cannot tell what an average person may earn. A local group also wants a development plan that benefits many people, but members disagree about what development should mean. The report must choose criteria that are fair to everyone and explain how each criterion fits the purpose of comparison.
activities.prompt: The teacher says the main purpose is to compare what income is available per person. Which approach should the classmates use?
options: Calculate income per person for each country and compare those results.
Compare total incomes and assume that the larger total also shows a higher average for people.
Choose the country with the lower total income on the assumption that its people must earn more.
Use either measure without linking the choice to the aim of the comparison.

why.Compare total incomes and assume that th: Comparing totals does not show what an average person may earn.
why.Choose the country with the lower total: A lower total alone does not establish that average earnings are higher.
why.Use either measure without linking the c: The appropriate criterion depends on the purpose of the comparison.

activities.explanation: Income per person, called average or per capita income, matches the stated purpose.

activities.context: Two classmates are preparing a report comparing two countries and deciding what counts as national development. One country has the higher total income, while their populations differ, so the classmates cannot tell what an average person may earn. A local group also wants a development plan that benefits many people, but members disagree about what development should mean. The report must choose criteria that are fair to everyone and explain how each criterion fits the purpose of comparison.
activities.prompt: The local group must choose among conflicting ideas for a development plan. What should it do to make the choice fair?
options: Test each idea against what is right for everyone and whether it benefits a broad section of the population.
Give priority to an idea because it is preferred by the few people who proposed it.
Choose the idea that produces agreement so the group can avoid making a difficult choice.
Let one side settle the conflict without considering whether many people benefit.

why.Give priority to an idea because it is p: A development plan should benefit many people rather than only a small group.
why.Choose the idea that produces agreement: Avoiding disagreement alone does not make the decision fair.
why.Let one side settle the conflict without: Ignoring the effects on people would not meet the idea of a fair path.

activities.explanation: A fair choice should consider what is right for everyone.

activities.context: Two classmates are preparing a report comparing two countries and deciding what counts as national development. One country has the higher total income, while their populations differ, so the classmates cannot tell what an average person may earn. A local group also wants a development plan that benefits many people, but members disagree about what development should mean. The report must choose criteria that are fair to everyone and explain how each criterion fits the purpose of comparison.
activities.prompt: If the report's new purpose is to compare the total income of the countries rather than income per person, which criterion should the classmates select?
options: Use total income because that is the measure matching the revised purpose.
Continue to use per capita income because it is the usual measure for every comparison.
Choose between the countries using whichever income measure makes one of them appear better.
Do not compare income because income has no importance when comparing countries.

why.Continue to use per capita income becaus: Per capita income does not match a comparison focused on total income.
why.Choose between the countries using which: The measure should be selected for its purpose, not to produce a preferred result.
why.Do not compare income because income has: Income is considered an important attribute when comparing countries.

activities.explanation: The criterion should match the revised purpose of the comparison.

activities.prompt:
Assertion (A): A comparison based only on total income may fail to show what an average person may earn in a country.
Reason (R): Comparing total incomes does not show what an average person may earn when countries have different populations.
options: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true but R is false.
A is false but R is true.
activities.explanation: The reason directly explains why total income alone may fail in the stated situation.

activities.prompt:
Assertion (A): A criterion for judging national development can differ with the purpose of the comparison.
Reason (R): People can hold different and conflicting ideas about national development.
options: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true but R is false.
A is false but R is true.
activities.explanation: Both statements are true, but disagreement about development does not explain why a criterion depends on the comparison's purpose.

activities.prompt: Explain the difference between using total income and using average income to compare countries.
activities.answer: Total income is not a very useful measure when countries have different populations because comparing total incomes does not show what an average person may earn. Average income is used to compare the income of people in different countries. It is also known as per capita income, meaning income per person. Therefore, if the purpose is to compare what people may earn on average, the students should select average income. This criterion fits the aim, while total income alone would not reveal the position of the average person in each country.
points: Explains why total income is less useful with different populations.
Identifies average income as income per person.
Explains that average income is used to compare people across countries.
Connects the choice of measure to the purpose of comparison.
activities.explanation: Compare your answer with the points a marker looks for.

activities.context: Two countries on a classroom income chart have the same average income. Country A’s income is distributed more equally, and people there are neither very rich nor extremely poor. The chart uses per capita income of US$2,300 or less as the lower cutoff and US$66,500 or more as the upper cutoff.
activities.prompt: Two countries have the same average income, and one of them is Country A. Which choice best explains why Country A should be preferred?
options: Country A should be chosen because its income is spread more evenly.
Country A should be chosen because its average is necessarily higher.
Country A should be chosen because every person earns exactly the average.
Country A should be chosen because income differences have disappeared completely.

why.Country A should be chosen because its a: Both countries have the same average, so the mean cannot explain the preference.
why.Country A should be chosen because every: An equal distribution does not mean that every person earns the average.
why.Country A should be chosen because incom: The absence of very rich and extremely poor people does not mean that all differences have disappeared.

activities.explanation: A more even distribution is the stated reason for preferring Country A.

activities.context: Two countries on a classroom income chart have the same average income. Country A’s income is distributed more equally, and people there are neither very rich nor extremely poor. The chart uses per capita income of US$2,300 or less as the lower cutoff and US$66,500 or more as the upper cutoff.
activities.prompt: A country’s per capita income in 2024 is exactly US$2,300. How should it be classified using the stated criteria?
options: It qualifies for the low-income category because its per capita income is US$2,300.
It qualifies for the high-income category because US$2,300 is a per capita figure.
It must be placed in the low middle income category because it is below US$66,500.
It fits neither category because the stated cutoff includes only amounts below US$2,300.

why.It qualifies for the high-income categor: US$2,300 does not meet the US$66,500-or-more high-income criterion.
why.It must be placed in the low middle inco: Being below the high-income threshold does not by itself establish low middle income status.
why.It fits neither category because the sta: The criterion says “or less,” so exactly US$2,300 is included.

activities.explanation: The stated limit includes per capita income of about US$2,300 or less.

activities.prompt:
Assertion (A): Country A may be preferred to another country with the same average income because its income is distributed more equally.
Reason (R): An average does not show how income is shared, so distribution must be considered separately.
options: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true but R is false.
A is false but R is true.
activities.explanation: Both statements are true, and the second explains why equal averages may still lead to different choices.

activities.prompt:
Assertion (A): A country with per capita income of US$66,500 in 2024 would be classified as high income.
Reason (R): Countries with per capita income of about US$2,300 or less are classified as low income.
options: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true but R is false.
A is false but R is true.
activities.explanation: Both statements are true, but the low-income criterion does not explain the high-income classification.

activities.prompt: Explain why the same average income may lead to different judgments about two countries, and why the average alone is not enough.
activities.answer: An average income provides one figure for comparing countries, and two countries can have exactly the same average. However, the average does not show how that income is shared among people. A figure may therefore look identical even when one country has greater inequality. In the case, Country A may be preferred because its income is distributed more equally, and its people are neither very rich nor extremely poor. The average is useful as a starting point, but it must be considered together with how income is distributed.
points: An average gives a single figure for comparison.
Two countries can have the same average income.
The average does not reveal how income is shared.
Distribution must be considered when judging equality.
activities.explanation: Compare your answer with the points a marker looks for.

activities.context: A study group compared Haryana, Bihar and Kerala. Haryana had the highest per capita income of the three, while Bihar had the lowest. In Kerala, 6 out of 1,000 children died before completing one year; Haryana's proportion was 28. About one-third of Bihar's 15–17-year-olds were not attending school. The group also learned that Kerala's low infant mortality is linked to adequate health and educational facilities.
activities.prompt: The group advises the Haryana government to improve public health and schooling while keeping per capita income unchanged. What should it expect?
options: Health and nutrition may improve because effective public services can support them.
Infant mortality will certainly become lower than Kerala's current level.
Children's health will remain unchanged because income is not changing.
A pollution-free environment will follow automatically from Haryana's higher income.

why.Infant mortality will certainly become l: The facts suggest a link, but they do not guarantee Kerala's rate.
why.Children's health will remain unchanged: The advice relies on improved services rather than higher income.
why.A pollution-free environment will follow: Money alone cannot buy a pollution-free environment.

activities.explanation: Effective public services can support better health and nutrition.

activities.context: A study group compared Haryana, Bihar and Kerala. Haryana had the highest per capita income of the three, while Bihar had the lowest. In Kerala, 6 out of 1,000 children died before completing one year; Haryana's proportion was 28. About one-third of Bihar's 15–17-year-olds were not attending school. The group also learned that Kerala's low infant mortality is linked to adequate health and educational facilities.
activities.prompt: Why might Kerala have fewer infant deaths than Haryana even though Haryana's per capita income is higher?
options: Kerala's public services give children stronger health and learning support.
Haryana's higher income automatically guarantees better child survival.
Kerala's lower income must mean that its health services are weaker.
A pollution-free environment alone explains Kerala's lower number of deaths.

why.Haryana's higher income automatically gu: A higher income does not automatically guarantee better survival.
why.Kerala's lower income must mean that its: Kerala's lower income does not show that its public services are weaker.
why.A pollution-free environment alone expla: The case does not identify environmental quality as the sole cause.

activities.explanation: Kerala's lower infant mortality is linked to adequate health and educational facilities.

activities.context: A study group compared Haryana, Bihar and Kerala. Haryana had the highest per capita income of the three, while Bihar had the lowest. In Kerala, 6 out of 1,000 children died before completing one year; Haryana's proportion was 28. About one-third of Bihar's 15–17-year-olds were not attending school. The group also learned that Kerala's low infant mortality is linked to adequate health and educational facilities.
activities.prompt: If Bihar improves access to education for 15–17-year-olds and uses collective provision to make the service work well, what change would the group most reasonably expect?
options: School participation among those ages would rise.
The proportion missing school would stay exactly one-third.
Bihar would immediately reach Haryana's per capita income.
The number of infant deaths in Bihar would immediately become lower than Kerala's.

why.The proportion missing school would stay: Collective provision being cheap does not mean participation cannot improve.
why.Bihar would immediately reach Haryana's: Improved education would not immediately change per capita income.
why.The number of infant deaths in Bihar wou: Improved schooling alone does not guarantee Kerala's infant mortality rate.

activities.explanation: Better access and effective collective services can improve school participation.

activities.prompt:
Assertion (A): Haryana's higher per capita income than Kerala does not by itself prove that Haryana is more developed.
Reason (R): Money alone cannot buy a pollution-free environment.
options: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true but R is false.
A is false but R is true.
activities.explanation: Both statements are true, but the environmental point does not explain why income alone gives an incomplete picture of development.

activities.prompt:
Assertion (A): If collective provision is often the cheapest method, public services will work well wherever per capita income is low.
Reason (R): Providing important goods and services collectively is often the cheapest method.
options: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true but R is false.
A is false but R is true.
activities.explanation: The reason is true, but it does not guarantee that public services will work well wherever income is low.

boss.title: Chapter challenge: Chapter 1: Development

activities.prompt: What does the wish for regular work, better wages and fair prices show?
options: Development has many goals
Development means only earning money
Everyone wants identical goals
Fair prices harm every producer
activities.explanation: The lesson lists regular work, better wages and fair prices as common hopes.

activities.prompt: People can have different and conflicting ideas about national development.
activities.explanation: Different people may want different things from development.

activities.prompt: India was placed in the ______ middle income category in 2024.
activities.hint: This word comes before “middle income”.
activities.explanation: India was placed in the low middle income category in 2024.

activities.prompt: Match each place with the correct comparison.
pairs: Highest per capita income among three states
Lowest per capita income among three states
Ahead of India in every comparison
activities.explanation: Each place is matched with the comparison given in your book.

activities.prompt: Put the states in order from highest to lowest per capita income.
activities.explanation: Haryana had the highest, while Bihar had the lowest. Kerala came between them.

activities.prompt: Which measure is used to compare people's incomes in different countries?
options: Average income
Total income
Income difference
Income growth
activities.explanation: Average income compares the income of people in different countries.

activities.prompt: Two countries with the same average income must have equal income distributions.
activities.explanation: The same average can hide different income distributions, including unequal ones.

activities.prompt: A BMI below the normal range can show that a student is ______.
activities.hint: This word describes having too little weight.
activities.explanation: A BMI below the normal range can indicate that a student is underweight.

activities.prompt: Which method finds BMI?
options: Divide weight by the square of height
Add weight to the square of height
Multiply weight by the square of height
Subtract weight from the square of height
activities.explanation: BMI is calculated by dividing weight by the square of height.

activities.prompt: Environmental harm stops at national or state boundaries.
activities.explanation: Environmental harm crosses boundaries, so places share a connected future.

chapters.title: Sectors of the Indian Economy
chapters.summary: In this chapter: economic activities and the three sectors; comparing production and calculating gdp; how the importance of sectors has changed; employment, underemployment and creating more jobs.

lessons.title: Economic Activities and the Three Sectors

activities.prompt: What helps us understand how people work, make things, and help each other?
activities.explanation: Now read on to find out.

activities.title: What are economic activities?
activities.body: Many people take part in economic activities. Some economic activities produce goods. Other economic activities produce services. Groups of economic activities are called sectors. The primary sector uses natural resources directly. The secondary sector changes natural products into other forms. The tertiary sector supports the production process and produces services rather than goods.
keyPoints: Economic activities produce goods or services.
Groups of economic activities are called sectors.
Each sector has a different role in production.
activities.explanation: Learning the sectors helps you understand different economic activities.

activities.prompt: A farmer grows cotton, a factory changes it, and a helper supports the work. Which sector is each job in?
steps: Growing cotton is primary because it uses natural resources directly.
Changing cotton is secondary because it changes a natural product into another form.
Helping production is tertiary because it supports the production process.
Therefore, the three jobs belong to three different sectors.
activities.explanation: Think it through with Hooty.

activities.title: Find the tertiary sector
activities.prompt: Which activity belongs to the tertiary sector?
options: Changing natural products into other forms
Supporting the production process
Using natural resources directly
Producing cotton
activities.explanation: The tertiary sector supports production and produces services instead of goods.

activities.title: Name the group
activities.prompt: Groups of economic activities are called ______.
activities.hint: Think of the word for a group or division.
activities.explanation: Groups of economic activities are called sectors.

activities.title: The foundation of production
activities.prompt: Which sector forms the base for other products?
options: Primary sector
Secondary sector
Tertiary sector
All three sectors
activities.explanation: The primary sector forms the base for other products.

activities.title: Match each sector
activities.prompt: Match each sector with its main role.
pairs: Changes natural products into other forms
activities.explanation: Each pair connects a sector with its role in production.

activities.title: Order the production path
activities.prompt: Put these activities in the order of the production path.
items: Change natural products into other forms
activities.explanation: Natural resources come first, then products change, and services support production.

activities.title: Cotton and natural factors
activities.prompt: Cotton production depends mainly on natural factors. Which sector does this show?
options: Tertiary sector
Secondary sector
Primary sector
Goods sector
activities.explanation: Cotton production uses natural factors. This fits the primary sector's direct use of natural resources.

activities.prompt: Many people work on a street. Some grow cotton, and others help production. What does this show?
options: Many people join different kinds of economic activities.
Only service workers join any kind of economic activity.
Every worker belongs to exactly one kind of activity.
Most people join economic activities but produce nothing.

why.Only service workers join any kind of ec: This mistake thinks only service workers take part.
why.Every worker belongs to exactly one kind: This mistake thinks everyone works in the same sector.
why.Most people join economic activities but: This mistake thinks economic activities produce neither goods nor services.

activities.explanation: This is right because many people take part in economic activities.

activities.prompt: A farm uses natural resources directly. A workshop changes those resources into other products. How do their roles differ?
options: The farm is primary, while the workshop is secondary.
The farm is secondary, while the workshop is primary.
The farm is tertiary, while the workshop is secondary.
The farm is tertiary, while the workshop is primary.

why.The farm is secondary, while the worksho: This mistake swaps the roles of the primary and secondary sectors.
why.The farm is tertiary, while the workshop: This mistake treats the farm as a service activity.
This mistake treats both places as service activities.

activities.explanation: This is right because the farm uses nature and the workshop changes products.

activities.prompt: Cotton grows mainly because of natural factors. It also forms the base for other products. What does this show?
options: Primary activity, because nature is used directly.
Secondary activity, because natural products are changed.
Tertiary activity, because production is supported.
Tertiary activity, because services are produced.

why.Secondary activity, because natural prod: This mistake applies the work of changing natural products.
why.Tertiary activity, because production is: This mistake treats cotton production as support work.
why.Tertiary activity, because services are: This mistake treats cotton production as service work.

activities.explanation: This is right because cotton production uses natural resources directly.

activities.prompt: A map shows a cotton field beside a workshop. The workshop receives cotton from the field. Which story fits the map?
options: The field produces first; the workshop changes the cotton later.
The workshop provides a service; the field makes goods for it.
Both places make services; neither place makes any goods.
Cotton is used first; the field grows it afterward.

why.The workshop provides a service; the fie: This mistake swaps the roles of the field and workshop.
why.Both places make services; neither place: This mistake says both places produce services.
why.Cotton is used first; the field grows it: This mistake reverses the order of growth and use.

activities.explanation: This is right because the field produces cotton before the workshop changes it.

activities.prompt: A worker repairs a machine while goods are being made. The worker makes no new goods. What is the worker's role?
options: Tertiary work, because it supports goods production.
Primary work, because it uses natural resources directly.
Secondary work, because it changes natural products.
Secondary work, because it produces a service.

why.Primary work, because it uses natural re: This mistake thinks every work activity uses natural resources.
why.Secondary work, because it changes natur: This mistake thinks the worker changes natural products.
why.Secondary work, because it produces a se: This mistake mixes service work with changing products.

activities.explanation: This is right because the worker supports production through a service.

activities.prompt: Last year, workers grew cotton. This year, workers changed it into new products. What changed between the years?
options: The work moved from primary activities to secondary activities.
The work moved from secondary activities to primary activities.
The work moved from producing goods to producing services.
The work moved from making services to using natural resources.

why.The work moved from secondary activities: This mistake reverses primary and secondary work.
why.The work moved from producing goods to p: This mistake thinks changing products produces services.
why.The work moved from making services to u: This mistake treats service work as direct use of nature.

activities.explanation: This is right because growing nature became changing natural products.

lessons.sceneAlt: A cotton farm in South-West Punjab, India, showing agriculture dependent on natural resources.
lessons.sceneCaption: A cotton farm in Punjab represents the primary sector, where natural resources are used to produce goods.

sceneCredit.text: A Cotton Farm (South-West Punjab) by Tizzythewhale, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons
sceneCredit.creator: Tizzythewhale

lessons.title: Comparing Production and Calculating GDP

activities.prompt: How can we measure what a country produces without counting twice?
activities.explanation: Now read on to find out.

activities.title: Understanding Production and GDP
activities.body: One or more sectors can dominate an economy in production and employment. Economists use values, not quantities, to compare goods and services. Wheat's value equals its quantity multiplied by its price. Intermediate goods are used up while making final goods and services. GDP is the value of all final goods and services produced within a country. It shows economic size. GVA adjusts sector contributions for taxes and subsidies.
keyPoints: Sectors can dominate production and employment.
Economists compare production using values.
GDP includes final goods and services.
activities.explanation: These ideas help you compare production and calculate GDP.

activities.prompt: A baker buys wheat, makes bread, and sells the bread. Should wheat and bread both be counted?
steps: Wheat is an intermediate good because it is used up while making bread.
Counting wheat and bread separately would count the same value many times.
Only final goods and services are included when counting total production.
So, count the bread, but do not count the wheat separately.
activities.explanation: Think it through with Hooty.

activities.title: Values or Quantities?
activities.prompt: When comparing goods and services, what do economists use instead of quantities?
options: Values
Quantities
Prices
Counts
activities.explanation: Values allow economists to compare goods and services.

activities.title: Intermediate Goods
activities.prompt: Intermediate goods are used up while producing final goods and services.
activities.explanation: Intermediate goods help producers make final goods and services.

activities.title: Match Economic Ideas
activities.prompt: Match each description with its correct term.
pairs: Adjusts contributions for taxes and subsidies
activities.explanation: Each pair connects an idea with its matching economic term.

activities.title: Avoiding Repeated Values
activities.prompt: Why are intermediate goods not counted separately in total production?
options: Counting them separately would repeat the same value.
They would remove the value of final goods.
They would change the prices of all goods.
They would ignore the country's final production.
activities.explanation: Counting them separately would count the same value many times.

activities.title: What GVA Adjusts
activities.prompt: GVA adjusts sector contributions without considering taxes or subsidies.
activities.explanation: GVA adjusts sector contributions for both taxes and subsidies.

activities.title: Describing GDP
activities.prompt: Which statement correctly describes GDP?
options: Shows jobs; uses quantities.
Uses values; shows size.
Shows prices; uses tax data.
Shows sectors; uses workers.
activities.explanation: GDP shows economic size. Its estimate uses information about goods, services and prices.

activities.prompt: A baker makes bread from wheat. How should production be counted?
options: Count only the bread, because it is final.
Count only the wheat, because it was bought.
Count both wheat and bread, because both were used.
Count neither good, because bread came from wheat.

why.Count only the wheat, because it was bou: It wrongly treats a bought intermediate good as final production.
why.Count both wheat and bread, because both: It counts intermediate and final goods separately, causing repeated counting.
why.Count neither good, because bread came f: It wrongly thinks an intermediate good has no value after use.

activities.explanation: Bread is final, while wheat is intermediate and used up in making it.

activities.prompt: Farming leads production and jobs in Place A. What does this show about its economy?
options: One sector can dominate the economy.
Farming must make every final good.
Place A must have only one sector.
Production and jobs must always match.

It assumes a dominant sector makes every final good.
It assumes other sectors cannot also matter in an economy.
It assumes production and employment must always have the same leader.

activities.explanation: One or more sectors can dominate production and employment.

activities.prompt: Wheat sales rise and its price falls. How is its total value checked?
options: Multiply the new quantity by the new price.
Add the new quantity and the new price.
Use only the new quantity of wheat.
Use only the new price of wheat.

It wrongly adds quantity and price instead of multiplying them.
It leaves out the price, which is needed to find value.
It leaves out the quantity, which is needed to find value.

activities.explanation: The value of wheat is its quantity multiplied by its price.

activities.prompt: A final good's price rises. Its quantity stays the same. How does its GDP value change?
options: It rises, because value uses quantity and price.
It falls, because economists prefer smaller quantities.
It stays, because GDP counts only quantities.
It stays, because only final goods matter.

why.It falls, because economists prefer smal: It reverses the effect of a higher price on value.
why.It stays, because GDP counts only quanti: It wrongly believes GDP adds quantities instead of values.
why.It stays, because only final goods matte: It wrongly believes final-good status removes the effect of price.

activities.explanation: The price rises while quantity stays the same, so the good's value rises.

lessons.title: How the Importance of Sectors Has Changed

activities.prompt: Why do people’s jobs change as societies become more developed?
activities.explanation: Now read on to find out.

activities.title: How sector importance changed
activities.body: The primary sector is farming. Early development made it the most important. Better farming methods produced much more food. More people became craft workers and traders. Later, many farm workers began working in factories. The secondary sector then became most important for production and work. The tertiary sector means services. In developed countries, services later became most important.
keyPoints: The primary sector was most important in early development.
The secondary sector became important as factory work grew.
The tertiary sector became most important later in developed countries.
activities.explanation: Farming was most important first. Factory work grew next, and services became most important later.

activities.prompt: Why does the most important sector change as a place develops?
steps: In early development, the primary sector is most important, so farming leads.
Farm workers move to factories, so the secondary sector becomes most important.
As primary and secondary sectors develop, they create demand for services.
Rising incomes raise service demand, so services later lead in developed countries.
activities.explanation: Think it through with Hooty.

activities.title: The first important sector
activities.prompt: Which sector was most important in the early stages of development?
options: Primary sector
Secondary sector
Service sector
Tertiary sector
activities.explanation: The primary sector was most important during the early stages of development.

activities.title: Early development
activities.prompt: In the early stages, the ______ sector was the most important.
activities.hint: Think about farming.
activities.explanation: The primary sector was most important in the early stages of development.

activities.title: Changes during early development
activities.prompt: Which change happened during the early stage of development?
options: Craft workers disappeared as trading grew.
Farm workers left all factory work.
Craft workers and traders increased.
Food production fell after farming improved.
activities.explanation: The number of craft workers and traders increased during the early stage.

activities.title: The changing order of importance
activities.prompt: Put these changes in the correct order.
items: Early development: the primary sector was most important.
Factory work grew: the secondary sector became most important.
Later in developed countries: the service sector became most important.
activities.explanation: The primary sector came first, followed by the secondary sector. The service sector became most important later.

activities.title: India's changing production
activities.prompt: Which statement about India's sectors from 1977–78 to 2017–18 is correct?
options: All sectors grew, but primary grew most.
All sectors grew, and tertiary grew most.
Only tertiary grew, while other sectors fell.
Primary grew most, while tertiary stayed still.
activities.explanation: Production increased in all three sectors. The tertiary sector grew more than the others.

activities.title: India's largest producing sector
activities.prompt: In India, the tertiary sector became the largest producing sector in ______.
activities.hint: Use the later year from the period.
activities.explanation: The tertiary sector became India's largest producing sector in 2017–18.

activities.prompt: A place is at an early stage of development. Another place is already developed. Which sector leads in the first place?
options: The primary sector in the first place.
The secondary sector in the first place.
The tertiary sector in the first place.
No sector leads in the first place.

This mistake uses the later factory stage for the early stage.
This mistake uses the developed-country stage for the early stage.
This mistake thinks no sector can be the most important.

activities.explanation: The primary sector is most important in the early stages of development.

activities.prompt: Farm workers move to factories. Which sector leads in production and jobs?
options: The secondary sector leads in production and jobs.
The primary sector leads in production and jobs.
The tertiary sector leads in production and jobs.
No sector leads in production and jobs.

why.The primary sector leads in production a: This mistake thinks farming stays most important after workers leave.
why.The tertiary sector leads in production: This mistake confuses the factory stage with the later service stage.
This mistake thinks the shift to factories creates no leading sector.

activities.explanation: The secondary sector becomes most important after workers move to factories.

activities.prompt: A worker provides a service using information and communication technology. Which sector does this work belong to?
options: The tertiary sector.
The primary sector.
The secondary sector.
No production sector.

This mistake treats information work as farming work.
This mistake treats a technology service as factory production.
This mistake assumes only farming and factory work count as sectors.

activities.explanation: This information and communication technology service belongs to the tertiary sector.

lessons.sceneCaption: A rural Tamil Nadu village with thatched huts contrasts with a modern factory, showing agriculture, handicrafts and industry together.

lessons.title: Employment, Underemployment and Creating More Jobs

activities.prompt: What can we discover about jobs, hidden unemployment, and ways to create work?
activities.explanation: Now read on to find out.

activities.title: Working and earning
activities.body: Production and employment did not grow at the same speed. Industrial production grew more than nine times, while industrial employment grew around three times. Service production grew fourteen times, but service employment grew around five times. Underemployment means people appear to work. It may be hidden, or disguised, unemployment. Cheap credit can help farmers. Education and rural employment schemes can also create work.
keyPoints: Production grew faster than employment.
Underemployment means people appear to be working.
Education and rural schemes can create more jobs.
activities.explanation: These ideas help you see why more production may not always mean more jobs.

activities.prompt: Industrial and service production grew faster than employment. What can we understand?
steps: Industrial production grew over nine times, so output rose very quickly.
Industry employment grew around three times, so jobs rose more slowly.
Service production grew fourteen times, while service employment grew around five times.
Thus, production outpaced employment in both sectors.
activities.explanation: Think it through with Hooty.

activities.prompt: Which name also means hidden underemployment?
options: Disguised unemployment
Rural employment
Service employment
Industrial employment
activities.explanation: Hidden underemployment is also called disguised unemployment.

activities.prompt: Industrial employment grew faster than industrial production.
activities.explanation: Industrial production grew more than nine times. Industrial employment grew around three times.

activities.prompt: Hidden underemployment is also called ______ unemployment.
activities.hint: This is another name for the same situation.
activities.explanation: The two names mean the same hidden underemployment situation.

activities.prompt: Match each area with its growth.
activities.explanation: Production and employment grew at different rates in both areas.

activities.prompt: By how much did service production grow?
options: Fourteen times
Around five times
Around three times
More than nine times
activities.explanation: Service production grew fourteen times. Service employment grew around five times.

activities.prompt: The government guaranteed 100 days of employment each year to every rural person.
activities.explanation: The guarantee was for eligible rural people, not every rural person.

activities.prompt: Which statement is fully correct?
options: The education sector alone can create nearly 20 lakh jobs.
The government guaranteed 100 days each year for every rural person.
Service sector employment grew fourteen times over the stated period.
Industrial sector employment grew around five times over the stated period.
activities.explanation: Education can create nearly 20 lakh jobs. The other statements confuse the eligible people, service production, or employment figures.

activities.prompt: Industry production grew over nine times. Industry employment grew about three times. What happened?
options: Production grew faster than employment.
Employment grew faster than production.
Production grew less than employment.
Production and employment grew equally.

Wrong: it reverses which of production and employment grew faster.
Wrong: it says employment grew faster than production.
Wrong: it wrongly treats the two growth rates as equal.

activities.explanation: Right: production grew over nine times, but employment only about three times.

activities.prompt: Service production grew fourteen times. Service employment grew about five times. What does this show?
options: Employment grew much faster than production.
Production grew much faster than employment.
Production and employment grew equally.
Service employment did not grow at all.

why.Employment grew much faster than product: Wrong: it reverses which of production and employment grew faster.
Wrong: it wrongly treats the two growth rates as equal.
Wrong: it wrongly treats five-times growth as no growth.

activities.explanation: Right: production grew fourteen times, but employment only around five times.

lessons.title: Organised and Unorganised Work

activities.prompt: How can we tell whether a job is organised or unorganised?
activities.explanation: Now read on to find out.

activities.title: Two Types of Work
activities.body: Organised work means jobs with clear employment terms and assured work. These enterprises register with the government and follow its rules. Workers have secure jobs and receive leave and holiday pay. Leave gives time off work. Holiday pay is pay for a holiday. The unorganised sector has small, scattered units. Its jobs are usually low-paid and irregular. Workers may face exploitation and not receive a fair wage.
keyPoints: Organised work has clear terms and assured work.
Organised workers have secure jobs and benefits.
Unorganised jobs are low-paid and often irregular.
Unorganised workers may face exploitation.
activities.explanation: These key differences help you recognise the two sectors.

activities.prompt: Ravi repairs cycles on the street. His pay is irregular, and he gets no paid leave. Why is his work different from organised work?
steps: Ravi repairs cycles on the street, so his work is unorganised.
His irregular pay contrasts with the assured work of organised employment.
His missing paid leave shows that organised benefits are absent.
Therefore, Ravi lacks the regular terms and security of organised work.
activities.explanation: Think it through with Hooty.

activities.prompt: What must an organised enterprise do with the government?
options: Pay workers extra rewards
Register with the government
Keep all records private
Use scattered work units
activities.explanation: Organised enterprises must register with the government. They must also follow its rules.

activities.prompt: Organised workers have security of employment.
activities.explanation: Yes. Organised workers enjoy security of employment.

activities.prompt: Match each group with the correct feature.
activities.explanation: Registration, benefits, scattered units and missing leave are clear sector features.

activities.prompt: Some unorganised workers sell on ______ and do repair work.
activities.hint: Choose the place used in your lesson.
activities.explanation: Street selling and repair work belong to the unorganised sector.

activities.prompt: Which description best fits unorganised jobs?
options: Usually low-paid and often irregular
Well-paid and always regular
Paid fairly with extra benefits
Secure with assured future work
activities.explanation: Unorganised jobs are usually low-paid and often irregular.

activities.prompt: A worker faces exploitation and does not receive a fair wage. Which statement fits?
options: It belongs to the unorganised sector.
It belongs to the organised sector.
It has assured employment.
It follows government rules.
activities.explanation: This points to the unorganised sector. Such workers are often not paid a fair wage.

activities.prompt: A repair workshop registers with the government and follows its rules. What kind of enterprise is it?
options: An organised, registered enterprise
An unorganised, unregistered enterprise
A regular, unregistered enterprise
A small, rule-free enterprise

why.An unorganised, unregistered enterprise: This workshop registers and follows rules, pointing to organised work.
why.A regular, unregistered enterprise: Regular work alone is not enough; registration is also needed.
why.A small, rule-free enterprise: The small size does not remove the need to register.

activities.explanation: Registration and government rules are required for organised enterprises.

activities.prompt: Amina is a rural landless labourer. Bhan loads bricks at a city construction site. What do they share?
options: Both belong to the unorganised sector
Both belong to the organised sector
Only Amina belongs to the unorganised sector
Only Bhan belongs to the unorganised sector

why.Both belong to the organised sector: Their listed work types belong to the unorganised sector.
why.Only Amina belongs to the unorganised se: Urban construction workers are also included in the unorganised sector.
why.Only Bhan belongs to the unorganised sec: Rural landless labourers are also included in the unorganised sector.

activities.explanation: The unorganised sector includes rural landless labourers and urban construction workers.

activities.prompt: A registered shop follows government rules. Its workers get paid leave and holiday pay. Street sellers usually get neither. Why?
options: Registered work gives organised workers employment benefits
Street selling gives workers more regular benefits
Paid leave and holidays belong only to street sellers
Holiday pay proves that street work is organised

why.Street selling gives workers more regula: Street sellers usually receive no paid leave or holiday benefits.
why.Paid leave and holidays belong only to s: These paid benefits belong to organised workers, not usually street sellers.
why.Holiday pay proves that street work is o: Holiday pay is an organised-worker benefit, not a street-seller benefit.

activities.explanation: Organised workers receive leave, holiday pay, provident fund and gratuity.

activities.prompt: A city map shows many tiny work units spread widely apart. What does this suggest?
options: The city has an unorganised sector
The city has an organised enterprise
The city has only organised work
The city has no unorganised work

why.The city has an organised enterprise: Scattered units alone do not show government registration.
why.The city has only organised work: Being in a city does not make every workplace organised.
why.The city has no unorganised work: Many scattered units show unorganised work, not its absence.

activities.explanation: Small, scattered units are a sign of the unorganised sector.

activities.prompt: A worker had no job security. The new firm registers with the government and follows its rules. Work now has regular terms. What changed?
options: The worker moved from unorganised to organised work
The worker moved from organised to unorganised work
The worker changed only the name of the job
The worker now has less secure, irregular terms

why.The worker moved from organised to unorg: The new security and regular terms show the opposite change.
why.The worker changed only the name of the: The change is in work security, not just the job's name.
why.The worker now has less secure, irregula: The new work has assured and regular terms, not irregular ones.

activities.explanation: Regular terms and assured work are marks of organised employment.

lessons.title: Public and Private Sectors

activities.prompt: How do we decide who should look after our shared services?
activities.explanation: Now read on to find out.

activities.title: Two Sectors, Different Responsibilities
activities.body: Public and private sectors are groups sorted by who owns assets and who provides services. Ownership means who owns something. The government owns most public assets and provides public services. Railways and post offices are public-sector examples. Private activities aim to earn profits. The public sector exists to serve people, not only to earn profits. Governments use taxes and other methods to pay for services.
keyPoints: Public and private sectors are classified by ownership and service responsibility.
Private activities aim to earn profits.
The public sector serves people and provides public services.
activities.explanation: These points help you see how ownership and service responsibility shape each sector.

activities.prompt: A small factory needs electricity, but high power bills make work difficult. Why might the government help?
steps: The factory needs electricity, so high power bills can hurt its work.
Government can supply electricity at affordable rates because this supports industries.
Private activities aim for profits, but public work does not exist only for profit.
So government help can support the factory without aiming only for profit.
activities.explanation: Think it through with Hooty.

activities.prompt: Who owns most public assets and provides public services?
options: The government
Private activities
Farmers
Post offices
activities.explanation: The government owns most public assets and provides public services.

activities.prompt: The government buys ______ and rice from farmers at a fair price.
activities.hint: This grain is bought with rice.
activities.explanation: Government buys wheat and rice from farmers at a fair price.

activities.prompt: Why do governments raise money through taxes and other methods?
options: To pay for services
To earn profits
To own private assets
To guide private activities
activities.explanation: Governments raise money to pay for services.

activities.prompt: Match each item with its correct description.
activities.explanation: Your matches connect examples and features with the correct sector or owner.

activities.prompt: Who receives the government's health and education facilities?
options: For everyone
For wealthy families
For city residents
For business owners
activities.explanation: Government provides health and education facilities for everyone.

activities.prompt: Why may some society-wide services remain in the public sector?
options: Private provision is not reasonable
Only officials need these services
Industries cannot use these services
Some people should be excluded
activities.explanation: Some society-wide services are not provided privately at a reasonable cost.

activities.prompt: Railways are public examples. Private food stalls aim for profits. Which comparison is best?
options: Railways serve the public, while private stalls mainly aim for profit.
Railways mainly aim for profit, while private stalls serve everyone without cost.
Both railways and private stalls work only to earn profits for owners.
Neither railways nor private stalls care about profit when they provide services.

why.Railways mainly aim for profit, while pr: This wrongly swaps the aims of the two sectors.
why.Both railways and private stalls work on: This wrongly treats every activity as profit-only.
why.Neither railways nor private stalls care: This wrongly ignores the profit aim of private activity.

activities.explanation: It matches public services and the profit aim of private activity.

activities.prompt: A map shows government-owned railways and government post offices. What does the map tell us?
options: These are public services because the government owns the assets.
These are private services because many people use them.
These are public services because private firms seek profits.
These are private services because the government owns the assets.

why.These are private services because many: This confuses public use with private ownership.
why.These are public services because privat: This confuses private profit aims with government ownership.
why.These are private services because the g: This wrongly calls government-owned assets private.

activities.explanation: Government ownership shows that these assets and services are public.

activities.prompt: The government supplies a factory with electricity at affordable rates. Why can this help?
options: Affordable electricity can support the factory because it costs less to run.
Affordable electricity can stop the factory because its power bills suddenly rise.
Affordable electricity can help farms because factories do not need power.
Affordable electricity can raise taxes because the factory pays extra money.

why.Affordable electricity can stop the fact: This reverses the effect of affordable power.
why.Affordable electricity can help farms be: This wrongly assumes that factories do not need electricity.
why.Affordable electricity can raise taxes b: This confuses power support with tax collection.

activities.explanation: Affordable power supports industries, as the fact states.

activities.prompt: A health service is too costly for most families to afford privately. What should the government do?
options: It should provide health facilities that everyone can use.
It should ask private firms to charge even higher prices.
It should close the service because most families cannot pay.
It should provide the service only to families who can pay.

why.It should ask private firms to charge ev: This wrongly makes higher private prices the main aim.
why.It should close the service because most: This wrongly gives up on a service people need.
why.It should provide the service only to fa: This wrongly makes payment decide who receives a public service.

activities.explanation: Public health must be available to everyone under this rule.

activities.prompt: The government buys wheat and rice from farmers at a fair price. What does this show?
options: Public-sector work can support people without existing only to earn profits.
Public-sector work must buy food only to earn higher profits.
Public-sector work helps farmers only when government taxes rise.
Public-sector work cannot include buying food at fair prices.

why.Public-sector work must buy food only to: This wrongly assumes all public work aims only for profit.
why.Public-sector work helps farmers only wh: This wrongly links fair-price buying to higher taxes.
why.Public-sector work cannot include buying: This wrongly says fair-price buying cannot be public work.

activities.explanation: Fair-price buying shows public work need not exist only for profit.

activities.prompt: Governments raise taxes to pay for services. If tax collection stops, what will likely happen?
options: Public services may stop because the government cannot pay for them.
Public services will improve because the government will have more money.
Private firms will pay for all services without collecting taxes.
Public services will grow because people will receive more tax money.

why.Public services will improve because the: This wrongly suggests less tax money gives the government more money.
why.Private firms will pay for all services: This wrongly assumes private firms will replace government funding.
why.Public services will grow because people: This wrongly treats stopped taxes as money still reaching services.

activities.explanation: Without tax money, the government cannot pay for services.

lessons.title: Test practice
lessons.sceneAlt: A cotton farm in South-West Punjab, India, showing agriculture dependent on natural resources.
lessons.sceneCaption: A cotton farm in Punjab represents the primary sector, where natural resources are used to produce goods.

sceneCredit.text: A Cotton Farm (South-West Punjab) by Tizzythewhale, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons
sceneCredit.creator: Tizzythewhale

activities.context: A cotton-growing area supplies cotton to a workshop. The workshop changes the cotton into another product. A nearby service centre provides support for the production process. Residents take part in these economic activities, and the groups they belong to form three sectors.
activities.prompt: If a change in natural conditions reduces cotton production, what is most likely to happen?
options: The workshop may have less cotton available for making its product.
The workshop may have more cotton available for making its product.
The workshop may continue with the same amount of cotton because sectors do not depend on one another.
The service centre may begin changing cotton into another product.

why.The workshop may have more cotton availa: Less cotton would reduce the supply available to the workshop.
why.The workshop may continue with the same: The primary sector forms the base for other products.
why.The service centre may begin changing co: The service centre supports production rather than changing natural products.

activities.explanation: Cotton production depends mainly on natural factors.

activities.context: A cotton-growing area supplies cotton to a workshop. The workshop changes the cotton into another product. A nearby service centre provides support for the production process. Residents take part in these economic activities, and the groups they belong to form three sectors.
activities.prompt: If the service centre stops providing support, what is the most likely result?
options: The production process may be disrupted.
Cotton may change into another product without the service centre's support.
The workshop may automatically receive more cotton.
The service centre may begin producing goods instead.

why.Cotton may change into another product w: Removing support can affect the production process.
why.The workshop may automatically receive m: The workshop depends on cotton as the base for its product.
why.The service centre may begin producing g: A change in support does not automatically change a sector's type.

activities.explanation: The tertiary sector supports the production process.

activities.prompt:
Assertion (A): Cotton production is part of the primary sector because it depends mainly on natural factors.
Reason (R): The primary sector uses natural resources directly.
options: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true but R is false.
A is false but R is true.
activities.explanation: The reason explains why cotton production belongs to the primary sector.

activities.prompt:
Assertion (A): The tertiary sector changes natural products into other forms.
Reason (R): Cotton production depends mainly on natural factors.
options: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true but R is false.
A is false but R is true.
activities.explanation: The statement is false because the secondary sector changes natural products, while the reason is true.

activities.prompt: Explain the difference between the primary sector and the secondary sector.
activities.answer: The primary sector uses natural resources directly and includes activities such as cotton production, which depends mainly on natural factors. It forms the base for other products. The secondary sector changes natural products into other forms. Thus, cotton production belongs to the primary sector, while changing cotton into another product belongs to the secondary sector. The main difference is that the primary sector works directly with natural resources, whereas the secondary sector transforms natural products into different forms for use.
points: Primary sector uses natural resources directly.
Cotton production is a primary-sector activity.
Primary sector forms the base for other products.
Secondary sector changes natural products into other forms.
activities.explanation: Compare your answer with the points a marker looks for.

activities.context: A village has farms that grow wheat, mills that make flour, and a bakery that sells bread. These sectors contribute to production and employment. The government wants to estimate the size of the economy, so it gathers information about goods, services and prices. In its estimate, the bread is counted as a final good, but flour is not counted separately because it was used up in making the bread.
activities.prompt: If the government mistakenly counts the flour separately as well as the bread, what would happen to its GDP estimate?
options: GDP would become smaller because fewer goods would be recorded.
GDP would be overstated because the flour's value would be included again.
GDP would remain unchanged because bread and flour are both goods.
GDP would show only the village's production and not the country's production.

why.GDP would become smaller because fewer g: This wrongly reduces the recorded production.
why.GDP would remain unchanged because bread: This wrongly treats intermediate goods as acceptable final goods.
why.GDP would show only the village's produc: This wrongly changes the territorial scope of GDP.

activities.explanation: This correctly identifies the repeated inclusion of value.

activities.context: A village has farms that grow wheat, mills that make flour, and a bakery that sells bread. These sectors contribute to production and employment. The government wants to estimate the size of the economy, so it gathers information about goods, services and prices. In its estimate, the bread is counted as a final good, but flour is not counted separately because it was used up in making the bread.
activities.prompt: Suppose farming provides more employment and production in the village than milling and baking. What can the village's production pattern show?
options: No sector can be important to an economy.
Farming can dominate the economy in production and employment.
Milling must dominate because its output is used later.
The size of the economy must decrease whenever one sector leads.

why.No sector can be important to an economy: This wrongly denies that one sector may dominate.
why.Milling must dominate because its output: This wrongly assumes that later use guarantees dominance.
why.The size of the economy must decrease wh: This wrongly links sector leadership to a smaller economy.

activities.explanation: This correctly applies the idea of sectoral dominance.

activities.prompt:
Assertion (A): Counting flour separately as well as bread can cause GDP to count the same value more than once.
Reason (R): Flour is an intermediate good used up while the final bread is produced.
options: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true but R is false.
A is false but R is true.
activities.explanation: The reason directly explains why counting the flour again would repeat value already included in the bread.

activities.prompt:
Assertion (A): GVA can be used when sector contributions need adjustment for taxes and subsidies.
Reason (R): GDP shows the size of an economy.
options: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true but R is false.
A is false but R is true.
activities.explanation: Both statements are true, but GDP's role does not explain the tax-and-subsidy adjustment made through GVA.

activities.prompt: Explain why the government counts the bread but not the flour separately when estimating GDP in the case.
activities.answer: GDP counts only final goods and services produced within a country. Bread sold by the bakery is a final good, so its value belongs in GDP. Flour is an intermediate good: it is used up while bread is produced. If the government counted the flour separately as well as the bread, it would include the flour's value again even though that value is already included in the bread. This would count the same value many times and make the measured total too large. Therefore, flour should not be counted separately when bread is counted.
points: Identifies bread as a final good
Identifies flour as an intermediate good
Explains the repeated counting of value
Explains why GDP would become overstated
activities.explanation: Compare your answer with the points a marker looks for.

activities.context: In a developing country, farming is initially the most important activity. Improved farming methods produce much more food, and the numbers of craft workers and traders rise. Many farm workers later begin working in factories, making the secondary sector increasingly important. In India, production rises in all three sectors between 1977–78 and 2017–18, while the tertiary sector grows the most and becomes the largest producing sector.
activities.prompt: After improved farming methods produce more food, what would most likely happen to many farm workers during the early stage of development?
options: They would begin working in factories.
Most would continue working on farms.
They would move into service-sector jobs.
They would become craft workers and traders.

Option 2: Remaining on farms does not show the shift towards factories.
why.They would move into service-sector jobs: Option 3: The case describes a shift towards factories, not services.
why.They would become craft workers and trad: Option 4: Craft workers and traders increased, but the later shift described was towards factories.

activities.explanation: Option 1: Many farm workers later began working in factories.

activities.context: In a developing country, farming is initially the most important activity. Improved farming methods produce much more food, and the numbers of craft workers and traders rise. Many farm workers later begin working in factories, making the secondary sector increasingly important. In India, production rises in all three sectors between 1977–78 and 2017–18, while the tertiary sector grows the most and becomes the largest producing sector.
activities.prompt: Which conclusion about India's sectors between 1977–78 and 2017–18 is best supported by the case?
options: By 2017–18, the tertiary sector had the highest production.
By 1977–78, the tertiary sector was already the largest producing sector.
The primary sector grew more than the tertiary sector.
The secondary sector grew more than all the other sectors.

why.By 1977–78, the tertiary sector was alre: Option 2: It became the largest producing sector in 2017–18, not in 1977–78.
why.The primary sector grew more than the te: Option 3: The tertiary sector, not the primary sector, grew the most.
why.The secondary sector grew more than all: Option 4: The tertiary sector, not the secondary sector, grew the most.

activities.explanation: Option 1: The tertiary sector grew the most and became India's largest producing sector.

activities.prompt:
Assertion (A): In the early stages of development, the primary sector was the most important.
Reason (R): Improved farming methods produced much more food than before.
options: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true but R is false.
A is false but R is true.
activities.explanation: Both statements are true, but increased food production does not directly explain why the primary sector was most important.

activities.prompt:
Assertion (A): The primary sector remained India's largest producing sector in 2017–18.
Reason (R): The tertiary sector grew more than the other sectors in India.
options: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true but R is false.
A is false but R is true.
activities.explanation: The assertion is false because the tertiary sector became India's largest producing sector, while the reason is true.

activities.prompt: What is the difference between the early-stage importance of sectors and their later importance in a developed country?
activities.answer: In the early stages of development, the primary sector is the most important, while improved farming methods produce more food and support increases in craft workers and traders. Many farm workers later move into factories, and the secondary sector becomes the most important in production and employment. In developed countries, the service sector later becomes the most important. This shift is linked to demand for services created by primary and secondary development, rising incomes, and the growing importance of information and communication technology services.
points: Early development is led by the primary sector.
The secondary sector becomes important as workers enter factories.
The service sector becomes most important in developed countries.
Service growth is linked to sectoral development, incomes and ICT.
activities.explanation: Compare your answer with the points a marker looks for.

activities.prompt:
Assertion (A): Service-sector production grew fourteen times, while service-sector employment grew around five times.
Reason (R): The education sector alone can create nearly 20 lakh jobs.
options: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true but R is false.
A is false but R is true.
activities.explanation: Both statements are true, but education-sector job creation does not explain the difference between service production and employment growth.

activities.prompt:
Assertion (A): Industrial employment increased at the same rate as industrial production.
Reason (R): Industrial production grew more than nine times, whereas industrial employment grew around three times.
options: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true but R is false.
A is false but R is true.
activities.explanation: The reason is true and explains the false assertion because industrial production grew much faster than industrial employment.

activities.prompt: Explain how the employment experience of industry differs from that of services.
activities.answer: Industrial production grew more than nine times, while employment in industry grew by around three times. In the service sector, production grew fourteen times, while employment grew around five times. The important difference is between growth in what was produced and growth in employment. In both sectors, production expanded more rapidly than employment. Therefore, higher output did not bring equal growth in employment, although employment in both sectors did increase over the stated period.
points: Industrial production grew more than nine times.
Industrial employment grew around three times.
Service production grew fourteen times.
Production grew faster than employment in both sectors.
activities.explanation: Compare your answer with the points a marker looks for.

boss.title: Chapter challenge: Sectors of the Indian Economy

activities.prompt: Which sector changes natural products into other forms?
options: Primary sector
Secondary sector
Tertiary sector
Goods sector
activities.explanation: The secondary sector changes natural products into other forms.

activities.prompt: Intermediate goods are used up while producing final goods and services.
activities.explanation: They are consumed while making final goods and services.

activities.prompt: GDP is the value of all ______ goods and services produced within a country.
activities.hint: These are ready for people to use or buy.
activities.explanation: GDP includes the value of all final goods and services produced within a country.

activities.prompt: Match each sector with its main role.
activities.explanation: Each sector has a main role in production.

activities.prompt: Put the steps for counting GDP production in order.
activities.explanation: GDP counts final goods and services. Intermediate goods are excluded.

activities.prompt: Which statement about GDP is correct?
options: Value of final goods and services
Number of workers in factories
Total quantity of goods produced
Value of intermediate goods only
activities.explanation: GDP measures the value of final goods and services produced within a country.

activities.prompt: Match each work group with the correct description.
activities.explanation: Organised work has regular terms. The unorganised sector has small, scattered units.

activities.prompt: Organised workers usually receive no paid leave or holiday benefits.
activities.explanation: Organised workers receive leave and holiday pay among other benefits.

activities.prompt: Which pair are examples of the public sector?
options: Railways and post offices
Street sellers and repair workers
Small farmers and sharecroppers
Construction and transport workers
activities.explanation: Your book gives railways and post offices as public sector examples.

activities.prompt: The education sector alone can create nearly ______ lakh jobs.
activities.hint: Think of a large number of teaching and education jobs.
activities.explanation: The education sector alone can create nearly 20 lakh jobs.
