chapters.title: Money and Credit
chapters.summary: In this chapter: money makes exchange easier; bank deposits, cheques and loans; credit, debt-traps and terms of credit; formal and informal sources of credit.

lessons.title: Money Makes Exchange Easier

activities.prompt: What if you could trade exactly what you wanted with anyone?
activities.explanation: Now read on to find out.

activities.title: How Money Makes Exchange Easier
activities.body: Money can buy any commodity or service you want. A commodity means a good someone wants. People prefer payment in money before buying. In barter, both parties must agree to sell and buy each other’s goods. This needs a double coincidence of wants: both sides want what the other offers. Money removes this need. Modern money includes paper notes and coins.
keyPoints: Money can buy any wanted commodity or service.
Currency means money used for buying, and the government authorises it.
The Reserve Bank of India issues currency notes for the central government.
activities.explanation: Money removes the need for both sides to want each other’s goods together.

activities.prompt: A boy wants a ball. The seller has one but does not want the boy's pen. How can they exchange?
steps: Because their wanted goods do not match, barter cannot start.
Both sides must agree because each must sell and buy.
This agreement needs a double coincidence of wants.
Money solves the problem because it can buy the ball.
activities.explanation: Think it through with Hooty.

activities.prompt: Which exchange can money support?
options: A trade for any wanted good
A trade for grains only
A trade for services only
A trade for cattle only
activities.explanation: Money can be exchanged for any commodity or service a person wants. It is not limited to one kind of good.

activities.prompt: In a ______ system, both parties must agree to sell and buy each other’s commodities.
activities.hint: Both parties trade commodities with each other.
activities.explanation: In barter, both parties must agree to sell and buy each other’s commodities.

activities.prompt: Match each idea with the correct term.
activities.explanation: Money can exchange for any wanted commodity or service. Barter needs both parties to agree. Government authorisation helps currency gain acceptance.

activities.prompt: Put these forms of money in the order given by the lesson.
items: Indians used grains and cattle as money
Gold, silver and copper were made into coins
Modern money includes paper notes and coins
activities.explanation: The lesson moves from grains and cattle to metallic coins. Paper notes and coins came later as modern money.

activities.prompt: Why do people prefer receiving payment in money before buying?
options: It can buy what they want
It must contain precious metal
It only works for food
It is made from cattle
activities.explanation: Money can buy any commodity or service a person wants. Receiving it first makes buying easier.

activities.prompt: Who issues currency notes for the central government?
options: The Reserve Bank of India
The owners of grain stores
The keepers of cattle markets
The managers of village shops
activities.explanation: The Reserve Bank of India issues currency notes for the central government.

activities.prompt: A girl wants the boy's kite. The boy wants the girl's pencils. What barter condition is now present?
options: Both people want what the other has.
Only the girl gets what she wants.
Only the boy gets what he wants.
Both people want money instead.

This misses the boy's matching want for pencils.
This misses the girl's matching want for the kite.
This changes barter into a money situation.

activities.explanation: This is a double coincidence of wants.

activities.prompt: A boy wants a fruit box. The seller does not want his pen. If he pays money, what problem disappears?
options: The need for both sides to want each other's goods.
The need for the seller to accept payment.
The need for the boy to want fruit.
The need to make more fruit boxes.

why.The need for the seller to accept paymen: In barter, matching wants matter more than accepting payment.
The boy's wish for fruit is already clear.
This confuses exchanging goods with making more goods.

activities.explanation: Money removes the need for a double coincidence of wants.

activities.prompt: People prefer to receive payments in money before buying wanted goods. How can this money help them buy later?
options: It can serve as a medium of exchange.
It can create a double coincidence of wants.
It can remove government permission for currency.
It can turn modern notes into precious metal.

why.It can create a double coincidence of wa: Money removes the barter need instead of creating it.
why.It can remove government permission for: This confuses what authorises money with what money does.
why.It can turn modern notes into precious m: Modern currency is not made of precious metal.

activities.explanation: Money can be exchanged for what a person wants.

lessons.title: Bank Deposits, Cheques and Loans

activities.prompt: How do banks keep your money safe, pay you, and help others borrow?
activities.explanation: Now read on to find out.

activities.title: How banks connect money and people
activities.body: Banks keep deposits safe and pay interest on them. Demand deposits can be withdrawn whenever you need the money. They have the quality of money. A cheque tells a bank to pay a sum from an account. Cheques can work without exchanging cash. Banks keep only a small part of deposits as cash. They use most deposits to give loans. Banks connect depositors with borrowers and earn money from the interest gap.
keyPoints: Demand deposits can be withdrawn whenever needed.
Cheques can move money without exchanging cash.
Banks use most deposits to provide loans.
activities.explanation: Banks protect deposits, make payments, and connect people who have money with people who need it.

activities.prompt: You have extra money, and someone else needs funds. What can the bank do for you both?
steps: Banks keep deposits safe and pay interest, so your money stays there.
Most deposits become loans, so the bank keeps only small cash.
The bank joins depositors with borrowers, so extra money meets needed funds.
Higher loan interest makes the interest gap the bank's main income.
activities.explanation: Think it through with Hooty.

activities.prompt: What do banks do with deposits?
options: Keep them safe and pay interest
Use all of them as cash
Give them to every borrower
Keep them away from borrowers
activities.explanation: Banks keep deposits safe and pay interest to depositors.

activities.prompt: You can withdraw money from a demand deposit whenever you need it.
activities.explanation: Demand deposits can be withdrawn whenever account holders need the money.

activities.prompt: A ______ instructs a bank to pay a stated sum from an account.
activities.hint: It is a written instruction to a bank.
activities.explanation: A cheque gives an instruction to pay a stated sum from an account.

activities.prompt: What can happen during a cheque transaction?
options: Cash is exchanged
Cash must be exchanged
Cash can be left out
Cash is always exchanged
activities.explanation: A cheque transaction can be completed without exchanging any cash.

activities.prompt: Match each banking part with its role.
activities.explanation: Banks connect depositors with borrowers. Most deposits are used to provide loans.

activities.prompt: Put the cheque transaction steps in order.
items: The bank pays the stated sum
activities.explanation: The cheque gives the instruction first. The bank pays the sum. The transaction can finish without exchanging cash.

activities.prompt: How do banks earn money?
options: Paying depositors more interest than borrowers pay
Charging borrowers more interest than depositors pay
Keeping most deposits as idle cash
Charging every borrower the same low interest
activities.explanation: Banks charge borrowers more interest than they pay depositors.

activities.prompt: The gap between loan interest and deposit interest is a bank's ______ income.
activities.hint: This is the bank's biggest income.
activities.explanation: The gap between loan interest and deposit interest is a bank's main income.

activities.prompt: A bank map shows small cash and large loan areas. What does this suggest about deposits?
options: Most deposits become loans, while little stays as cash.
Most deposits stay idle, while all become cash.
Every deposit becomes a cheque, while none stays cash.
All deposits are lent to one borrower at a time.

why.Most deposits stay idle, while all becom: This mistake reverses what the map shows about cash and loans.
why.Every deposit becomes a cheque, while no: This mistake thinks every deposit becomes a cheque instead of a loan.
why.All deposits are lent to one borrower at: This mistake thinks all loans must go to one borrower.

activities.explanation: Right: banks keep only a small part of deposits as cash.

activities.prompt: First, you hold cash. Later, you keep it in a demand deposit. What stays similar about them?
options: Both can be used when a payment is needed.
Both earn interest only while held as cash.
Both become useless for meeting a need.
Both must first become a loan.

why.Both earn interest only while held as ca: This mistake thinks only bank deposits earn interest.
This mistake thinks money-like deposits cannot meet needs.
This mistake thinks using money always requires taking a loan.

activities.explanation: Right: demand deposits have money's important quality, like cash.

lessons.title: Credit, Debt-Traps and Terms of Credit

activities.prompt: How can borrowing help someone today, and what should you watch out for later?
activities.explanation: Now read on to find out.

activities.title: Understanding Credit
activities.body: Credit is an agreement. A borrower receives money, goods or services now. The borrower promises to pay the lender later. A lender may ask for collateral, which is an asset owned by the borrower. If the borrower does not repay, the lender can take the collateral. Terms of credit include interest, collateral, documents and repayment methods. The complete repayment arrangement is part of these terms. Swapna’s situation became a debt-trap.
keyPoints: Credit gives something now for payment later.
Collateral is an asset owned by the borrower.
Swapna’s situation became a debt-trap.
activities.explanation: Credit moves payment to later, but its terms explain repayment and security.

activities.prompt: A shop gives a cycle now and asks for payment later. Is this credit, and what happens if the buyer cannot pay?
steps: The cycle comes now and payment comes later, so this is credit.
The borrower promises to pay later, which is part of credit.
If the cycle is collateral, the lender can take it after nonpayment.
Therefore, credit can include taking collateral when the borrower does not repay.
activities.explanation: Think it through with Hooty.

activities.prompt: The borrower receives money, goods or services now.
activities.explanation: Credit lets the borrower receive something now. Payment comes later.

activities.prompt: What does the borrower promise to do?
options: To return goods immediately
To lend money to the lender
To pay the lender later
To stop the agreement
activities.explanation: The borrower promises the lender that payment will come later.

activities.prompt: Credit helped Salim pay the continuing costs of producing ______.
activities.hint: He makes these for his order.
activities.explanation: This credit helped him complete his order on time and increase his earnings.

activities.prompt: Swapna’s situation stayed free from debt.
activities.explanation: Swapna’s situation became a debt-trap.

activities.prompt: Whose asset is the collateral?
options: The borrower
The lender
Salim
Swapna
activities.explanation: Collateral is an asset owned by the borrower, not the lender.

activities.prompt: Which group includes only parts of the terms of credit?
options: Interest, savings, documents and repayment methods
Interest, collateral, clothes and repayment methods
Interest, collateral, documents and repayment methods
Interest, collateral, documents and visiting methods
activities.explanation: These are all listed parts of the terms of credit. The complete repayment arrangement is also part of them.

activities.prompt: A borrower receives money now and leaves the lender. What must the borrower have agreed to do?
options: Pay the lender at a later time.
Return the money at the same time.
Give the lender another good now.
Stop using the money after receiving it.

This wrongly treats receiving money now as requiring immediate return.
This wrongly makes credit depend on receiving another good now.
This wrongly treats credit as a ban on using the money.

activities.explanation: The borrower receives money now and promises to pay later.

activities.prompt: Salim uses credit for continuing shoe production costs. He completes his order on time. What can happen next?
options: His earnings can increase because the order was completed on time.
His earnings must fall because he borrowed money earlier.
His order will become late because the loan was repaid.
His production costs will stop because his order was completed.

why.His earnings must fall because he borrow: This wrongly assumes that borrowing must reduce earnings.
why.His order will become late because the l: This wrongly links repayment to a later delay in the order.
why.His production costs will stop because h: This wrongly assumes completed production must stop all costs.

activities.explanation: Completing his order on time helped Salim increase his earnings.

activities.prompt: A borrower offers a bicycle as security for a loan. The bicycle belongs to the borrower. Why can the lender take it if repayment does not happen?
options: It is collateral, so the lender can take it after nonpayment.
It is the loan amount, so the lender can take it after nonpayment.
It is a repayment method, so the lender can take it after nonpayment.
It is a loan document, so the lender can take it after nonpayment.

why.It is the loan amount, so the lender can: The bicycle is security, not the amount of money borrowed.
why.It is a repayment method, so the lender: A repayment method is not an asset owned by the borrower.
why.It is a loan document, so the lender can: A document is not the borrower's asset offered as security.

activities.explanation: Collateral is the borrower's asset, which the lender can take after nonpayment.

activities.prompt: A lender asks for security against a loan. The borrower's own asset is offered, and repayment does not happen. Which action can the lender take?
options: Take the borrower's asset offered as collateral.
Take any asset belonging to another person.
Take the borrower's promised future payment.
Take the borrower's asset before making the loan.

why.Take any asset belonging to another pers: The fact allows taking the borrower's own offered asset.
why.Take the borrower's promised future paym: Future payment is not the borrower's owned asset.
why.Take the borrower's asset before making: The lender can take collateral after nonpayment, not before making the loan.

activities.explanation: The lender can take collateral when the borrower does not repay.

lessons.title: Formal and Informal Sources of Credit

activities.prompt: Which kind of credit can help a family grow without adding worries?
activities.explanation: Now read on to find out.

activities.title: Borrowing Can Be Costly
activities.body: Informal lenders usually charge much higher interest than formal lenders. These loans therefore cost borrowers more. High borrowing costs leave borrowers with less income for themselves. High interest can push borrowers into a debt-trap. Poor households often pay a large amount for borrowing. Formal lenders meet only about half of rural credit needs.
keyPoints: Informal lenders usually charge much higher interest.
High borrowing costs leave less income for borrowers.
Formal lenders meet only about half of rural credit needs.
activities.explanation: This card shows how borrowing costs can affect borrowers.

activities.prompt: A rural family needs a loan, but formal lenders meet only half of rural needs. It uses an informal lender. Why might the family have less money later?
steps: Formal lenders meet only about half of rural credit needs, so the family may turn to an informal lender.
Informal lenders usually charge much higher interest than formal lenders, so the informal loan may cost more.
The higher cost leaves the family with less income for itself.
High borrowing costs can push the family into a debt-trap, so the extra cost matters.
activities.explanation: Think it through with Hooty.

activities.title: Informal Lending
activities.prompt: Which statement about informal lenders is correct?
options: They charge much higher interest.
They charge much lower interest.
They charge the same interest.
They charge no interest at all.
activities.explanation: Informal lenders usually charge much higher interest than formal lenders. This makes informal loans costly for borrowers.

activities.prompt: Informal loans usually cost borrowers more than formal loans.
activities.explanation: Informal loans cost borrowers more because their interest charges are usually much higher.

activities.title: What Borrowers Keep
activities.prompt: High borrowing costs leave borrowers with less ______ for themselves.
activities.hint: Borrowers keep less of this after high borrowing costs.
activities.explanation: High borrowing costs leave borrowers with less income for themselves.

activities.title: The Danger of High Interest
activities.prompt: What can happen because of high interest?
options: Borrowers enter a debt-trap.
Borrowers gain more income.
Borrowing becomes cheaper.
Borrowers pay less interest.
activities.explanation: High interest can push borrowers into a debt-trap.

activities.title: Why Income Becomes Less
activities.prompt: Why can an informal loan leave a borrower with less income?
options: The lender charges higher interest.
The lender charges lower interest.
The lender charges no interest.
The lender charges the same interest.
activities.explanation: Informal lenders usually charge much higher interest. This raises borrowing costs and leaves less income for borrowers.

activities.title: Effects of Informal Credit
activities.prompt: Put these effects in the correct order.
activities.explanation: Higher interest makes loans costly and leaves less income. It can also push borrowers into a debt-trap.

activities.prompt: Informal lenders usually charge much higher interest than formal lenders. Why can this hurt the borrower?
options: High costs leave the borrower with less income.
High costs leave the borrower with more income.
High costs leave the borrower’s income unchanged.
High costs leave the borrower with less credit.

why.High costs leave the borrower with more: This reverses the effect of high borrowing costs.
why.High costs leave the borrower’s income u: It wrongly says high costs do not change income.
why.High costs leave the borrower with less: It confuses less income with less credit.

activities.explanation: High borrowing costs leave borrowers with less income for themselves.

activities.prompt: A map shows formal lenders meet only about half of rural credit needs. What does this suggest?
options: Formal lenders do not meet all rural credit needs.
Formal lenders meet only half of all credit needs.
Formal lenders meet more than all rural credit needs.
Formal lenders meet no rural credit needs.

why.Formal lenders meet only half of all cre: It changes rural credit needs into all credit needs.
why.Formal lenders meet more than all rural: It reverses the meaning of only about half.
why.Formal lenders meet no rural credit need: It mistakes a small share for no credit at all.

activities.explanation: Formal lenders meet only about half, not all, rural credit needs.

activities.prompt: Formal lenders meet only about half of rural credit needs. Why might a rural household use an informal lender?
options: It may need credit that formal lenders do not meet.
It may find all needed credit easily from formal lenders.
It may expect to pay much lower interest.
It may receive more rural credit than formal lenders.

why.It may find all needed credit easily fro: This wrongly assumes formal lenders meet every need.
why.It may expect to pay much lower interest: Informal loans usually cost more, not less.
why.It may receive more rural credit than fo: Formal lenders meet fewer rural credit needs, not more.

activities.explanation: Formal lenders meet only about half of rural credit needs.

activities.prompt: Poor households often pay a large amount for borrowing. Why can this leave them with less money?
options: High borrowing costs leave less income for themselves.
High borrowing costs leave more income for themselves.
High borrowing costs leave their income unchanged.
High borrowing costs leave them with more credit.

why.High borrowing costs leave more income f: This reverses the effect of high borrowing costs.
why.High borrowing costs leave their income: It wrongly says high costs do not change income.
why.High borrowing costs leave them with mor: It confuses less income with more credit.

activities.explanation: High borrowing costs leave borrowers with less income for themselves.

activities.prompt: High borrowing costs leave borrowers with less income for themselves. What serious danger can follow?
options: The borrower may fall into a debt-trap.
The borrower may become free from all debt.
The borrower may pay lower interest on the loan.
The borrower may have more money left after paying.

why.The borrower may become free from all de: It wrongly suggests less income removes the danger of debt.
why.The borrower may pay lower interest on t: It confuses less income with lower borrowing costs.
why.The borrower may have more money left af: It reverses the effect of high borrowing costs.

activities.explanation: High interest can push borrowers into a debt-trap.

lessons.title: Self-Help Groups and Credit for the Poor

activities.prompt: What can poor women gain by pooling their savings and supporting each other?
activities.explanation: Now read on to find out.

activities.title: How groups support each other
activities.body: Small Self Help Groups organise rural poor, especially women, to pool savings. Members regularly meet and save together. Members can take small loans from their own group. These loans charge less interest than moneylender loans. Regular saving can help a group become eligible for bank loans. The group lends bank loans to members for self-employment. This means work that earns money. Collateral means security for a loan.
keyPoints: Members pool savings through regular meetings.
A typical group has 15 to 20 members.
Organised poor women may receive loans without collateral.
activities.explanation: Regular saving helps groups support members and work towards bank loans.

activities.prompt: A Self Help Group wants loans for members. What should it do?
steps: Members should meet and save together, because this pools their savings.
The group can offer small loans, because members borrow from it.
Regular saving can bring a bank loan for members' self-employment.
The group must repay that bank loan, so it should lend carefully.
activities.explanation: Think it through with Hooty.

activities.prompt: A typical Self Help Group has 15 to 20 members.
activities.explanation: This is the usual number of members in a typical Self Help Group.

activities.prompt: Members meet and save separately.
activities.explanation: Members regularly meet and save together.

activities.prompt: Self Help Group loans charge ______ interest than moneylender loans.
activities.hint: Compare the interest charged by each kind of loan.
activities.explanation: Self Help Group loans charge less interest than moneylender loans.

activities.prompt: Who is responsible for repaying the bank loan?
options: A member alone
The group
A moneylender
The village shop
activities.explanation: The group receives the bank loan and lends it to members. The group repays the bank.

activities.prompt: Match each clue with the correct detail.
activities.explanation: The clues describe group size, borrowing, repayment and bank lending.

activities.prompt: Put the path from regular saving to member lending in order.
items: Members regularly meet and save together
The group becomes eligible for a bank loan
The group receives the bank loan
The group lends it to members
activities.explanation: The group saves first, then qualifies, receives and lends the bank loan.

activities.prompt: Grameen Bank had over 9 million members in 2018. Almost all borrowers were women. Which statement is also true?
options: Banks always need collateral, and women can run small activities.
Banks may lend without collateral, but women cannot run small activities.
Banks may lend without collateral, and women can run small activities.
Banks always need collateral, but women cannot run small activities.
activities.explanation: Organised poor women can receive bank loans without collateral. They can successfully run small income-generating activities.

activities.prompt: The lesson says the poor should receive a much greater share of formal loans. Which action follows this advice?
options: Give poor people a smaller share of formal loans.
Give poor people a greater share of formal loans.
Give poor people no formal loans to use today.
Give poor people only moneylender loan support.
activities.explanation: Giving poor people a greater share of formal loans follows this advice.

activities.prompt: A Self Help Group gets bank support. How can members borrow before and after?
options: From the group first, then through the group's bank loan.
From a bank first, then through the group's own savings.
From moneylenders first, then through their own group.
From their group both before and after bank support.

why.From a bank first, then through the grou: This reverses the order of group saving and bank support.
why.From moneylenders first, then through th: The group's own loans come before any moneylender borrowing.
why.From their group both before and after b: This ignores the new bank loan after the group receives support.

activities.explanation: The group first lends its own savings, then its bank loan.

activities.prompt: Why do women in a Self Help Group save together regularly?
options: To pool savings and become eligible for a bank loan.
To avoid meeting their group and managing savings.
To make moneylender loans charge less interest.
To lend bank loans without responsibility for repayment.

why.To avoid meeting their group and managin: Group saving requires regular meetings, not avoiding them.
why.To make moneylender loans charge less in: The lower interest applies to group loans, not moneylender loans.
why.To lend bank loans without responsibilit: The group must repay the bank loan, so it cannot ignore repayment.

activities.explanation: Regular saving pools savings and can make the group bank-eligible.

lessons.sceneCaption: Sher Shah Suri issued this silver rupee between 1540 and 1545 CE.

activities.context: A person wants a carpenter’s service but owns only some grain. The carpenter does not need grain and instead wants payment in money. The buyer therefore gets money first, then uses it to pay the carpenter and buy the service. Earlier, when metallic coins were used, money was made from gold, silver or copper. Today, currency consists of paper notes and coins, although it is not made of precious metal.
activities.prompt: If the carpenter refuses money and asks for grain instead, what would have to change for the exchange to proceed?
options: The carpenter would also need to want something the buyer offers.
The buyer would no longer need the carpenter’s service.
The government would need to order the carpenter to accept grain.
The buyer would only need paper notes instead of grain.

why.The buyer would no longer need the carpe: The buyer still wants the carpenter’s service.
why.The government would need to order the c: Government authorisation does not force acceptance of grain.
why.The buyer would only need paper notes in: Having notes would not remove the carpenter’s refusal.

activities.explanation: This would create a double coincidence of wants.

activities.context: A person wants a carpenter’s service but owns only some grain. The carpenter does not need grain and instead wants payment in money. The buyer therefore gets money first, then uses it to pay the carpenter and buy the service. Earlier, when metallic coins were used, money was made from gold, silver or copper. Today, currency consists of paper notes and coins, although it is not made of precious metal.
activities.prompt: If a community used gold, silver and copper coins instead of modern paper notes and coins, what would happen?
options: Money could still support exchange, although this would differ from the modern system.
A double coincidence of wants would become necessary because metals were used to make coins.
Government authorisation would become unnecessary because the coins contain precious metals.
Grains and cattle would have to be used together with the metallic coins.

why.A double coincidence of wants would beco: Money removes the need for a double coincidence of wants.
why.Government authorisation would become un: Government authorisation remains important for currency acceptance.
why.Grains and cattle would have to be used: The old forms of money need not be used together.

activities.explanation: Metallic coins can still function as money.

activities.prompt:
Assertion (A): Money removes the need for a double coincidence of wants.
Reason (R): Money can be exchanged for any commodity or service that a person wants.
options: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true but R is false.
A is false but R is true.
activities.explanation: Money’s ability to buy any commodity or service explains why it removes the need for matching wants in barter.

activities.prompt:
Assertion (A): The Reserve Bank of India issues currency notes for the central government.
Reason (R): Currency is accepted because the government authorises it.
options: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true but R is false.
A is false but R is true.
activities.explanation: Both statements are true, but the issuing role does not explain why currency is accepted.

activities.prompt: How does money make exchange easier than a barter system?
activities.answer: In barter, both parties must agree to sell and buy each other’s commodities. This creates a double coincidence of wants because each side must want what the other side offers. Money removes this problem because it can be exchanged for any commodity or service that a person wants. People also prefer to receive payments in money before buying what they want. Thus, exchange becomes easier without requiring the two sides to have matching wants.
points: Barter requires both parties to agree to trade.
Barter creates a double coincidence of wants.
Money can buy any commodity or service wanted.
Money removes the need for matching wants.
activities.explanation: Compare your answer with the points a marker looks for.

activities.context: A shopkeeper deposits spare money in a bank. The deposit earns interest and can be withdrawn whenever needed. When the shopkeeper pays a supplier by cheque, no cash changes hands. The bank keeps only a small part of its deposits as cash and uses most deposits to give loans. It charges borrowers more interest than it pays depositors, and this difference is its main income.
activities.prompt: The shopkeeper now needs some of the deposited money. What is the most appropriate action?
options: Withdraw the required amount from the demand deposit.
Keep the money in the account and take out a loan instead.
Ask the bank to exchange the deposit for a cheque.
Use the deposit receipt to withdraw money without involving the bank.

why.Keep the money in the account and take o: Taking a loan is unnecessary when the required money is already available.
why.Ask the bank to exchange the deposit for: A cheque instructs a bank to pay a stated sum; it is not an exchange for a deposit.
why.Use the deposit receipt to withdraw mone: The bank handles withdrawals from accounts.

activities.explanation: Demand deposits can be withdrawn whenever account holders need the money.

activities.context: A shopkeeper deposits spare money in a bank. The deposit earns interest and can be withdrawn whenever needed. When the shopkeeper pays a supplier by cheque, no cash changes hands. The bank keeps only a small part of its deposits as cash and uses most deposits to give loans. It charges borrowers more interest than it pays depositors, and this difference is its main income.
activities.prompt: The bank uses most deposits to provide loans. Why does this help the bank earn its main income?
options: The interest collected from borrowers exceeds the interest paid to depositors.
The interest paid to borrowers exceeds the interest collected from depositors.
Borrowers receive more interest because banks keep all deposits as cash.
Depositors receive no interest because banks use their deposits for loans.

why.The interest paid to borrowers exceeds t: The relationship between these interests is reversed.
why.Borrowers receive more interest because: Banks keep only a small part of deposits as cash and use most for loans.

activities.explanation: Banks charge borrowers more interest than they pay depositors.

activities.prompt: Explain how banks connect depositors with borrowers and earn their main income.
activities.answer: Banks connect depositors who have extra money with borrowers who need funds. Depositors can keep their money safely in banks and receive interest on it. Banks use most deposits to provide loans and keep only a small part as cash. The bank charges borrowers more interest than it pays depositors. The difference between loan interest and deposit interest is the bank's main income. Thus, the same deposits can meet the needs of both depositors and borrowers.
points: Banks connect depositors with borrowers.
Deposits are kept safely and earn interest.
Most deposits are used to provide loans.
The interest difference is the bank's main income.
activities.explanation: Compare your answer with the points a marker looks for.

activities.context: Salim needs to pay the continuing costs of producing shoes, so he borrows money from a lender. He receives the money now and promises to repay it later. With the credit, Salim can complete his order on time and increase his earnings. The arrangement includes interest, collateral, documents and repayment methods. If Salim owns an asset offered as collateral and does not repay, the lender can take that asset.
activities.prompt: What would be likely to happen after Salim completes the order on time?
options: He would be able to earn more.
He would have to stop producing shoes immediately.
He would need to return the borrowed money at once.
He would have less money for continuing production.

why.He would have to stop producing shoes im: Nothing in the facts says that he must stop producing.
why.He would need to return the borrowed mon: Credit involves repayment later, not immediate repayment.
why.He would have less money for continuing: The credit helped him pay continuing production costs.

activities.explanation: Completing the order on time helped Salim increase his earnings.

activities.context: Salim needs to pay the continuing costs of producing shoes, so he borrows money from a lender. He receives the money now and promises to repay it later. With the credit, Salim can complete his order on time and increase his earnings. The arrangement includes interest, collateral, documents and repayment methods. If Salim owns an asset offered as collateral and does not repay, the lender can take that asset.
activities.prompt: What could the lender do if Salim failed to repay?
options: Claim the borrower's asset used to secure the loan.
Demand a written apology instead of taking any asset.
Cancel the agreement while keeping the borrowed money.
Ask the borrower for more production costs instead of repayment.

why.Demand a written apology instead of taki: An apology is not stated as a remedy in the facts.
why.Cancel the agreement while keeping the b: Cancelling the agreement is not the stated lender remedy.
why.Ask the borrower for more production cos: The relevant consequence concerns repayment and collateral.

activities.explanation: The lender can take collateral when repayment is not made.

activities.prompt:
Assertion (A): Terms of credit set out how a borrower will repay a loan.
Reason (R): The terms include repayment methods and the complete repayment arrangement.
options: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true but R is false.
A is false but R is true.
activities.explanation: The repayment arrangement explains the borrower's obligation and therefore explains the assertion.

activities.prompt: Explain why credit helped Salim complete his order on time and increase his earnings.
activities.answer: Credit helped Salim because it provided money when he needed to pay the continuing costs of producing shoes. In return, he promised to pay the lender later. The credit gave him the resources to complete his order on time. Completing the order on time helped him increase his earnings. Thus, credit supported both the production of the shoes and his ability to earn more, while creating a repayment obligation.
points: Credit provided money when Salim needed it.
He used it to pay continuing shoe-production costs.
The credit helped him complete his order on time.
Completing the order helped him increase his earnings.
activities.explanation: Compare your answer with the points a marker looks for.

activities.context: A rural household needs credit, but formal lenders meet only about half of rural credit needs. The household therefore turns to an informal lender, which charges much higher interest than a formal lender. The loan costs the household a large amount, leaving it with less income for itself. The household struggles to repay, and the high interest begins to push it toward a debt-trap.
activities.prompt: What is likely to happen to the household after it takes the informal loan?
options: The household will have less money left after repayment.
The household will be able to save all of the remaining income.
The interest charged will fall below the formal interest rate.
The household will avoid any difficulty in repaying the loan.

why.The household will be able to save all o: Borrowing costs reduce, rather than protect, the remaining income.
why.The interest charged will fall below the: Informal lenders usually charge more than formal lenders.
why.The household will avoid any difficulty: High interest can make repayment difficult and lead to a debt-trap.

activities.explanation: High interest raises the repayment burden and reduces the money left.

activities.context: A rural household needs credit, but formal lenders meet only about half of rural credit needs. The household therefore turns to an informal lender, which charges much higher interest than a formal lender. The loan costs the household a large amount, leaving it with less income for itself. The household struggles to repay, and the high interest begins to push it toward a debt-trap.
activities.prompt: Why did the household in the case face such high borrowing costs?
options: Formal lenders cover only part of rural credit needs, while informal loans carry much higher interest.
Formal lenders charge much higher interest than informal lenders.
Informal loans cost borrowers less, so the household chose one to save money.
High borrowing costs increase the amount of income left for borrowers.

why.Informal loans cost borrowers less, so t: Informal loans cost more because their interest rates are usually higher.
why.High borrowing costs increase the amount: High borrowing costs reduce, rather than increase, the income left.

activities.explanation: The limited formal credit and high informal interest explain the household's costly loan.

activities.prompt:
Assertion (A): Informal loans usually cost borrowers more than formal loans.
Reason (R): Informal lenders usually charge much higher interest than formal lenders.
options: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true but R is false.
A is false but R is true.
activities.explanation: Both statements are true, and the higher interest rate explains why informal loans cost more.

activities.prompt: Explain why a rural household using an informal lender may face a debt-trap.
activities.answer: Informal lenders usually charge much higher interest than formal lenders. As a result, informal loans cost borrowers more, and poor households often pay a large amount for borrowing. High borrowing costs leave borrowers with less income for themselves. When a large part of their income must go towards repayment, high interest can push them into a debt-trap. This problem is important for rural households because formal lenders meet only about half of rural credit needs.
points: Informal interest rates are much higher
Poor households often pay large amounts
Borrowing costs reduce available income
High interest can cause a debt-trap
activities.explanation: Compare your answer with the points a marker looks for.

activities.context: In a rural area, 15 to 20 poor women formed a Self Help Group. They meet regularly and pool small savings. A member facing a need can borrow a small amount from the group at less interest than a moneylender charges. Regular saving can make the group eligible for bank finance, even though the women have no collateral. The group receives the bank loan, lends it to members for self-employment, and is responsible for repaying the bank.
activities.prompt: After the group becomes eligible for a bank loan, what should it do next?
options: Use the money for members' self-employment while keeping repayment of the bank loan as the group's responsibility.
Let each member repay the bank directly, because the money will be lent to the members.
Keep the bank loan as group savings and continue lending only from the savings already pooled.
Use the bank loan to replace regular saving and stop lending money to members.

why.Let each member repay the bank directly,: The group receives the bank loan, so it remains responsible for repayment.
why.Keep the bank loan as group savings and: Keeping the loan as savings would prevent members from using it for self-employment.
why.Use the bank loan to replace regular sav: Regular saving supports eligibility, while the bank loan is meant to be lent to members.

activities.explanation: This follows the group's role of lending bank finance to members for self-employment.

activities.context: In a rural area, 15 to 20 poor women formed a Self Help Group. They meet regularly and pool small savings. A member facing a need can borrow a small amount from the group at less interest than a moneylender charges. Regular saving can make the group eligible for bank finance, even though the women have no collateral. The group receives the bank loan, lends it to members for self-employment, and is responsible for repaying the bank.
activities.prompt: Why might a member choose a small loan from the Self Help Group instead of borrowing from a moneylender?
options: The group charges less interest, so the member's small loan costs less.
The group charges more interest, but it can lend without any regular savings.
The group charges the same interest, but members must wait for bank finance before borrowing.
The group charges less interest, but only members who have collateral may borrow.

why.The group charges more interest, but it: The group lends from members' pooled savings rather than charging a higher rate.
why.The group charges the same interest, but: Group loans can be made from pooled savings before the group receives bank finance.
why.The group charges less interest, but onl: Collateral is not required for bank loans to organised poor women.

activities.explanation: Self Help Group loans charge less interest than moneylender loans.

boss.title: Chapter challenge: Money and Credit

activities.prompt: A grain seller wants shoes. A baker wants grain but does not need shoes. What barter need is missing?
options: A match of both parties’ wants
Only the baker wants an exchange
Only the seller wants an exchange
Neither party wants an exchange
activities.explanation: Barter needs a double coincidence of wants. Their wants do not match.

activities.prompt: Money removes the need for a double coincidence of wants.
activities.explanation: One side can pay money for what it wants. The other side need not offer a wanted good.

activities.prompt: Why do banks keep only some deposits as cash?
options: They use most deposits to provide loans.
They use most deposits to keep them safe.
They use most deposits to buy currency notes.
They use most deposits to pay all borrowers.
activities.explanation: Banks keep only a small part as cash. They use most deposits to provide loans.

activities.prompt: Match each item with its correct meaning.
pairs: Instruction to pay a stated sum
activities.explanation: Each pair shows a key idea from the lesson. Check the links between money, payments and borrowing.

activities.prompt: Informal lenders usually charge much higher interest than formal lenders.
activities.explanation: Their loans therefore cost borrowers more. High borrowing costs can leave borrowers with less income.

activities.prompt: How does a Self Help Group use a bank loan?
options: It lends the money to members.
It keeps all the money as cash.
It gives the money to officials.
It charges members higher interest.
activities.explanation: The group lends the bank loan to members for self-employment. The group remains responsible for repaying the bank.

activities.prompt: Formal lenders meet only about ______ of rural credit needs.
activities.hint: Think of the share shown in your lesson.
activities.explanation: Formal lenders meet only about half of rural credit needs. This leaves a large gap.

activities.prompt: Which list shows all terms of credit?
options: Interest, collateral, documents and repayment methods
Deposits, cheques, currency notes and borrowers
Demand deposits, loans, cheques and currencies
Collateral, lenders, borrowers and exchanged goods
activities.explanation: Terms of credit include interest, collateral, documents and repayment methods. The repayment arrangement is part of these terms.

chapters.title: Globalisation and the Indian Economy
chapters.summary: In this chapter: production across countries and interlinking; foreign trade and integration of markets; technology and globalisation; liberalisation and the world trade organisation.

lessons.title: Production Across Countries and Interlinking

activities.prompt: Why might your favorite everyday object have parts made around the world?
activities.explanation: Now read on to find out.

activities.title: How Production Crosses Borders
activities.body: Before the middle of the twentieth century, production was mostly organised within countries. Colonies such as India exported raw materials and food. They imported finished goods. Multinational companies, or MNCs, own or control production in more than one nation. MNCs divide production into small parts and spread them across the globe. Their business relationships link production in widely separated places.
keyPoints: Production was mostly organised within countries before the middle of the twentieth century.
MNCs divide production into small parts and spread them across the globe.
Business relationships link production in widely separated places.
activities.explanation: This shows how production has become linked across countries.

activities.prompt: An MNC makes components in China and other parts elsewhere. Why does it split its production?
steps: The MNC divides production into small parts because it can spread them across countries.
It places parts where labour and other resources are cheap.
This lowers production costs because the work uses cheaper resources.
The linked work can then help the MNC earn higher profits.
activities.explanation: Think it through with Hooty.

activities.prompt: What is an MNC?
options: A company owning or controlling production in more than one nation
A company selling goods in only one country
A colony exporting raw materials and food
A business investing money in foreign assets
activities.explanation: An MNC owns or controls production in more than one nation.

activities.prompt: Colonies such as India imported ______ goods.
activities.hint: These goods were already made.
activities.explanation: Colonies such as India imported finished goods.

activities.prompt: Why do MNCs set up factories where labour and resources are cheap?
options: Low production costs and higher profits
High production costs and lower profits
High production costs and higher profits
Low production costs and lower profits
activities.explanation: Cheap labour and resources help MNCs keep costs low and profits higher.

activities.prompt: Match each term with its meaning.
pairs: A company owning or controlling production in more than one nation
Divided into small parts and spread across the globe
Spending money on assets such as land, buildings and machines
activities.explanation: Each pair connects an idea with its definition from the lesson.

activities.prompt: Put these steps in the order described.
items: Set up factories where labour and resources are cheap
activities.explanation: MNCs choose cheap locations to lower costs and raise profits.

activities.prompt: How does an MNC connect production in widely separated places?
options: MNCs and business relationships
Exports of raw materials alone
Imports of finished goods alone
Production organised within one country
activities.explanation: MNCs and their business relationships link production in widely separated places.

activities.prompt: An MNC can make its products in different countries. Labour and resources are cheaper in one country. Where should it produce, and why?
options: It should choose the cheaper country to keep production costs low.
It should choose the costly country because higher wages always help.
It should choose the cheaper country because all profits must remain there.
It should choose either country because labour costs do not change profits.

why.It should choose the costly country beca: This wrongly treats higher labour costs as helpful to the MNC.
why.It should choose the cheaper country bec: This confuses lower costs with where the MNC profits must stay.
why.It should choose either country because: This wrongly believes labour costs have no effect on profits.

activities.explanation: Cheap labour and resources help the MNC lower costs and raise profits.

activities.prompt: Before the middle of the twentieth century, production mostly stayed within countries. Today, MNCs spread production across countries. What is the main change?
options: Production is now often divided and linked across different countries.
Production is now mostly kept inside one country by each business.
Production is now moved abroad only to exchange raw materials.
Production is now spread abroad without links between separate places.

why.Production is now mostly kept inside one: This keeps production within countries, like the earlier period.
why.Production is now moved abroad only to e: This wrongly limits foreign production to exchanging raw materials.
why.Production is now spread abroad without: This misses the business links between widely separated production places.

activities.explanation: MNCs now divide production and link it across different countries.

activities.prompt: A map shows components made in China and finished goods made elsewhere. What does this tell us about the MNC?
options: The MNC splits production into parts made in different countries.
The MNC keeps every production step inside one country.
The MNC makes parts only where finished goods are finally sold.
The MNC avoids foreign production because foreign work cannot be controlled.

why.The MNC keeps every production step insi: This contradicts the map, which places production in another country.
why.The MNC makes parts only where finished: This wrongly ties every production part to the final sales place.
why.The MNC avoids foreign production becaus: This wrongly claims an MNC cannot control production in another nation.

activities.explanation: The map shows the MNC dividing production across different countries.

activities.prompt: An MNC spends money on a factory in another nation. Why is this foreign investment?
options: Because an MNC is spending money on assets in another nation.
Because only factories count as investment, while land and buildings do not.
Because spending money in any country automatically makes every company an MNC.
Because the factory must employ workers from the MNC home country.

why.Because only factories count as investme: This wrongly leaves out land and buildings as investment assets.
why.Because spending money in any country au: This wrongly believes every company becomes an MNC after spending money.
why.Because the factory must employ workers: This invents a rule about workers that the facts do not give.

activities.explanation: The MNC is investing money on assets in another nation.

lessons.title: Foreign Trade and Integration of Markets

activities.prompt: How does trade connect us to the rest of the world?
activities.explanation: Now read on to find out.

activities.title: How Foreign Trade Connects Countries
activities.body: Foreign trade connects markets in different countries. Producers can sell beyond their home market and compete overseas. Imports give buyers more choice. As trade grows, similar goods tend to have similar prices in different markets. This connection is part of globalisation, the rapid integration of countries. People also connect countries by seeking income, jobs or education.
keyPoints: Foreign trade connects different countries.
Imports give buyers more choice.
Growing trade brings similar prices closer.
Globalisation means rapid integration of countries.
activities.explanation: Foreign trade links markets, choices and people across countries.

activities.prompt: Why do Chinese toys sell well while Indian toy makers lose money?
steps: Chinese toys become popular because they are cheaper and have new designs.
Indian buyers choose them because price and design attract them.
Indian toy makers face losses because fewer customers buy their toys.
So foreign trade can help buyers while hurting some local producers.
activities.explanation: Think it through with Hooty.

activities.title: The Main Channel
activities.prompt: Which statement about foreign trade is correct?
options: It keeps different markets separate.
It stops producers from selling abroad.
It connects markets in different countries.
It gives buyers fewer choices.
activities.explanation: Foreign trade has long connected markets in different countries.

activities.title: More Choices
activities.prompt: Imports give buyers more choice.
activities.explanation: Imports add goods produced in another country to the market.

activities.title: Selling Beyond Home
activities.prompt: Foreign trade lets producers sell beyond their ______ market.
activities.hint: This is the market where producers first sell their goods.
activities.explanation: Foreign trade helps producers sell in other countries.

activities.title: Popular Chinese Toys
activities.prompt: What made Chinese toys popular in India?
options: Cheaper prices and new designs
Higher prices and old designs
Cheaper prices but no designs
Higher prices and new designs
activities.explanation: Chinese toys became popular because they were cheaper and had new designs.

activities.title: Indian Toy Makers
activities.prompt: Indian toy makers made profits because more customers bought their toys.
activities.explanation: Indian toy makers faced losses because fewer customers bought their toys.

activities.title: MNCs and World Trade
activities.prompt: Which statement about MNCs is correct?
options: Investment is falling, and they control a small part of trade.
Investment is rising, and they control a large part of trade.
Investment is rising, and they control no foreign trade.
Investment is falling, and they control all foreign trade.
activities.explanation: Foreign investment by MNCs is rising. They control a large part of foreign trade.

activities.title: Prices Across Markets
activities.prompt: How does growing trade affect prices of similar goods across markets?
options: They tend to become equal.
They tend to become different.
They tend to lose all value.
They tend to stop being sold.
activities.explanation: Prices of similar goods tend to become equal as trade grows.

activities.prompt: Chinese toys are cheap in India and have new designs. What follows?
options: Indian toy makers faced losses because fewer buyers came.
Indian toy makers gained customers because Chinese toys looked old.
Indian buyers lost choice because all toys came from China.
Chinese trade stopped because Indian makers disliked the competition.

why.Indian toy makers gained customers becau: This mistake assumes new designs made Chinese toys less attractive.
why.Indian buyers lost choice because all to: This mistake assumes popularity removed all other goods from buyers' choices.
why.Chinese trade stopped because Indian mak: This mistake assumes price and design competition stopped foreign trade.

activities.explanation: This is right because fewer customers buying Indian toys caused their losses.

activities.prompt: As trade grows, prices of the same phone in two countries will...
options: Their prices will tend to become equal.
Their prices will tend to stay different.
Their prices will change in only one country.
Their prices will rise in both countries together.

why.Their prices will tend to stay different: This mistake assumes trade does not make prices more similar.
why.Their prices will change in only one cou: This mistake assumes price changes stay in only one market.
why.Their prices will rise in both countries: This mistake assumes trade causes equal rises instead of similar prices.

activities.explanation: Right, because similar goods' prices tend to equalize as trade grows.

lessons.sceneCaption: The container ship India at Rotterdam shows how shipping links European and South Asian markets.

lessons.title: Technology and Globalisation

activities.prompt: How does technology connect people, places, and ideas?
activities.explanation: Now read on to find out.

activities.title: Technology Connects the World
activities.body: Rapid technology improvement has been a major factor in globalisation. Better transport has made delivery faster and cheaper. Containers stay intact across ships, railways, planes and trucks. They reduce port handling costs. Telecommunications help people contact others and access information instantly. Computers enter almost every field of activity. The Internet lets people share information about almost anything.
keyPoints: Technology has driven globalisation.
Better transport lowers delivery costs.
Containers reduce port handling costs.
activities.explanation: Technology makes transport, communication and information sharing easier.

activities.prompt: A remote shop must contact a supplier and find information. It must also pay for a magazine design. How can modern communication tools help?
steps: The Internet helps because it gives access to information about almost anything.
Electronic mail helps because it transfers magazine payment instantly at low cost.
A satellite device helps because it allows communication from remote places.
So modern communication tools can handle contact, information, and payment needs.
activities.explanation: Think it through with Hooty.

activities.title: Fast Communication Across Distances
activities.body: Lower air transport costs let airlines carry much larger volumes of goods. Telecommunication facilities help people contact others and access information instantly. Satellite communication devices help people communicate from remote areas. The Internet lets people obtain and share information about almost anything. Electronic mail and voice-mail can cross the world at very low cost. Money for magazine design and printing can move instantly through the Internet.
keyPoints: Cheaper air transport carries more goods.
Satellite devices help remote communication.
The Internet shares information and moves money instantly.
activities.explanation: Communication technology makes distant contact, information and money transfers easier.

activities.prompt: Which change has better transport technology made possible?
options: Faster delivery at lower costs
Faster delivery at higher costs
Slower delivery at lower costs
Slower delivery at higher costs
activities.explanation: Better transport technology has made delivery faster and cheaper.

activities.prompt: Match each technology with its result.
activities.explanation: Each technology helps transport goods or share information more easily.

activities.prompt: Containers can be loaded intact onto ships, railways, planes and trucks.
activities.explanation: Yes! Containers can stay intact across all these transport methods.

activities.prompt: What did falling air transport costs allow airlines to do?
options: Carry much smaller volumes of goods
Carry much larger volumes of goods
Carry only very small volumes of goods
Carry goods only within nearby areas
activities.explanation: Falling costs have allowed airlines to carry much larger volumes of goods.

activities.prompt: Technology in ______, computers and the Internet has changed rapidly.
activities.hint: This means contacting people and accessing information.
activities.explanation: Telecommunications, computers and the Internet have all changed rapidly.

activities.prompt: A designer needs to transfer money for designing and printing a magazine. Which technology can do this?
options: Containers
The Internet
Ships
Trucks
activities.explanation: The Internet can transfer this money instantly.

activities.prompt: A business sends boxes to another country. Better transport technology makes delivery faster and cheaper. What follows?
options: The boxes arrive sooner, and delivery costs less.
The boxes arrive later, but delivery costs less.
The boxes arrive sooner, but delivery costs more.
The boxes arrive later, and delivery costs more.

why.The boxes arrive later, but delivery cos: This wrongly treats better transport as making delivery slower.
why.The boxes arrive sooner, but delivery co: This wrongly assumes that faster delivery must cost more.
why.The boxes arrive later, and delivery cos: This wrongly reverses both effects of better transport.

activities.explanation: This follows because better transport makes delivery faster and cheaper.

activities.prompt: A cargo must stay intact while moving between ships, trains, planes, and trucks. Which choice best fits?
options: Use one container, which also lowers port costs.
Load each item separately at every stop.
Repack the cargo whenever its vehicle changes.
Open the cargo box at every port.

This ignores that containers keep cargo together.
why.Repack the cargo whenever its vehicle ch: This adds needless repacking, which containers avoid.
This wrongly treats every port as a place to open cargo.

activities.explanation: Containers stay intact across all listed transports and cut port costs.

activities.prompt: A picture shows sealed boxes moving from a ship to a truck. What does the picture suggest?
options: The boxes stay intact across different transport modes.
The boxes must be opened at every port.
Each loose item is handled separately.
The boxes can travel only by sea.

This assumes all cargo must be opened at ports.
This wrongly treats each item as loose cargo.
This wrongly limits the cargo to ships.

activities.explanation: The sealed boxes show that cargo can stay intact during transport.

activities.prompt: A remote student needs to contact others. A city student can use the Internet. Which device helps the remote student?
options: A satellite communication device.
A container for carrying goods.
A railway cargo box.
A packing box for magazines.

Containers carry goods, but they do not help people contact others.
Railway cargo boxes move goods, but they do not help remote communication.
Packing boxes hold magazine pages, but they do not help communication.

activities.explanation: Satellite devices allow people to communicate from remote areas.

activities.prompt: A designer needs magazine ideas from another country. Payment must also reach the designer today. Which tools best help?
options: The Internet and electronic mail.
Containers and cargo ships.
Satellite containers and railways.
Air freight and paper post.

Containers move goods, but they do not share ideas or pay designers.
Satellite containers cannot provide either of these services.
Air freight moves goods, but cannot share ideas or transfer payment.

activities.explanation: The Internet and electronic mail share ideas and transfer payment quickly.

activities.prompt: An airline can carry much larger volumes of goods because air transport now costs less. What effect on globalisation is likely?
options: More goods can move across long distances.
More goods must be made close to each buyer.
People stop needing quick transport services.
Countries stop sharing news and information.

why.More goods must be made close to each bu: This wrongly says nearby production must replace long-distance movement.
why.People stop needing quick transport serv: This wrongly assumes quick transport is no longer useful.
why.Countries stop sharing news and informat: This wrongly assumes more air cargo stops information sharing.

activities.explanation: Falling air transport costs let airlines carry much larger volumes.

lessons.title: Liberalisation and the World Trade Organisation

activities.prompt: Why did India open its doors to the world of trade?
activities.explanation: Now read on to find out.

activities.title: How India's Trade Policy Changed
activities.body: After Independence, India used trade barriers to protect domestic producers. These barriers included import taxes. India first allowed only essential imports, such as machinery and fertilisers. Around 1991, the government removed many barriers. This policy change is called liberalisation. The World Trade Organisation, or WTO, aims to liberalise international trade.
keyPoints: Trade barriers protect domestic producers.
Liberalisation means removing government restrictions.
The WTO aims to liberalise international trade.
activities.explanation: This card introduces liberalisation and the WTO.

activities.prompt: After Independence, India taxes imported toys. Why might buyers pay more while local makers feel safer?
steps: Buyers pay more because the tax raises the price of imported toys.
The tax is a trade barrier because it limits imported goods.
India used trade barriers to protect domestic producers from foreign competition.
So buyers pay more, while domestic producers gain protection from foreign competition.
activities.explanation: Think it through with Hooty.

activities.title: Competition and the WTO
activities.body: India wanted competition from foreign producers so Indian producers would improve quality. The change began around 1991. About 160 countries were WTO members when the chapter was written. It aims to liberalise international trade. However, developed countries have unfairly kept some trade barriers in practice.
keyPoints: Competition was meant to improve Indian producers' quality.
About 160 countries were WTO members.
Some developed countries still keep trade barriers.
activities.explanation: Some countries still keep unfair trade barriers.

activities.title: The Effect of an Import Tax
activities.prompt: What happens when a tax is placed on imported toys?
options: A toy becomes cheaper for buyers.
Buyers pay a higher price.
Foreign toys reach shops more easily.
Toys disappear from shops.
activities.explanation: A tax raises the price buyers pay for imported toys.

activities.title: Name the Trade Barrier
activities.prompt: A tax on imports is an example of a ______ barrier.
activities.hint: This barrier controls trade between countries.
activities.explanation: A tax on imports is a trade barrier.

activities.title: Match Trade Ideas
activities.prompt: Match each trade idea with its matching name or aim.
activities.explanation: Each pair connects a trade idea with its matching name or aim.

activities.title: Why India Wanted Competition
activities.prompt: Why did the government want competition for Indian producers?
options: Help producers improve their quality.
Help producers make poorer quality.
Stop competition between producers.
Keep all imports banned.
activities.explanation: The government wanted competition to improve producers' quality.

activities.title: India's Trade Policy Timeline
activities.prompt: Put India's trade policy events in time order.
items: During the changes: many barriers are removed
activities.explanation: The events move from barriers to policy changes and removal.

activities.title: WTO Aims and Practice
activities.prompt: Which statement best matches the WTO's aim and practice?
options: It seeks liberal trade, but some developed countries keep barriers.
It seeks liberal trade, but every country removed all barriers.
It seeks protected trade, and all barriers are unfair.
It seeks liberal trade, but India kept every barrier.
activities.explanation: The WTO promotes liberal trade, while some developed countries still keep barriers.

activities.prompt: A country taxes imported toys. Why might it use this rule?
options: To keep some foreign trade under control.
To help shoppers pay less for imported toys.
To remove limits on foreign investment.
To make imported toys free for shoppers.

why.To help shoppers pay less for imported t: This mistake treats a tax as a way to lower prices.
This mistake confuses trade barriers with liberalisation.
This mistake treats a tax as removing the toy price.

activities.explanation: This is right because governments use barriers to regulate trade.

activities.prompt: A map shows about 160 WTO member countries. What does this suggest?
options: The WTO had a large group of member countries.
The WTO had a small group of member countries.
The WTO had no members from foreign countries.
The WTO had members from only one country.

why.The WTO had a small group of member coun: This mistake reads about 160 countries as only a few.
why.The WTO had no members from foreign coun: This mistake treats WTO members as countries without foreign trade.
why.The WTO had members from only one countr: This mistake ignores the many countries shown on the map.

activities.explanation: This is right because about 160 countries shows a large membership.

activities.prompt: WTO wants liberal trade, but some barriers remain. What does this show?
options: WTO aims for liberal trade, but practice can be unfair.
WTO aims for liberal trade, but all practice is fair.
WTO aims for unfair trade, so all practice is unfair.
WTO aims for liberal trade, so no barriers can remain.

why.WTO aims for liberal trade, but all prac: This mistake ignores the unfair barriers kept by developed countries.
why.WTO aims for unfair trade, so all practi: This mistake treats unfair barriers as the WTO's main aim.
why.WTO aims for liberal trade, so no barrie: This mistake assumes liberalisation removes every barrier everywhere.

activities.explanation: This is right because the aim is liberal trade, but practice can be unfair.

lessons.title: Globalisation’s Impact on Consumers and Producers

activities.prompt: How does globalisation affect what we buy, make, and earn?
activities.explanation: Now read on to find out.

activities.title: Different People, Different Benefits
activities.body: Globalisation means changes linked to competition and MNC investment in India. It has not affected every producer and worker in the same way. Competition has benefited consumers, especially well-off people in urban areas. MNCs are multinational companies investing more in India. They created new jobs, and local suppliers prospered. Well-off urban consumers now have higher living standards than earlier. Indian companies invested in newer technology and raised production standards.
keyPoints: Competition has especially benefited well-off urban consumers.
MNCs have created jobs and helped local suppliers prosper.
Indian companies have raised their production standards.
activities.explanation: Different groups can gain different benefits from globalisation.

activities.prompt: MNCs invested more in India. Why might one producer improve while another does not?
steps: Globalisation affects producers and workers unevenly, so one producer may gain more.
MNC investment can create jobs and help local suppliers prosper, so some producers may gain.
Indian companies can adopt newer technology and raise production standards, so some firms may improve.
Therefore, globalisation creates opportunities, but producers will not all benefit in the same way.
activities.explanation: Think it through with Hooty.

activities.title: More Opportunities for Producers
activities.body: Consumers are not the only group gaining from globalisation. MNCs have created new jobs, and local suppliers to their industries have prospered. Indian companies have invested in newer technology. They have raised their production standards. Globalisation has also opened new opportunities for service companies, especially in IT. These changes can affect producers, workers and service firms in different ways.
keyPoints: MNC industries have created new jobs.
Indian companies have invested in newer technology.
Service companies have gained new opportunities, especially in IT.
activities.explanation: Globalisation can bring gains to producers, workers and service companies.

activities.title: Who Benefits from Competition?
activities.prompt: Which group has clearly benefited from competition?
options: Well-off urban consumers
All rural workers equally
Every producer in India
Workers in every industry
activities.explanation: Competition has benefited consumers, especially well-off people in urban areas.

activities.title: An Industry for MNC Investment
activities.prompt: MNCs have invested in cell phones, cars, ______ and soft drinks.
activities.hint: This is one of the industries named for MNC investment.
activities.explanation: Electronics is one of the industries in which MNCs have invested.

activities.title: Match Each Change with Its Result
activities.prompt: Match each group or change with the result described in the lesson.
activities.explanation: Each pair joins a group or change with its result in the lesson.

activities.title: Why Set Up Economic Zones?
activities.prompt: Why is the government setting up Special Economic Zones?
options: To attract foreign companies
To stop all MNC investment
To remove workplace facilities
To keep firms outside India
activities.explanation: These zones are intended to attract foreign companies. They should offer world-class facilities.

activities.title: The Development Sequence
activities.prompt: Put these developments in the order described in the lesson.
activities.explanation: The lesson links industry investment with new jobs and prosperous local suppliers.

activities.title: Understanding the Overall Impact
activities.prompt: Well-off urban consumers benefit from competition. Some producers and workers gain differently. What can you conclude?
options: Globalisation affects groups differently
Every producer gains equally
All workers benefit equally
Only consumers are affected
activities.explanation: Competition benefits well-off urban consumers, but effects differ among producers and workers.

activities.prompt: Competition reaches a city market. Who is most likely to benefit?
options: Well-off urban consumers, because competition benefited them.
All workers equally, because every producer is affected equally.
Small producers equally, because globalisation helps every producer.
Rural consumers, because competition mainly helps rural areas.

why.All workers equally, because every produ: This confuses consumer benefits with equal effects on every producer and worker.
why.Small producers equally, because globali: This assumes globalisation shares gains equally, contrary to.
why.Rural consumers, because competition mai: This reverses the urban focus stated in.

activities.explanation: says competition especially benefited well-off people in urban areas.

activities.prompt: An MNC invests in an Indian industry. Which effect can follow?
options: New jobs can appear, and local suppliers can prosper.
Every producer will gain equally from the investment.
Consumers will lose all competition from the MNC.
Indian companies will stop using newer technology.

why.Every producer will gain equally from th: This mistakes possible gains for equal effects on every producer and worker.
why.Consumers will lose all competition from: This treats new investment as removing the competition described in.
why.Indian companies will stop using newer t: This reverses, which says Indian companies invest in newer technology.

activities.explanation: says MNC industries can create jobs and help local suppliers prosper.

activities.prompt: Tata Motors invests in newer technology. What can result?
options: It can raise Tata Motors' production standards.
It can lower Tata Motors' production standards.
It can raise every producer's standards equally.
It can remove competition from the Indian market.

why.It can lower Tata Motors' production sta: This reverses the effect of investing in newer technology.
why.It can raise every producer's standards: This assumes one company's change reaches every producer equally, contrary to.
why.It can remove competition from the India: This mistakes one company's higher standards for competition disappearing.

activities.explanation: says Indian companies have raised production standards through newer technology.

activities.prompt: A map marks MNC investment in four industries. What can we infer?
options: MNC investment reached several industries, not just one.
Every producer in these industries gained equally.
Only service companies received MNC investment.
The map shows why Special Economic Zones were set up.

why.Every producer in these industries gaine: This confuses investment in industries with equal effects on every producer.
why.Only service companies received MNC inve: This overlooks, which names industries beyond services.
why.The map shows why Special Economic Zones: This assumes the map proves why Special Economic Zones were set up, which it cannot show.

activities.explanation: Facts 5.4 and 5.5 show investment across several named industries.
