lessons.title: Small Producers, Workers and Fair Globalisation

activities.prompt: How can globalisation become fairer for small producers and workers?
activities.explanation: Now read on to find out.

activities.title: Challenges for Small Producers and Workers
activities.body: Globalisation has created major challenges for many small producers and workers. Many small units have closed, leaving workers without jobs. Flexible employment has made many jobs less secure. Some factories employ workers only temporarily. Workers may also face very long hours or regular night shifts. Fair globalisation should create opportunities for everyone and share benefits more equally.
keyPoints: Many small units have closed.
Flexible employment can reduce job security.
Fair globalisation should share benefits more equally.
activities.explanation: This lesson explores work, fairness, and support for small producers.

activities.prompt: A small workshop closes, and its workers lose jobs. What can fair globalisation do for them?
steps: Globalisation creates major challenges, so some small units may close.
When units close, workers lose jobs, so benefits are unequal.
Fair globalisation should share benefits more equally, including with workers.
Government support can help small producers compete, so action is needed.
activities.explanation: Think it through with Hooty.

activities.title: Unequal Benefits and Workers’ Conditions
activities.body: Some factories use temporary workers. Workers may face very long hours or regular night shifts. Jobs in the organised sector increasingly resemble unorganised-sector working conditions. Not everyone has benefited equally from globalisation. People’s organisations have influenced important trade and investment decisions at the WTO.
keyPoints: Some workers face insecure employment.
Not everyone benefits equally from globalisation.
People’s organisations have influenced WTO decisions.
activities.explanation: Fair globalisation must consider workers’ conditions and unequal benefits.

activities.title: A Major Globalisation Challenge
activities.prompt: Which change has affected many small producers and workers?
options: Challenges from globalisation
More equal benefits now
Fewer foreign orders
Strong support from government
activities.explanation: Globalisation has created major challenges for many small producers and workers.

activities.title: Match Each Idea
activities.prompt: Match each idea to its lesson meaning.
pairs: Employ the largest number of workers in India
Makes many workers’ jobs less secure
activities.explanation: Each idea matches its meaning from the lesson.

activities.title: The Impact of Flexible Employment
activities.prompt: What has happened to many workers’ jobs because of flexible employment?
options: They have become less secure.
They have become more secure.
They now work fewer hours.
They now have permanent jobs.
activities.explanation: Flexible employment has made many workers’ jobs less secure.

activities.title: A Large Foreign Order
activities.prompt: A garment exporter wants a large foreign order. What may the exporter try to do?
options: Reduce labour costs
Create more factories
Share equal benefits
Close small units
activities.explanation: Garment exporters try to reduce labour costs to win large foreign orders.

activities.title: Making Globalisation Fair
activities.prompt: Fair globalisation should create ______ for everyone and share benefits more equally.
activities.hint: This means chances for people to gain benefits.
activities.explanation: Fair globalisation should create opportunities for everyone.

activities.title: Supporting a Small Producer
activities.prompt: A small producer needs help to compete. What can the government do?
options: Support it until it can compete.
End all support immediately.
Use temporary workers instead.
Give support only to large exporters.
activities.explanation: The government can support small producers until they become strong enough to compete.

activities.prompt: A small workshop closes. Workers lose their jobs. How can the government help?
options: Support small producers until they become strong enough to compete.
Give every worker a permanent job in organised factories.
Tell garment exporters to reduce labour costs for foreign orders.
Wait until small workshops close before offering any help.

why.Give every worker a permanent job in org: This wrongly treats job creation as the stated government response.
why.Tell garment exporters to reduce labour: This confuses exporter cost-cutting with government support.
why.Wait until small workshops close before: This reverses the rule, which supports producers before they become strong.

activities.explanation: This matches the rule that government can support small producers until they can compete.

activities.prompt: A garment exporter cuts labour costs to win a large foreign order. What may happen to workers?
options: Workers may work very long hours and regular night shifts.
Workers may receive more secure permanent jobs.
Workers may work fewer hours and no night shifts.
Workers may leave factories because hours become shorter.

why.Workers may receive more secure permanen: This mistakes cost-cutting for better job security.
why.Workers may work fewer hours and no nigh: This reverses the possible effect on working hours.
why.Workers may leave factories because hour: This confuses long working hours with factory closure.

activities.explanation: This is a possible effect when exporters reduce labour costs to win orders.

activities.prompt: Flexible work replaces a secure job. What may happen to the worker?
options: The job may become less secure.
The job may become more secure.
The worker may gain a permanent contract.
The worker may get more regular working hours.

This reverses the effect of flexible employment.
why.The worker may gain a permanent contract: This confuses temporary employment with greater job security.
why.The worker may get more regular working: This confuses flexible work with regular working hours.

activities.explanation: Flexible employment can make workers’ jobs less secure.

activities.prompt: A report says small and medium industries employ India’s most workers. What does this show?
options: Many workers depend on these small and medium industries.
Only a few workers work in these industries.
All these workers have secure permanent jobs.
These industries never face challenges from globalisation.

why.Only a few workers work in these industr: This wrongly reverses the meaning of employing the largest number of workers.
why.All these workers have secure permanent: This confuses high employment with secure jobs.
why.These industries never face challenges f: This confuses large employment with an absence of challenges.

activities.explanation: Employing the largest number of workers shows that many workers depend on them.

activities.prompt: People’s organisations influence trade and investment decisions at the WTO. Why might they do this?
options: To help globalisation share its benefits more equally.
To make sure only large exporters gain from trade decisions.
To keep every worker in a temporary job forever.
To stop small producers from facing any challenges.

why.To make sure only large exporters gain f: This assumes trade decisions should favour only large exporters, not everyone.
why.To keep every worker in a temporary job: This mistakes temporary work for a goal of people’s organisations.
why.To stop small producers from facing any: This seeks to remove challenges instead of helping producers meet them.

activities.explanation: This matches fair globalisation’s aim of sharing benefits more equally.

activities.prompt: Some small units close, while other people gain from globalisation. What does this show?
options: Globalisation’s benefits are not shared equally among people.
Globalisation gives every person exactly the same benefits.
Small producers no longer face major challenges.
All workers become more secure after globalisation begins.

why.Globalisation gives every person exactly: This wrongly assumes that everyone receives equal benefits.
why.Small producers no longer face major cha: This ignores the major challenges faced by small producers.
why.All workers become more secure after glo: This confuses unequal benefits with better security for every worker.

activities.explanation: Different outcomes show that not everyone benefits equally from globalisation.

activities.context: Before the middle of the twentieth century, production was mostly organised within countries. Colonies such as India exported raw materials and food while importing finished goods. In another situation, consider an MNC that manufactures components in China. It divides production into small parts and spreads them across the globe, placing offices and factories where labour and other resources are cheap. Production in widely separated places becomes linked through the MNC and its business relationships.
activities.prompt: If labour and other resources become cheaper in a country where the MNC already operates, what is the most likely next step?
options: Shift some production there to lower costs and increase profits.
Move every stage of production there so that it no longer operates across countries.
Stop production because dividing it among countries always raises costs.
Buy raw materials there but continue importing all finished goods from abroad.

why.Move every stage of production there so: MNCs may spread different production parts across countries.
why.Stop production because dividing it amon: This contradicts the reason for locating production where resources are cheap.
why.Buy raw materials there but continue imp: The case shows that different parts may be produced in different countries.

activities.explanation: Cheaper resources can reduce production costs and raise profits.

activities.context: Before the middle of the twentieth century, production was mostly organised within countries. Colonies such as India exported raw materials and food while importing finished goods. In another situation, consider an MNC that manufactures components in China. It divides production into small parts and spreads them across the globe, placing offices and factories where labour and other resources are cheap. Production in widely separated places becomes linked through the MNC and its business relationships.
activities.prompt: The MNC wants to expand production in another country. What is the most common route for its investment?
options: Purchase an existing local company.
Avoid spending money on any assets there.
Use only borrowed workers without acquiring a company.
Wait for the country to stop producing goods and services.

why.Avoid spending money on any assets there: MNC investment involves spending money on assets.
why.Use only borrowed workers without acquir: Acquiring a company is a common form of MNC investment.
why.Wait for the country to stop producing g: The passage does not suggest that expansion requires production to stop.

activities.explanation: Buying an existing local company is the most common route.

activities.prompt:
Assertion (A): An MNC can divide a production process into small parts and spread them across different countries.
Reason (R): This helps the MNC locate production where labour and other resources are cheap.
options: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true but R is false.
A is false but R is true.
activities.explanation: Locating different parts where resources are cheap helps explain why an MNC spreads production across countries.

activities.prompt:
Assertion (A): Production in widely separated places becomes linked through MNCs and their business relationships.
Reason (R): The most common route for MNC investment is buying existing local companies.
options: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true but R is false.
A is false but R is true.
activities.explanation: Both statements are true, but the investment route does not explain how widely separated production becomes linked.

activities.prompt: Explain how an MNC organises production across countries and how this links widely separated places.
activities.answer: An MNC divides a production process into small parts and places them in different countries. This allows it to set up offices and factories where labour and other resources are cheap. As a result, production costs can be kept low and profits can be higher. The parts made in widely separated places are then linked through the MNC and its business relationships. This is how production across countries becomes interlinked, while the MNC organises and controls the different stages of production.
points: The production process is divided into small parts.
Different parts are spread across countries.
Cheap labour and resources help reduce costs.
MNCs and business relationships link distant production.
activities.explanation: Compare your answer with the points a marker looks for.

activities.prompt:
Assertion (A): As foreign trade grows, prices of similar goods in different markets tend to become equal.
Reason (R): Foreign trade connects markets in different countries through integration.
options: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true but R is false.
A is false but R is true.
activities.explanation: Both statements are true, and market integration through trade explains why similar goods tend to have more equal prices.

activities.prompt:
Assertion (A): MNCs control only a small part of foreign trade.
Reason (R): Foreign investment by MNCs in developing countries has been rising.
options: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true but R is false.
A is false but R is true.
activities.explanation: The first statement is false because MNCs control a large part of foreign trade, while the second statement is true.

activities.prompt: Explain how foreign trade integrates markets and affects the prices of similar goods.
activities.answer: Foreign trade integrates markets in different countries by allowing producers to sell beyond their home market and buyers to obtain goods made elsewhere. Imports add choice to buyers, and competition from producers in other countries can affect local producers. As trade grows, prices of similar goods in different markets tend to become equal. Thus, integration links producers and buyers and can reduce price differences between markets.
points: Foreign trade allows producers to sell beyond their home market.
Imports give buyers more choice.
Trade links markets in different countries.
Prices of similar goods tend to become equal as trade grows.
activities.explanation: Compare your answer with the points a marker looks for.

activities.context: A publisher sends copies of a new magazine to partners in several countries. It loads sealed shipping containers onto a ship, then uses air transport for the remaining copies. Email and satellite communication help the team contact suppliers and partners instantly. The publisher transfers money through the Internet for designing and printing the magazine. The containers reduce port handling costs, while cheaper air transport allows the airline to carry much larger volumes of goods.
activities.prompt: If the cost of air transport fell further, how would the publisher’s use of air transport most likely change?
options: Airlines would be able to move a greater quantity of the magazine copies.
Airlines would move fewer magazine copies despite the lower transport cost.
The quantity moved by air would stay the same, since only containers affect shipment size.
No magazine copies could be moved by air because containers are suitable only for ships.

why.Airlines would move fewer magazine copie: A lower transport cost does not reduce carrying capacity.
why.The quantity moved by air would stay the: Cheaper air transport also affects the volume airlines can carry.
why.No magazine copies could be moved by air: Containers can be loaded onto planes as well as ships.

activities.explanation: Lower costs make larger air shipments possible.

activities.context: A publisher sends copies of a new magazine to partners in several countries. It loads sealed shipping containers onto a ship, then uses air transport for the remaining copies. Email and satellite communication help the team contact suppliers and partners instantly. The publisher transfers money through the Internet for designing and printing the magazine. The containers reduce port handling costs, while cheaper air transport allows the airline to carry much larger volumes of goods.
activities.prompt: Suppose the Internet service became unavailable when the designer needed payment. What would most likely happen?
options: The instant payment route described in the case would no longer work.
The payment would move with the containers and arrive when the copies reached their destinations.
Satellite communication would automatically transfer the money in place of the Internet.
Voice-mail would automatically carry the payment across the world.

why.Satellite communication would automatica: Satellite devices help communication but do not transfer money.

activities.explanation: Instant Internet payment requires access to the Internet.

activities.prompt:
Assertion (A): The falling cost of air transport allows airlines to carry much larger volumes of goods.
Reason (R): Better transport technology has made faster delivery possible at lower costs.
options: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true but R is false.
A is false but R is true.
activities.explanation: Better transport technology can reduce costs, allowing airlines to carry larger volumes of goods.

activities.prompt:
Assertion (A): Containers can be loaded intact onto ships, railways, planes and trucks.
Reason (R): Satellite communication devices help people communicate from remote areas.
options: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true but R is false.
A is false but R is true.
activities.explanation: Both statements are true, but satellite communication does not explain why containers can be loaded onto different forms of transport.

activities.prompt: How does transport technology contribute to globalisation differently from communication technology?
activities.answer: Transport technology helps goods move faster and at lower cost. Better transport technology makes fast delivery possible while reducing expenses. Containers can be loaded intact onto ships, railways, planes and trucks, and they greatly reduce port handling costs. The falling cost of air transport allows airlines to carry much larger volumes of goods. In contrast, telecommunication technology helps people contact others, access information instantly and communicate from remote areas. The Internet supports cheap worldwide email and instant money transfers.
points: Better transport technology enables faster, lower-cost delivery.
Containers reduce port handling costs and can travel by several transport modes.
Cheaper air transport allows airlines to carry larger volumes of goods.
Telecommunication technology enables instant contact, information access and communication from remote areas.
activities.explanation: Compare your answer with the points a marker looks for.

activities.context: After Independence, India used trade barriers to protect domestic producers, and it initially allowed imports only of essential items such as machinery and fertilisers. A tax on imported toys then made buyers pay more. Starting around 1991, the government removed many barriers on foreign trade and foreign investment so that competition could push Indian producers to improve quality. The WTO, with about 160 member countries at the time, aimed to liberalise international trade.
activities.prompt: If India removes the tax on imported toys as part of liberalisation, what is the most likely effect for buyers?
options: They would pay less for imported toys.
They would pay more for imported toys.
The price would remain exactly the same.
They would pay the same amount under a differently named tax.

That would reverse the stated effect of the tax.
Nothing given predicts an unchanged price.
why.They would pay the same amount under a d: Renaming a tax would not remove its burden.

activities.explanation: Removing the tax reverses its price-raising effect.

activities.context: After Independence, India used trade barriers to protect domestic producers, and it initially allowed imports only of essential items such as machinery and fertilisers. A tax on imported toys then made buyers pay more. Starting around 1991, the government removed many barriers on foreign trade and foreign investment so that competition could push Indian producers to improve quality. The WTO, with about 160 member countries at the time, aimed to liberalise international trade.
activities.prompt: An importer describes the tax on imported toys as a barrier used to regulate foreign trade. Which conclusion follows most directly from the case?
options: The tax can regulate foreign trade, but it also raises buyers' prices.
The tax raises prices but has no connection with trade regulation.
Using this tax would remove the need for other trade barriers.
The tax means that only essential items may be imported.

why.The tax raises prices but has no connect: This wrongly denies its stated regulatory use.
why.Using this tax would remove the need for: One barrier does not remove all other restrictions.
why.The tax means that only essential items: The tax does not make only essentials importable.

activities.explanation: Both its barrier role and price effect are stated.

activities.prompt:
Assertion (A): India's liberalisation beginning around 1991 involved removing many barriers on foreign trade and foreign investment.
Reason (R): The government wanted competition to encourage Indian producers to improve quality.
options: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true but R is false.
A is false but R is true.
activities.explanation: Removing barriers allowed competition to create pressure for better quality.

activities.prompt:
Assertion (A): India initially allowed imports of only essential items such as machinery and fertilisers.
Reason (R): A tax on imports is an example of a trade barrier.
options: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true but R is false.
A is false but R is true.
activities.explanation: The tax being a trade barrier does not explain India's initial restriction to essential imports.

activities.prompt: Explain how liberalisation changed India's trade policy and what result the government wanted.
activities.answer: After Independence, India used barriers to protect domestic producers from foreign competition. It also allowed imports only of essential items such as machinery and fertilisers. Starting around 1991, the government made far-reaching policy changes and removed many barriers on foreign trade and foreign investment. This process is called liberalisation. The government wanted competition to encourage Indian producers to improve quality. Thus, liberalisation reduced government restrictions while seeking better quality from domestic producers through competition.
points: Before liberalisation, India used trade barriers.
Initially, only essential items could be imported.
From around 1991, many barriers were removed.
Competition was intended to encourage better quality.
activities.explanation: Compare your answer with the points a marker looks for.

boss.title: Chapter challenge: Globalisation and the Indian Economy

activities.title: Meaning of globalisation
activities.prompt: What does globalisation mean?
options: The rapid integration of countries.
The local isolation of markets.
The slower movement of workers.
The fall in all production costs.
activities.explanation: Globalisation means the rapid integration or interconnection of countries.

activities.title: MNC production
activities.prompt: MNCs spread production across countries to keep production costs low.
activities.explanation: MNCs divide production and spread parts across the globe. Cheap resources help lower costs.

activities.title: Meaning of investment
activities.prompt: Money spent on assets such as land, buildings and machines is called ______.
activities.hint: Think about buying property or machines.
activities.explanation: Investment means spending money on assets such as land, buildings and machines.

activities.title: Match the terms
activities.prompt: Match each term with its correct meaning.
pairs: A company owning production in more than one nation.
Removing restrictions on trade and investment.
A box loaded intact onto ships, railways, planes and trucks.
A device that helps communication from remote areas.
activities.explanation: These terms describe business, government policy, transport and communication.

activities.title: Popular Chinese toys
activities.prompt: Why did Chinese toys become popular in India?
options: They were cheaper and had new designs.
They were heavier and had old designs.
They were larger and cost more money.
They were softer and used less fuel.
activities.explanation: Chinese toys became popular because they were cheaper and had new designs.

activities.title: Prices across markets
activities.prompt: Prices of similar goods tend to become equal as foreign trade grows.
activities.explanation: Growing trade links markets, so similar goods tend to have similar prices.

activities.title: How MNC production spreads
activities.prompt: Put these steps in the order described by an MNC's global production.
items: MNC divides production into small parts.
MNC spreads those parts across the globe.
Production in widely separated places becomes linked.
activities.explanation: An MNC divides and spreads production. Business relationships then link widely separated places.

activities.title: Meaning of liberalisation
activities.prompt: What does liberalisation mean in this lesson?
options: Removing restrictions on trade and investment.
Adding limits on foreign buyers.
Raising taxes on every imported item.
Giving all factories to MNC owners.
activities.explanation: Liberalisation means removing government restrictions on foreign trade and foreign investment.

activities.title: Rising foreign investment
activities.prompt: Foreign investment by MNCs in developing countries has stayed unchanged.
activities.explanation: Foreign investment by MNCs in developing countries has been rising.

activities.title: Unequal effects
activities.prompt: Not everyone has benefited equally from globalisation.
activities.explanation: Effects differ among producers and workers. Some face losses or insecure jobs.

chapters.title: Consumer Rights
chapters.summary: In this chapter: consumers in the marketplace; the consumer movement; rights to safety and information; choice and seeking justice.

lessons.title: Consumers in the marketplace

activities.prompt: How can you make sure sellers treat you fairly in the marketplace?
activities.explanation: Now read on to find out.

activities.title: Consumers in the marketplace
activities.body: Consumers join the market when they buy goods and services they need. The goods they buy are final goods because people use them. Rules and regulations help protect consumers. Buyers may feel weak because sellers may blame them, give less weight, add charges, or sell defective goods. Producers can also use wealth, power and reach to shape the market. False information may spread through media.
keyPoints: Consumers join the market by buying needed goods and services.
Rules and regulations help protect consumers.
Buyers may face weak positions, unfair practices and false information.
activities.explanation: This card introduces how buyers and sellers can affect the marketplace.

activities.prompt: A shopper buys food from a stall. The seller gives short weight and adds a hidden charge. What should the shopper do?
steps: Short weight harms the consumer because the buyer gets less goods.
Hidden charges also harm the consumer because the final cost becomes higher.
The seller may blame the buyer, but buyers often have weak positions.
The shopper should complain about both problems because rules protect consumers.
activities.explanation: Think it through with Hooty.

activities.title: Joining the market
activities.prompt: Which action means a consumer takes part in the market?
options: Buying needed goods and services
Giving less weight to goods
Adding unmentioned charges
Passing false information
activities.explanation: Consumers take part in the market when they buy goods and services they need.

activities.title: Protecting consumers
activities.prompt: Rules and ______ are needed to protect consumers in the marketplace.
activities.hint: This word works with rules to protect buyers.
activities.explanation: Rules and regulations are needed to protect consumers in the marketplace.

activities.title: Final goods
activities.prompt: Final goods are goods that people use.
activities.explanation: Goods bought by consumers are final goods because people use them.

activities.title: The position of buyers
activities.prompt: Which statement about buyers is true?
options: Individual buyers often feel weak.
Shopkeepers always give full weight.
Consumers usually buy large amounts.
Traders always mention every charge.
activities.explanation: Individual consumers often find themselves in a weak position.

activities.title: How consumers buy
activities.prompt: Consumers usually purchase goods in ______ amounts and are scattered.
activities.hint: Think about the usual quantity bought by each consumer.
activities.explanation: Consumers usually purchase goods in small amounts and are scattered.

activities.title: Why rules matter
activities.prompt: Why do rules and regulations matter when traders add unmentioned charges?
options: They are needed to protect consumers.
They make consumers buy larger amounts.
They allow traders to add extra charges.
They give consumers greater market power.
activities.explanation: Traders may add unmentioned charges, so rules and regulations are needed to protect consumers.

activities.prompt: A powerful producer has wide reach. False information appears in the media. What may happen?
options: The producer will soon lose all power in the market.
Small buyers will gain control over the producer's market.
The producer may use false information to manipulate the market.
Every media message will give buyers equal power.

why.The producer will soon lose all power in: The producer lacks the power or reach to affect many buyers.
why.Small buyers will gain control over the: Small buyers do not gain market power just because false information appears.
why.Every media message will give buyers equ: The fact says media can pass information, not give buyers equal power.

activities.explanation: Its wealth and reach can spread false information and manipulate the market.

activities.prompt: First, a market has no rules. Later, seller rules are introduced. A buyer complains about a hidden charge. What changes?
options: Consumer protection is stronger in the later market.
Sellers have less need to follow fair market rules.
Buyers now have more power over every seller.
Hidden charges become easier for sellers to add.

why.Sellers have less need to follow fair ma: This reverses the purpose of rules and regulations in the marketplace.
why.Buyers now have more power over every se: One complaint does not give buyers power over every seller.
why.Hidden charges become easier for sellers: Rules protect consumers, but they do not give every buyer equal power.

activities.explanation: Rules and regulations are needed to protect consumers from hidden charges.

activities.prompt: A government rule says sellers must show every charge before sale. A trader adds a new fee later. What should happen?
options: The trader should be allowed to add the fee later.
The consumer should have to accept the extra charge.
The rule should apply only to large companies.
The consumer should be able to challenge the extra charge.

why.The trader should be allowed to add the: This allows hidden charges, which consumer rules should prevent.
why.The consumer should have to accept the e: The consumer does not have to accept charges that were never mentioned.
why.The rule should apply only to large comp: Rules protect all consumers in the marketplace, not only large companies.

activities.explanation: The fee was not mentioned, and rules are needed to protect consumers.

activities.prompt: A consumer complains about short weight. The seller says the buyer chose the goods. Why might the seller do this?
options: The seller may shift blame to avoid responsibility.
The seller may want to protect every consumer equally.
The seller may think short weight helps the buyer.
The seller may expect the buyer to thank the seller.

why.The seller may want to protect every con: Protecting consumers does not mean shifting blame away from sellers.
why.The seller may think short weight helps: Giving short weight helps the seller, not the buyer.
why.The seller may expect the buyer to thank: A complaint about less weight is not likely to make the buyer grateful.

activities.explanation: Sellers may put the blame for complaints on buyers.

activities.prompt: Many consumers each buy a little. One large company has great wealth and reach. Who can more easily affect the market?
options: The large company can use its wealth and reach.
Each small consumer can control the large company.
Every consumer can affect the whole market alone.
The shopkeeper can control all producers together.

why.Each small consumer can control the larg: Small, scattered consumers usually do not have equal market power.
why.Every consumer can affect the whole mark: Buying a small amount does not give one consumer control of the market.
why.The shopkeeper can control all producers: The facts show large companies have power, not shopkeepers controlling producers.

activities.explanation: Large companies can use wealth, power, and reach to manipulate the market.

lessons.title: The consumer movement

activities.prompt: How did people unite to make unfair treatment stop?
activities.explanation: Now read on to find out.

activities.title: Why the consumer movement began
activities.body: Many consumers were unhappy with sellers. They had no legal system for protection from exploitation. Food shortages, hoarding, black marketing and adulteration helped start the movement. Unhappy buyers sometimes stopped buying a brand or visiting a shop. Over many years, organisations built awareness and made the movement a strong social force.
keyPoints: Many consumers were dissatisfied with sellers.
Food shortages and unfair trading helped start the movement.
Organisations created awareness and protected consumers' interests.
activities.explanation: These problems explain why the movement focused on fair treatment.

activities.prompt: Food is being hoarded during a shortage. What should consumers do?
steps: Consumers should speak out because hoarding helped start the movement.
They should spread awareness because people need consumer protection.
They should use COPRA because consumers once lacked legal protection.
Consumer pressure can protect interests because it can correct unfair conduct.
activities.explanation: Think it through with Hooty.

activities.title: The movement and consumer law
activities.body: The organised consumer movement in India began during the 1960s. The United Nations adopted its Consumer Protection Guidelines in 1985. India enacted the Consumer Protection Act 1986, called COPRA. COPRA was amended in 2019. The movement became a social force for protecting consumers' interests.
keyPoints: The organised movement began during the 1960s.
The United Nations adopted its guidelines in 1985.
India enacted COPRA in 1986 and amended it in 2019.
activities.explanation: The lesson links the movement's organisation with later legal protection.

activities.title: Why did the movement begin?
activities.prompt: Why did the consumer movement begin in India?
options: Many consumers were dissatisfied with sellers.
Most buyers were pleased with every shop.
Consumer organisations had already finished their work.
Food shortages had completely ended.
activities.explanation: Many consumers were dissatisfied with sellers, so they started the movement.

activities.title: What unhappy buyers did
activities.prompt: Unhappy consumers often stopped buying a brand or visiting a shop.
activities.explanation: This was one way consumers showed their dissatisfaction with sellers.

activities.title: Parts of the consumer movement
activities.prompt: Match each part of the consumer movement with its description.
activities.explanation: Buyers once checked products, while the movement later protected their interests.

activities.title: When the movement began
activities.prompt: The organised consumer movement in India began during the ______.
activities.hint: Choose the decade from your book.
activities.explanation: The organised consumer movement in India began during the 1960s.

activities.title: Put the events in date order
activities.prompt: Put these events in date order, from earliest to latest.
items: United Nations adopts Consumer Protection Guidelines — 1985
India enacts Consumer Protection Act, known as COPRA — 1986
activities.explanation: The dates run from the 1960s through 2019.

activities.title: A need for legal protection
activities.prompt: A buyer faces exploitation without legal protection. Which later development best addresses this problem?
options: India enacted COPRA in 1986.
Sellers began checking products for buyers.
Buyers were told to check every product carefully.
The movement supported unfair business conduct.
activities.explanation: The lesson says India enacted COPRA after consumers lacked legal protection.

activities.prompt: A buyer dislikes how a seller behaves. What might the buyer do?
options: Stop buying that brand or visiting that shop
Ask the seller to treat buyers more fairly
Check every product carefully before buying it
Wait for other buyers to decide what to do

why.Ask the seller to treat buyers more fair: This assumes one buyer can make the seller change alone.
why.Check every product carefully before buy: This repeats the old duty of buyers to check products.
why.Wait for other buyers to decide what to: This overlooks the direct action unhappy consumers often took.

activities.explanation: Unhappy consumers often stopped buying a brand or visiting a shop.

activities.prompt: A timeline shows two consumer events. Which one came first?
options: India's organised movement began in the 1960s
The UN adopted its consumer guidelines in 1985
The Indian government enacted COPRA in 1986
The Indian government amended COPRA in 2019

why.The UN adopted its consumer guidelines i: The UN guidelines came after India's 1960s movement began.
why.The Indian government enacted COPRA in 1: COPRA in 1986 came after India's 1960s movement began.
why.The Indian government amended COPRA in 2: The 2019 amendment came after India's 1960s movement began.

activities.explanation: The 1960s came before the other listed events.

activities.prompt: A shop notice tells buyers to check products. What does it show?
options: Buyers once had to check products themselves
Sellers once received legal protection from buyers
Consumers once had a national protection law
Shops once faced organised consumer pressure

why.Sellers once received legal protection f: This swaps the roles of buyers and sellers in the notice.
why.Consumers once had a national protection: This confuses the old buyer duty with later legal protection.
why.Shops once faced organised consumer pres: This confuses buyer duties with the movement's pressure on businesses.

activities.explanation: The notice shows that buyers were responsible for checking products.

activities.prompt: An organisation teaches consumer protection for years. Why might this take long?
options: Many people still needed to learn about consumer protection
Buyers already knew every seller treated them fairly
Shops wanted people to keep checking products
The law already protected every consumer everywhere

why.Buyers already knew every seller treated: This assumes buyers already knew how to protect themselves.
why.Shops wanted people to keep checking pro: This confuses awareness work with the old duty to check products.
why.The law already protected every consumer: This confuses awareness work with legal protection through COPRA.

activities.explanation: Creating awareness among people took many years.

activities.prompt: A consumer group pressures an unfair business. What change may follow?
options: The business corrects its unfair conduct
The business keeps every unfair practice unchanged
Buyers must again check every product
The business begins hoarding food during shortages

why.The business keeps every unfair practice: This is the opposite of what consumer pressure seeks to achieve.
why.Buyers must again check every product: This repeats the old burden placed on buyers.
why.The business begins hoarding food during: Hoarding helped start the movement; it was not its goal.

activities.explanation: Consumer pressure can make businesses correct unfair conduct.

lessons.title: Rights to safety and information

activities.prompt: What should you do when a product feels unsafe or too mysterious?
activities.explanation: Now read on to find out.

activities.title: Your safety and information rights
activities.body: Consumers have rights to safety and information. They can know product details, including ingredients, dates, price, and side effects. Producers must obey safety rules. Consumers have the right to protection from hazardous services. You can get a defective product replaced within its expiry period. You can also bargain for a price below the MRP.
keyPoints: Consumers have the right to protection from hazardous services.
Packaging can show ingredients, price, dates, and batch number.
Medicine packets can show side effects and linked risks.
Defective products within expiry can be replaced.
Consumers can bargain below the MRP.
activities.explanation: These rights help you stay safe and make informed choices.

activities.prompt: A shop sells medicine after its expiry date. Why can the seller face severe action?
steps: The medicine's expiry date has passed, so it is expired.
The replacement rule applies to defective products found within their expiry period.
Severe action can be taken against sellers of expired medicines.
Therefore, the seller can face severe action because the medicine is expired.
activities.explanation: Think it through with Hooty.

activities.prompt: Which right protects you from hazardous services?
options: Protection from hazardous services
Knowledge of product particulars
Compensation from every hospital
Replacement of every product
activities.explanation: Protection from hazardous services is a consumer safety right.

activities.prompt: Producers may ignore required safety rules.
activities.explanation: Producers must follow the required safety rules and regulations.

activities.prompt: A medicine packet can show side effects and ______.
activities.hint: These may be linked with using the medicine.
activities.explanation: Medicine packets can show side effects and risks linked with using the medicine.

activities.prompt: A pressure cooker has a defective safety valve. What can happen?
options: A lower price below MRP
A product replacement
A serious accident
Severe seller action
activities.explanation: A defective safety valve in a pressure cooker can cause a serious accident.

activities.prompt: Consumers can bargain with sellers for a price below the MRP.
activities.explanation: Consumers can bargain with sellers to sell goods below the MRP.

activities.prompt: Which account matches Reji’s case?
options: A defective valve caused brain abnormalities; sellers faced severe action.
Improper anaesthesia caused brain abnormalities; the Commission directed compensation.
Expired medicine caused brain abnormalities; sellers faced severe action.
Unsafe packaging caused brain abnormalities; the Commission directed compensation.
activities.explanation: Improper anaesthesia caused Reji’s brain abnormalities and crippling. The National Commission directed the hospital to pay compensation.

activities.prompt: A packet shows ingredients, price, batch number, manufacture date, and expiry date. Which right does this packet support?
options: The right to know the goods' particulars.
The right to receive compensation from hospitals.
The right to bargain for prices below MRP.
The right to replace every defective product.

why.The right to receive compensation from h: This mixes product information with hospital compensation.
why.The right to bargain for prices below MR: This mixes the right to know with the right to bargain.
why.The right to replace every defective pro: This ignores that replacement applies within the expiry period.

activities.explanation: This is right because consumers can know the particulars of goods and services.

activities.prompt: A producer sells pressure cookers, and a buyer wants a lower price. Who must follow which rule?
options: Producer follows safety rules; consumer can bargain below MRP.
Consumer follows safety rules; producer can bargain below MRP.
Producer replaces expired items; consumer reads medicine risks.
Consumer follows safety rules; producer ignores required rules.

why.Consumer follows safety rules; producer: This wrongly swaps the duties and rights of producers and consumers.
why.Producer replaces expired items; consume: This mixes producer duties with expiry rules and medicine information.
why.Consumer follows safety rules; producer: This wrongly gives the producer's duty to the consumer and ignores safety rules.

activities.explanation: This is right because producers follow safety rules and consumers can bargain below MRP.

activities.prompt: One product is defective but within its expiry date. Another medicine is expired. Which seller can face severe action?
options: The seller of the expired medicine.
The seller of the defective product.
Both sellers can face the same severe action.
Neither seller can face any severe action.

This confuses replacement for defective products with action against expired medicine sellers.
why.Both sellers can face the same severe ac: This wrongly treats defective products and expired medicines as the same case.
why.Neither seller can face any severe actio: This wrongly ignores the rule about sellers of expired medicines.

activities.explanation: This is right because severe action can be taken against sellers of expired medicines.

lessons.sceneCaption: Medicine package inserts help patients learn about risks and adverse events.

lessons.title: Choice and seeking justice

activities.prompt: What should you do when a service feels unfair?
activities.explanation: Now read on to find out.

activities.title: Your rights as a consumer
activities.body: Consumers can choose whether to keep receiving a service. Redressal means seeking a fair solution to an unfair trade practice. Abirami’s refund request for one year was denied. The District Commission directed her institute to refund Rs 28,000. The State Commission fined the institute for a frivolous appeal. You can complain without a lawyer or join a class action suit. Video conferencing lets you join a commission case through video.
keyPoints: You can choose whether to continue receiving a service.
You can seek redressal for unfair trade practices.
You can complain without a lawyer or with other consumers.
activities.explanation: Learning these rights helps you make choices and seek fair solutions.

activities.prompt: Several consumers face the same unfair trade practice. Some suffer different damage. How can they seek justice together?
steps: They can seek redressal, because unfair trade practices need fair answers.
They can complain without a lawyer, because legal help is not needed.
They can join a class action suit, because consumers can complain together.
Compensation should match each person's damage, because payment depends on its degree.
activities.explanation: Think it through with Hooty.

activities.prompt: Consumers can choose whether to continue receiving a service.
activities.explanation: Every consumer has this right. It lets you decide whether to keep the service.

activities.prompt: What happened to Abirami’s refund request for one year?
options: The request was denied
Her request was accepted
Her complaint was withdrawn
Her case was dismissed
activities.explanation: Her request was denied. Later, the District Commission directed a refund of Rs 28,000.

activities.prompt: Gas suppliers cannot force new customers to buy their ______.
activities.hint: Choose the item named in the lesson.
activities.explanation: New gas customers cannot be forced to buy the gas suppliers’ stoves.

activities.prompt: Match each idea with the correct rule.
pairs: Cannot force new customers to buy stoves
activities.explanation: These pairs connect service choice, gas purchases, unfair practices, and group complaints.

activities.prompt: A consumer faces an unfair trade practice. What can they seek?
options: Seek redressal
Buy a new stove
Choose a new supplier
Attend a class action
activities.explanation: Redressal is the route for unfair trade practices. It means seeking a fair solution.

activities.prompt: Put the events in the correct order.
items: District Commission directs a refund of Rs 28,000
State Commission fines the institute for a frivolous appeal
activities.explanation: The State Commission acted after the institute made a frivolous appeal.

activities.prompt: What guides the amount of compensation for a consumer?
options: The degree of damage
The number of complaints
The consumer’s age
The supplier’s address
activities.explanation: Compensation depends on how much damage occurred. The degree of damage guides its amount.

activities.prompt: Consumers may use video conferencing and may complain without a lawyer.
activities.explanation: Both options are allowed. A consumer can use video conferencing and need not use a lawyer.

activities.prompt: A new gas customer does not want a stove. The customer wants to choose whether to continue service. What should the supplier do?
options: Let the customer continue or leave and refuse the stove.
Force the customer to buy a stove before continuing.
Make the customer continue until the stove is bought.
Stop gas service because the customer refuses the stove.

why.Force the customer to buy a stove before: This wrongly treats buying the stove as a condition of service.
why.Make the customer continue until the sto: This wrongly removes the customer's choice to continue or leave.
why.Stop gas service because the customer re: This wrongly punishes the customer for making a free choice.

activities.explanation: The customer can choose whether to continue, and the stove cannot be forced.

activities.prompt: A consumer suffers loss from an unfair trade practice. The shop refuses to solve it. What can the consumer do next?
options: Use the right to seek redressal for the unfair practice.
Keep buying because the shop's refusal ends the right.
Wait because redressal applies only to service choices.
Avoid complaints because the loss is already known.

why.Keep buying because the shop's refusal e: This wrongly thinks the shop's refusal removes the consumer's right.
why.Wait because redressal applies only to s: This wrongly limits redressal to choosing whether to continue a service.
why.Avoid complaints because the loss is alr: This wrongly thinks knowing the loss removes the need for redressal.

activities.explanation: Unfair trade practices give consumers a right to seek redressal.

lessons.title: Forums and redressal

activities.prompt: What can you do when a consumer problem feels too big to handle alone?
activities.explanation: Now read on to find out.

activities.title: How consumers seek justice
activities.body: Consumer forums and consumer protection councils help you seek justice. They show you how to file cases. They sometimes represent individual consumers before commissions. The government supports these voluntary organisations for awareness work. Residents’ Welfare Associations can take up cases for members. COPRA created a three-tier system with district, state and national levels for deciding consumer claims. You can also represent yourself before commissions.
keyPoints: Consumer forums and councils help you seek justice.
They guide case filing and may represent you.
COPRA created district, state and national levels.
Residents’ Welfare Associations can support members.
You can represent yourself before commissions.
activities.explanation: These bodies give consumers several paths to justice.

activities.prompt: A consumer has a problem, does not know how to file a case, and wants help.
steps: Start with a consumer forum or council because these organisations help consumers seek justice.
Ask the organisation for filing help because it shows consumers how to file cases.
If the consumer cannot speak alone, the organisation may speak for them because it sometimes represents individual consumers.
So the consumer can use the organisation’s help or represent themselves before a consumer commission.
activities.explanation: Think it through with Hooty.

activities.prompt: What do consumer forums and consumer protection councils help consumers do?
options: Seek justice
Select members
Set claim limits
Give financial support
activities.explanation: These organisations help consumers seek justice.

activities.prompt: Consumer protection councils sometimes represent individual consumers before commissions.
activities.explanation: The councils sometimes represent individual consumers before commissions.

activities.prompt: Residents’ Welfare Associations can take up cases for their ______.
activities.hint: These are the people whose cases the associations can take up.
activities.explanation: Residents’ Welfare Associations can take up cases for their members.

activities.prompt: What is the government’s financial support for these voluntary organisations used for?
options: Awareness work
Member selection
Claim decisions
Case representation
activities.explanation: The government gives financial support for awareness work.

activities.prompt: COPRA gives consumers the right to represent themselves before consumer commissions.
activities.explanation: Consumers have this right under COPRA.

activities.prompt: Match each commission with the claims it deals with.
pairs: Claims from Rs 1 crore to Rs 10 crore
activities.explanation: These pairs show the claim limits given in the lesson.

activities.prompt: A consumer can appeal from a district commission only to a state commission.
activities.explanation: Consumers can appeal to both state and national commissions.

activities.prompt: Put these consumer commission levels in order from district to national.
activities.explanation: COPRA created these levels from district to national.

activities.prompt: Government gives voluntary organisations money for awareness work. What can this support help consumers do?
options: Consumers should learn how to file cases.
Consumers should receive direct payments for complaints.
Consumers should stop needing consumer forums and councils.
Consumer commissions should receive all this support directly.

why.Consumers should receive direct payments: This wrongly assumes that support is used to pay consumers directly.
why.Consumers should stop needing consumer f: This wrongly assumes that awareness work makes justice organisations unnecessary.
why.Consumer commissions should receive all: This wrongly assumes that the support goes to commissions instead of voluntary organisations.

activities.explanation: Awareness support helps consumers learn where and how to file cases.

lessons.title: Well-informed consumers and the movement ahead

activities.prompt: How can I become a smarter, more confident consumer?
activities.explanation: Now read on to find out.

activities.title: Becoming a well-informed consumer
activities.body: Consumers who know their rights can distinguish between choices and make informed decisions. Becoming a well-informed consumer needs knowledge and skill. Quality certification helps consumers feel confident. Producers may use quality logos only if they follow required standards. Certain products that affect health and safety need compulsory certification. Consumer movements work best when consumers take active part.
keyPoints: Consumer rights support informed decisions.
Knowledge and skill help consumers decide well.
Active participation helps consumer movements.
activities.explanation: Your rights, knowledge and skills help you make informed decisions.

activities.prompt: A child wants to buy a product with a quality logo. How can the child be a well-informed consumer?
steps: Check the quality certification, because it can build your confidence.
Check the producer’s standards, because logos are allowed only with them.
Learn your rights, because knowledge and skill support informed choices.
Therefore, you can choose confidently instead of choosing without information.
activities.explanation: Think it through with Hooty.

activities.title: Your rights help you choose
activities.prompt: What can consumers do when they know their rights?
options: They can no longer compare products.
They must accept the first product offered.
They can distinguish between choices.
They lose the ability to decide.
activities.explanation: Knowing your rights helps you compare choices and decide wisely.

activities.title: Using quality logos
activities.prompt: When may producers use quality logos?
options: Even when required standards are ignored.
Only if they follow required standards.
Whenever competitors use the same logo.
After changing the product's colour.
activities.explanation: Quality logos are allowed only when required standards are followed.

activities.title: National Consumers’ Day
activities.prompt: India observes National Consumers’ Day on ______ in December.
activities.hint: Use the date given in the lesson.
activities.explanation: India observes National Consumers’ Day on 24 December.

activities.title: Connect consumer issues
activities.prompt: Match each consumer issue with its correct meaning.
pairs: May be used only with required standards
activities.explanation: Each pair connects a consumer issue with the correct lesson idea.

activities.title: Changes in consumer protection
activities.prompt: Which statement about consumer protection is correct?
options: Internet purchases count, but redressal is always quick.
Internet purchases count, and makers answer for defects.
Internet purchases do not count, and makers avoid responsibility.
Redressal is simple, but makers never answer for defects.
activities.explanation: Internet purchases are covered by amended COPRA. Makers can be held responsible for defects and service deficiencies. Redressal can be costly, slow and complicated.

activities.title: India’s consumer movement
activities.prompt: Which statement best describes India’s consumer movement?
options: No groups exist, and consumers act together.
Many groups exist, but consumers should stay inactive.
More than 2000 groups exist, and consumers act.
More than 2000 groups exist, but consumers stay inactive.
activities.explanation: India has more than 2000 consumer groups. Consumer movements work best when consumers take active part.

activities.prompt: A girl compares two products with quality logos. She checks the producer’s standards. What will happen?
options: She can feel confident and make a better informed choice.
She can be sure every product is safe, whatever its standards.
She must reject both products because logos need standards.
She should choose the logo and stop checking.

why.She can be sure every product is safe, w: Wrong: A quality logo does not remove the need to follow required standards.
why.She must reject both products because lo: Wrong: Logos are allowed when standards are followed, not rejected for having them.
why.She should choose the logo and stop chec: Wrong: Checking rights and standards helps an informed decision, so checking should continue.

activities.explanation: Right: Certification builds confidence, and checking standards supports an informed choice.

activities.prompt: A product can affect people’s health and safety. A shop wants to sell it. What must the shop do?
options: Get the required certification before selling it.
Use any logo without checking the standards.
Wait for consumers to form a group.
Give buyers a promise instead of certification.

why.Use any logo without checking the standa: Wrong: This treats a logo as a substitute for compulsory certification.
Wrong: Consumer groups do not replace health and safety certification.
why.Give buyers a promise instead of certifi: Wrong: A promise is not the required certification for such products.

activities.explanation: Right: Certification is compulsory for products that affect health and safety.

activities.prompt: Ravi buys a product online and finds a service problem. Which rule now helps him?
options: The amended COPRA can cover his internet purchase.
The old rule covers only purchases made in shops.
Online purchases are never covered by COPRA.
He must leave his internet purchase out of his claim.

why.The old rule covers only purchases made: Wrong: This wrongly limits COPRA to purchases made in physical shops.
why.Online purchases are never covered by CO: Wrong: This confuses old coverage with the amended rule.
why.He must leave his internet purchase out: Wrong: This assumes internet purchases cannot be included in a claim.

activities.explanation: Right: The amended COPRA includes purchases made through the internet.

activities.prompt: A consumer has a defective product and poor service. A claim may take time and money. What should the consumer expect?
options: The maker may be responsible, while claims can be costly and slow.
The maker can never be responsible, and every claim is easy.
Only a quality logo can fix the product and service.
The consumer should stop trying because all claims fail.

why.The maker can never be responsible, and: Wrong: This wrongly assumes makers have no responsibility for faults.
why.Only a quality logo can fix the product: Wrong: This confuses quality certification with a remedy for every fault.
why.The consumer should stop trying because: Wrong: This assumes a difficult process means no claim can succeed.

activities.explanation: Right: Makers can be responsible, while redressal can be costly, slow, and complicated.
