chapters.title: Human Development
chapters.summary: In this chapter: the pre-modern world; a nineteenth-century world economy; technology, colonialism and rinderpest; indentured labour and indian trade.

lessons.title: The Pre-modern World

activities.prompt: How did distant places and new foods become connected before modern times?
activities.explanation: Now read on to find out.

activities.title: How the World Connected
activities.body: Long-distance trade connected far-off places. Coastal trade linked the Indus valley with West Asia. Silk routes crossed land and sea, carrying Chinese pottery. Buddhism spread in different directions from eastern India. In the sixteenth century, the pre-modern world became much smaller. The origins of spaghetti and noodles may never be known. Smallpox spread, while American crops transformed trade and lives.
keyPoints: Coastal trade joined the Indus valley and West Asia.
Silk routes carried Chinese pottery over land and by sea.
The pre-modern world became smaller in the sixteenth century.
activities.explanation: Trade, travel, disease and American crops connected far-off lives.

activities.prompt: A poor Irish family depends heavily on potatoes. Disease destroys the crop. What may happen to the family's food supply?
steps: Poor Irish families relied on potatoes, so the crop mattered greatly.
The disease destroyed that crop, so an important food source was lost.
Their heavy dependence made this loss especially dangerous for their food supply.
Therefore, the crop failure could cause serious hunger among poor Irish families.
activities.explanation: Think it through with Hooty.

activities.prompt: Which places were linked by long-distance coastal trade?
options: The Indus valley and West Asia
The Indus valley and China
The Maldives and East Africa
China and eastern India
activities.explanation: This trade joined the Indus valley with West Asia by 3000 BCE.

activities.prompt: Many common foods were unknown to our ancestors until about ______ centuries ago.
activities.hint: Think about a long gap in time.
activities.explanation: Many common foods were unknown to our ancestors until about five centuries ago.

activities.prompt: Match each item with its matching detail.
activities.explanation: These pairs show the routes, pottery and faith described in the lesson.

activities.prompt: What happened to the potato crop in the mid-1840s?
options: Disease destroyed it.
Trade enlarged it.
Rain improved it.
Salt protected it.
activities.explanation: Poor Irish peasants depended on potatoes. Disease destroyed their crop in the mid-1840s.

activities.prompt: Put these changes in time order from earliest to latest.
items: Coastal trade linked the Indus valley with West Asia by 3000 BCE.
The pre-modern world became much smaller in the sixteenth century.
Disease destroyed the potato crop in the mid-1840s.
activities.explanation: These dates run from the earliest event to the latest.

activities.prompt: What did smallpox do before Europeans arrived in the continent?
options: It spread deep into the continent.
It stayed in eastern India.
It ended coastal trade.
It saved potato crops.
activities.explanation: Smallpox spread deep into the continent ahead of Europeans.

activities.prompt: By 3000 BCE, coastal trade linked the Indus valley with West Asia. Cowrie shells from the Maldives reached China and East Africa. What do these facts show?
options: Long-distance trade connected many distant places.
All trade stayed inside the Indus valley.
Trade happened only after Europeans arrived.
Every trade route carried only one kind of good.

why.All trade stayed inside the Indus valley: This wrongly assumes trade stayed inside one region.
why.Trade happened only after Europeans arri: The facts show trade without needing European traders.
why.Every trade route carried only one kind: This assumes each route carried just one kind of good.

activities.explanation: Both facts directly show trade reaching distant places.

activities.prompt: Historians identified several silk routes, both over land and by sea. Chinese pottery also travelled along these routes. What does the pottery's journey suggest?
options: These routes carried goods besides silk.
Silk routes were used only by sea traders.
All pottery came from eastern India.
Potatoes were the main trade of Asia.

why.Silk routes were used only by sea trader: This mistakes sea routes for the only routes.
This wrongly links pottery to Buddhism's origin.
This confuses pottery with another traded food.

activities.explanation: The pottery proves the routes carried more than silk.

activities.prompt: Buddhism emerged from eastern India and spread in different directions. Many common foods were unknown until about five centuries ago. What do these facts show?
options: Ideas and diets changed across different times and places.
Trade always moved beliefs faster than foods.
All foods spread in the same directions as Buddhism.
People had every common food five centuries ago.

why.Trade always moved beliefs faster than f: The facts give no speed or comparison for spreading.
why.All foods spread in the same directions: The facts do not say foods followed religion's directions.
why.People had every common food five centur: It reverses the fact that many foods were once unknown.

activities.explanation: Buddhism spread, while many familiar foods were once unknown.

activities.prompt: The exact origins of spaghetti and noodles may never be known. Many common foods were unknown until about five centuries ago. What do both facts suggest about food history?
options: Food histories can have gaps and major changes.
Every common food has one fully known beginning.
People always ate every food found today.
All new foods came from long-distance trade.

why.Every common food has one fully known be: This assumes every origin can be traced clearly.
why.People always ate every food found today: It assumes people already knew every food.
why.All new foods came from long-distance tr: The facts do not say all new foods came through trade.

activities.explanation: One origin may be unknown, and food use changed greatly.

activities.prompt: Poor Irish peasants became very dependent on potatoes. Disease destroyed the potato crop in the mid-1840s. What was likely to happen next?
options: Their food supply was put in serious danger.
Their dependence on potatoes suddenly ended.
Ireland gained many different food sources.
Long-distance trade across the world stopped.

why.Their dependence on potatoes suddenly en: Losing a crop does not remove their dependence on it.
why.Ireland gained many different food sourc: No fact says new food sources appeared in Ireland.
why.Long-distance trade across the world sto: A local crop failure does not end all world trade.

activities.explanation: Destroying a crop they depended on endangered their food supply.

activities.prompt: The pre-modern world became much smaller in the sixteenth century. America's crops and minerals began transforming trade and lives everywhere. Smallpox spread deep into the continent ahead of Europeans. Which explanation fits all three facts?
options: Connections moved trade, disease, and new goods across regions.
Europeans controlled every earlier movement across regions.
American trade alone caused the world to become smaller.
Disease and trade had no effect on distant lives.

why.Europeans controlled every earlier movem: This ignores disease spreading before Europeans and earlier trade.
why.American trade alone caused the world to: This leaves out disease and gives trade too much power.
why.Disease and trade had no effect on dista: This denies the stated changes to trade and lives.

activities.explanation: Trade, disease, and American goods all affected wider regions.

lessons.sceneCaption: The Hexi Corridor forms part of the ancient Silk Road route.

lessons.title: A Nineteenth-century World Economy

activities.prompt: How did people, goods, and money connect the nineteenth-century world?
activities.explanation: Now read on to find out.

activities.title: How the world economy changed
activities.body: The nineteenth century changed economies, societies and international relations. International exchange had three kinds of flow. These were trade in goods, people seeking work, and capital for investment. The Corn Laws let Britain restrict corn imports. Land was cleared in several regions to produce food for Britain. Money came from financial centres such as London. By 1890, a worldwide agricultural economy had taken shape.
keyPoints: Trade, workers and capital formed international flows.
Land was cleared to produce food for Britain.
By 1890, a worldwide agricultural economy had formed.
activities.explanation: Great start. These connections changed economies across the world.

activities.prompt: A child sees imported food, people leaving Europe, and money sent from London. Why did the world economy change this way?
steps: British farming could not compete with imported food, so the Corn Laws restricted corn imports.
Land was cleared in several regions to produce food for Britain.
Money came from financial centres such as London to pay for these changes.
Trade, people, and capital moved, forming a worldwide agricultural economy by 1890.
activities.explanation: Think it through with Hooty.

activities.prompt: Which flow involved cloth and wheat?
options: Trade in goods
Movement of workers
Movement of capital
Clearing for farming
activities.explanation: Cloth and wheat were goods traded between places.

activities.prompt: Movement of people looking for work was one of the three flows.
activities.explanation: Yes. People seeking work formed one of the three international flows.

activities.prompt: Capital moved for short-term or ______ investments.
activities.hint: This investment lasted for a longer time.
activities.explanation: Capital could move for both short-term and long-term investments.

activities.prompt: Put the three kinds of flow in the order presented in the lesson.
items: Movement of people looking for work
activities.explanation: Well done. The lesson presents trade, people and capital as the three flows.

activities.prompt: Which statement about the world economy by 1890 is correct?
options: A worldwide agricultural economy had formed.
International exchange had just one flow.
British farming could compete with imports.
All capital moved for short-term investment.
activities.explanation: By 1890, a worldwide agricultural economy had taken shape.

activities.prompt: Which places received nearly 50 million people from Europe?
options: America and Australia
Europe and America
London and Australia
Europe and London
activities.explanation: Nearly 50 million people moved from Europe to America and Australia.

activities.prompt: Britain restricts corn imports under the Corn Laws. British farming cannot compete with imported food. What is likely?
options: It gives British farming less competition from imported food.
It makes imported corn easier for British buyers to get.
It makes British farming need fewer workers.
It gives British shoppers more imported food choices.

why.It makes imported corn easier for Britis: This confuses restricting imports with making imports easier.
why.It makes British farming need fewer work: The facts do not say that fewer imports means fewer farm workers.
why.It gives British shoppers more imported: This confuses a limit on imports with more choices for shoppers.

activities.explanation: This is right because restricting imports gives British farming less competition.

activities.prompt: Nearly 50 million people moved from Europe to America and Australia. Why did they move?
options: They wanted mainly to trade cloth and wheat.
They were looking for work in those places.
They wanted mainly to invest money in farms.
They wanted mainly to ease corn import limits.

why.They wanted mainly to trade cloth and wh: This confuses people moving with trade in goods.
why.They wanted mainly to invest money in fa: This confuses people moving with capital moving for investment.
why.They wanted mainly to ease corn import l: This confuses people moving with government rules about corn imports.

activities.explanation: This is right because one flow was people moving to look for work.

activities.prompt: Money from London is invested in another place for many years. What does this show?
options: Trade goods moved there for a long-term investment.
People moved there to make a long-term investment.
Capital moved there for a long-term investment.
Capital moved there to trade cloth and wheat.

why.Trade goods moved there for a long-term: This mistakes the movement of goods for the movement of capital.
why.People moved there to make a long-term i: This mistakes people looking for work for money used for investment.
why.Capital moved there to trade cloth and w: This confuses investment money with the trade of goods.

activities.explanation: This is right because capital moved for short-term or long-term investments.

activities.prompt: Imagine a map from 1890 showing farming linked across many regions. What change does this show?
options: Only Britain had taken part in world farming.
International exchange had only one kind of flow.
People and capital had stopped moving between places.
A worldwide agricultural economy had taken shape.

why.Only Britain had taken part in world far: This mistakes worldwide farming for farming in Britain only.
why.International exchange had only one kind: This confuses a worldwide economy with only one flow of exchange.
why.People and capital had stopped moving be: This wrongly treats the other flows as if they had stopped.

activities.explanation: This is right because a worldwide agricultural economy had taken shape by 1890.

activities.prompt: Imagine a record showing money flowing from London to pay for land clearing. What does this tell us?
options: Money for these changes came from a financial centre.
People looking for work came from London.
Cloth and wheat were sent from London as trade.
Land was moved from London to other regions.

why.People looking for work came from London: This confuses the flow of money with the movement of people.
why.Cloth and wheat were sent from London as: This confuses investment money with trade in goods.
why.Land was moved from London to other regi: This confuses money flowing with land moving.

activities.explanation: This is right because money flowed from financial centres such as London.

lessons.title: Technology, Colonialism and Rinderpest

activities.prompt: How could new technology change the world—and hurt people too?
activities.explanation: Now read on to find out.

activities.title: How changes connected
activities.body: Railways, steamships and the telegraph transformed the nineteenth-century world. Advances grew from social, political and economic factors. Refrigerated ships carried perishable foods over long distances. Live animals used ship space, but could be slaughtered before voyages. Frozen meat lowered shipping costs and meat prices in Europe. Expanding trade caused losses of freedom and livelihoods. Britain and France added overseas territories. Explorations supported imperial projects. Fast-spreading rinderpest destroyed African livelihoods.
keyPoints: Technology changed travel, communication and food transport.
Trade and colonialism caused losses of freedom and livelihoods.
Rinderpest spread quickly and destroyed African livelihoods.
activities.explanation: This lesson connects technology, trade, colonialism and rinderpest.

activities.prompt: A family in Europe wants cheaper meat from far away. How can ships help?
steps: Live animals use much ship space, so they leave less room.
They let perishable foods travel far, so distant buyers can get meat.
Slaughter at the start means animals need not travel alive.
Frozen meat cuts shipping costs, so Europe gets lower meat prices.
activities.explanation: Think it through with Hooty.

activities.title: Important inventions
activities.prompt: Which group includes three important inventions?
options: Live animals and frozen meat
Rinderpest and African borders
Railways, steamships and telegraph
Colonial projects and perishable food
activities.explanation: Railways, steamships and the telegraph were important nineteenth-century inventions.

activities.title: Food travelled farther
activities.prompt: Refrigerated ships helped perishable foods travel over ______ distances.
activities.hint: Choose the word placed before 'distances' in the lesson.
activities.explanation: Refrigerated ships allowed perishable foods to travel over long distances.

activities.title: Effects of frozen meat
activities.prompt: What did frozen meat do?
options: Lowered shipping costs
Raised meat prices in Europe
Stopped all food travel
Increased live animal travel
activities.explanation: Frozen meat reduced shipping costs and lowered meat prices in Europe.

activities.title: Make connections
activities.prompt: Match each item to its closest link in the lesson.
activities.explanation: Each pair shows a direct connection described in the lesson.

activities.title: The impact of rinderpest
activities.prompt: Put the impact of rinderpest in order.
activities.explanation: Rinderpest spread quickly, caused cattle losses and destroyed African livelihoods.

activities.title: Exploration and empire
activities.prompt: What did explorations of Africa directly support?
options: Lower meat prices
Long-distance food travel
Rinderpest control
Imperial projects
activities.explanation: Explorations of Africa directly supported imperial projects.

activities.prompt: Britain and France made vast additions to their overseas territories. Explorations of Africa directly supported imperial projects. A colonial government wants more territory. Which action fits?
options: Explore Africa to support imperial expansion.
Explore Africa to protect every local livelihood.
Explore Africa to lower frozen meat prices.
Explore Africa to stop overseas territorial growth.

why.Explore Africa to protect every local li: Protection of livelihoods does not explain imperial expansion.
why.Explore Africa to lower frozen meat pric: Frozen meat prices were linked to shipping, not exploration.
why.Explore Africa to stop overseas territor: Stopping territorial growth is opposite to imperial expansion.

activities.explanation: Exploration directly supported imperial projects, so it fits.

activities.prompt: Live animals take much ship space. Animals can be slaughtered at the starting point. Which meat choice avoids carrying them?
options: Frozen meat, because animals can be slaughtered at the start.
Live animals, because animals are slaughtered after the voyage.
Live animals, because frozen meat needs more ship space.
Frozen meat, because frozen meat raises shipping costs.

why.Live animals, because animals are slaugh: It keeps animals alive even though they can be slaughtered earlier.
why.Live animals, because frozen meat needs: It reverses the fact that live animals use much ship space.
why.Frozen meat, because frozen meat raises: It wrongly says frozen meat raises shipping costs.

activities.explanation: Animals can be slaughtered before the voyage, so they need not travel.

activities.prompt: Rinderpest spreads quickly among cattle. An African farmer depends on these animals for a livelihood. What is likely to happen?
options: It can be destroyed by the loss of cattle.
It will be protected by straight African borders.
It will improve when meat prices fall in Europe.
It will stay safe because cattle diseases spread quickly.

why.It will be protected by straight African: Straight borders do not protect a farmer from rinderpest.
why.It will improve when meat prices fall in: European price changes do not improve this farmer’s livelihood.
why.It will stay safe because cattle disease: It reverses the danger of a fast-spreading cattle disease.

activities.explanation: Losing cattle can destroy African livelihoods.

activities.prompt: Frozen meat lowered meat prices in Europe. Rinderpest destroyed cattle and African livelihoods. Which comparison is correct?
options: Europe saw lower meat prices; Africa lost cattle-based livelihoods.
Europe lost cattle livelihoods; Africa saw lower meat prices.
Both regions lost freedom and livelihoods from frozen meat.
Both regions gained cheaper meat from rinderpest.

why.Europe lost cattle livelihoods; Africa s: It swaps the effects happening in Europe and Africa.
why.Both regions lost freedom and livelihood: It wrongly makes frozen meat cause freedom and livelihood losses.
why.Both regions gained cheaper meat from ri: It wrongly links cheaper European meat to rinderpest.

activities.explanation: It matches lower European prices and destroyed African livelihoods.

lessons.title: Indentured Labour and Indian Trade

activities.prompt: What tempted workers to cross the sea, and what did they bring along?
activities.explanation: Now read on to find out.

activities.title: Indentured Labour and Indian Trade
activities.body: Indentured labour moved Indian and Chinese workers across the world. Labourers were promised return travel to India after five years. Agents sometimes lied or forced unwilling workers to sea. Destinations included Caribbean islands. Nineteenth-century indenture was called new slavery. Cultures mixed and changed. Indian communities later grew. Nationalist leaders opposed indenture from the 1900s. Indian traders financed export farming. Britain had a trade surplus with India.
keyPoints: Indian and Chinese labourers moved across the world.
Agents sometimes lied or forced unwilling workers to sea.
Indian communities later lived in many destination countries.
Nationalist leaders began opposing indenture from the 1900s.
Indian traders financed export farming in Central and Southeast Asia.
Britain had a trade surplus with India.
activities.explanation: This lesson connects migration, trade, and later Indian communities.

activities.prompt: An agent promises return travel to India after five years. Why might a family still worry?
steps: The five-year return promise could attract families seeking work abroad.
Agents sometimes lied or forced people, so workers might lose choice.
Nineteenth-century indenture was called a new slavery, so freedom was not assured.
activities.explanation: Think it through with Hooty.

activities.prompt: Caribbean islands were main destinations for Indian indentured migrants.
activities.explanation: Yes. Caribbean islands were among the main destinations for Indian indentured migrants.

activities.prompt: Match each group with its role or result.
activities.explanation: These pairs connect migrants, agents, trade, and Indian communities.

activities.prompt: Agents always gave migrants correct information.
activities.explanation: False. Agents sometimes gave migrants false information, so they did not always tell the truth.

activities.prompt: Put these developments in the order they happened.
items: Different cultural forms mixed and changed.
Large communities of Indian descent lived there.
activities.explanation: Different forms met first. They then mixed and changed. Indian communities later lived in those countries.

activities.prompt: Which action used force against a migrant's wishes?
options: Giving migrants false information
Forcibly taking unwilling migrants to sea
Promising return travel to India
Describing indenture as new slavery
activities.explanation: This action used force. It shows how agents could take unwilling migrants to sea.

activities.prompt: In Central and Southeast Asia, which statement correctly describes two parts of Indian trade?
options: Traders financed import farming; Britain had a trade surplus with India.
Traders financed export farming; Britain had a trade deficit with India.
Bankers stopped farming finance; Britain had a trade surplus with India.
Traders financed export farming; Britain had a trade surplus with India.
activities.explanation: Indian traders financed export farming. Britain also had a trade surplus with India.

activities.prompt: A recruiter offers indentured labour abroad. He promises return travel to India after five years. What should the migrant know about this promise?
options: The promise could be false if agents gave wrong information.
The promise always stopped forced journeys to sea.
The promise meant migrants could refuse all work.
The promise ended the system called new slavery.

why.The promise always stopped forced journe: This mistake assumes that a promise always stopped forced journeys.
why.The promise meant migrants could refuse: This mistake assumes return travel removed a migrant's choice.
why.The promise ended the system called new: This mistake thinks promising return ended the slavery-like system.

activities.explanation: This is right because agents sometimes gave migrants false information.

activities.prompt: Nineteenth-century indenture was described as a new system of slavery. Indian nationalist leaders began opposing it from the 1900s. Why did they oppose it?
options: It always gave workers a safe return home.
It could deceive workers and take away their freedom.
It prevented all communities from forming abroad.
It ended all trade between India and Britain.

why.It always gave workers a safe return hom: This mistake treats the promised return as proof of safety.
why.It prevented all communities from formin: This mistake assumes communities of Indian descent never formed abroad.
why.It ended all trade between India and Bri: This mistake links opposition to indenture with ending India-Britain trade.

activities.explanation: This is right because deception and force took away workers' freedom.

activities.prompt: Britain had a trade surplus with India. Which statement best explains that balance?
options: Britain bought more from India than it sold to India.
Britain sold and bought exactly the same goods value.
India sold more goods than Britain could buy.
Britain sold more to India than it bought from India.

why.Britain bought more from India than it s: This mistake reverses the meaning of a trade surplus.
why.Britain sold and bought exactly the same: This mistake treats a surplus as equal buying and selling.
why.India sold more goods than Britain could: This mistake says India sold more than Britain bought.

activities.explanation: This is right because a surplus means more sold than bought.

lessons.title: The Inter-war Economy

activities.prompt: How did the world’s economy change after the First World War?
activities.explanation: Now read on to find out.

activities.title: How the Inter-war Economy Changed
activities.body: The First World War affected economies worldwide. It was the first modern industrial war. The United States changed from owing money to receiving money. Recovery proved difficult. In the 1920s, mass production became important in the US economy. Mass production means making many goods. Assembly lines made vehicles faster and cheaper. Mass production lowered the costs and prices of engineered goods. The Great Depression began around 1929. It had several causes.
keyPoints: The First World War affected economies worldwide and was the first modern industrial war.
The United States changed from owing money to receiving money after the war.
Mass production lowered costs and prices during the 1920s.
activities.explanation: This lesson connects war, recovery, mass production, and the Great Depression.

activities.prompt: A car maker wants to sell vehicles at lower prices. How can mass production help?
steps: The maker can use assembly lines because they allow faster and cheaper vehicle production.
Mass production lowers the costs of making engineered goods.
When costs fall, goods can be sold at lower prices.
Therefore, the maker can offer vehicles more cheaply by using mass production.
activities.explanation: Think it through with Hooty.

activities.prompt: Where was the First World War’s impact felt?
options: Only in Britain
Only in Europe
Only in the United States
Across the world
activities.explanation: The lesson says the war’s impact was felt around the world.

activities.prompt: Assembly lines allowed faster and cheaper ______ production.
activities.hint: Choose the word for the things made faster and more cheaply.
activities.explanation: Assembly lines allowed faster and cheaper vehicle production.

activities.prompt: Which effect did mass production have?
options: Engineered goods became cheaper.
All goods became dearer.
Vehicle production stopped.
Vehicle prices stopped changing.
activities.explanation: Mass production lowered both costs and prices for engineered goods.

activities.prompt: Match each economic feature with its result.
pairs: One in five workers was out of work
activities.explanation: Each pair shows an economic change or result described in the lesson.

activities.prompt: How did assembly lines change vehicle production?
options: It made production slower and dearer.
It made production faster but costlier.
It made production faster and cheaper.
It made production slower but cheaper.
activities.explanation: Assembly lines made vehicle production faster and cheaper.

activities.prompt: Put this economic chain in order.
items: Mass production became important in the 1920s
Assembly lines allowed faster and cheaper vehicle production
Mass production lowered costs and prices for engineered goods
activities.explanation: Mass production used assembly lines for faster, cheaper vehicles. This lowered costs and prices.

activities.prompt: Assembly lines let a car maker produce vehicles faster and more cheaply. What happens next?
options: Lower costs can lead to lower prices for engineered goods.
Higher costs can lead to higher prices for engineered goods.
Faster production can make vehicles harder for families to buy.
Cheaper production can make workers lose their jobs.

why.Higher costs can lead to higher prices f: This reverses the lesson that mass production lowers costs and prices.
why.Faster production can make vehicles hard: This wrongly treats faster production as making goods less affordable.
why.Cheaper production can make workers lose: This wrongly links cheaper production to job loss, which the facts do not show.

activities.explanation: This is right because mass production lowers costs and prices.

activities.prompt: After the war, one country owes the United States money. The United States is owed more overall. What does this show?
options: The United States had become an international creditor.
The United States had become an international debtor.
The United States had stopped trading with all other countries.
The United States had the same debt position as before the war.

why.The United States had become an internat: This reverses the meaning of a creditor and a debtor.
why.The United States had stopped trading wi: This confuses being a creditor with ending international trade.
why.The United States had the same debt posi: This ignores the change from an international debtor to a creditor.

activities.explanation: This is right because being owed more money makes the United States a creditor.

activities.prompt: A town has many people looking for work after the war. Why might recovery be difficult?
options: High unemployment shows that post-war economic recovery was difficult.
High unemployment shows that post-war economic recovery was easy.
High unemployment shows that mass production had completely stopped.
High unemployment shows that the war affected only one country.

why.High unemployment shows that post-war ec: This confuses unemployment with an easy economic recovery.
why.High unemployment shows that mass produc: This wrongly treats unemployment as proof that mass production stopped.
why.High unemployment shows that the war aff: This confuses local unemployment with the war's worldwide effects.

activities.explanation: This is right because high unemployment shows that recovery was difficult.

activities.prompt: A shop owner says business became much harder around 1929. What lesson explains this change?
options: The Great Depression began around 1929 and had several causes.
The Great Depression began after 1929 and had only one cause.
The Great Depression began before the 1920s mass production period.
The Great Depression began when British unemployment had disappeared.

why.The Great Depression began after 1929 an: This gets both the starting time and the number of causes wrong.
why.The Great Depression began before the 19: This wrongly puts the Depression before the 1920s production change.
why.The Great Depression began when British: This wrongly treats earlier unemployment facts as having disappeared.

activities.explanation: This is right because the Depression began around 1929 and had several causes.

activities.prompt: Source A calls the war the first modern industrial war. Source B shows effects in many countries. Source C reports 9 million deaths and 20 million injuries. What combined lesson fits?
options: The war was industrial, worldwide, and caused huge death and injury.
The war was industrial, stayed in one country, and caused huge losses.
The war lacked industry, was worldwide, and caused huge death and injury.
The war was industrial and worldwide, but caused only small losses.

why.The war was industrial, stayed in one co: This wrongly limits the worldwide effects of the war.
why.The war lacked industry, was worldwide,: This wrongly denies that the war was an industrial war.
why.The war was industrial and worldwide, bu: This wrongly treats the reported deaths and injuries as small losses.

activities.explanation: This is right because the war was industrial, worldwide, and caused huge losses.

lessons.title: Rebuilding the World Economy

activities.prompt: How did the world rebuild after World War II?
activities.explanation: Now read on to find out.

activities.title: A New World Economy
activities.body: After the Second World War, the United States led the Western world. It became dominant economically, politically and militarily. The Soviet Union was the second major influence on rebuilding. The Bretton Woods conference established the International Monetary Fund. The World Bank financed post-war rebuilding. World trade grew by over 8 per cent yearly from 1950 to 1970. The Bretton Woods system of fixed exchange rates later collapsed.
keyPoints: The United States led the Western world.
The Soviet Union was the second major influence.
The Bretton Woods system later collapsed.
activities.explanation: These points show how the world economy changed after the war.

activities.prompt: A toy factory makes many toys quickly. Most families buy very few. What could happen, and why?
steps: The factory can make more toys than families buy.
This creates a large supply without enough buyers.
Mass production cannot be sustained without mass consumption.
So more people must buy toys to keep mass production going.
activities.explanation: Think it through with Hooty.

activities.title: Independence, Production and Consumption
activities.body: Most colonies in Asia and Africa became free, independent nations. Developing countries organised themselves as the Group of 77, also called G-77. Companies called MNCs began shifting production in the late 1970s. They moved production to low-wage Asian countries. Mass production could not be sustained without mass consumption. Production therefore depended on many people buying goods.
keyPoints: Most colonies became free, independent nations.
Developing countries formed the Group of 77.
MNCs shifted production in the late 1970s.
activities.explanation: These points connect independence, economic organisation and production.

activities.prompt: Which organisation was set up to finance post-war reconstruction?
options: The World Bank
The Group of 77
The Bretton Woods conference
The International Monetary Fund
activities.explanation: The World Bank was set up to finance post-war reconstruction.

activities.prompt: The Second World War killed at least 60 million people.
activities.explanation: The lesson says that at least 60 million people died.

activities.prompt: World trade grew by over ______ per cent each year from 1950 to 1970.
activities.hint: Think of the yearly growth rate.
activities.explanation: World trade grew by over 8 per cent each year during this period.

activities.prompt: Match each description with the correct name.
pairs: Body set up to finance post-war reconstruction
Companies shifting production to low-wage Asian countries
Conference that established the International Monetary Fund
activities.explanation: The World Bank financed rebuilding, and developing countries formed the Group of 77. The other clues describe MNCs and the Bretton Woods conference.

activities.prompt: Put these dates in order from earliest to latest.
activities.explanation: Trade grew each year from 1950 to 1970. MNCs began shifting production in the late 1970s.

activities.prompt: Which statement is correct?
options: Mass production needed mass consumption.
The Bretton Woods system did not collapse.
MNCs shifted production to high-wage Asian countries.
Most colonies remained under colonial rule.
activities.explanation: Mass production needed mass consumption. The exchange-rate system collapsed, and the other claims were false.

activities.prompt: A post-war map gives the United States and Soviet Union largest symbols. What does this suggest about world power?
options: The United States led the West; the Soviet Union shaped rebuilding.
The United States and Soviet Union controlled every other country.
The Soviet Union led Africa, while the United States led Asia.
Both countries gained equal power in every part of the world.

why.The United States and Soviet Union contr: This wrongly says the two countries controlled all other countries.
why.The Soviet Union led Africa, while the U: This wrongly limits Soviet influence to Africa and United States influence to Asia.
why.Both countries gained equal power in eve: This wrongly says both countries had equal power everywhere.

activities.explanation: Right: the United States led the West; the Soviet Union ranked second.

activities.prompt: Most colonies in Asia and Africa become free nations. What do these developing countries do next?
options: They organised themselves as the Group of 77.
They created the International Monetary Fund instead.
They set fixed exchange rates for all countries.
They led the Western world during reconstruction.

why.They created the International Monetary: This confuses the IMF with a group of developing countries.
why.They set fixed exchange rates for all co: This confuses a country group with an exchange-rate system.
why.They led the Western world during recons: This wrongly gives the United States the work of G-77.

activities.explanation: Right: developing countries organised themselves as the Group of 77.

activities.prompt: In the late 1970s, an MNC moves production to an Asian country. Why might it choose this place?
options: The country offers workers lower wages than other places.
The country has no factories or workers for production.
The company wants to stop selling products to local people.
The country bans all production by large companies.

why.The country has no factories or workers: This wrongly says Asian countries lacked factories and workers.
why.The company wants to stop selling produc: This wrongly says MNCs wanted fewer buyers.
why.The country bans all production by large: This wrongly says large companies faced a production ban.

activities.explanation: Right: MNCs shifted production to low-wage Asian countries.

activities.prompt: A family expects the exchange rate to stay fixed. Later, the Bretton Woods system collapses. What should they conclude?
options: They cannot expect the old fixed rates to continue.
They should expect the fixed-rate system to become stronger.
The same fixed rates will soon start working again.
Exchange rates will now decide where factories operate.

why.They should expect the fixed-rate system: This wrongly treats collapse as stronger fixed-rate control.
why.The same fixed rates will soon start wor: This wrongly assumes the same fixed rates will simply restart.
why.Exchange rates will now decide where fac: This wrongly connects exchange rates to factory locations.

activities.explanation: Right: a collapse means the old fixed-rate system ended.

activities.context: A merchant travels the silk routes by sea, carrying Chinese pottery and cowrie shells from the Maldives toward China and East Africa. In a separate report from Ireland, disease has destroyed the potato crop in the mid-1840s, and poor Irish peasants are deeply worried because they depend so heavily on potatoes. News also arrives that American crops and minerals are transforming trade and lives far away. The merchant must explain how these connected changes affect different communities.
activities.prompt: If the Irish had become less dependent on potatoes before the crop was destroyed, what would likely happen?
options: The harm to their food supply would be smaller.
The disruption would remain exactly the same.
The disruption would become greater.
The disruption would affect only coastal traders.

why.The disruption would remain exactly the: Less dependence should reduce, rather than preserve, the disruption.
Reducing dependence works in the opposite direction.
why.The disruption would affect only coastal: A crop failure affecting food would not be limited to coastal traders.

activities.explanation: Reduced reliance on potatoes would limit the effect of losing the crop.

activities.context: A merchant travels the silk routes by sea, carrying Chinese pottery and cowrie shells from the Maldives toward China and East Africa. In a separate report from Ireland, disease has destroyed the potato crop in the mid-1840s, and poor Irish peasants are deeply worried because they depend so heavily on potatoes. News also arrives that American crops and minerals are transforming trade and lives far away. The merchant must explain how these connected changes affect different communities.
activities.prompt: If American crops and minerals enter other regions, what result would be consistent with the information in the case?
options: Trade and everyday life in other regions could begin to change.
Trade and daily life everywhere would remain unchanged.
Local products would immediately disappear from all markets.
Only American communities would experience any change.

why.Trade and daily life everywhere would re: The stated effect extends beyond America.
why.Local products would immediately disappe: Transformation does not mean that local goods completely disappear.
why.Only American communities would experien: The changes were not confined to American communities.

activities.explanation: American crops and minerals were transforming trade and lives everywhere.

activities.prompt:
Assertion (A): American crops and minerals began transforming trade and lives everywhere.
Reason (R): Long-distance trade and the movement of goods, diseases, and ideas made distant societies more closely connected.
options: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true but R is false.
A is false but R is true.
activities.explanation: Closer connections helped American crops and minerals affect trade and lives in distant regions.

activities.prompt:
Assertion (A): Cowrie shells from the Maldives reached China and East Africa.
Reason (R): Smallpox spreading deep into the continent ahead of Europeans increased the movement of cowrie shells to those regions.
options: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true but R is false.
A is false but R is true.
activities.explanation: Cowrie shells did reach both regions, but smallpox spreading ahead of Europeans is not given as a reason for that trade.

activities.prompt: How did long-distance connections change the pre-modern world?
activities.answer: Long-distance connections linked distant regions and made the pre-modern world smaller by the sixteenth century. By 3000 BCE, coastal trade connected the Indus valley with West Asia. Cowrie shells from the Maldives reached China and East Africa, while Chinese pottery also travelled along the silk routes, which ran both over land and by sea. These exchanges brought goods between societies. Buddhism emerged from eastern India and spread in different directions, while American crops and minerals began transforming trade and lives everywhere.
points: Coastal trade connected the Indus valley with West Asia by 3000 BCE.
Cowrie shells reached China and East Africa.
Chinese pottery travelled along land and sea silk routes.
Buddhism and American crops and minerals show wider connections and effects.
activities.explanation: Compare your answer with the points a marker looks for.

activities.context: By 1890, a British policymaker debated how food reached the country. British farming could not compete with imported food, and the government had restricted corn imports under the Corn Laws. Land was cleared in several regions to produce food for Britain, while money for these changes flowed from financial centres such as London. Migrants were also moving from Europe toward America and Australia.
activities.prompt: If the government stopped using the Corn Laws to restrict corn imports, which result would most likely follow?
options: British farmers would face greater competition from imported food.
British farmers would automatically gain an advantage over imported food.
Imported food would be discouraged even without the Corn Laws.
The government would still be able to limit corn imports under those laws.

why.British farmers would automatically gain: Removing a restriction would not automatically give domestic farmers an advantage over imported food.
why.Imported food would be discouraged even: Without the Corn Laws restricting them, imports would not be deliberately discouraged.
why.The government would still be able to li: The Corn Laws provided the government's power to restrict corn imports.

activities.explanation: British farming could not compete with imported food, so easier import access would increase pressure on farmers.

activities.context: By 1890, a British policymaker debated how food reached the country. British farming could not compete with imported food, and the government had restricted corn imports under the Corn Laws. Land was cleared in several regions to produce food for Britain, while money for these changes flowed from financial centres such as London. Migrants were also moving from Europe toward America and Australia.
activities.prompt: Given the trade, migration, and capital flows described, what broad development by 1890 is the most reasonable conclusion?
options: A worldwide agricultural economy had taken shape.
A worldwide economy based only on trade in goods had taken shape.
A worldwide economy based only on movement of people had taken shape.
A worldwide economy based only on short-term capital movement had taken shape.

why.A worldwide economy based only on trade: International exchange included people and capital as well as goods, so it was not based only on trade.
why.A worldwide economy based only on moveme: Movement of people was one flow, but trade and capital movement also mattered.
why.A worldwide economy based only on short-: Capital could be moved for short-term or long-term investments, and other flows also mattered.

activities.explanation: The linked changes in food production, trade, migration, and investment support this conclusion.

activities.prompt:
Assertion (A): The Corn Laws let Britain's government restrict corn imports.
Reason (R): Restricting imports was relevant because British farming could not compete with imported food.
options: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true but R is false.
A is false but R is true.
activities.explanation: The reason explains why the government had reason to restrict corn imports.

activities.prompt:
Assertion (A): International exchange involved trade in goods, movement of people seeking work, and movement of capital for investment.
Reason (R): Nearly 50 million people moved from Europe to America and Australia.
options: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true but R is false.
A is false but R is true.
activities.explanation: The migration supports one flow but does not explain the other two kinds of flow.

activities.prompt: How does the movement of goods differ from the other two flows of international exchange in the nineteenth century?
activities.answer: Trade in goods moved products such as cloth and wheat across borders. The movement of people was different because it involved people leaving Europe to look for work; nearly 50 million moved to America and Australia. The third flow moved money for short-term or long-term investments, with money coming from financial centres such as London. Thus, the exchange of goods, movement of people, and movement of capital were connected, but each had a different purpose within the changing world economy.
points: Trade in goods included products such as cloth and wheat.
People moved mainly in search of work.
Nearly 50 million people moved from Europe to America and Australia.
Capital moved for short-term or long-term investments from financial centres such as London.
activities.explanation: Compare your answer with the points a marker looks for.

activities.context: A merchant firm has begun shipping frozen meat on refrigerated steamships to Europe, where prices have fallen, and its traders are mapping the interior of Africa. Colonial officials follow these routes, claim territory, and draw African borders in ruler-straight lines. Meanwhile rinderpest, a fast-spreading cattle disease, has reached the region, and communities are losing both their cattle and their livelihoods. The firm asks whether this new trade and technology will bring Africa only benefits.
activities.prompt: If frozen meat keeps making meat cheaper in Europe, what is the most likely effect on African cattle owners who are already hit by rinderpest?
options: They face even less demand for their cattle, so their income falls further.
They would sell their remaining cattle more easily, because European buyers suddenly want local cattle.
Rinderpest would spread faster in Africa, because cheap meat attracts more ships and more herders.
African borders would be redrawn to follow the cattle routes of the new trade.

why.They would sell their remaining cattle m: European demand for African cattle would fall, not rise, when cheaper imported meat arrives.
why.Rinderpest would spread faster in Africa: Rinderpest spreads through infected cattle; meat prices do not decide how the disease travels.
why.African borders would be redrawn to foll: Border drawing is a political act by officials, not an effect of meat prices.

activities.explanation: Cheap imported meat reduces what European buyers will pay for local cattle, hurting owners whose herds have already been destroyed.

activities.context: A merchant firm has begun shipping frozen meat on refrigerated steamships to Europe, where prices have fallen, and its traders are mapping the interior of Africa. Colonial officials follow these routes, claim territory, and draw African borders in ruler-straight lines. Meanwhile rinderpest, a fast-spreading cattle disease, has reached the region, and communities are losing both their cattle and their livelihoods. The firm asks whether this new trade and technology will bring Africa only benefits.
activities.prompt: If the firm had kept sending live animals on its ships instead of frozen meat in refrigerated holds, what would probably have happened?
options: Each voyage would need more space and the meat might spoil, so European prices would stay higher.
The meat would have travelled even farther in good condition, because animals stay fresh while at sea.
The ships would have needed less space, so the firm could carry more animals for the same cost.
African borders would have been drawn earlier, since ships arriving with animals needed new ports.

why.The meat would have travelled even farth: It was refrigeration, not live animals, that let perishable foods travel over long distances.
why.The ships would have needed less space,: This reverses the fact that live animals took up a lot of space on ships.
why.African borders would have been drawn ea: Borders were drawn from exploration and imperial ambition, not from the cargo ships carried.

activities.explanation: Live animals used a lot of space and meat without refrigeration could spoil, while frozen meat cut shipping costs and prices.

activities.prompt:
Assertion (A): Explorations of Africa directly supported imperial projects.
Reason (R): European journeys produced maps and knowledge of the interior that helped colonial powers claim African territory.
options: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true but R is false.
A is false but R is true.
activities.explanation: Both statements are true, and the knowledge gained in exploration is what made claiming and dividing territory easier.

activities.prompt:
Assertion (A): Rinderpest was a fast-spreading cattle disease with a terrifying impact.
Reason (R): Refrigerated ships allowed perishable foods to travel over long distances.
options: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true but R is false.
A is false but R is true.
activities.explanation: Both statements are true, but refrigeration explains long-distance food shipping, not the spread of rinderpest or its devastation.

activities.prompt: Explain why new transport technology helped European consumers more than African communities, and how it added to African losses.
activities.answer: New transport technology helped European consumers more than African ones. Live animals took up much space on ships, but refrigerated ships let meat travel long distances, and animals could be slaughtered at the starting point instead of after the voyage. Frozen meat therefore reduced shipping costs and lowered meat prices in Europe. Yet expanding trade also caused losses of freedom and livelihoods for African communities, and technological advances often resulted from wider social, political and economic factors rather than from choice alone. Cheap European meat added pressure on herders already ruined by rinderpest, whose spread destroyed cattle and livelihoods.
points: Live animals used a lot of ship space, while refrigeration let perishables travel long distances.
Animals could be slaughtered at the starting point instead of after the voyage.
Frozen meat reduced shipping costs and lowered meat prices in Europe.
Expanding trade caused losses of freedom and livelihoods, with rinderpest destroying cattle and herders' livelihoods.
activities.explanation: Compare your answer with the points a marker looks for.

activities.context: An agent recruits workers for work on a Caribbean island. He says their five-year term includes a return journey to India. A worker who feels unwilling is taken to sea after receiving misleading details about the destination and conditions. The worker joins a community where Indian and other cultural forms influence one another. Later, Indian nationalist leaders begin calling for an end to this labour system.
activities.prompt: Which long-term outcome best matches what can happen after Indian migrants settle in the destination country?
options: A lasting community of Indian descent could emerge as cultural exchange continues.
The community would keep only one cultural form because interaction prevents exchange.
Every migrant would leave when the promised period ended, erasing the community.
The presence of Indian migrants would have no effect on later communities.

why.The community would keep only one cultur: Meeting different cultural forms can change them rather than preserve only one.
why.Every migrant would leave when the promi: Some migrants formed long-term communities despite the promise of return.
why.The presence of Indian migrants would ha: Indian migration contributed to large communities in the destination countries.

activities.explanation: Cultural interaction could support lasting communities of Indian descent.

activities.context: An agent recruits workers for work on a Caribbean island. He says their five-year term includes a return journey to India. A worker who feels unwilling is taken to sea after receiving misleading details about the destination and conditions. The worker joins a community where Indian and other cultural forms influence one another. Later, Indian nationalist leaders begin calling for an end to this labour system.
activities.prompt: What position would best represent the response of Indian nationalist leaders to this system?
options: Continue expanding the recruitment system without any change.
Oppose the system because recruitment depended on indenture.
Support the system because every migrant travelled willingly.
Leave the system unchanged because the return promise was sufficient.

why.Continue expanding the recruitment syste: Nationalist leaders called for an end to indenture.
why.Support the system because every migrant: Some migrants were deceived or taken unwillingly.
why.Leave the system unchanged because the r: The return promise did not remove the system's problems.

activities.explanation: Their opposition was directed at the recruitment system itself.

activities.prompt:
Assertion (A): Forcible removal of unwilling migrants is one reason nineteenth-century indenture was described as a new system of slavery.
Reason (R): Some agents gave migrants false information and took them to sea.
options: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true but R is false.
A is false but R is true.
activities.explanation: The statement and reason are true, and deception and force explain the description of indenture as a new system of slavery.

boss.title: Chapter challenge: Human Development

activities.prompt: Which two flows formed part of international exchange?
options: Trade in goods and workers moving
Trade in goods and capital moving
People moving and corn restrictions
Corn restrictions and overseas colonies
activities.explanation: International exchange included goods, people and capital as three flows.

activities.prompt: Poor Irish peasants depended on potatoes before disease destroyed the crop.
activities.explanation: Their dependence grew before disease destroyed the potato crop in the mid-1840s.

activities.prompt: International exchange involved three kinds of ______.
activities.hint: Think about goods, people and capital moving across countries.
activities.explanation: Trade, movement of people and movement of capital were the three flows.

activities.prompt: Match each flow or policy with its description.
activities.explanation: Each pair shows one flow or policy and its example.

activities.prompt: Put the food-shipping changes in order, from the old problem to the final result.
items: Live animals used a lot of space on ships
Refrigerated ships allowed perishable foods to travel over long distances
Animals could be slaughtered at the starting point instead of after the voyage
Frozen meat reduced shipping costs and lowered meat prices in Europe
activities.explanation: The sequence moves from crowded animal transport to cheaper meat shipping.

activities.prompt: Why did some indentured migrants have a difficult journey?
options: Agents protected every migrant during sea travel
Agents gave every migrant correct work details
Agents lied and forced unwilling migrants to sea
Agents guaranteed return travel before departure
activities.explanation: Agents sometimes lied and forced unwilling migrants to sea.

activities.prompt: After the Second World War, most colonies in Asia and Africa stayed under colonial rule.
activities.explanation: Most colonies in Asia and Africa became free, independent nations.

activities.prompt: The Bretton Woods conference established the International Monetary ______.
activities.hint: This organisation was set up at the Bretton Woods conference.
activities.explanation: The conference established the International Monetary Fund.

activities.prompt: Match each organisation or power with its role.
pairs: Dominant Western economic, political and military power
Second major influence on post-war reconstruction
Established by the Bretton Woods conference
activities.explanation: These organisations and powers shaped the post-war world.

activities.prompt: Put these global changes in time order, from earliest to latest.
items: Coastal trade linked the Indus valley with West Asia by 3000 BCE
The pre-modern world became much smaller in the sixteenth century
The nineteenth century deeply changed economies, societies and international relations
World trade grew by over 8 per cent each year from 1950 to 1970
MNCs began shifting production to low-wage Asian countries in the late 1970s
activities.explanation: These changes progress from 3000 BCE to the late 1970s.

chapters.title: The Age of Industrialisation
chapters.summary: In this chapter: progress, machines and proto-industrialisation; the coming of factories and the pace of industrial change; hand labour and the lives of workers; indian textiles and colonial control.

lessons.title: Progress, machines and proto-industrialisation

activities.prompt: How can a simple picture reveal a whole world changing?
activities.explanation: Now read on to find out.

activities.title: Progress before factories
activities.body: Modernity means a way of life shaped by rapid technological change. In 1900, a music publisher showed progress as a goddess-like angel. She carried a new century’s flag while standing on a winged wheel. The image linked modernity with rapid change, machines, factories, railways and steamships. The chapter studies Britain first, then India, where colonial rule shaped industrial change. Proto-industrialisation means large-scale production before factories became common.
keyPoints: Progress appears as a goddess-like angel.
Modernity links change, machines and new transport.
Large-scale production began before factories became common.
activities.explanation: This picture shows how progress became closely linked with industry.

activities.prompt: A merchant cannot work in town. Why might production move to the countryside?
steps: Powerful town guilds make it hard for new merchants to start businesses.
The merchant moves to the countryside and supplies money.
Peasants and artisans produce goods for the merchant's trade network.
Most production stays outside towns, showing proto-industrialisation before common factories.
activities.explanation: Think it through with Hooty.

activities.title: The Cover Announcement
activities.prompt: What did the book cover announce?
options: Dawn of the Century
Close of the Century
Music of New Machines
Railways Across Britain
activities.explanation: The cover announced the Dawn of the Century in 1900.

activities.title: Name the Early Phase
activities.prompt: Historians call this early phase of industrialisation ______.
activities.hint: Large-scale production came before factories became common.
activities.explanation: Well done! Proto-industrialisation names this early phase of industrialisation.

activities.title: People and Changes
activities.prompt: Match each group or change to its description.
activities.explanation: You matched each group with its description from the lesson.

activities.title: The Main Production Site
activities.prompt: Where did most proto-industrial production happen?
options: In town centres
In the countryside
Inside factories
On steamships
activities.explanation: Most production was in the countryside, although merchants lived in towns.

activities.title: Signs of Modernity
activities.prompt: Put these signs of modernity in the order given in the lesson.
activities.explanation: Your lesson lists these signs in this order.

activities.title: Merchants in the Countryside
activities.prompt: What did European merchants do after moving to the countryside?
options: They enclosed common lands against merchants.
They gave town factories to old guilds.
They supplied money to peasants and artisans.
They ended all large-scale rural production.
activities.explanation: They supplied money to peasants and artisans after moving to the countryside.

activities.prompt: Powerful town guilds stop new merchants from opening businesses. Where will production most likely continue?
options: In countryside workshops, because town business is blocked.
In town workshops, because guilds support new merchants.
In factories, because factories already work everywhere.
On common lands, because enclosure has not started.

why.In town workshops, because guilds suppor: This wrongly assumes guilds helped new merchants enter town trade.
why.In factories, because factories already: This wrongly assumes factories were common before proto-industrialisation.
why.On common lands, because enclosure has n: This wrongly treats common lands as land open for new factories.

activities.explanation: The countryside housed most production because merchants financed rural workers.

activities.prompt: India was under colonial rule during the period studied. What will happen if a researcher ignores this context?
options: The explanation may miss how colonial rule shaped industrial change.
Colonial rule will correctly seem irrelevant to industrial change.
Early production will appear only after factories became common.
Merchants will wrongly appear to control town production.

why.Colonial rule will correctly seem irrele: This confuses ignoring colonial rule with correctly explaining it.
why.Early production will appear only after: This mistakes proto-industrial production for production after factories.
why.Merchants will wrongly appear to control: This confuses rural production under merchant control with town production.

activities.explanation: Colonial rule shaped industrial change, so ignoring it weakens the explanation.

activities.prompt: A book cover from 1900 shows an angel carrying a flag. It also shows a winged wheel below her. What idea does this cover present?
options: A new century brings progress through modern technology.
A new century will return progress to old traditions.
A new century will stop factories and railways.
A new century will end merchants' control of trade.

why.A new century will return progress to ol: This wrongly treats progress as a return to older traditions.
why.A new century will stop factories and ra: Modernity was linked to factories, railways and steamships, not stopping them.
why.A new century will end merchants' contro: The cover says nothing about ending merchant control of trade.

activities.explanation: The winged wheel and progress signs point to modern technology.

activities.prompt: A town rule lets only old guild members start new businesses. What will likely happen?
options: New merchants may move to production in the countryside.
New merchants may take over the old town guilds.
Peasants may stop making goods for rural merchants.
Common lands may become open fields for peasants.

why.New merchants may take over the old town: Guild restrictions did not let new merchants take over guilds.
why.Peasants may stop making goods for rural: Blocked merchants may still need rural workers to produce goods.
why.Common lands may become open fields for: Enclosure removed common lands rather than restoring them.

activities.explanation: Blocked merchants can finance production in the countryside.

activities.prompt: A map shows merchants living in towns and workshops in the countryside. What does this suggest?
options: Merchants organised rural production while living in towns.
Most production took place inside the town centres.
Peasants and artisans controlled the whole trade network.
Factories had already replaced most countryside workshops.

why.Most production took place inside the to: This reverses the map's location of most production.
why.Peasants and artisans controlled the who: This wrongly gives trade control to the rural producers.
why.Factories had already replaced most coun: This assumes factories were common before proto-industrialisation.

activities.explanation: Merchants controlled trade while most production remained in the countryside.

activities.prompt: Enclosure reduces common lands. How can this affect proto-industrialisation?
options: Peasants may depend more on money from countryside merchants.
Peasants may gain more control of shared fields.
Town guilds may remove barriers for new merchants.
Merchants may stop funding all rural production.

why.Peasants may gain more control of shared: Enclosure removed common lands instead of giving peasants more control.
why.Town guilds may remove barriers for new: Guild barriers made new business harder, and enclosure did not remove them.
why.Merchants may stop funding all rural pro: Enclosure can increase dependence on merchant money rather than stop it.

activities.explanation: Losing common lands can push peasants towards merchant funding.

lessons.sceneCaption: The 1900 cover portrays Progress as an angelic woman standing on a winged wheel amid modern inventions.

lessons.title: The coming of factories and the pace of industrial change

activities.prompt: How did new ideas transform Britain’s factories and everyday work?
activities.explanation: Now read on to find out.

activities.title: How industry changed
activities.body: Factories began appearing in England by the 1730s. Their number multiplied mainly in the late eighteenth century. Inventions made cotton production more efficient at each stage. Richard Arkwright created a cotton mill that brought processes together. Cotton was the leading industrial sector during the first phase. After the 1840s, iron and steel led. New ideas also helped older trades, while steam engines spread slowly.
keyPoints: Factories appeared by the 1730s.
Cotton led during the first industrial phase.
New ideas improved production and older trades.
activities.explanation: Industry changed through factories, inventions and improvements across many trades.

activities.prompt: Why did cotton become a leading industrial sector?
steps: Because eighteenth-century inventions made each stage more efficient, cotton production could improve.
Richard Arkwright's cotton mill brought production processes together, so production was better organised.
Raw cotton imports rose from 2.5 million pounds in 1760 to 22 million pounds in 1787, showing a much larger supply.
Together, these facts help explain why cotton led the first phase of industrialisation.
activities.explanation: Think it through with Hooty.

activities.title: The first factories
activities.prompt: By when had the earliest factories appeared in England?
activities.explanation: The earliest factories in England had appeared by the 1730s.

activities.title: Rising cotton imports
activities.prompt: Raw cotton imports reached 22 million pounds in which year?
activities.explanation: Britain’s raw cotton imports reached 22 million pounds by 1787.

activities.title: Changes in industry
activities.prompt: Match each change with its result.
pairs: Helped pottery, furniture and food processing
activities.explanation: These changes affected cotton production, traditional trades and steam power.

activities.title: The typical worker
activities.prompt: The typical mid-nineteenth-century worker was a ______ or labourer.
activities.hint: This word describes someone skilled with their hands.
activities.explanation: The typical worker was a craftsperson or labourer, not a machine operator.

activities.title: Traditional trades and new ideas
activities.prompt: Which traditional trades did small innovations help?
options: Pottery and furniture making
Cotton and raw cotton imports
Steam engines and cotton mills
Iron and steel sectors
activities.explanation: Small innovations helped traditional trades such as pottery, furniture making and food processing.

activities.prompt: A trade record shows 2.5 million pounds of raw cotton imported in 1760 and 22 million in 1787. What does this show?
options: Raw cotton imports became much larger.
Raw cotton imports became much smaller.
Raw cotton imports stayed exactly the same.
Raw cotton imports changed only slightly.

This mistakes a large increase for a decrease.
why.Raw cotton imports stayed exactly the sa: This mistakes changing imports for unchanged imports.
why.Raw cotton imports changed only slightly: This mistakes a large increase for a small change.

activities.explanation: The rise from 2.5 million to 22 million pounds was large.

activities.prompt: Richard Arkwright's cotton mill brought production processes together. Eighteenth-century inventions made each stage more efficient. What change does this suggest?
options: More organised cotton production with efficient stages.
Less organised cotton production with slower stages.
Cotton production without any connected stages.
Cotton production using only the newest machines.

why.Less organised cotton production with sl: This mistakes bringing processes together for separating them.
why.Cotton production without any connected: This mistakes connected stages for having no stages.
why.Cotton production using only the newest: This mistakes improved stages for using only new machines.

activities.explanation: Connected processes and efficient stages supported organised cotton production.

activities.prompt: Cotton led the first phase of industrialisation. Iron and steel became leading sectors after the 1840s. What does this show?
options: The leading industrial sector changed over time.
The leading industrial sector never changed.
Only cotton remained important throughout industry.
Iron and steel led before cotton did.

why.The leading industrial sector never chan: This mistakes a changing sequence for no change.
why.Only cotton remained important throughou: This assumes cotton stayed the only important sector.
This reverses the order of the leading sectors.

activities.explanation: Cotton led first, while iron and steel led after the 1840s.

activities.prompt: The typical mid-nineteenth-century worker was a craftsperson or labourer, not a machine operator. What does this tell us?
options: Most workers did not mainly operate machines.
Most workers spent all day operating machines.
Workers never used any machines at work.
Machines had no place in mid-nineteenth-century work.

why.Most workers spent all day operating mac: This mistakes the typical worker for a machine operator.
This turns not mainly operating machines into never using them.
why.Machines had no place in mid-nineteenth-: This mistakes limited machine roles for no machine use.

activities.explanation: The typical worker was a craftsperson or labourer, not a machine operator.

activities.prompt: A pottery maker uses a small innovation in traditional pottery work. What does this show?
options: Small innovations could help traditional industries.
Traditional industries always became large factories.
Only cotton production received useful innovations.
Small innovations always ended traditional work.

why.Traditional industries always became lar: This assumes all traditional industries became factories.
why.Only cotton production received useful i: This limits helpful innovations to cotton production.
why.Small innovations always ended tradition: This mistakes helpful changes for the end of traditional work.

activities.explanation: The fact says small innovations helped traditional industries.

lessons.sceneCaption: This 1775 carding machine represents the eighteenth-century mechanisation of cotton production.
