lessons.title: Hand labour and the lives of workers

activities.prompt: Why did some factories choose hand labour instead of machines?
activities.explanation: Now read on to find out.

activities.title: Why workers turned to hand labour
activities.body: Industrialists often preferred hand labour when seasonal production rose. Their varied products needed human skill, not mechanical technology. Poor peasants and vagrants moved to cities for work. Plentiful labour kept wages low. Machines often cost too much in capital. Seasonal work could leave workers unemployed for long periods. During economic slumps, unemployment sometimes reached 35 to 75 per cent. Sharp price rises also reduced workers’ real earnings.
keyPoints: Industrialists preferred hand labour when seasonal production rose.
Workers moved to cities because they wanted employment.
Seasonal work and economic slumps caused unemployment.
activities.explanation: Hand labour suited seasonal products, while plentiful workers kept wages low.

activities.prompt: A workshop makes different goods and production rises in one season. Should it hire hand workers or buy a machine?
steps: Different products need human skill, so hand labour is suitable.
Production rises during a season, when industrialists usually preferred hand labour.
A labour-saving machine needs a large capital investment, so it is costly.
Therefore, the owner should hire hand workers when capital is limited.
activities.explanation: Think it through with Hooty.

activities.title: Workers moving to cities
activities.prompt: Poor peasants and vagrants moved to cities in large numbers seeking work.
activities.explanation: Many people left rural areas and moved to cities because they wanted work.

activities.title: Choosing hand labour
activities.prompt: Why did industrialists usually prefer hand labour?
options: When production rose during a season
When varied products needed little skill
When machines needed no capital
When seasonal jobs became permanent
activities.explanation: Production often rose during a season. Industrialists usually preferred hand labour then.

activities.title: The cost of machines
activities.prompt: Industrialists avoided labour-saving machines because they needed large ______ investments.
activities.hint: The important kind of investment named in your book.
activities.explanation: Labour-saving machines needed large capital investments, so industrialists often avoided them.

activities.title: Finding factory work
activities.prompt: People with relatives or friends in factories were more likely to find work quickly.
activities.explanation: Connections with relatives or friends helped people obtain factory work more quickly.

activities.title: Workers defending their jobs
activities.prompt: Which workers attacked machines that threatened their jobs?
options: Women who depended on hand spinning
Poor peasants who moved to cities
Vagrants who wanted factory work
Industrialists who preferred hand labour
activities.explanation: Women who depended on hand spinning attacked machines because those machines threatened their jobs.

activities.title: Unemployment during slumps
activities.prompt: What happened to unemployment in some regions during economic slumps?
options: It fell below 35 per cent
It rose to between 35 and 75 per cent
It stayed below 35 per cent
It rose above 75 per cent
activities.explanation: Your book says unemployment rose to between 35 and 75 per cent in some regions.

activities.title: Workers’ real earnings
activities.prompt: Workers’ real earnings rose when prices rose sharply during the Napoleonic War.
activities.explanation: Workers’ real earnings fell when prices rose sharply during the Napoleonic War.

activities.prompt: A factory is busy each festival season. What happens next?
options: Many workers stay without work for long periods.
All workers gain steady work throughout the year.
All workers lose their real earnings at once.
Workers begin attacking the machines instead.

why.All workers gain steady work throughout: A seasonal factory does not give every worker steady work all year.
why.All workers lose their real earnings at: Ending a busy season does not automatically make real earnings fall.
why.Workers begin attacking the machines ins: People attacked machines when their own jobs were threatened.

activities.explanation: Seasonal work can leave people without employment for long periods.

activities.prompt: Two maps show unemployment. One has 35 per cent. The other has 75 per cent. Which town faced the stronger job shortage?
options: It was the town with 75 per cent unemployment.
It was the town with 35 per cent unemployment.
It was the town with more factory machinery.
It was the town with fewer seasonal jobs.

why.It was the town with 35 per cent unemplo: The town with 35 per cent had the lower unemployment rate.
why.It was the town with more factory machin: The maps show unemployment rates, not numbers of machines.
why.It was the town with fewer seasonal jobs: The maps show unemployment rates, not details of seasonal jobs.

activities.explanation: A higher unemployment rate shows a stronger job shortage in that town.

lessons.sceneCaption: Brilliant-coloured silk threads form an exquisite sari on a handloom in Kanchipuram, Tamil Nadu.

lessons.title: Indian textiles and colonial control

activities.prompt: Why did India’s textile trade change so dramatically during colonial rule?
activities.explanation: Now read on to find out.

activities.title: How India’s textile trade changed
activities.body: Before machine industries, India dominated the international market in fine textiles. Armenian and Persian merchants carried Indian textiles towards Afghanistan and Central Asia. During the 1750s, the merchant-controlled textile trade network began to break down. European trading companies gradually gained power over Indian trade. This shift changed where trade centred.
keyPoints: India dominated the fine textile market before machine industries.
Armenian and Persian merchants carried Indian textiles.
European trading companies gradually gained power over trade.
activities.explanation: This shows how trade power shifted from merchants to European companies.

activities.prompt: A merchant asks why traders now find it harder to get credit. What changed?
steps: India dominated the fine textile trade before machine industries.
European trading companies gradually gained power over Indian trade.
The old ports lost their exports, so merchants had less trade to support credit.
Therefore, credit dried up as the merchant-controlled network broke down.
activities.explanation: Think it through with Hooty.

activities.prompt: Before machine industries, India dominated the international market in fine textiles.
activities.explanation: This statement matches India’s leading place in fine textiles.

activities.prompt: Who carried Indian textiles towards Afghanistan and Central Asia?
options: East India Company
Gomasthas
Armenian and Persian merchants
European trading companies
activities.explanation: The lesson names Armenian and Persian merchants as these carriers.

activities.prompt: Surat’s trade value fell from Rs ______ million to Rs 3 million by the 1740s.
activities.hint: Use the starting value for Surat’s trade.
activities.explanation: Surat’s trade began at Rs 16 million before it fell.

activities.prompt: Put these changes in the order described in the lesson.
items: European trading companies gradually gained power over Indian trade
Credit for the earlier trade dried up
Bombay and Calcutta grew as colonial trade centres shifted
activities.explanation: Each step comes directly from the lesson’s account of changing trade.

activities.prompt: Match each part of trade with what happened to it.
activities.explanation: These pairs show the shift in trade power and centres.

activities.prompt: After gaining political power, what did the East India Company want?
options: Expand Indian textile exports
End Indian textile production
Restore credit for the earlier trade
Return trade to the old ports
activities.explanation: The Company wanted more exports after gaining political power.

activities.prompt: A merchant’s old port has lost its cloth exports. Traders now give less credit. What best explains this change?
options: Credit dried up because exports from old ports fell.
Credit grew because European trading companies gained more power.
Credit fell because Indian weavers stopped producing fine textiles.
Credit changed because Surat became a centre of colonial trade.

why.Credit grew because European trading com: This reverses the effect of losing exports on credit.
why.Credit fell because Indian weavers stopp: This blames weavers, but the cause was lost port exports.
why.Credit changed because Surat became a ce: This misplaces the shift of colonial trade to Bombay and Calcutta.

activities.explanation: This is right because losing exports made credit dry up.

activities.prompt: The East India Company has political power. It wants more Indian textile exports. What is the best rule for this situation?
options: Pay weavers very low prices and collect their cloth.
Let merchants control all routes so exports can grow freely.
End textile production because political power is enough.
Give weavers loans and let them keep all their cloth.

why.Let merchants control all routes so expo: This wrongly assumes that old merchant control would expand exports.
why.End textile production because political: This confuses political power with a reason to stop production.
why.Give weavers loans and let them keep all: This forgets that accepting loans required handing over cloth.

activities.explanation: This is right because low prices and cloth collection helped expand exports.

activities.prompt: A weaver accepts a loan from the Company. The agreement says the cloth must go to the Company. Why would the weaver accept?
options: The weaver wants credit, but the loan ties cloth to the Company.
The weaver expects to sell the cloth freely to Central Asian merchants.
The weaver believes the loan removes all pressure from the Company.
The weaver wants fewer working hours and more time away from weaving.

why.The weaver expects to sell the cloth fre: This assumes the weaver could ignore the loan agreement.
why.The weaver believes the loan removes all: This confuses accepting credit with freedom from Company pressure.
why.The weaver wants fewer working hours and: This links accepting a loan with less weaving, which the facts do not show.

activities.explanation: This is right because accepting a loan meant handing over the cloth.

activities.prompt: Many weavers lease their land and spend all their time weaving. Gomasthas pay very low prices. What is a likely result?
options: More cloth is produced, but weavers may earn very little.
Weavers will lease less land because weaving gives them high profits.
Textile exports may fall because weavers stop making cloth.
Old trade routes may recover because weavers now work alone.

why.Weavers will lease less land because wea: This misreads low prices as high profits.
why.Textile exports may fall because weavers: This assumes full-time weaving will stop textile production.
why.Old trade routes may recover because wea: This connects weaver work to old routes without any stated link.

activities.explanation: Full-time weaving may increase cloth, while low prices reduce earnings.

lessons.title: Factories, entrepreneurs and workers in India

activities.prompt: Why did people travel far from home to work in India’s new factories?
activities.explanation: Now read on to find out.

activities.title: Early industry and factory work
activities.body: India’s first cotton mill came up in Bombay in 1854. By 1862, four Bombay mills had 94,000 spindles and 2,150 looms. Elgin Mill began production in Kanpur during the 1860s. Dwarkanath Tagore used China-trade wealth for joint-stock companies. European Managing Agencies controlled much industrial production. Machinery and railways were mostly imported. Workers travelled far for mill jobs. Industrialists used jobbers to recruit and control workers.
keyPoints: First cotton mill: Bombay, 1854.
Four Bombay mills by 1862.
Workers travelled far for mill jobs.
Jobbers recruited and controlled workers.
activities.explanation: These are the main people, places and changes in this lesson.

activities.prompt: A worker leaves home and travels far to work in a mill. Why might this happen?
steps: Workers travelled long distances because mills offered employment.
Mill owners wanted workers, so they usually used jobbers.
Jobbers recruited and controlled new workers for industrialists.
Therefore, travelling and jobbers were linked to finding and controlling mill workers.
activities.explanation: Think it through with Hooty.

activities.title: India’s first cotton mill
activities.prompt: When did the first cotton mill in Bombay come up?
options: During the 1860s
Before 1854
activities.explanation: The first cotton mill in Bombay came up in 1854.

activities.title: The Elgin Mill
activities.prompt: The Elgin Mill began production in Bombay during the 1860s.
activities.explanation: The Elgin Mill began production in Kanpur during the 1860s.

activities.title: A starting year
activities.prompt: The first cotton mill in Bombay came up in ______.
activities.hint: This was the mill’s starting year.
activities.explanation: The first cotton mill in Bombay came up in 1854.

activities.title: People and industrial development
activities.prompt: Match each name or group with its result or feature.
activities.explanation: Each pair shows an entrepreneur, organisation or feature described in your lesson.

activities.title: Using trade wealth
activities.prompt: What did Dwarkanath Tagore establish with his China-trade wealth?
options: Joint-stock companies
Cotton mills
Railway workshops
Managing agencies
activities.explanation: Dwarkanath Tagore used his wealth to establish joint-stock companies.

activities.title: Controlling production
activities.prompt: Who controlled a large part of Indian industrial production?
options: Indian workers
European Managing Agencies
Chinese merchants
Bombay mill owners
activities.explanation: European Managing Agencies controlled a large part of Indian industrial production.

activities.title: Hiring factory workers
activities.prompt: Industrialists usually used jobbers to recruit and control new workers.
activities.explanation: Industrialists used jobbers because they recruited and controlled new workers.

activities.prompt: In 1854, Bombay had its first cotton mill. By 1862, four Bombay mills had 94,000 spindles and 2,150 looms. What changed?
options: Bombay’s cotton industry grew in mills and equipment.
Bombay’s cotton industry stayed at one small mill.
Cotton mills in Bombay stopped using looms.
Only one type of mill worked in Bombay.

why.Bombay’s cotton industry stayed at one s: This ignores the four mills reported in 1862.
why.Cotton mills in Bombay stopped using loo: This disagrees with the 2,150 looms working in 1862.
This confuses the first cotton mill with the only type of mill.

activities.explanation: This is right because the number of mills and machines grew.

activities.prompt: Bombay had a cotton mill in 1854. Kanpur’s Elgin Mill began production in the 1860s. What can we compare?
options: Both places had factory production during this period.
Both places had the same number of mills.
Kanpur started before Bombay’s mill began.
Both places produced only cotton cloth.

why.Both places had the same number of mills: This is wrong because the facts give no matching mill numbers.
why.Kanpur started before Bombay’s mill bega: This is wrong because Bombay’s mill began earlier.
This is wrong because Kanpur’s production is not limited to cloth.

activities.explanation: This is right because both places had mills producing goods.

lessons.title: Industrial growth, small workshops and advertising

activities.prompt: How did Indian factories, handloom workers, and advertisements transform cloth and markets?
activities.explanation: Now read on to find out.

activities.title: Industry, cloth and advertising
activities.body: European industrialists often produced goods mainly for export, not for sale in India. Early Indian cotton mills mainly made coarse yarn for people who wove cloth by hand. Later, industrialists made cloth too. Handloom cloth production nearly trebled between 1900 and 1940. Advertising expanded markets and helped create a consumer culture. This means people bought more goods. Nationalists promoted swadeshi, a movement to avoid buying foreign cloth.
keyPoints: Early Indian mills mainly produced coarse yarn.
Indian industrialists shifted from yarn to cloth.
Advertising expanded markets and created a consumer culture.
activities.explanation: These changes linked mills, handloom weaving and new buying habits.

activities.prompt: Why did Indian cloth makers win more home buyers after the war?
steps: British mills supplied the war effort, so Manchester’s imports into India declined.
Indian industrial production boomed during the First World War, so local makers grew stronger.
Nationalists encouraged a boycott of foreign cloth, giving local makers more support.
Therefore, local industrialists captured the home market from British manufactures after the war.
activities.explanation: Think it through with Hooty.

activities.title: Industry during and after the war
activities.body: India’s industrial production boomed during the First World War. British mills supplied the war effort, meaning they sent goods for the war. Goods brought from Manchester into India declined at this time. After the war, local industrialists captured the home market from British makers. Indian industry shifted from making yarn to making cloth. Indian cotton cloth production doubled between 1900 and 1912. The fly shuttle increased workers’ productivity and reduced labour needs.
keyPoints: Indian industrial production boomed during the war.
Local industrialists captured the home market after the war.
The fly shuttle raised productivity and reduced labour needs.
activities.explanation: These changes show Indian industry gaining strength during and after the war.

activities.prompt: What did European industrialists often do with the goods they produced?
options: Sell them mainly for export
Sell them mainly within India
Keep them only for local use
Give them only to Indian mills
activities.explanation: European makers often produced goods mainly for sale outside India.

activities.prompt: Early Indian cotton mills mainly produced coarse yarn for handloom weavers.
activities.explanation: These mills supported handloom weavers by making the coarse yarn they used.

activities.prompt: Indian cotton piecegoods production doubled between ______ and 1912.
activities.hint: This is the starting year for both periods of production growth.
activities.explanation: Indian cotton piecegoods production doubled between 1900 and 1912.

activities.prompt: Match each item to its partner from the lesson.
activities.explanation: Each pair shows an action and its connection with people or markets.

activities.prompt: How did Manchester labels try to gain customers’ trust?
options: Using unfamiliar gods and goddesses
Using familiar gods and goddesses
Using names of British machines
Using pictures of Indian factories
activities.explanation: Familiar gods and goddesses helped customers feel more comfortable with Manchester products.

activities.prompt: What did expanded advertising help create?
options: A new export market
A new mill system
A new consumer culture
A new home market
activities.explanation: Advertising did more than sell goods. It helped create a new consumer culture.

activities.prompt: Manchester’s imports into India declined while British mills supplied the war effort. What was a likely result for Indian producers?
options: Indian industrial production boomed during the war.
Indian buyers wanted more British cloth after the war.
Manchester’s imports rose sharply during the war.
Indian handloom production stopped growing.

why.Indian buyers wanted more British cloth: This reverses the effect of fewer Manchester imports.
why.Manchester’s imports rose sharply during: This ignores the stated fall in Manchester’s imports.
why.Indian handloom production stopped growi: The facts show handloom production expanded, not stopped.

activities.explanation: Indian production grew as fewer goods came from Manchester.

activities.prompt: Indian cotton piecegoods production doubled from 1900 to 1912. Handloom cloth production nearly trebled from 1900 to 1940. Which conclusion fits both facts?
options: Industrial and handloom cloth production both grew.
Industrial cloth grew faster than handloom cloth.
Handloom cloth production fell over these years.
Only British mills increased cloth production.

why.Industrial cloth grew faster than handlo: Nearly trebling is greater growth than doubling, not less.
why.Handloom cloth production fell over thes: Nearly trebled means production increased greatly.
why.Only British mills increased cloth produ: The growth facts concern Indian production, not British mills.

activities.explanation: Doubling and nearly trebling both show clear growth.

activities.prompt: Nationalists encouraged people to boycott foreign cloth. If Indian buyers respond, how might Indian industrialists change?
options: Shift from making yarn to making cloth.
Make more yarn and no cloth at all.
Stop cloth making and import more cloth.
Use only handloom cloth in their factories.

This misses the shift from yarn towards cloth.
Boycotting foreign cloth does not encourage importing more.
why.Use only handloom cloth in their factori: The facts connect local cloth demand with industrial cloth production.

activities.explanation: A cloth boycott encouraged industrialists to make more cloth.

activities.prompt: A government rule gives Indian cloth first place in shops. What result would fit the swadeshi movement?
options: Local makers could capture more of the home market.
Foreign makers could win more home buyers.
Indian mills would return to making yarn.
Manchester would gain more power in India.

why.Foreign makers could win more home buyer: This reverses the direction of the boycott.
why.Indian mills would return to making yarn: Indian industrialists shifted towards cloth, not back towards yarn.
why.Manchester would gain more power in Indi: Giving Indian cloth first place would not help Manchester makers.

activities.explanation: A boycott and priority for Indian cloth could help local makers.

activities.prompt: A workshop starts using the fly shuttle. The same workers can make more cloth. What may happen next?
options: Fewer workers may be needed for the same output.
More workers may be needed for the same output.
The workshop may stop making cloth altogether.
The output may fall because workers work less.

why.More workers may be needed for the same: Higher productivity means fewer workers may be needed.
why.The workshop may stop making cloth altog: Greater productivity does not mean cloth production must stop.
why.The output may fall because workers work: The new tool increased output rather than reducing it.

activities.explanation: The fly shuttle raised productivity and reduced labour needs.

activities.prompt: A maker uses advertisements with familiar gods and goddesses on cloth labels. What is the maker trying to achieve?
options: Gain trust and create a new consumer culture.
Reduce demand and close many small workshops.
Stop buyers from choosing cloth at all.
Show that handloom weaving has ended.

why.Reduce demand and close many small works: Advertisements seek more buyers, not fewer buyers.
Advertising encourages people to choose the advertised cloth.
Nothing in the facts says handloom weaving ended.

activities.explanation: Familiar labels can gain trust, while advertising can create consumer culture.

activities.prompt:
Assertion (A): Most proto-industrial production occurred in the countryside even though the merchants lived in towns.
Reason (R): European merchants financed countryside peasants and artisans and controlled the proto-industrial trade network.
options: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true but R is false.
A is false but R is true.
activities.explanation: Both statements are true, and the organisation of merchants, finance and production explains the rural location of production.

activities.prompt: Explain the difference between proto-industrialisation and production based on the later spread of factories.
activities.answer: Proto-industrialisation was the early phase of industrialisation, when large-scale production already existed but factories had not yet become common in England and Europe. It was organised mainly through European merchants who supplied money to peasants and artisans and controlled the trade network. Production usually took place in the countryside, although merchants lived in towns. As factories became common, modernity became closely associated with machines, factories, railways and steamships. The key difference is not whether production was large-scale, but where and how it was organised.
points: Proto-industrialisation was an early phase of industrialisation.
Large-scale production existed before factories became common.
Merchants financed rural peasants and artisans.
Most production occurred in the countryside.
activities.explanation: Compare your answer with the points a marker looks for.

activities.context: At a British cotton mill, the manager studies the factory's growth. The business began as part of the early factories seen in England by the 1730s, and cotton expanded strongly during the late eighteenth century. Raw cotton imports rose from 2.5 million pounds in 1760 to 22 million pounds by 1787. Production stages are brought together in the cotton mill, while small improvements also help pottery, furniture making and food processing.
activities.prompt: If the mill continues the production method shown, what is the most likely result?
options: Production would become more efficient at each stage.
Raw cotton would no longer be needed.
Cotton would immediately lose its leading industrial position.
The workforce would immediately consist only of machine operators.

Greater efficiency would not remove the need for raw cotton.
why.Cotton would immediately lose its leadin: Cotton was the leading sector during the first phase of industrialisation.
why.The workforce would immediately consist: The typical mid-nineteenth-century worker was still a craftsperson or labourer.

activities.explanation: Eighteenth-century inventions made each stage of cotton production more efficient.

activities.context: At a British cotton mill, the manager studies the factory's growth. The business began as part of the early factories seen in England by the 1730s, and cotton expanded strongly during the late eighteenth century. Raw cotton imports rose from 2.5 million pounds in 1760 to 22 million pounds by 1787. Production stages are brought together in the cotton mill, while small improvements also help pottery, furniture making and food processing.
activities.prompt: Suppose the owner makes plans for the period after the 1840s. Which sector should the owner treat as the likely industrial leader?
options: Iron and steel
Cotton
Pottery
Furniture making

why.Cotton: Cotton led during the first phase of industrialisation.
why.Pottery: Small innovations helped pottery, but it is not identified as the later leading sector.
why.Furniture making: Small innovations helped furniture making, but it is not identified as the later leading sector.

activities.explanation: Iron and steel became the leading sectors after the 1840s.

activities.prompt:
Assertion (A): The large increase in raw cotton imports helped supply the expansion of factories in the late eighteenth century.
Reason (R): Britain imported 2.5 million pounds of raw cotton in 1760 and 22 million pounds by 1787.
options: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true but R is false.
A is false but R is true.
activities.explanation: The stated rise in imports supports the claim that more raw cotton was available as factories multiplied.

activities.prompt:
Assertion (A): By 1800, powerful steam engines were already operating widely across England.
Reason (R): Only 321 powerful steam engines were operating across England around 1800.
options: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true but R is false.
A is false but R is true.
activities.explanation: The reason confirms that steam engines spread slowly and contradicts the assertion that they were widespread.

activities.prompt: Explain why cotton became increasingly important in Britain between 1760 and 1787.
activities.answer: Britain's raw cotton imports rose from 2.5 million pounds in 1760 to 22 million pounds by 1787, showing that the cotton industry expanded rapidly during the late eighteenth century. Eighteenth-century inventions made each stage of cotton production more efficient. Richard Arkwright's cotton mill brought production processes together, so production could be organised in one system. These developments helped cotton become the leading industrial sector during the first phase of industrialisation.
points: Raw cotton imports rose from 2.5 million to 22 million pounds.
Inventions made each stage of cotton production more efficient.
Richard Arkwright brought production processes together in the cotton mill.
Cotton led industry during the first phase of industrialisation.
activities.explanation: Compare your answer with the points a marker looks for.

activities.context: In an industrial city, production rose during a season, so a factory owner preferred hand labour because the products varied and required human skill. Many poor peasants and vagrants had moved to the city seeking work. One migrant found a job quickly because relatives worked in the factory. When the season ended, however, many workers faced long periods without employment.
activities.prompt: If the owner considered buying a labour-saving machine but could not make a large capital investment, what would he most likely do?
options: Continue using hand labour for the varied products
Install the machine and find the large capital investment later
Use machines because they were better suited to varied products
End the season's production because hand labour could not meet higher demand

why.Install the machine and find the large c: The machine required a large capital investment that the owner lacked.
why.Use machines because they were better su: Varied products required human skill rather than mechanical technology.
why.End the season's production because hand: Industrialists usually preferred hand labour when seasonal production rose.

activities.explanation: Hand labour avoided the large investment required for a machine.

activities.context: In an industrial city, production rose during a season, so a factory owner preferred hand labour because the products varied and required human skill. Many poor peasants and vagrants had moved to the city seeking work. One migrant found a job quickly because relatives worked in the factory. When the season ended, however, many workers faced long periods without employment.
activities.prompt: If many more poor peasants and vagrants arrived in the city during the busy season, what would most likely happen to wages?
options: Wages would remain low because labour would be abundant
Wages would rise because every newcomer would find a job
Wages would rise because industrialists would have to use machines
Wages would rise because seasonal unemployment had ended

why.Wages would rise because every newcomer: A large supply of labour did not guarantee that every worker would find employment.
why.Wages would rise because industrialists: Industrialists avoided labour-saving machines because they required large capital investments.
why.Wages would rise because seasonal unempl: Seasonal production was ending for many workers, so seasonal unemployment had not ended.

activities.explanation: The large number of workers would maintain an abundance of labour, which kept wages low.

activities.prompt:
Assertion (A): Industrialists usually preferred hand labour when production rose during a season.
Reason (R): Varied products required human skill rather than mechanical technology.
options: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true but R is false.
A is false but R is true.
activities.explanation: The need for human skill in varied products directly explains the preference for hand labour.

activities.prompt:
Assertion (A): Machines guaranteed more work for women who depended on hand spinning.
Reason (R): Machines threatened the jobs of women who depended on hand spinning.
options: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true but R is false.
A is false but R is true.
activities.explanation: The statement about guaranteed work is false, while the statement about threatened jobs is true.

activities.prompt: Explain why an abundance of labour kept wages low and how seasonal work made workers' lives uncertain.
activities.answer: When poor peasants and vagrants moved to cities in large numbers to seek work, the supply of labour became abundant. Because industrialists could find many workers, wages stayed low. Seasonal production created a different kind of insecurity. Production rose during the busy season, but seasonal work then ended, leaving many people without employment for long periods. Workers therefore faced both low pay and periods when no work was available.
points: Large-scale movement of workers increased the supply of labour
An abundance of labour kept wages low
Seasonal production rose during busy periods
Seasonal work left many people unemployed for long periods
activities.explanation: Compare your answer with the points a marker looks for.

activities.context: A Surat merchant sees trade changing. Before machine industries, India dominated the market in fine textiles, while Armenian and Persian merchants carried Indian textiles towards Afghanistan and Central Asia. From the 1750s, the merchant-controlled network began breaking down as European trading companies gained power. The East India Company then wanted more Indian textile exports. Gomasthas paid weavers very low prices, and weavers who leased land and accepted loans had to hand over their cloth to the Company.
activities.prompt: Based on the merchant’s situation, which development best fits the emerging Company-controlled trade system?
options: The Company would seek larger Indian textile exports while keeping weavers under control through gomasthas and loan terms.
The old merchant network would recover its strength because credit was returning to Surat.
The Company would allow weavers to set their own prices because textile production had become more important.
The Company would stop exporting textiles because low payments discouraged weavers from working.

why.The old merchant network would recover i: The old network was weakening, and credit for the earlier trade was drying up.
why.The Company would allow weavers to set t: The Company sought exports, while gomasthas paid weavers very low prices.
why.The Company would stop exporting textile: The Company wanted expansion, so low payments did not lead it to abandon textile exports.

activities.explanation: This matches the Company’s aim to expand exports and the controls exercised through gomasthas and loans.

activities.context: A Surat merchant sees trade changing. Before machine industries, India dominated the market in fine textiles, while Armenian and Persian merchants carried Indian textiles towards Afghanistan and Central Asia. From the 1750s, the merchant-controlled network began breaking down as European trading companies gained power. The East India Company then wanted more Indian textile exports. Gomasthas paid weavers very low prices, and weavers who leased land and accepted loans had to hand over their cloth to the Company.
activities.prompt: A weaver accepts a Company loan and is then offered a very low price by a gomastha. What must the weaver do under the arrangement described?
options: The weaver would need to deliver the woven cloth to the East India Company.
The weaver could keep the cloth until the end of the trading season.
The weaver would be free to sell the cloth directly to Armenian or Persian merchants.
The weaver would only need to give the cloth to the gomastha, not to the Company.

why.The weaver could keep the cloth until th: The loan arrangement did not permit the weaver to delay delivery.
why.The weaver would be free to sell the clo: The arrangement required Company delivery rather than a direct merchant sale.
why.The weaver would only need to give the c: The cloth had to reach the Company, not merely be given to the gomastha.

activities.explanation: Accepting a loan made delivery of the woven cloth to the Company compulsory.

activities.prompt:
Assertion (A): The merchant-controlled textile trade network began breaking down during the 1750s.
Reason (R): European trading companies gradually gained power over Indian trade.
options: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true but R is false.
A is false but R is true.
activities.explanation: The growth of European companies’ power helps explain why the merchant-controlled network weakened.

activities.prompt:
Assertion (A): Surat’s trade value rose from Rs 3 million to Rs 16 million by the 1740s.
Reason (R): The loss of old-port exports caused credit for the earlier merchant trade to dry up.
options: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true but R is false.
A is false but R is true.
activities.explanation: Surat’s value actually fell, while the drying up of earlier credit is stated as a fact.

activities.prompt: Explain how the East India Company’s political power changed Indian textile trade after the merchant-controlled network began to weaken.
activities.answer: Earlier, India dominated the international market in fine textiles. Armenian and Persian merchants carried Indian textiles towards Afghanistan and Central Asia, while the merchant-controlled trade network began breaking down during the 1750s. European trading companies gradually gained power over Indian trade, credit for the earlier trade dried up as old ports lost exports, and Bombay and Calcutta grew as colonial trade centres shifted. After gaining political power, the East India Company wanted to expand Indian textile exports. Gomasthas then paid weavers very low prices, and weavers who accepted loans had to hand over their cloth to the Company.
points: India earlier dominated the international fine-textile market.
European trading companies gained power and the merchant network weakened.
Old-port losses reduced earlier trade credit while Bombay and Calcutta grew.
The Company promoted exports and controlled weavers through gomasthas and loan conditions.
activities.explanation: Compare your answer with the points a marker looks for.

activities.context: After earning wealth in the China trade, Dwarkanath Tagore used it to establish joint-stock companies. Jamsetjee Nusserwanjee Tata built a huge industrial empire. Meanwhile, European Managing Agencies controlled a large part of Indian industrial production. When an industrialist needed mill workers, people travelled long distances to seek employment, and industrialists usually used jobbers to recruit and control the new workers.
activities.prompt: Why could Dwarkanath Tagore establish joint-stock companies after working in the China trade?
options: His China-trade earnings gave him money to invest in the companies.
His control over European Managing Agencies gave him the needed investment.
His control over imported railways and locomotives gave him the needed investment.
His recruitment of workers through jobbers gave him the needed investment.

why.His control over European Managing Agenc: Managing Agency control was not the source of his investment.
why.His control over imported railways and l: Railway and locomotive imports were not his investment income.
why.His recruitment of workers through jobbe: Jobbers recruited workers rather than providing capital.

activities.explanation: His wealth from the China trade financed the joint-stock companies.

chapters.title: Markets Around Us
chapters.summary: In this chapter: first printed books; print comes to europe; the print revolution and its impact; the reading mania.

lessons.title: First Printed Books

activities.prompt: How did people turn stories into books before modern printing presses?
activities.explanation: Now read on to find out.

activities.title: How early printing grew
activities.body: Printing began in China, Japan and Korea. Chinese printers rubbed paper against inked woodblocks. Accordion books were folded and stitched at the side. China’s imperial state printed many materials and sponsored examination textbooks. As urban culture grew, printing gained more uses. Readers then wanted fiction, poetry, autobiographies and plays.
keyPoints: Early printing developed in China, Japan and Korea.
China's imperial state sponsored examination textbooks.
Urban growth led to more printing uses and new readers.
activities.explanation: These early methods helped printed books spread and grow.

activities.prompt: A reader in a growing Chinese city wants a story book. How might printing change?
steps: Urban culture grows, so print is used for more purposes.
New readers want fiction, poetry, autobiographies and plays.
Therefore, printed books can meet more kinds of reading needs.
activities.explanation: Think it through with Hooty.

activities.prompt: Where was the earliest kind of print technology developed?
options: China and Japan only
China, Japan and Korea
Japan and Korea only
China and Korea only
activities.explanation: The earliest print technology developed in China, Japan and Korea.

activities.prompt: Chinese accordion books were folded and stitched at the ______.
activities.hint: Think about where the stitching joined the folded pages.
activities.explanation: Accordion books were folded and stitched at the side.

activities.prompt: What did China’s imperial state sponsor?
options: Large numbers of examination textbooks
Large numbers of imperial storybooks
Large numbers of urban poetry books
Large numbers of Buddhist picture books
activities.explanation: The imperial state sponsored large numbers of examination textbooks.

activities.prompt: What did the Buddhist Diamond Sutra contain?
options: Poetry and printed pictures
Plays and handwritten notes
Fiction and painted portraits
Text and woodcut illustrations
activities.explanation: The Diamond Sutra contained text and woodcut illustrations.

activities.prompt: Match each printing fact with its correct detail.
activities.explanation: These pairs connect each development with its place or method.

activities.prompt: Put the steps for printing a Chinese book in order.
activities.explanation: Printing starts with the inked woodblock, then rubbing transfers the print.

activities.prompt: Urban culture in China grows. Print is used for more purposes. Readers begin to want stories, poems, life stories and plays. What is the best prediction?
options: New books will focus more on what readers want to read.
Print will stop because readers already have enough books.
Only examination textbooks will be printed in the future.
Fiction will completely replace every other kind of book.

why.Print will stop because readers already: This wrongly assumes that more readers reduce the need for books.
why.Only examination textbooks will be print: This wrongly assumes that print would serve only examinations.
why.Fiction will completely replace every ot: This wrongly assumes that one new kind would remove all others.

activities.explanation: This follows because urban growth made print serve more purposes.

activities.prompt: China's imperial state needs many copies of examination textbooks. It sponsors large numbers of them. What is the likely result?
options: More students can receive printed textbooks for their examinations.
No one will print books because the state does everything.
Readers will ask only for fiction, poetry and plays.
Books will be printed only by missionaries in distant Japan.

why.No one will print books because the stat: This wrongly assumes state support stops all other printing.
why.Readers will ask only for fiction, poetr: This wrongly assumes printed reading needs will ignore fiction and poems.
why.Books will be printed only by missionari: This wrongly gives Japanese missionaries the work of Chinese printing.

activities.explanation: State sponsorship can provide large numbers of textbooks to students.

activities.prompt: China imports Western printing techniques and mechanical presses. A workshop changes its printing process. What does this situation show?
options: China has adopted printing methods brought from the West.
China has stopped printing because its older methods failed.
Japanese missionaries have introduced hand-printing to China.
Imperial examination textbooks are no longer needed in China.

why.China has stopped printing because its o: This wrongly assumes importing methods means ending printing.
why.Japanese missionaries have introduced ha: This reverses the direction of the missionary printing transfer.
why.Imperial examination textbooks are no lo: This wrongly assumes new presses remove the need for exam textbooks.

activities.explanation: The imported Western techniques and presses explain the workshop's change.

lessons.title: Print Comes to Europe

activities.prompt: What made books become faster to make and share?
activities.explanation: Now read on to find out.

activities.title: How Printing Spread
activities.body: Chinese silk and spices reached Europe through the silk route. Chinese paper arrived in the eleventh century. Marco Polo brought woodblock printing knowledge to Italy. Italians then made books with woodblocks. Printed books were cheaper than handwritten ones. Demand grew too quickly for manuscripts. Gutenberg developed the first-known printing press in the 1430s. Woodblocks also printed textiles, cards and religious pictures.
keyPoints: Paper reached Europe in the eleventh century.
Italians produced books with woodblocks.
Printed copies cost less than manuscripts.
Gutenberg developed the first-known press in the 1430s.
activities.explanation: Printing helped Europe meet its growing demand for books.

activities.prompt: A bookshop has more readers than it can serve with handwritten books. How can it meet the growing demand?
steps: More readers want books, so the shop needs many copies.
Handwritten manuscripts cannot satisfy this demand, so they cannot do it alone.
A printing press can make printed copies, and merchants and students buy cheaper ones.
Therefore, printed books should meet the shop's growing demand.
activities.explanation: Think it through with Hooty.

activities.prompt: Marco Polo brought woodblock printing knowledge back to Italy.
activities.explanation: Marco Polo brought woodblock printing knowledge from China to Italy.

activities.prompt: Chinese paper reached Europe in the ______ century.
activities.hint: Remember the century named for paper's arrival.
activities.explanation: Chinese paper reached Europe in the eleventh century.

activities.prompt: Match each change with its detail from the lesson.
pairs: Reached Europe in the eleventh century
activities.explanation: Each person, place and invention played a part in printing's arrival.

activities.prompt: Why did merchants and students buy printed copies?
options: They were cheaper
They were handwritten
They used costly vellum
They were rare imports
activities.explanation: Merchants and students bought cheaper printed copies.

activities.prompt: Handwritten manuscripts could satisfy the growing demand for books.
activities.explanation: Handwritten manuscripts could not satisfy the growing demand for books.

activities.prompt: Put the development of printed books in order.
items: Italians begin making books with woodblocks
Merchants and students buy cheaper copies
Booksellers begin exporting books to many countries
activities.explanation: The knowledge came first, followed by production, buying and exporting.

activities.prompt: Why did Gutenberg's printing press matter?
options: It met growing demand
It stopped book copying
It ended book exports
It stopped paper arriving
activities.explanation: His press helped meet demand that handwritten manuscripts could not satisfy.

activities.prompt: Printed copies cost less than vellum copies. Which will many buyers choose?
options: The cheaper printed copy, because it costs less.
The costly vellum copy, because it is handwritten.
The vellum copy, because paper cannot be used.
The printed copy, because all books were printed.

why.The costly vellum copy, because it is ha: This wrongly assumes handwritten books would attract buyers despite their higher cost.
why.The vellum copy, because paper cannot be: This wrongly assumes buyers would pay more for vellum copies.
why.The printed copy, because all books were: This wrongly assumes every book was printed, while luxury books stayed handwritten.

activities.explanation: This is right because merchants and students bought cheaper printed copies.

activities.prompt: A source says booksellers exported books widely. What does this show?
options: Books travelled beyond their home country.
Every family owned a printing press.
All exported books were made on vellum.
Only students could read exported books.

This wrongly assumes exporting books meant owning printing presses.
This wrongly assumes every exported book was a luxury vellum manuscript.
This wrongly limits readers to students, though merchants also bought books.

activities.explanation: This is right because booksellers exported books to many countries.

lessons.sceneCaption: This mosaic depicts Marco Polo, who brought woodblock printing knowledge from China to Italy.

sceneCredit.creator: Salviati

lessons.title: The Print Revolution and Its Impact

activities.prompt: How did printing change the way people read, learn, and share ideas?
activities.explanation: Now read on to find out.

activities.title: How Printing Changed the World
activities.body: The print revolution changed how people related to information and knowledge. The printing press created a new reading public. Print culture includes oral culture, so hearing and reading publics became mixed. Print reduced book costs and allowed ideas to circulate widely. Some authorities feared rebellious and irreligious thoughts might spread. Martin Luther used print to criticise practices in the Roman Catholic Church.
keyPoints: Printing created a new reading public.
Print reduced book costs and spread ideas.
Luther used print to criticise Church practices.
activities.explanation: Printing changed what people read, how they shared ideas, and how authorities responded.

activities.prompt: A village gets a printing press. Why might this change what people know and how they live together?
steps: Printing lowers book costs, so more people can read them.
A new reading public can share ideas through printed books.
Wide circulation can make authorities fear rebellious or irreligious thoughts.
Therefore, printing changes how people relate to information and knowledge.
activities.explanation: Think it through with Hooty.

activities.prompt: What did printing do to the cost of books?
options: It reduced them.
It doubled them.
It removed them.
It fixed them.
activities.explanation: Printing reduced the cost of books.

activities.prompt: The printing press created a new reading public.
activities.explanation: The printing press brought together people who could read printed material.

activities.prompt: Oral culture entered ______ culture.
activities.hint: This culture grew through printed books.
activities.explanation: Oral culture entered print culture.

activities.prompt: Why did some authorities fear the spread of print?
options: Rebellious thoughts might spread.
Irreligious thoughts might remain rare.
Reading publics might stay separate.
Book costs might become higher.
activities.explanation: Some authorities feared that rebellious and irreligious thoughts might spread.

activities.prompt: Match each person or group with what they did.
pairs: Began an Index of Prohibited Books
activities.explanation: Luther's writings helped begin the Protestant Reformation, while Menocchio studied books independently.

activities.prompt: Hearing and reading publics stayed completely separate.
activities.explanation: Hearing and reading publics became mixed together.

activities.prompt: What did Menocchio do after reading books?
options: He developed his own Bible interpretation.
He stopped reading the Bible.
He followed the Church's fixed view.
He began an Index of Prohibited Books.
activities.explanation: Menocchio read books and developed his own interpretation of the Bible.

activities.prompt: Printing makes books cost less for families. What is one likely result?
options: More families can read books and share ideas.
Fewer families can read books and share ideas.
Most families stop buying and sharing books.
Books become harder to share with others.

why.Fewer families can read books and share: This reverses the effect of lower book costs and wider circulation.
why.Most families stop buying and sharing bo: Lower costs make stopping less likely, not more likely.
why.Books become harder to share with others: Print supports sharing ideas rather than making sharing harder.

activities.explanation: Lower costs and wider circulation let more people read and share ideas.

activities.prompt: An authority sees a printed book with rebellious ideas. Why might it try to stop the book?
options: They fear rebellious or irreligious thoughts may spread.
They think books will make people stop reading.
They want every spoken story to remain unchanged.
They believe lower prices will reduce church attendance.

why.They think books will make people stop r: This mistakes book reading for a reason to stop reading.
why.They want every spoken story to remain u: This mistakes control of spoken stories for the real fear about printed ideas.
why.They believe lower prices will reduce ch: This confuses lower book prices with the authority's main fear.

activities.explanation: Authorities feared that rebellious or irreligious thoughts might spread.

lessons.sceneCaption: Relief on Strasbourg's Gutenberg monument showing the printing press bringing printed laws and civilisation to Africa.

lessons.title: The Reading Mania

activities.prompt: What made people want to read, think, and talk so much?
activities.explanation: Now read on to find out.

activities.title: Books spread across Europe
activities.body: Europe had a virtual reading mania. Literacy means being able to read and write. Literacy rates rose through the seventeenth and eighteenth centuries. In parts of Europe, literacy reached 60 to 80 per cent. Churches set up village schools. Pedlars carried small books to villages. Penny chapbooks helped poor people buy books. The periodical press developed from the early eighteenth century.
keyPoints: Literacy rose and Europe experienced a reading mania.
Schools, pedlars and cheap books spread reading.
The periodical press developed from the early eighteenth century.
activities.explanation: Several changes helped more people read and buy books.

activities.prompt: How could books and new ideas spread through villages when some people were poor?
steps: Churches set up village schools, so villagers could learn to read.
Pedlars brought books to villages, so village readers could get them.
Penny chapbooks let poor people buy books, so they could also read.
Print spread new ideas and created debate, though it did not shape every reader’s mind.
activities.explanation: Think it through with Hooty.

activities.title: Print changes how people think
activities.body: Print did more than carry stories. It popularised the ideas of Enlightenment thinkers. It created a culture of dialogue and debate. Literature could mock royalty and question the existing social order. Print opened ways for people to think differently. It did not directly shape every reader’s mind. Readers could still respond differently to the same printed ideas.
keyPoints: Print spread the ideas of Enlightenment thinkers.
Print encouraged dialogue, debate and criticism.
Print opened possibilities without shaping every reader.
activities.explanation: Print encouraged new ideas, but readers did not all react in the same way.

activities.prompt: Penny chapbooks allowed poor people to buy books.
activities.explanation: Penny chapbooks made books possible for poor people to buy.

activities.prompt: Churches set up village schools to spread ______.
activities.hint: This means being able to read and write.
activities.explanation: Churches used village schools to spread literacy.

activities.prompt: What did newspapers and journals report?
options: church schools and village lessons
pedlar routes and village visits
wars, trade and developments elsewhere
penny prices and cheap books
activities.explanation: Newspapers and journals reported wars, trade and developments elsewhere.

activities.prompt: Match each beginning to what happened.
pairs: allowed poor people to buy books
developed from the early eighteenth century
reported wars, trade and developments elsewhere
activities.explanation: Each pair shows how reading and printing spread through Europe.

activities.prompt: Which statement best describes print’s influence?
options: Print shaped every reader’s mind in one fixed way.
Print stopped all dialogue and debate between readers.
Print made every book teach one social order.
Print opened possibilities for thinking differently.
activities.explanation: Print opened new ways of thinking, but did not directly shape every reader’s mind.

activities.prompt: Literature supported the existing social order without questioning it.
activities.explanation: Literature mocked royalty and questioned the existing social order.

activities.prompt: Pedlars carried small books to villages. What would this most likely help happen?
options: More village people could obtain and read books.
Most village people would stop buying other goods.
Village people would have fewer reasons to read.
Books would become less useful in villages.

why.Most village people would stop buying ot: This wrongly assumes wider book access changed other buying habits.
why.Village people would have fewer reasons: This mistakes easier access for weaker interest in reading.
why.Books would become less useful in villag: This wrongly assumes books became less useful in villages.

activities.explanation: This is right because pedlars made books easier to get.

activities.prompt: Churches set up village schools to spread literacy. What result would this most likely produce?
options: Literacy rates would rise in those villages.
Literacy rates would fall in those villages.
Royalty would gain more power in those villages.
Print would stop spreading through European villages.

why.Literacy rates would fall in those villa: This reverses the link between schools and literacy.
why.Royalty would gain more power in those v: This confuses literacy teaching with changes in political power.
why.Print would stop spreading through Europ: This wrongly treats literacy schools as a barrier to print.

activities.explanation: This is right because village schools helped spread literacy.

activities.prompt: Literacy rose through the seventeenth and eighteenth centuries. In some parts of Europe, it reached 60 to 80 per cent. What does this show?
options: Reading became common in some European parts.
Every European person could read by then.
Reading stayed rare in every European part.
Print began only after literacy had risen.

why.Every European person could read by then: This wrongly changes some European parts into every part.
why.Reading stayed rare in every European pa: This turns high literacy in some places into rarity everywhere.
why.Print began only after literacy had rise: This treats rising literacy as the only cause of print’s growth.

activities.explanation: This is right because high literacy rates show reading became common.

activities.prompt: From the early eighteenth century, the periodical press developed. Newspapers and journals reported wars, trade, and developments elsewhere. What did this help readers do?
options: Learn about events beyond their own places.
Know less about trade and distant events.
Take part in every war they read about.
Villages stopped reading because reports covered distant events.

why.Know less about trade and distant events: This reverses the purpose of newspapers and journals.
This confuses learning about wars with joining them.
why.Villages stopped reading because reports: This wrongly assumes news about distant events stopped village reading.

activities.explanation: This is right because the reports gave news from elsewhere.

activities.prompt: Print spread Enlightenment ideas. Literature mocked royalty and questioned the existing social order. What could this lead to?
options: A culture of dialogue and debate, with readers thinking differently.
One shared belief among every reader, with no further debate.
Less reading, because old ideas became harder to question.
More silence, because print stopped readers from debating.

why.One shared belief among every reader, wi: This wrongly assumes that print made all readers agree.
why.Less reading, because old ideas became h: This mistakes questioning the old order as stopping learning.
why.More silence, because print stopped read: This reverses print’s role in opening discussion.

activities.explanation: This is right because print encouraged debate but did not shape every mind.

lessons.title: The Nineteenth Century

activities.prompt: How did new technology and education change who could read?
activities.explanation: Now read on to find out.

activities.title: Reading and Printing Change
activities.body: Reading and writing improved across Europe. Women became readers and writers. Lending libraries educated workers and lower-middle-class families. Shorter working days gave time for self-improvement. Compulsory primary education made children important readers. The Grimm Brothers collected traditional folk tales. Presses began to use metal. Richard M. Hoe developed a power-driven cylindrical press. It printed 8,000 sheets in one hour. The offset press printed up to six colours at once.
keyPoints: The nineteenth century brought large gains in literacy across Europe.
Libraries, shorter working days and compulsory education encouraged reading.
The Grimm Brothers collected and edited traditional folk tales.
New printing presses printed many sheets and several colours.
activities.explanation: These changes helped more people read, write and learn.

activities.prompt: A worker finishes earlier and visits a lending library. How can this help learning?
steps: Shorter working days give workers free time, because they work fewer hours.
Libraries gave workers books, because they educated workers and lower-middle families.
With time and books, the worker can improve reading and writing.
This change supports learning and self-improvement for working people.
activities.explanation: Think it through with Hooty.

activities.title: The Grimm Brothers
activities.prompt: The Grimm Brothers collected and edited traditional ______ tales.
activities.hint: These were traditional stories passed among people.
activities.explanation: The Grimm Brothers collected and edited traditional folk tales.

activities.title: Women and Literature
activities.prompt: Women became important as readers and writers.
activities.explanation: Women became important as readers and writers during the nineteenth century.

activities.title: Changes for Readers
activities.prompt: Match each group or change with its result.
activities.explanation: Libraries and shorter working days supported learning. Education also made children important readers.

activities.title: A Change in Printing Presses
activities.prompt: What material began to be used for printing presses?
options: Glass
Metal
Paper
Cloth
activities.explanation: Printing presses began to be made of metal.

activities.title: The Cylindrical Press
activities.prompt: What could the cylindrical press print in one hour?
options: 8,000 sheets
8,000 colours
six sheets
six colours
activities.explanation: The power-driven cylindrical press could print 8,000 sheets in one hour.

activities.title: Printing Developments
activities.prompt: Put these printing developments in the order presented in your book.
items: Printing presses began to be made of metal.
Richard M. Hoe developed the power-driven cylindrical press.
The cylindrical press could print 8,000 sheets in one hour.
The offset press could print up to six colours at a time.
activities.explanation: Your book introduces metal presses, then the cylindrical press and its speed. It ends with the offset press and its colours.

activities.prompt: Workers have shorter days and visit a lending library. What change is most likely?
options: Workers will have more time and chances for self-improvement.
Children will become the main readers in town.
Women will stop being readers and writers.
Printing presses will print six colours at once.

why.Children will become the main readers in: This confuses workers' self-improvement with children's schooling.
why.Women will stop being readers and writer: This wrongly treats women as losing their reading and writing roles.
why.Printing presses will print six colours: This confuses library education with printing technology.

activities.explanation: This combines free time with access to educational books.

activities.prompt: Primary schooling is compulsory for children in a town. What is most likely to change?
options: Children will become important readers in the town.
Children will need school books less often.
Adult workers will become the only readers.
Women will become unimportant readers and writers.

why.Children will need school books less oft: This confuses attending school with needing less reading.
why.Adult workers will become the only reade: This wrongly treats adults as the only readers.
why.Women will become unimportant readers an: This wrongly treats women's importance as something that ends.

activities.explanation: Compulsory primary education made children an important group of readers.

activities.prompt: A map marks a lending library in a workers' area. What can we best infer?
options: Workers and lower-middle families can gain education.
Everyone in the area can already read well.
The library mainly prints six-colour pages.
Children there must attend primary school.

why.Everyone in the area can already read we: This wrongly treats one library as proof that everyone can read.
why.The library mainly prints six-colour pag: This confuses a lending library with an offset press.
why.Children there must attend primary schoo: This assumes compulsory schooling without evidence from the map.

activities.explanation: Lending libraries educated workers and lower-middle-class families.

activities.prompt: A reading group wants more voices after women's writing grew in importance. What should the leader do?
options: Invite women to read, write, and discuss books.
Invite only children to read and discuss books.
Give workers longer days and less free time.
Replace books with metal printing presses.

why.Invite only children to read and discuss: This focuses on children while ignoring women's important reading and writing roles.
why.Give workers longer days and less free t: This confuses literacy with working hours and reduces workers' free time.
why.Replace books with metal printing presse: This confuses reading groups with the development of printing technology.

activities.explanation: Women became important as readers and writers, so their voices belong.

lessons.title: India and the World of Print

activities.prompt: How did printing change the way people read, argue, and share ideas in India?
activities.explanation: Now read on to find out.

activities.title: From Manuscripts to Print
activities.body: India had a rich, old tradition of handwritten manuscripts. Manuscripts were copied on palm leaves or handmade paper. The printing press first reached India with Portuguese missionaries in Goa. A lithographic press is a cheap press for publishing text. Print encouraged reading, debate, and new kinds of writing.
keyPoints: Manuscripts were copied on palm leaves or handmade paper.
The printing press first reached India with Portuguese missionaries in Goa.
Print encouraged reading, debate, and new kinds of writing.
activities.explanation: This card connects India's old manuscript tradition with the spread of print.

activities.prompt: Two classmates want to study a religious text and compare ideas. How can print help?
steps: Printed copies let both classmates read the text, because print encourages people to read.
They can then compare ideas in public, because religious debates were carried out publicly and in print.
Their reading can lead them to try new writing, because print creates an appetite for new writing.
Thus print supports shared learning and debate, though officials may control or suppress it.
activities.explanation: Think it through with Hooty.

activities.prompt: Manuscripts were copied only on handmade paper.
activities.explanation: Good spotting! Manuscripts were also copied on palm leaves.

activities.prompt: Match each person or group with the related printing detail.
pairs: The printing press first reached India with them in Goa
Used cheap lithographic presses to publish their views
activities.explanation: You matched each group with the correct detail from the lesson.

activities.prompt: Who used cheap lithographic presses to publish their views?
options: Muslim scholars
Jesuit priests
Portuguese missionaries
Colonial government
activities.explanation: Muslim scholars used cheap lithographic presses to publish their views.

activities.prompt: Muslim scholars used cheap ______ presses to publish their views.
activities.hint: This word names the type of press used.
activities.explanation: Great work! Lithographic presses helped scholars publish their views cheaply.

activities.prompt: Put these printing developments in their historical order.
items: Manuscripts are copied on palm leaves or handmade paper
The printing press reaches India with Portuguese missionaries
Jesuit priests print several tracts in Konkani
activities.explanation: Handwritten copying came first. Jesuit printing followed the press's arrival in Goa.

activities.prompt: Match each place or group with the related detail.
pairs: The first printing press reached India there
Used cheap lithographic presses to publish their views
Very cheap books were sold there in the nineteenth century
activities.explanation: You linked each place or group with its related detail from the lesson.

activities.prompt: Neighbours read different religious texts and argue. Why can print cause this?
options: Print lets people read religious texts and debate them.
Print makes everyone agree after reading the same pages.
Print keeps religious debates hidden inside printed books.
Print stops people from sharing religious views with others.

why.Print makes everyone agree after reading: This wrongly assumes that shared reading must create agreement.
why.Print keeps religious debates hidden ins: This wrongly treats printing as a way to keep debates hidden.
why.Print stops people from sharing religiou: This wrongly assumes that print prevents the sharing of views.

activities.explanation: This is right because print encouraged reading and debate of religious texts.

activities.prompt: In Goa, a missionary prints a religious tract in Konkani. Why?
options: Jesuit priests used a press brought by Portuguese missionaries.
Jesuit priests avoided printing in Konkani and other languages.
The printing press arrived in India only after the colonial government.
Handwritten palm leaves were replaced by printed Konkani tracts.

why.Jesuit priests avoided printing in Konka: This wrongly assumes that priests did not print in Konkani.
why.The printing press arrived in India only: This wrongly assumes that the government introduced India's first press.
why.Handwritten palm leaves were replaced by: This wrongly assumes that palm leaves were replaced by printed tracts.

activities.explanation: This is right because missionaries brought the press and Jesuits printed Konkani tracts.

activities.prompt: Colonial prints oppose government rule. What will officials likely do?
options: They will control and suppress the printed material.
They will spread more copies among local readers.
They will leave every printed work completely untouched.
They will ask printers to publish only handwritten copies.

why.They will spread more copies among local: This wrongly assumes that opposition makes the government support printing.
why.They will leave every printed work compl: This wrongly assumes that government control means taking no action.
why.They will ask printers to publish only h: This wrongly assumes that officials ordered a return to handwriting.

activities.explanation: This is right because the government controlled and suppressed printed material.

activities.prompt: A palm-leaf manuscript and a later printed tract show which change?
options: India moved from copied manuscripts toward the first printing press.
The first printing press came before India had any manuscripts.
Palm leaves became the usual support for every printed book.
Handwritten copying continued only after the printing press arrived.

why.The first printing press came before Ind: This wrongly reverses the order of manuscripts and printing.
why.Palm leaves became the usual support for: This wrongly confuses the material used for copying with printing.
why.Handwritten copying continued only after: This wrongly assumes that copying began only after printing arrived.

activities.explanation: This is right because old manuscripts existed before the press reached Goa.
