activities.context: A student in a growing Chinese city asks a bookseller for a collection of fiction, poetry, an autobiography, and a play. The bookseller explains that readers’ interests have broadened as urban culture has grown. The imperial state also produces much printed material and sponsors large numbers of examination textbooks. The student wonders whether newer Western printing techniques and mechanical presses could improve production. The bookseller says these techniques have been imported into China.
activities.prompt: Based on the case, which set of materials would the bookseller most likely recommend to the student?
options: Stories, poems, personal-life narratives, and stage drama
Stories, poems, personal-life narratives, and woodcut pictures
Stories, poems, examination textbooks, and imported presses
Stories, examination textbooks, accordion books, and imported presses

why.Stories, poems, personal-life narratives: Woodcut pictures belonged to the Diamond Sutra, not every requested work.
why.Stories, poems, examination textbooks, a: Imported presses are methods, not a kind of written work.
why.Stories, examination textbooks, accordio: This option mixes popular literature, textbooks, book formats, and machinery.

activities.explanation: These are the four kinds of writing wanted by new readers.

activities.context: A student in a growing Chinese city asks a bookseller for a collection of fiction, poetry, an autobiography, and a play. The bookseller explains that readers’ interests have broadened as urban culture has grown. The imperial state also produces much printed material and sponsors large numbers of examination textbooks. The student wonders whether newer Western printing techniques and mechanical presses could improve production. The bookseller says these techniques have been imported into China.
activities.prompt: If a printer adopts imported Western mechanical presses while older Chinese methods continue, which result is most reasonable?
options: Both mechanical presses and rubbing against inked woodblocks may be used to produce printed material.
Mechanical presses would replace woodblock rubbing and end the production of accordion books.
Accordion books would be used only for examination textbooks.
All printed material would be limited to text and woodcut illustrations like the Buddhist Diamond Sutra.

why.Mechanical presses would replace woodblo: The facts do not say that imported presses replace every older method.
why.Accordion books would be used only for e: Accordion books are not described as textbooks.
why.All printed material would be limited to: One illustrated work does not mean that all printing became illustrated.

activities.explanation: Imported presses can exist alongside the older woodblock-rubbing method.

activities.prompt:
Assertion (A): The growth of urban culture in China helped print become useful for more purposes.
Reason (R): New readers wanted fiction, poetry, autobiographies and plays.
options: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true but R is false.
A is false but R is true.
activities.explanation: The new interests of readers explain why print was used for more purposes as urban culture grew.

activities.prompt:
Assertion (A): The spread of Western mechanical presses caused Buddhist missionaries to introduce hand-printing to Japan.
Reason (R): Buddhist missionaries from China introduced hand-printing to Japan.
options: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true but R is false.
A is false but R is true.
activities.explanation: The introduction of hand-printing is true, but the assertion wrongly connects it to Western mechanical presses.

activities.prompt: How did growing urban culture and the imperial state influence printing in China?
activities.answer: As urban culture grew in China, print became used for more purposes because new readers wanted fiction, poetry, autobiographies and plays. The imperial state also played an important role as a major producer of printed material. It sponsored large numbers of examination textbooks, giving further support to the production of books. Thus, urban readers encouraged a wider range of printed works, while the imperial state helped produce and sponsor printed material for examinations.
points: Urban growth led print to be used for more purposes
New readers wanted fiction, poetry, autobiographies and plays
The imperial state was a major producer of printed material
The state sponsored large numbers of examination textbooks
activities.explanation: Compare your answer with the points a marker looks for.

activities.context: A student in eleventh-century Europe hears that Chinese paper has reached Europe. After Marco Polo brings woodblock printing knowledge back to Italy, Italians begin producing books with woodblocks. Yet a wealthy reader wants a luxury book that is handwritten on expensive vellum. Meanwhile, handwritten manuscripts cannot satisfy the growing demand for books. Merchants and students buy cheaper printed copies, and booksellers begin exporting books to many countries.
activities.prompt: In the case, what is likely to happen to the wanted luxury book as printed copies become more common?
options: The hand-copied luxury volume would continue to use costly vellum.
The hand-copied luxury volume would be replaced by a standard woodblock-printed book.
The hand-copied luxury volume would become cheaper because more books are printed.
The hand-copied luxury volume would be sent to students instead of wealthy readers.

why.The hand-copied luxury volume would be r: This wrongly treats every book like a cheaper printed copy.
why.The hand-copied luxury volume would beco: Printing more books did not make luxury vellum production cheaper.
why.The hand-copied luxury volume would be s: There is no reason to change the reader who wants the luxury book.

activities.explanation: Luxury books remained handwritten on expensive vellum.

activities.context: A student in eleventh-century Europe hears that Chinese paper has reached Europe. After Marco Polo brings woodblock printing knowledge back to Italy, Italians begin producing books with woodblocks. Yet a wealthy reader wants a luxury book that is handwritten on expensive vellum. Meanwhile, handwritten manuscripts cannot satisfy the growing demand for books. Merchants and students buy cheaper printed copies, and booksellers begin exporting books to many countries.
activities.prompt: What should a bookseller do when buyers in many countries want the books available in Italy?
options: Send copies to buyers in the other countries.
Keep every copy in one country, even if buyers elsewhere want them.
Stop making books and print only textiles, cards and religious pictures.
Wait for handwritten manuscripts to supply all the new demand.

why.Keep every copy in one country, even if: This ignores the demand for books in other countries.
why.Stop making books and print only textile: Printed textiles, cards and religious pictures were separate uses of woodblocks.
why.Wait for handwritten manuscripts to supp: Handwritten manuscripts could not satisfy the growing demand for books.

activities.explanation: Booksellers began exporting books to many countries.

activities.prompt:
Assertion (A): Handwritten manuscripts could not satisfy the growing demand for books.
Reason (R): Luxury books were handwritten on expensive vellum, so hand-copying could not keep pace with growing demand.
options: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true but R is false.
A is false but R is true.
activities.explanation: Both statements are true, and the difficulty of hand-copying explains why manuscripts could not meet the demand.

activities.prompt:
Assertion (A): European woodblocks were used only for printing books.
Reason (R): European woodblocks were also used for textiles, cards and religious pictures.
options: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true but R is false.
A is false but R is true.
activities.explanation: The assertion is false because woodblocks had several uses, while the reason is true.

activities.prompt: How did the coming of paper and printing change book production and distribution in Europe?
activities.answer: Chinese silk and spices entered Europe through the silk route, and Chinese paper reached Europe in the eleventh century. Marco Polo brought woodblock printing knowledge back to Italy, where Italians began producing books with woodblocks. Merchants and students bought cheaper printed copies, and booksellers began exporting books to many countries. Johann Gutenberg developed the first-known printing press in the 1430s. These developments increased the supply of books, although luxury books remained handwritten on expensive vellum and manuscripts could not satisfy the growing demand for books.
points: Chinese paper reached Europe in the eleventh century.
Marco Polo brought woodblock printing knowledge to Italy.
Italians used woodblocks to produce books.
Printed copies were cheaper and could be exported widely.
activities.explanation: Compare your answer with the points a marker looks for.

activities.context: Menocchio reads books and develops his own interpretation of the Bible. More generally, printing reduces the cost of books and makes ideas circulate widely. Some authorities fear that rebellious and irreligious thoughts will spread. Martin Luther uses print to criticise practices in the Roman Catholic Church, and his writings help divide the Church and begin the Protestant Reformation. The Roman Church begins an Index of Prohibited Books in 1558.
activities.prompt: If Luther's printed criticisms reached more readers, what would be a likely result?
options: More divisions would grow within the Church
The Church would become united again
People would return entirely to oral culture
The Index of Prohibited Books would become unnecessary

why.The Church would become united again: More readers encountering his criticisms would not restore Church unity.
why.People would return entirely to oral cul: Print expanded print culture rather than making people abandon it for oral culture.
why.The Index of Prohibited Books would beco: More circulating ideas would increase, not remove, the perceived need for restrictions.

activities.explanation: Wider circulation helped Luther's criticism spread and divide the Church.

activities.context: Menocchio reads books and develops his own interpretation of the Bible. More generally, printing reduces the cost of books and makes ideas circulate widely. Remove all restrictions on books

Encourage only oral explanations of religion

why.Stop the circulation of all printed idea: Stopping all circulation would go beyond the response shown in the case.
why.Encourage only oral explanations of reli: The case shows a response involving printed books, not oral explanations.

activities.explanation: The Roman Church responded by creating an Index of Prohibited Books.

activities.prompt:
Assertion (A): The printing press created a new reading public.

options: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true but R is false.

activities.prompt:
Assertion (A): The Roman Church's Index of Prohibited Books in 1558 showed no concern about rebellious and irreligious thoughts.

options: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true but R is false.
A is false but R is true.
activities.explanation: The Index represented concern about such thoughts, so the reason is true while the statement is false.

activities.prompt: Explain why print changed the way people related to information and knowledge.
activities.answer: Print changed how people related to information and knowledge by creating a new reading public and reducing the cost of books. Ideas could now circulate widely, and oral culture entered print culture. Hearing and reading publics became mixed together, so people encountered knowledge through both spoken and printed forms. Print also enabled people to engage with written ideas. Menocchio, for example, read books and developed his own interpretation of the Bible. This shows how access to printed knowledge could lead to personal interpretation and new ways of understanding information.
points: Created a new reading public
Reduced the cost of books
Mixed hearing and reading publics
Enabled personal interpretation, as shown by Menocchio
activities.explanation: Compare your answer with the points a marker looks for.

activities.context: In a European village, a church opened a school so that children could become literate. A pedlar later arrived carrying small books, and even a poor villager bought a penny chapbook. As the periodical press developed, newspapers and journals brought news of wars, trade, and developments elsewhere. Printed literature also mocked royalty and questioned the existing social order, encouraging villagers to debate and think differently, although it did not shape every reader’s mind in the same way.
activities.prompt: If the pedlar stopped visiting the village, what would most likely happen?
options: Small books would become less easily available in the village.
Most villagers would begin attending the church school.
Newspapers would replace small books as the only form of print.
The village would immediately lose all interest in reading.

why.Most villagers would begin attending the: Village schools continued to spread literacy.
why.Newspapers would replace small books as: Other forms of print, such as newspapers, also existed.
why.The village would immediately lose all i: Print did not determine every reader’s interest.

activities.explanation: The pedlar brought books directly to the village.

activities.context: In a European village, a church opened a school so that children could become literate. why.The church school will no longer teach l: Church schools continued to spread literacy.
why.The pedlar will stop selling small books: Pedlars continued to carry books to villages.

activities.explanation: Mocking royalty could prompt discussion of the social order.

activities.context: In the nineteenth century, a printing workshop adopted Richard M. Hoe’s power-driven cylindrical press as presses began to be made of metal. Nearby, a lending library opened for workers and lower-middle-class families, while shorter working days gave some workers time to read and improve themselves. Children attended compulsory primary school and became important readers. Women also read and wrote more visibly, and the workshop began printing the Grimm Brothers’ collected folk tales.
activities.prompt: The workshop wants to publish a new series of books. What should it prioritize?
options: Print more books for pupils, because mandatory schooling created a new reading market.
Print mainly for women, because their reading and writing became more prominent.
Print only folk tales, because the Grimm Brothers had collected them.
Print fewer school books, because compulsory schooling reduced children’s interest in reading.

why.Print mainly for women, because their re: Women became important readers and writers, but this does not make them the best target for a school-book series.
why.Print only folk tales, because the Grimm: The Grimm Brothers’ work supports printing folk tales, but it does not show that they were the only useful subject.
why.Print fewer school books, because compul: Compulsory schooling increased children’s participation in reading rather than reducing their interest.

activities.explanation: This correctly connects compulsory primary education with children’s importance as readers.

lessons.title: Power-sharing and Belgium

activities.title: Power-sharing and Belgium
activities.body: A democracy should not give power to one organisation alone. Power is shared among the legislature, executive and judiciary. Belgium is a small European country with a complex ethnic population. Flemish speakers form 59 per cent of Belgium’s people. Most people in Brussels speak French. Dutch speakers are a minority in Brussels, although they are a majority in Belgium overall.
keyPoints: Power should be shared among the legislature, executive and judiciary.
Belgium has different language groups across the country.
Most people in Brussels speak French, while Dutch speakers are a minority there.
activities.explanation: The lesson links power-sharing with Belgium’s different language groups.

activities.prompt: Which country borders Belgium?

Spain
Italy
Portugal

activities.prompt: Power should be shared among the ______, executive and judiciary.
activities.hint: The lesson names this part with executive and judiciary.
activities.explanation: The legislature, executive and judiciary share power in a democracy.

activities.explanation: Each pair joins a place or group with its population detail.

activities.explanation: Dutch speakers are a minority in Brussels. They are a majority in Belgium as a whole.

lessons.title: Sri Lanka and majoritarianism

activities.title: Power, policies and conflict
activities.body: Sri Lanka is an island near Tamil Nadu’s southern coast. Tamil-speakers form 18 per cent of its people. Indian Tamils come from families of plantation workers who came from India. After independence in 1948, Sinhala leaders sought majority power and Sinhala dominance. An Act made Sinhala the only official language in 1956. Policies favoured Sinhala applicants, increasing Tamil alienation. Tamil leaders demanded regional autonomy and equality in education. The conflict became a civil war.
keyPoints: Sri Lanka became independent in 1948.
Sinhala leaders wanted majority power and dominance.
Tamil leaders demanded regional autonomy and equality in education.
activities.explanation: These ideas show how language and government policies affected Sri Lanka.

A city on Tamil Nadu’s southern coast

lessons.title: Accommodation in Belgium

activities.title: Living Together in Belgium
activities.body: Accommodation means accepting differences and sharing rules. Belgium accepted regional differences and cultural diversity. Its constitution changed four times between 1970 and 1993. Dutch and French-speaking ministers have equal numbers. Special laws need support from both linguistic groups. No group can decide alone. Many powers belong to state governments, which are not subordinate to central government. Both communities have equal representation in Brussels.
keyPoints: Belgium chose a different path from Sri Lanka.
Regional differences and cultural diversity were accepted.
Fair sharing of power helped communities live together.
activities.explanation: Fair rules helped Belgium's different communities live together.

activities.title: A Different Path

Regional differences and cultural diversity
Decisions by one community alone
A single path like Sri Lanka

lessons.title: Why power-sharing is desirable

activities.title: Power-sharing and democracy
activities.body: Belgium reached mutually acceptable arrangements for sharing power. Sri Lanka shows how refusing to share power can weaken national unity. Power-sharing can reduce conflict between social groups, and it is an important part of democracy. People have a right to be consulted about how they will be governed. The chapter calls the first set of reasons prudential and the second moral. Majority rule can harm the majority and the minority.
keyPoints: Power-sharing can reduce conflict.
It supports national unity and democracy.
People have a right to be consulted.
activities.explanation: These ideas show why sharing power can support unity and democracy.

Government without consultation

lessons.title: Democratic and federal power-sharing

activities.title: How power is shared
activities.body: In democracy, people are the source of all political power. People rule themselves through institutions of self-government. A good democratic government respects diverse groups and views. Everyone has a voice in shaping public policies. Power sharing can work across government levels and among organs at the same level. This sharing supports checks, balance and self-government.
keyPoints: People are the source of political power.
Power is shared among levels and organs.
Separation of powers creates balance.
activities.explanation: These ideas show how people share power and keep government balanced.

activities.prompt: In democracy, people are the source of all political power.
activities.explanation: That is the basic democratic idea: people hold political power.

activities.prompt: How do people rule themselves in democracy?
options: Institutions of self-government
Central government power alone
Power without public rule
No government institutions
activities.explanation: People rule themselves through institutions of self-government.

activities.prompt: Everyone has a voice in shaping public policies.
activities.explanation: A democratic government gives everyone a voice in public policies.

activities.prompt: Sharing power among government organs at the same level is ______ distribution.
activities.hint: This word names the direction of power sharing.
activities.explanation: Sharing power among organs at the same level is horizontal distribution.

activities.prompt: Sharing power among organs at the same level is vertical division of power.
activities.explanation: The same-level sharing is horizontal distribution, not vertical division.

activities.prompt: Match each power-sharing idea to its meaning.
pairs: Power sharing at the same level
activities.explanation: The pairs show how sharing, different powers and checks support balance.

activities.prompt: Government organs at the same level have different powers. Each organ checks the others. Which idea is shown?
options: Centralised government power
Unchecked organ power
Separation of powers
Power without mutual checks
activities.explanation: Different powers and mutual checks create balance among institutions.

activities.prompt: Which statement correctly describes vertical division of power?
options: Power among organs at the same level
Power among higher and lower levels
Power among diverse groups and views
Power without checks between organs
activities.explanation: Vertical division means sharing power among higher and lower government levels.

lessons.title: Sharing power among social groups and political actors

activities.title: Sharing Power Fairly
activities.body: Power can be shared among religious, linguistic and social groups. Belgium’s community government shows this sharing. Reserved constituencies give weaker groups and women representation. Political parties, pressure groups and movements influence those in power. Parties compete, and alliances may form coalition governments. Citizens need free choices among different contenders.
keyPoints: Power can be shared among social groups.
Reserved constituencies support representation and fair shares.
Competition, alliances and pressure groups influence power.
activities.explanation: This lesson connects shared power, representation, choice and alliances.

activities.prompt: Which arrangement shares power among social groups?
options: Belgium’s community government
One party holding all power
Citizens losing choice
An alliance contesting elections
activities.explanation: Belgium’s community government is an example of sharing power among social groups.

activities.prompt: Reserved constituencies give diverse social groups space in government.
activities.explanation: Yes, reserved constituencies give diverse social groups space in government.

activities.prompt: Belgium’s ______ government shares power among social groups.
activities.hint: This word describes the groups sharing power.
activities.explanation: Belgium’s community government is an example of shared power among social groups.

activities.prompt: Match each group with the result of reserved constituencies.
pairs: Receive a fair share of power
activities.explanation: Reserved constituencies support weaker groups, women and minority communities.

activities.prompt: What can political parties, pressure groups and movements do?
options: End all competition
Influence those in power
Remove political choices
Join every coalition
activities.explanation: Political parties, pressure groups and movements influence those in power.

activities.prompt: Put these events in the correct order.
items: Two or more parties form an alliance
A winning alliance forms a coalition government
activities.explanation: Parties may form an alliance, contest elections and form a coalition government after winning.

activities.prompt: Which situation best shows citizens choosing freely?
options: Citizens can choose among parties
Only one party is allowed
Pressure groups leave committees
Minority groups lose representation
activities.explanation: Citizens must be free to choose among different contenders for power.

The legislature and executive only

chapters.title: Federalism
chapters.summary: In this chapter: what is federalism?; what makes india a federal country?; how federalism is practised: linguistic states; centre-state relations and language policy.

lessons.title: What is federalism?

activities.prompt: How can one country have different levels of government working together?
activities.explanation: Now read on to find out.

activities.title: Sharing government power
activities.body: Federalism is a system that divides government power between a central authority and the country's units. A federation usually has a national government and governments for provinces or states. The national government handles matters of common national interest. State governments handle much day-to-day work. Each level, also called a tier, has independent power. The constitution sets its authority.
keyPoints: Power is divided between central and state governments.
Each tier has independent power.
The constitution sets each tier's authority.
activities.explanation: Federalism shares power while keeping each level of government independent.

activities.prompt: Two levels of government handle different duties. Why can both act without taking over each other?
steps: Power is divided because common national work differs from daily state work.
Each tier stays independent because one level must not control the other.
The constitution sets legal areas so each tier's authority is clear.
Unity and diversity can stay because powers need not cancel each other.
activities.explanation: Think it through with Hooty.

activities.title: How is power shared?
activities.prompt: Which statement shows how federalism divides power?
options: Central and state governments share power.
Only central leaders hold governmental power.
The central government holds every power.
States make every national decision.
activities.explanation: Federalism divides power between the central authority and the country's units.

activities.title: Parts of a federation
activities.prompt: A federation usually has a national government and governments for provinces or ______.
activities.hint: These are parts of the country.
activities.explanation: A federation usually has governments for provinces or states.

activities.title: Roles and responsibilities
activities.prompt: Match each part of a federation with its responsibility.
activities.explanation: Each part has a clear role under the constitution.

activities.title: Changing fundamental provisions
activities.prompt: Put the steps for changing the constitution's fundamental provisions in order.
items: Someone wants to change the fundamental provisions.
Both tiers of government give consent.
activities.explanation: Consent comes before the change, so both tiers have a say.

activities.title: Who must consent?
activities.prompt: What is needed to change the constitution's fundamental provisions?
options: Only the national government must consent.
Both tiers of government must consent.
Only state governments must consent.
Courts must approve the change instead.
activities.explanation: Changing fundamental provisions needs the consent of both tiers.

activities.title: Unity and diversity
activities.prompt: Federalism aims to protect national unity while accepting regional ______.
activities.hint: This means differences between regions.
activities.explanation: Federalism aims for national unity and accepts regional diversity.

activities.prompt: The national government handles common interests. States handle daily work. They govern the same citizens. What follows?
options: Each tier has power within its own legal area.
Every citizen belongs to only one government tier.
Both levels control every part of citizens' lives.
Each state creates all rules for national matters.

why.Every citizen belongs to only one govern: This mistake thinks governing the same citizens means only one tier governs them.
why.Both levels control every part of citize: This mistake confuses separate authority with control over every area.
why.Each state creates all rules for nationa: This mistake confuses state administration with power over national rules.

activities.explanation: This is right because each tier has its own legal authority.

activities.prompt: One area has one tier. Another has national and state governments. Which area shows federalism?
options: The second area, because power is divided between government levels.
The first area, because one level is enough for a federation.
The second area, because one level must control the other.
The first area, because citizens need only one legal area.

why.The first area, because one level is eno: This mistake assumes a federation can work with only one tier.
why.The second area, because one level must: This mistake treats divided power as control by one level.
why.The first area, because citizens need on: This mistake thinks citizens need only one legal area.

activities.explanation: This is right because a federation divides power between government levels.

activities.prompt: A document lists the revenue source for each tier. Why does this make federal funding clearer?
options: Each tier knows the revenue source it may use.
Each tier can take revenue from every other tier.
Only the national tier may use any public revenue.
Each tier's money source comes from daily state work.

why.Each tier can take revenue from every ot: This mistake treats separate revenue sources as permission to take any money.
why.Only the national tier may use any publi: This mistake assumes only the national tier may use revenue.
why.Each tier's money source comes from dail: This mistake confuses daily state work with control over revenue sources.

activities.explanation: This is right because each tier's revenue source is clearly specified.

activities.prompt: A proposed change changes the constitution's fundamental provisions. The national tier agrees. A state tier refuses. Can it happen?
options: No, because both tiers must consent to fundamental changes.
Yes, because the national tier's agreement is enough.
Yes, because the state tier cannot change national powers.
No, because only courts may approve constitutional changes.

why.Yes, because the national tier's agreeme: This mistake thinks national approval alone is enough.
why.Yes, because the state tier cannot chang: This mistake treats state independence as power to ignore consent.
why.No, because only courts may approve cons: This mistake confuses courts settling disputes with approving constitutional changes.

activities.explanation: This is right because both tiers must consent to fundamental changes.

activities.prompt: People want one united country, but they also want each region to keep its identity. Why support federalism?
options: It can protect national unity while still accepting regional diversity.
It can remove regional differences and keep all power at the centre.
It can give each region complete freedom from national authority.
It can place both national and local powers in one tier.

why.It can remove regional differences and k: This mistake thinks unity requires removing regional differences.
why.It can give each region complete freedom: This mistake confuses accepting diversity with leaving national authority completely alone.
why.It can place both national and local pow: This mistake thinks federalism places all power in one tier.

activities.explanation: This is right because federalism protects unity while accepting diversity.

lessons.title: What makes India a federal country?

activities.prompt: How does India share power across its different levels of government?
activities.explanation: Now read on to find out.

activities.title: How India shares law-making power
activities.body: India is a Union of States based on federalism. This means Union and State Governments share law-making work. The Union List holds subjects of national importance. Only the Union Government makes laws on them. The State List holds subjects of state and local importance. Only State Governments make laws on them. Both levels can make concurrent laws. If these conflict, the Union law prevails.
keyPoints: India is a Union of States based on federalism.
Union and State Governments have different areas of law-making.
The Union law prevails when concurrent laws conflict.
activities.explanation: Federalism shares law-making work between Union and State Governments.

activities.prompt: A child asks: Who makes a law about a local matter?
steps: India is a Union of States, so it has both a Union Government and State Governments.
Federalism places different subjects in different lists, so each level has a clear law-making role.
Local importance points to the State List, so only State Governments can make such laws.
Panchayats and Municipalities later added a third tier, so India's federal system includes local bodies.
activities.explanation: Think it through with Hooty.

activities.title: Special features of India's federal structure
activities.body: India later added a third tier of federalism through Panchayats and Municipalities. This created an extra level within the Union of States. Some states enjoy special powers. Assam, Nagaland, Arunachal Pradesh and Mizoram have these powers. Lakshadweep and Delhi are both called Union Territories.
keyPoints: Panchayats and Municipalities form a third tier of federalism.
Some states enjoy special powers.
Lakshadweep and Delhi are called Union Territories.
activities.explanation: These features add more levels and special arrangements to India's federal structure.

activities.title: Choose the national list
activities.prompt: Which list contains subjects of national importance?
options: State List
Union List
Concurrent subjects
Residuary subjects
activities.explanation: These subjects have national importance. Only the Union Government can make laws on them.

activities.title: Who makes State List laws?
activities.prompt: Only the Union Government can make laws on subjects in the State List.
activities.explanation: State List subjects have state and local importance. Only State Governments make laws on them.

activities.title: Match each clue
activities.prompt: Match each clue with its correct term.
activities.explanation: Each clue points to the correct part of India's federal structure.

activities.title: When laws conflict
activities.prompt: Union and State laws conflict on a concurrent subject. Which law prevails?
options: State law
Neither law
Union law
Both laws
activities.explanation: Both levels can make concurrent laws. The Union law prevails when they conflict.

activities.title: Fill in the law-maker
activities.prompt: Only the ______ Government can make laws on residuary subjects.
activities.hint: Which level of government makes these laws?
activities.explanation: The Union Government can make laws on residuary subjects.

activities.title: Choose the Union Territories
activities.prompt: Which pair consists of Union Territories?
options: Assam and Nagaland
Delhi and Mizoram
Lakshadweep and Delhi
Arunachal Pradesh and Assam
activities.explanation: Lakshadweep and Delhi are called Union Territories.

activities.prompt: A rule affects the whole country. It is a subject of national importance. Which government can make its law?
options: Only the Union Government can make the law.
Only State Governments can make the law.
Both governments can make laws on it.
Local bodies can make the law instead.

This confuses national subjects with State List subjects.
This mistake treats a national subject as a concurrent subject.
This mistake gives law-making power to the local tier.

activities.explanation: Union List subjects need laws from the Union Government only.

activities.prompt: A map compares Assam with Delhi. Which comparison is correct?
options: Assam enjoys special powers, while Delhi is a Union Territory.
Delhi enjoys special powers, while Assam is a Union Territory.
Both are ordinary States with no special status.
Both are Union Territories without State status.

why.Delhi enjoys special powers, while Assam: This swaps the special status of Assam and Delhi.
why.Both are ordinary States with no special: This mistake ignores the special status given to Assam.
why.Both are Union Territories without State: This mistake treats both places as Union Territories.

activities.explanation: Assam has special powers, while Delhi is called a Union Territory.

activities.prompt: A new subject is left over after the Lists are considered. Who can make a law on it?
options: Only the Union Government can make the law.
Only State Governments can make the law.
Both governments can make laws on it.
Local bodies can make the law instead.

This mistake treats a residuary subject as a State List subject.
This mistake treats a residuary subject as a concurrent subject.
This mistake gives law-making power to the local tier.

activities.explanation: The Union Government can make laws on residuary subjects.

activities.prompt: Panchayats and Municipalities were added later. What does this show about India?
options: India began with States, then gained a third tier.
India always had three tiers from its start.
India lost its States when tiers were added.
India had no local tier before this change.

why.India always had three tiers from its st: This mistake thinks the third tier existed from the beginning.
why.India lost its States when tiers were ad: This mistake thinks adding a tier removed the States.
why.India had no local tier before this chan: This mistake ignores the fact that a third tier was added later.

activities.explanation: India was a Union of States before a third tier was added.

activities.prompt: A matter concerns local importance in a state. Which government can make its law?
options: Only State Governments can make the law.
Only the Union Government can make the law.
Both governments can make laws on it.
Panchayats and Municipalities can make its law.

why.Only the Union Government can make the l: This confuses State List subjects with Union List subjects.
This mistake treats a State List subject as a concurrent subject.
why.Panchayats and Municipalities can make i: This mistake assumes the third tier makes State List laws.

activities.explanation: Only State Governments can make laws on State List subjects.

lessons.title: How federalism is practised: Linguistic States

activities.prompt: How can speaking different languages help bring a country closer together?
activities.explanation: Now read on to find out.

activities.title: How linguistic states support federalism
activities.body: Creating linguistic states was a major test for Indian democracy. These states helped people speaking the same language live together. In 1947, several old states changed boundaries. Some states recognised cultural, ethnic or geographical differences. Federalism needs constitutional provisions, but they are not enough alone. Respect for diversity and living together became shared ideals. Flexibility helped India avoid Sri Lanka's situation. Hindi was not imposed on states using another language.
keyPoints: People speaking the same language could live in the same state.
Constitutional provisions are needed, but are not enough alone.
Respect for diversity and living together became shared ideals.
Linguistic states made India more united and administration easier.
activities.explanation: This shows how language, constitutional rules and shared ideals can support federalism.

activities.prompt: How did the new state boundaries help people?
options: Live with people speaking the same language.
Speak one language in every state.
Move to another country easily.
Stop needing state governments.
activities.explanation: The changed boundaries helped people speaking the same language live in the same state.

activities.prompt: In ______, the boundaries of several old states were changed.
activities.hint: Choose the year given in the lesson.
activities.explanation: The boundaries of several old states changed in 1947.

activities.prompt: Which statement about constitutional provisions is correct?
options: They are needed, but are not enough alone.
They work without any respect for diversity.
They make every state use one language.
They remove the need to live together.
activities.explanation: Constitutional provisions are necessary. Respect for diversity and living together also matter.

activities.prompt: Match each part of the lesson with its matching fact.
pairs: Could live in the same state
Respect for diversity and living together
activities.explanation: Each pair shows how new boundaries, constitutional rules and shared ideals supported linguistic states.

activities.prompt: Why did some national leaders oppose linguistic states?
options: They feared that India might break apart.
They wanted Hindi imposed on every state.
They wanted all old boundaries unchanged.
They thought language groups should stay apart.
activities.explanation: Some leaders feared that linguistic states would break up India. The Central Government resisted them for some time.

activities.prompt: Put these steps in the order in which they took place.
items: Change the boundaries of several old states.
Help people speaking the same language live in the same state.
activities.explanation: Changing boundaries brought language groups together and made administration easier.

activities.prompt: A state contains groups with different languages and cultures. Some groups ask for new states. What may happen?
options: Administration can become easier, and India can become more united.
Administration can become harder, and India can break into pieces.
The Centre can force Hindi on states using other languages.
The Centre can support all new state demands immediately.

why.Administration can become harder, and In: This mistake reverses the effect because linguistic states made administration easier and India more united.
why.The Centre can force Hindi on states usi: This mistake confuses promoting Hindi with imposing it on states.
why.The Centre can support all new state dem: This mistake ignores that the Centre resisted linguistic states for some time.

activities.explanation: This is right because recognising differences can make administration easier and unity stronger.

activities.prompt: Before 1947, several old states had different boundaries. After some boundaries changed, what result followed?
options: Same-language speakers could live together in one state more easily.
Same-language speakers could no longer live together in one state.
Every old state boundary stayed exactly the same.
Hindi became compulsory in every state after the change.

why.Same-language speakers could no longer l: This mistake reverses the effect of bringing same-language speakers together.
why.Every old state boundary stayed exactly: This mistake assumes no change, although several old state boundaries changed.
why.Hindi became compulsory in every state a: This mistake confuses promoting Hindi with imposing it on states.

activities.explanation: This is right because boundary changes helped same-language speakers live in the same state.

activities.prompt: A government has constitutional rules for federalism. People also respect diversity and want to live together. What must we understand?
options: Constitutional rules help, but shared ideals are also needed.
Constitutional rules alone are enough for federalism to succeed.
Shared ideals matter only when constitutional rules are missing.
State changes succeed only when everyone speaks one language.

why.Constitutional rules alone are enough fo: This mistake treats necessary constitutional provisions as sufficient by themselves.
why.Shared ideals matter only when constitut: This mistake makes shared ideals seem unnecessary when constitutional rules exist.
why.State changes succeed only when everyone: This mistake assumes one language is needed instead of respecting diversity.

activities.explanation: This is right because constitutional provisions are necessary but not sufficient.

activities.prompt: Some national leaders fear that linguistic states will break up India. What is likely to happen next?
options: The Central Government may resist the states for some time.
The Central Government may support all the states at once.
The Central Government may force Hindi on states using other languages.
The Central Government may remove all state boundaries at once.

why.The Central Government may support all t: This mistake assumes fear led to immediate support for linguistic states.
why.The Central Government may force Hindi o: This mistake confuses promoting Hindi with imposing it on states.
why.The Central Government may remove all st: This mistake confuses reorganising states with removing all boundaries.

activities.explanation: This is right because the Centre resisted linguistic states for some time.

lessons.title: Centre-State relations and language policy

activities.prompt: How do the Centre and states balance power while shaping India’s language policy?
activities.explanation: Now read on to find out.

activities.title: Sharing power and using languages
activities.body: When one party ruled Centre and states, states did not use their autonomy fully. When parties differed, the Centre sometimes weakened state power. A judgement made it harder to dismiss state governments. Regional parties rose after 1990. Coalition governments required national parties to form alliances. Power-sharing developed and became more effective today. No language received national-language status. Hindi became official. English continued with it for official work.
keyPoints: Same-party rule reduced the full use of state autonomy.
Different-party rule brought Centre attempts to weaken state power.
No language received national-language status.
activities.explanation: These changes shaped Centre-state relations and language policy.

activities.prompt: The Centre and a state have the same party. How does this affect state autonomy?
steps: Same-party rule can stop states using their full autonomy.
This happens because the Centre and state share one party.
Different-party rule can make the Centre weaken state power.
So party differences can shape how much state power is used.
activities.explanation: Think it through with Hooty.

activities.title: Same-party rule
activities.prompt: What happened when the same party ruled the Centre and states?
options: State governments did not use autonomy fully.
The Centre always shared power fairly.
English replaced Hindi for official work.
activities.explanation: The same party's rule stopped states using their autonomy fully.

activities.title: Hindi and English
activities.prompt: Hindi was identified as the official language.
activities.explanation: Hindi was identified as the official language.

activities.title: No national-language status
activities.prompt: The Constitution did not give ______-language status to any language.
activities.hint: This status was given to no language.
activities.explanation: No language received national-language status under the Constitution.

activities.title: Match situations and results
activities.prompt: Match each situation with its result.
pairs: Same party ruled Centre and states
State autonomy was not fully used
Different parties ruled Centre and states
Coalition governments began at the Centre
activities.explanation: Each situation matches the result described in the lesson.

activities.title: An important judgement
activities.prompt: What made it harder for the Centre to dismiss state governments?
options: Regional party alliances
Hindi's official status
The later judgement
English's official use
activities.explanation: The judgement made it difficult for the Centre to dismiss state governments.

activities.title: English's status
activities.prompt: The Constitution gave English national-language status.
activities.explanation: No language received national-language status. English continued with Hindi for official purposes.

activities.prompt: Same party rules Centre and state. What happens to state autonomy?
options: State governments use less of their autonomy.
State governments use more of their autonomy.
State governments ignore all Centre rules.
State governments become fully independent powers.

why.State governments use more of their auto: This reverses what happened under same-party rule.
why.State governments ignore all Centre rule: This wrongly treats same-party rule as complete Centre control.
why.State governments become fully independe: This wrongly assumes that states became fully independent.

activities.explanation: This matches the fact that states did not use their full autonomy.

activities.prompt: Different parties rule Centre and state. What may the Centre do?
options: The Centre may weaken state power.
The Centre may protect state power.
The Centre may leave state power unchanged.
The Centre may give states more power.

This wrongly assumes different parties always cooperate.
why.The Centre may leave state power unchang: This wrongly assumes party differences make no difference.
This reverses the effect of different-party rule.

activities.explanation: The fact says the Centre sometimes tried to weaken state power.

activities.prompt: After 1990, regional parties began to rise. What did national parties do?
options: They entered alliances with many parties.
They stopped seeking regional support.
They gave up all national elections.
They formed one-party rule everywhere.

This wrongly suggests they avoided regional support.
This wrongly turns alliances into giving up elections.
This wrongly suggests alliances led to one-party rule.

activities.explanation: Major national parties had to enter alliances with many parties.

activities.prompt: Hindi is official; English is used too. What national rule applies?
options: No language has national-language status.
Hindi is the only official language.
English has national-language status.
Hindi and English both have national status.

This forgets that English also continued for official work.
This confuses official use with national-language status.
why.Hindi and English both have national sta: This confuses official use with national-language status.

activities.explanation: The Constitution gave no language national-language status.

activities.prompt: A new culture values power-sharing and state autonomy. How effective is sharing today?
options: Federal power-sharing is more effective now.
Federal power-sharing is less effective now.
Federal power-sharing is exactly the same now.
Federal power-sharing is no longer connected to states.

why.Federal power-sharing is less effective: This reverses the change in federal power-sharing.
why.Federal power-sharing is exactly the sam: This wrongly denies the change from the early years.
why.Federal power-sharing is no longer conne: This wrongly denies the connection with state autonomy.

activities.explanation: Federal power-sharing is more effective today than in the early years.

lessons.title: Decentralisation and local government

activities.prompt: How can your neighbourhood shape the decisions that affect your daily life?
activities.explanation: Now read on to find out.

activities.title: What is decentralisation?
activities.body: India's large and diverse states need to share power within them. Federal power-sharing needs another tier below state governments. This tier is local government. Decentralisation means giving power to this local tier. People can take part directly in making decisions. Before 1992, state governments controlled local bodies directly. A major step came in 1992, making the third tier stronger. Regular elections must now happen by law.
keyPoints: Decentralisation gives power to local government.
Local government lets people join decisions directly.
The 1992 amendment strengthened the third tier.
activities.explanation: Local government gives people a direct role in decisions.

activities.prompt: Your town wants to decide its own priorities. Why should power come down to the town?
steps: India's states are large and diverse, so power must be shared inside them.
Another tier below state governments lets shared power reach local areas.
Local government gives people power and lets them join decisions directly.
The 1992 change made this third tier more effective, with regular elections required.
activities.explanation: Think it through with Hooty.

activities.title: The meaning of decentralisation
activities.prompt: Decentralisation means giving power to local government.
activities.explanation: Yes. Local government is the tier below state governments.

activities.title: Choose the decentralised system
activities.prompt: Which change shows decentralisation?
options: Giving power to local government.
Keeping local bodies under state control.
Taking away local government powers.
Stopping regular local elections.
activities.explanation: Decentralisation moves some power towards local government and local people.

activities.title: Match the facts
activities.prompt: Match each clue with the correct term.
activities.explanation: Local government is below states, while each state has its own election body.

activities.title: The year of the major step
activities.prompt: A major step towards decentralisation was taken in ______.
activities.hint: Think about the year of the major decentralisation step.
activities.explanation: The major step towards decentralisation was taken in 1992.

activities.title: After the amendment
activities.prompt: What happened after the 1992 amendment?
options: The third tier became more effective.
The third tier lost its powers.
State control became stronger.
Local elections became optional.
activities.explanation: The amendment made the third tier of democracy more powerful and effective.

activities.title: Sharing power and revenue
activities.prompt: State governments may keep all powers and revenue for themselves.
activities.explanation: State governments must share some powers and revenue with local bodies.

activities.title: Order the stages
activities.prompt: Put these decentralisation stages in order.
items: After the amendment: a stronger third tier
activities.explanation: The order moves from state control to a major step, then a stronger local tier.

activities.prompt: After 1992, how did the local tier of democracy become stronger?
options: The third tier grew stronger, and regular elections became required.
The third tier grew stronger, but regular elections stayed optional.
The third tier stayed weak, but regular elections became required.
The third tier stayed weak, and regular elections stayed optional.

why.The third tier grew stronger, but regula: This wrongly treats constitutionally mandatory elections as optional.
why.The third tier stayed weak, but regular: This wrongly says the third tier stayed weak after the amendment.
why.The third tier stayed weak, and regular: This wrongly says both the third tier stayed weak and elections stayed optional.

activities.explanation: The amendment made the third tier powerful, effective, and regularly elected.

activities.prompt: A group has few members in local elected bodies. What can help?
options: Reserved seats and executive posts can give them places.
Only state elected seats can be reserved for them.
All local seats must belong to one group.
Reservation means no one can vote for local leaders.

why.Only state elected seats can be reserved: This mistakes reservation in local bodies for reservation in state bodies.
why.All local seats must belong to one group: This confuses reserved places with giving every seat to one group.
why.Reservation means no one can vote for lo: This confuses reserved places with removing the right to vote.

activities.explanation: Seats in local elected bodies and executive posts are reserved.

lessons.title: Local government structure and participation

activities.prompt: Who makes local decisions, and how can young people have their say?
activities.explanation: Now read on to find out.

activities.title: How local government works
activities.body: A gram panchayat serves a village or villages. Its members are elected by adults. All voters in a village are gram sabha members. Several gram panchayats form a panchayat samiti. District samitis form a zilla parishad, while big cities have municipal corporations. Porto Alegre shows how residents can help make city budgets. India's local government is the world's largest experiment in democracy. Constitutional status has helped it deepen democracy.
keyPoints: Gram panchayats serve villages.
Samitis group panchayats and form district zilla parishads.
Residents can help shape local budgets.
activities.explanation: Local government works through different levels and encourages citizen participation.

activities.prompt: How did Porto Alegre stop city money from favouring only rich colonies?
steps: Porto Alegre combined decentralisation with participative democracy.
Residents helped make the city's budget.
The municipality made the final decision on local meeting proposals.
This stopped money from being spent only for rich colonies.
activities.explanation: Think it through with Hooty.

activities.prompt: Who elects gram panchayat members?
options: Children in the village school
Adults in their ward or village
District samiti members
City corporation officers
activities.explanation: Adults in their ward or village elect gram panchayat members.

activities.prompt: Match each local government body with its role.
pairs: Serves a village or group of villages
activities.explanation: These pairs show how local government bodies are organised.

activities.prompt: The body containing all village voters is called gram ______.
activities.hint: Think of the two-word name for the village group.
activities.explanation: All voters in a village are members of the gram sabha.

activities.prompt: Which action did Porto Alegre residents take?
options: Choosing the zilla parishad
Selecting every city officer
Making the city's budget
Writing national laws
activities.explanation: Porto Alegre combined decentralisation with participative democracy, and residents helped make the city's budget. The municipality made final decisions on local proposals, stopping money favouring only rich colonies.

activities.prompt: What has constitutional status helped local government do?
options: Stop local elections
Remove gram sabhas
Help deepen democracy
End local voting
activities.explanation: India's local government is called the world's largest experiment in democracy. Constitutional status has helped it deepen democracy.

activities.prompt: Put these bodies from the village level to the district level.
activities.explanation: Gram panchayats come first, then samitis, and district samitis form the zilla parishad.

activities.prompt: Adult voters live in a village. Which two local roles can they have?
options: They vote for panchayat members and belong to the gram sabha.
They join a panchayat samiti and elect a zilla member.
They attend city meetings and choose a municipal corporation.
They belong to a district body and become adult voters.

why.They join a panchayat samiti and elect a: This confuses a group of panchayats with an elected district member.
why.They attend city meetings and choose a m: This confuses city meetings with voting in a village.
why.They belong to a district body and becom: This reverses adult voting with membership in a district body.

activities.explanation: This joins voting for members with membership in the gram sabha.

activities.prompt: Residents of Porto Alegre help make the city's budget. What does this show about local power?
options: Decentralisation and participation work together in city decisions.
Central officials make every decision without resident help.
Money goes only to rich colonies after local meetings.
Final decisions disappear whenever residents join local meetings.

why.Central officials make every decision wi: This mistakes local participation for central-only decision making.
why.Money goes only to rich colonies after l: This treats one past effect as the whole local power system.
why.Final decisions disappear whenever resid: This thinks participation removed the final decision.

activities.explanation: This is the correct link between local power and participation.

activities.prompt: Porto Alegre used local meetings for budget proposals. Why did this stop money favouring only rich colonies?
options: Residents' budget proposals reached the municipality's final decision.
The municipality ignored all proposals from local meetings.
Only rich residents could attend the local meetings.
The city removed the municipality's power to decide.

why.The municipality ignored all proposals f: Final authority does not mean proposals were ignored.
why.Only rich residents could attend the loc: Participation included residents, not only rich ones.
why.The city removed the municipality's powe: Participation did not remove the municipality's final power.

activities.explanation: Residents' budget ideas reached the body making the final choice.

activities.prompt: Several village bodies form groups. Those groups will join. Which pair fits?
options: A gram sabha and a municipal corporation, at two levels.
A gram panchayat and a panchayat samiti, at two levels.
A panchayat samiti and a zilla parishad, at two levels.
A municipal corporation and a gram panchayat, at two levels.

why.A gram sabha and a municipal corporation: Neither body forms the stated levels of village groups.
why.A gram panchayat and a panchayat samiti,: This starts with a village body instead of the group it forms.
why.A municipal corporation and a gram panch: This mixes city government with the grouping of village bodies.

activities.explanation: A samiti groups panchayats, and district samitis form the zilla parishad.

activities.prompt: India's local government has constitutional status. It is the world's largest democracy experiment. What does this suggest?
options: Local democracy is very large and can become deeper.
Local democracy is limited to Porto Alegre and rich colonies.
Only big cities can receive constitutional local status.
Local democracy needs central orders to work properly.

why.Local democracy is limited to Porto Aleg: This confuses Porto Alegre's example with all Indian local government.
why.Only big cities can receive constitution: This confuses constitutional status with a rule for big cities.
why.Local democracy needs central orders to: This mistakes constitutional status for detailed central control.

activities.explanation: India's scale is very large, and constitutional status has deepened democracy.
