activities.context: A state government is considering a rule for matters in the State List, while the Union government is considering a rule for matters in the Union List. The two governments also need to address a concurrent matter, but their proposed rules may conflict. A committee asks which government can decide each issue, what happens if the concurrent rules conflict, and how a third tier through Panchayats and Municipalities fits into the federal arrangement.
activities.prompt: If the Union and State Governments make conflicting laws on the concurrent matter, what would happen next?
options: The Union law would prevail.
The State law would prevail.
Both laws would have equal force.
Neither law could be enforced.

This reverses the rule about Union supremacy.
This ignores the special rule for a conflict.
This is not the result stated in the federal arrangement.

activities.explanation: This is the stated rule for conflicting concurrent laws.

activities.context: A state government is considering a rule for matters in the State List, while the Union government is considering a rule for matters in the Union List. The two governments also need to address a concurrent matter, but their proposed rules may conflict. A committee asks which government can decide each issue, what happens if the concurrent rules conflict, and how a third tier through Panchayats and Municipalities fits into the federal arrangement.
activities.prompt: How should the committee describe the additional tier that works through Panchayats and Municipalities?
options: It is a third tier of federalism.
It replaces the State Governments.
It becomes part of the Union List.
It has the same law-making power as the Union.

The State Governments remain part of the federal system.
The additional tier is not described as a Union List subject.
why.It has the same law-making power as the: Its powers are not stated to equal those of the Union.

activities.explanation: Panchayats and Municipalities added a third tier to federalism.

activities.prompt:
Assertion (A): Only the Union Government can make laws on subjects in the Union List.
Reason (R): The Union List contains subjects of national importance.
options: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true but R is false.
A is false but R is true.
activities.explanation: The reason explains why law-making on Union List subjects is reserved for the Union Government.

activities.prompt:
Assertion (A): Both Union and State Governments can make laws on concurrent subjects.
Reason (R): Only the Union Government can make laws on concurrent subjects.
options: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true but R is false.
A is false but R is true.
activities.explanation: The assertion is true, but the reason is false because both governments can make concurrent laws.

activities.prompt: How do the Union List, State List and concurrent subjects distribute law-making powers in India?
activities.answer: The Constitution declared India as a Union of States based on federal principles. The Union List contains subjects of national importance, and only the Union Government can make laws on them. The State List contains subjects of state and local importance, and only State Governments can make laws on those subjects. Both the Union and State Governments can make laws on concurrent subjects. If their concurrent laws conflict, the Union law prevails. The Union Government can also make laws on residuary subjects.
points: Union List: national importance; only the Union Government legislates.
State List: state and local importance; only State Governments legislate.
Both levels can legislate on concurrent subjects.
A conflicting Union law prevails; the Union also legislates on residuary subjects.
activities.explanation: Compare your answer with the points a marker looks for.

activities.context: After 1947, several old states had their boundaries changed so that people speaking the same language could live together. When proposals were made to create states recognising cultural, ethnic or geographical differences, some national leaders feared that this would break up India. The Central Government resisted the proposals for some time. The country’s shared ideals of respecting diversity and the desire to live together became important. Later, linguistic states made India more united and administration easier.
activities.prompt: If the proposed linguistic states were created, what result could reasonably be expected?
options: India would become more unified, and governing the states would become easier.
The Centre would gain power to impose Hindi on every state.
Constitutional safeguards would no longer be needed for federalism to succeed.
Language-based divisions would remove the need to respect diversity.

why.The Centre would gain power to impose Hi: The Centre could not impose Hindi on states using another language.
why.Constitutional safeguards would no longe: Constitutional provisions remained necessary even when linguistic states were created.
why.Language-based divisions would remove th: Respect for diversity remained important for living together.

activities.explanation: Linguistic states strengthened unity and simplified administration.

activities.context: After 1947, several old states had their boundaries changed so that people speaking the same language could live together. When proposals were made to create states recognising cultural, ethnic or geographical differences, some national leaders feared that this would break up India. The Central Government resisted the proposals for some time. The country’s shared ideals of respecting diversity and the desire to live together became important. Later, linguistic states made India more united and administration easier.
activities.prompt: As further state proposals are considered, what should decision-makers do?
options: Use constitutional rules while allowing flexibility and respecting diversity.
Rely only on constitutional wording and ignore the desire to live together.
Promote one language uniformly and disregard differences among states.
Reject every proposal because flexibility could weaken the country.

why.Rely only on constitutional wording and: Respect for diversity and the desire to live together support federalism.
why.Promote one language uniformly and disre: Promoting Hindi did not authorise imposing it on states using another language.
why.Reject every proposal because flexibilit: Flexibility helped India avoid the situation faced by Sri Lanka.

activities.explanation: Constitutional provisions are necessary, but they are not sufficient alone.

activities.prompt:
Assertion (A): The Central Government resisted linguistic states for some time.
Reason (R): Some national leaders feared that linguistic states would break up India.
options: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true but R is false.
A is false but R is true.
activities.explanation: The fear of national division helps explain the Central Government’s resistance.

activities.prompt:
Assertion (A): Constitutional provisions alone made linguistic states successful in India.
Reason (R): Linguistic states made India more united and administration easier.
options: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true but R is false.
A is false but R is true.
activities.explanation: The reason is true, but the assertion is false because constitutional provisions alone were not sufficient.

activities.prompt: How did the creation of linguistic states help India practise federalism successfully?
activities.answer: India practised federalism through linguistic states by changing several old state boundaries after 1947. This allowed people who spoke the same language to live in the same state. Some states were also created to recognise cultural, ethnic or geographical differences. Although constitutional provisions were necessary for federalism, they were not sufficient on their own. Success also depended on respect for diversity, the desire to live together and flexibility. These features helped India become more united and made administration easier. They also helped India avoid the situation faced by Sri Lanka.
points: Old state boundaries were changed after 1947.
People speaking the same language could live in the same state.
Cultural, ethnic and geographical differences were recognised.
Constitutional provisions, diversity, unity and flexibility all mattered.
activities.explanation: Compare your answer with the points a marker looks for.

activities.context: After 1990, regional parties began to rise, and coalition governments began at the Centre. A major national party therefore formed alliances with many parties. In a state ruled by a different party from the Centre, officials believed the Centre might misuse the Constitution to dismiss the state government. A court judgement made such dismissal difficult, encouraging a culture of power-sharing and greater respect for state autonomy.
activities.prompt: If coalition government continues and the judgement remains in force, what is the Centre most likely to do when a differently ruled state resists its decision?
options: Negotiate with state leaders and follow a power-sharing approach
Try to weaken the state government's authority at the first opportunity
Use constitutional misuse to remove the state government
End its alliances and rely only on its own strength

why.Try to weaken the state government's aut: Different-party rule sometimes encouraged the Centre to weaken state power.
why.Use constitutional misuse to remove the: The judgement made dismissal difficult, so this is unlikely.
why.End its alliances and rely only on its o: The coalition era required national parties to maintain broad alliances.

activities.explanation: This matches the culture of power-sharing and respect for state autonomy.

activities.context: After 1990, regional parties began to rise, and coalition governments began at the Centre. A major national party therefore formed alliances with many parties. In a state ruled by a different party from the Centre, officials believed the Centre might misuse the Constitution to dismiss the state government. A court judgement made such dismissal difficult, encouraging a culture of power-sharing and greater respect for state autonomy.
activities.prompt: Why did the major national party need many alliance partners?
options: It needed a wider support base to run the coalition government
Alliances would give it more chances to dismiss opposing state governments
Alliances would allow it to end power-sharing altogether
Alliances would help it give one partner's language national-language status

why.Alliances would give it more chances to: Alliances did not create unrestricted power to dismiss state governments.
why.Alliances would allow it to end power-sh: The new political culture encouraged power-sharing.
why.Alliances would help it give one partner: The Constitution did not give national-language status to any language.

activities.explanation: Coalition government required major national parties to build broad support.

activities.context: After 1990, regional parties began to rise, and coalition governments began at the Centre. A major national party therefore formed alliances with many parties. In a state ruled by a different party from the Centre, officials believed the Centre might misuse the Constitution to dismiss the state government. A court judgement made such dismissal difficult, encouraging a culture of power-sharing and greater respect for state autonomy.
activities.prompt: Suppose the same party begins ruling both the Centre and the state. How might the state government's behaviour change?
options: It might not use its autonomy fully
It would become completely independent of the Centre
State autonomy would become stronger than under different-party rule
Power-sharing between the Centre and the state would disappear entirely

why.It would become completely independent o: State autonomy meant cooperation within the federal system, not complete independence.
why.State autonomy would become stronger tha: The same-party pattern had weakened the full use of autonomy.
why.Power-sharing between the Centre and the: Power-sharing had become more effective, even though it did not continue unchanged.

activities.explanation: The same party previously did not allow full use of state autonomy.

activities.prompt:
Assertion (A): Major national parties formed many alliances because coalition governments began at the Centre.
Reason (R): Regional parties began to rise after 1990, increasing the need for broad political support.
options: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true but R is false.
A is false but R is true.
activities.explanation: Both statements are true, and the rise of regional parties increased the need for the alliances that coalition government required.

activities.prompt:
Assertion (A): English was used with Hindi for official purposes.
Reason (R): Hindi was the only language granted official-language status.
options: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true but R is false.
A is false but R is true.
activities.explanation: The assertion is true, but the reason is false because English also continued to be used for official purposes.

activities.prompt: Explain how the rise of regional parties and the beginning of coalition governments changed Centre-State relations.
activities.answer: After 1990, regional parties began to rise, and coalition governments began at the Centre. Major national parties therefore had to enter into alliances with many parties. This development encouraged a new culture of power-sharing and respect for state autonomy. The judgement also made it difficult for the Centre to dismiss state governments. Together, these changes made federal power-sharing more effective than it had been in the early years and increased the importance of respecting state autonomy in Centre-State relations.
points: Regional parties began to rise after 1990.
The coalition era began at the Centre.
National parties had to form alliances with many parties.
Power-sharing and respect for state autonomy developed, while dismissals became harder.
activities.explanation: Compare your answer with the points a marker looks for.

activities.context: A large and diverse state is considering how local communities can influence decisions that affect them. Residents want a stronger local tier, but the state still controls local bodies and provides them few powers or resources. The 1992 amendment made the third tier more powerful and effective, made regular local elections constitutionally mandatory, and required reserved seats. Each state has an independent State Election Commission, while state governments must share some powers and revenue with local bodies.
activities.prompt: If the state continues to control local bodies directly and denies them their own resources, what is the likely result?
options: Local people will have less direct influence over local decisions.
The third tier will be able to exercise greater authority than before.
Local bodies will gain independent decision-making power automatically.
People will be able to participate more directly because local bodies exist.

why.The third tier will be able to exercise: Continued state control does not strengthen the third tier.
why.Local bodies will gain independent decis: Local bodies do not gain autonomy automatically.
why.People will be able to participate more: Their existence alone does not give local people direct influence.

activities.explanation: Without powers or resources, local participation becomes limited.

activities.context: A large and diverse state is considering how local communities can influence decisions that affect them. Residents want a stronger local tier, but the state still controls local bodies and provides them few powers or resources. The 1992 amendment made the third tier more powerful and effective, made regular local elections constitutionally mandatory, and required reserved seats. Each state has an independent State Election Commission, while state governments must share some powers and revenue with local bodies.
activities.prompt: What should the state government do if it wants local people to participate directly and local bodies to function effectively?
options: Share some powers and revenue with local bodies.
Keep all decisions at state level but announce them locally.
Allow local bodies to exist but give them no resources.
Wait for another constitutional amendment before sharing anything.

why.Keep all decisions at state level but an: Announcing state decisions is not the same as sharing power.
why.Allow local bodies to exist but give the: Local bodies need resources to function effectively.
why.Wait for another constitutional amendmen: The existing requirement already makes state governments share powers and revenue.

activities.explanation: Sharing powers and revenue gives local bodies real responsibilities.

activities.prompt: Which statement best describes federalism?
options: Power divided among levels of government
Power held only by central government
Power given to foreign governments
Power shared by political parties
activities.explanation: Federalism divides governmental power among different levels of government.

activities.prompt: In a federation, each level of government has independent power.
activities.explanation: Each level has power independent of the other.

activities.prompt: The constitution specifies the authority of each ______ of government.

activities.prompt: Match each list or authority with its correct meaning.

can make laws on concurrent subjects

activities.prompt: Which government can make laws on subjects in the State List?
options: Union Government
State Governments
Both governments
Local governments

activities.explanation: These bodies form different parts of India's local government system.

chapters.title: Gender, Religion and Caste
chapters.summary: In this chapter: gender division and everyday work; women’s inequality and rights; women’s political representation; religion and communal politics.

lessons.title: Gender division and everyday work

activities.prompt: Why do people call some everyday jobs “men’s work” and others “women’s work”?
activities.explanation: Now read on to find out.

activities.title: How work is divided
activities.body: Gender division means different work is expected from women and men. The lesson calls it a hierarchical social division based on social expectations and stereotypes, not biology. Women often do housework and other daily tasks, while men are expected to work outside the home. Men can do housework, and many accept it when paid. Women’s paid work often goes unrecognised, and their public role stays small.
keyPoints: Gender division is based on social expectations and stereotypes.
Men are not physically unable to do housework.
Women’s paid and domestic work often goes unrecognised.
activities.explanation: Good start! You now know why work is divided differently.

activities.prompt: A father refuses to cook because it is a woman’s duty. His wife cooks, cleans and has paid work. What explains this?
steps: Social expectations assign housework to women because people see it as their duty.
Men are not physically unable to do it because this division is based on stereotypes.
Many men will take up housework when paid because money changes what they accept.
His wife’s paid work can go unrecognised, so the result is a hierarchical gender division.
activities.explanation: Think it through with Hooty.

activities.prompt: Which are the main social differences discussed in the lesson?
options: Gender, religion and caste
Age, religion and gender
Caste, class and gender
Religion, income and caste
activities.explanation: The lesson discusses gender, religion and caste as the main social differences.

activities.prompt: Gender division rests on social ______ and stereotypes, not biology.
activities.hint: These ideas come from society.
activities.explanation: Well done! Gender division is based on social expectations and stereotypes, not biology.

activities.prompt: Social diversity does not threaten democracy.
activities.explanation: That is correct. The lesson clearly states that social diversity does not threaten democracy.

activities.prompt: Match each group with the work or role described.
pairs: Fetch water, collect fuel and work in fields
Work as domestic helpers in middle-class homes
Do paid work as well as domestic work
Have a minimal role in most societies
activities.explanation: Excellent matching! These examples show the many kinds of work women do.

activities.prompt: Why do many people think housework is women’s duty?
options: Social expectations and stereotypes
Biology makes men unable to clean
Women are born with more energy
Men have no time for housework
activities.explanation: The lesson says this belief comes from society. Men are not physically unable to do housework.

activities.prompt: Match each idea with the correct lesson statement.
pairs: Is based on expectations, not biology
Are physically able to do housework
Have a minimal role in most societies
activities.explanation: Great work! You have connected the main ideas about diversity, work and social roles.

activities.prompt: A man says he will cook and clean if paid. What does this show?
options: He sees housework as women’s duty unless payment changes it.
He believes paid housework is harder than unpaid housework.
He thinks cooking needs skills that women learn first.
He thinks payment proves he already wants a housework job.

why.He believes paid housework is harder tha: This mistake assumes that payment makes the work physically harder.
why.He thinks cooking needs skills that wome: This mistake treats social training as a natural difference in ability.
why.He thinks payment proves he already want: This mistake treats payment as proof that he wants to change jobs.

activities.explanation: This is right because payment changes his readiness to do housework.

activities.prompt: A democracy has citizens of different genders, religions and castes. A leader says diversity threatens it. What should citizens conclude?
options: The leader is wrong because social diversity does not threaten democracy.
The leader is right because different groups make different choices.
Citizens should choose one social group to protect democracy.
Elections should stop until one social group remains.

why.The leader is right because different gr: This mistake wrongly treats social diversity as a threat to democracy.
why.Citizens should choose one social group: This mistake wrongly believes democracy works best with one group.
why.Elections should stop until one social g: This mistake wrongly believes elections need only one social group.

activities.explanation: This is right because social diversity does not threaten democracy.

activities.prompt: A father says housework is women’s duty, although he can do it. How does this show gender division?
options: Social expectations put women’s work inside and men’s work outside.
Bodies decide that women should stay inside and men go outside.
Payments decide that women should cook while men earn money.
Elections decide that women should clean while men lead politics.

why.Bodies decide that women should stay ins: This mistake mistakes social stereotypes for biological differences.
why.Payments decide that women should cook w: This mistake wrongly treats payment as the cause of the division.
why.Elections decide that women should clean: This mistake wrongly treats politics as the cause of housework roles.

activities.explanation: This is right because gender division rests on expectations, not biology.

activities.prompt: A woman cooks, cleans and has a paid job. Why can her total work still be missed?
options: Her domestic and paid work can both go unrecognised.
She has one paid job, so people miss her domestic work.
She works only at home, so her paid work cannot exist.
She works fewer hours than men, so her work matters less.

why.She has one paid job, so people miss her: This mistake ignores that she also does domestic work.
why.She works only at home, so her paid work: This mistake wrongly assumes domestic and paid work cannot happen together.
why.She works fewer hours than men, so her w: This mistake wrongly treats unequal hours as the reason for missing her work.

activities.explanation: This is right because women often do both kinds of work without recognition.

lessons.title: Women’s inequality and rights

activities.prompt: Why should girls and women have equal chances to learn, work, and thrive?
activities.explanation: Now read on to find out.

activities.title: Understanding women’s inequality and rights
activities.body: A feminist believes in equal rights and opportunities for women and men. Feminist movements campaign for equality in personal and family life. Agitations sought better legal and political status for women. India remains male-dominated and patriarchal. Women’s literacy was 54 per cent, compared with 76 for men. Some girls leave school because parents spend more on sons. Women also work longer than men, often without pay.
keyPoints: Fewer girls go on to higher studies.
The Equal Remuneration Act, 1976 says that equal work should receive equal wages.
Sex-selective abortion caused the child sex ratio to fall to 919 girls per thousand boys.
activities.explanation: These points show why equal rights and opportunities matter.

activities.prompt: A woman earns less for the same work. She campaigns for equality at home. What do these show?
steps: She earns less even though she does exactly the same work.
Equal work should receive equal wages, so her pay is unequal.
Her belief in equal rights and family campaign fit a feminist movement.
Therefore, her pay should equal his pay.
activities.explanation: Think it through with Hooty.

activities.title: Women’s literacy rate
activities.prompt: The literacy rate among women was ______ per cent.
activities.hint: Use the rate for women from the lesson.
activities.explanation: Women’s literacy was 54 per cent, while men’s was 76 per cent.

activities.title: Match the terms
activities.prompt: Match each term with its meaning from the lesson.
pairs: Believes in equal rights and opportunities
Campaign for equality in personal and family life
Demand better legal and political status
Says equal work should receive equal wages
activities.explanation: Each pair joins a person, movement, demand, or law with its main idea.

activities.title: Pay for equal work
activities.prompt: Which statement best matches what often happens at work?
options: Women are paid less for the same work.
Women are paid more for the same work.
Men and women always receive equal pay.
Women are paid only for office work.
activities.explanation: The Equal Remuneration Act, 1976 says equal work should receive equal wages.

activities.title: Women’s extra work
activities.prompt: What is often true about the extra work done by women?
options: It is unpaid and often not valued.
It is always paid at a higher rate.
It is done only by men.
It is always included in official wages.
activities.explanation: An average Indian woman works one hour more each day than an average man. Much of this extra work is unpaid and often not valued.

activities.title: Why do some girls leave school?
activities.prompt: According to the lesson, why do some girls leave school?
options: Parents spend more on their sons’ education.
Parents spend more on their daughters’ education.
Parents spend less on all children’s education.
Parents spend more on buying school clothes.
activities.explanation: The lesson links some school leaving to unequal resources for sons and daughters.

activities.prompt: Some parents spend more resources on their sons’ education. What may happen to girls going to higher studies?
options: Fewer girls may enter higher studies.
More girls may enter higher studies.
Girls may receive more family money.
Parents may give boys more family time.

This reverses the effect on girls’ higher studies.
This assumes girls receive more family resources.
This confuses resources spent on education with family time.

activities.explanation: When resources favour sons, some girls may leave school.

activities.prompt: India is described as a male-dominated and patriarchal society. Women’s literacy is 54 per cent. Men’s literacy is 76 per cent. What does this difference show?
options: Education has not reached equal levels.
Women have more education than men.
Men and women have equal literacy.
Only girls have a stated literacy rate.

This reverses the two given literacy rates.
Different rates do not show equal literacy.
The given rates include both women and men.

activities.explanation: The lower women’s rate shows that education is not equal.

activities.prompt: The Equal Remuneration Act, 1976 says equal work gets equal wages. A woman does the same work as a man but earns less. What should happen?
options: The same pay for the same work.
More pay for the man’s work.
Less pay for the woman’s work.
Different pay in different workplaces.

This accepts unequal pay for the same work.
This accepts lower pay for the same work.
The rule depends on the work, not the workplace.

activities.explanation: The Act requires equal pay for equal work.

activities.prompt: Feminist movements campaign for equality in personal and family life. Women’s rights agitations sought better legal and political status. The Equal Remuneration Act supports equal pay. What connects all three?
options: Equality should reach many parts of life.
Rights should apply only in families.
Equal pay should replace all other rights.
Legal change should stop family equality.

This limits rights to families and ignores paid work.
why.Equal pay should replace all other right: This treats equal pay as more important than other equality.
why.Legal change should stop family equality: This wrongly opposes equality in family life.

activities.explanation: All three facts support equality in different parts of life.

lessons.title: Women’s political representation

activities.prompt: Why should more women have a voice in deciding our country’s future?
activities.explanation: Now read on to find out.

activities.title: Why women’s representation matters
activities.body: Many feminists believe women’s problems will not receive proper attention unless women control power. Electing more women as representatives can improve this situation. India still has low women’s representation in its legislatures. One solution is to require a fair proportion of women’s election by law. The Women’s Reservation Act provides such a reservation.
keyPoints: Women need control over power for attention to their problems.
Electing more women can improve representation.
Legal reservation provides a fair proportion of women’s seats.
activities.explanation: These ideas connect political power, women’s representation, and legal reform.

activities.prompt: A panchayat has some seats reserved for women. Why might this help women gain political power?
steps: Women’s problems may not get proper attention without women controlling power.
Electing more women representatives can improve this situation.
Reserved panchayat and municipality seats give women a chance to win.
Therefore, reserved seats can help women gain political power.
activities.explanation: Think it through with Hooty.

activities.prompt: What do many feminists believe?
options: Women should control power
Women must avoid elected posts
Women’s problems need less attention
Political power does not matter
activities.explanation: Many believe women’s problems need attention unless women control power.

activities.prompt: Electing more women as representatives can improve women’s representation.
activities.explanation: This is one important way suggested for improving the situation.

activities.prompt: The Women’s Reservation Act was passed in ______.
activities.hint: This is the year given for the law’s passage.
activities.explanation: The Women’s Reservation Act was passed in 2023.

activities.prompt: Where are there more than 10 lakh elected women representatives?
options: rural and urban local bodies
state assemblies
the Lok Sabha
government cabinets
activities.explanation: More than 10 lakh elected women represent people in local bodies.

activities.prompt: Government cabinets are fully balanced by women and men.
activities.explanation: Government cabinets remain largely all-male, even when the leader is a woman.

activities.prompt: Match each item with its correct detail.
pairs: 33 per cent of seats for women
activities.explanation: Each pair connects a measure or situation with the correct detail.

activities.prompt: Put the legal response in process order.
items: Women’s share in state assemblies is low.
Fair representation by law is suggested.
The Women’s Reservation Act was passed in 2023.
The law provides 33 per cent reservation of seats for women.
activities.explanation: The sequence moves from low representation to a legal solution and its provision.

activities.prompt: Government cabinets stay mostly all-male, even when the leader is a woman. What does this show?
options: Having one woman leader does not ensure women control cabinet power.
All cabinet decisions will automatically favour women’s problems.
Women leaders must always choose an entirely male cabinet.
Cabinet power becomes fully equal when a woman leads.

why.All cabinet decisions will automatically: One leader cannot make every cabinet decision favour women.
why.Women leaders must always choose an enti: The fact does not say women leaders always choose male cabinets.
why.Cabinet power becomes fully equal when a: A woman leader does not make cabinet representation equal.

activities.explanation: One woman leader does not mean women control cabinet power.

activities.prompt: A map places India in the bottom group for women’s representation in legislatures. What does this tell us?
options: Women’s representation is low compared with other nations.
India gives women more legislative seats than every nation.
India has no women elected in any legislature.
India’s local elections are also included on that map.

why.India gives women more legislative seats: Being in the bottom group does not mean India leads every nation.
why.India has no women elected in any legisl: A low national share does not mean no women are elected.
why.India’s local elections are also include: The map compares legislatures, not all local elections.

activities.explanation: The bottom group means India has low women’s representation.

lessons.title: Religion and communal politics

activities.prompt: How can we keep faith in public life without letting religion divide us?
activities.explanation: Now read on to find out.

activities.title: Religion and political life
activities.body: Religion can shape political demands when members of religious communities speak about their needs. Political power may protect people from discrimination or oppression. Acts based on religion are acceptable only when they treat every religion equally. Communal politics uses religion in an exclusive way, favouring one group. It may claim one religion is better than others and sometimes lead to violence.
keyPoints: Members of religious communities can state their needs and demands.
Political power can prevent discrimination or oppression.
Religion-based political acts must treat every religion equally.
activities.explanation: Equal treatment and equal political rights help keep religion fair.

activities.prompt: A leader says one religion should guide the country. How should citizens respond?
steps: People in each religious community should state their needs, because every community contains different voices with rights.
Political acts are acceptable when they treat every religion equally, because fairness requires equal respect.
Calling one religion superior turns religion into exclusive politics, because it supports one group over others.
The nation should not be based on one religion, because that ignores the rights of different voices.
activities.explanation: Think it through with Hooty.

activities.title: Understanding communal politics
activities.body: Communal politics treats religion in an exclusive way and favours one group. It may claim one religion is better than others. It often uses religious prejudices, fixed ideas, symbols, leaders, emotions and fear. This religious mobilisation unites followers politically. Every community has many voices with a right to be heard. Its ugliest forms include communal violence, riots and massacres.
keyPoints: Communal politics may claim one religion is better than others.
Religious mobilisation unites followers using symbols, leaders, emotions and fear.
Every community contains many voices with a right to be heard.
activities.explanation: Fair politics must hear every voice and reject religious prejudice.

activities.prompt: Religious differences are often expressed in which field?
options: politics
gardening
painting
weather
activities.explanation: The lesson says religious differences often appear in political life.

activities.prompt: Using religion in an exclusive and partisan way in politics is called ______ politics.
activities.hint: This politics favours one religious group.
activities.explanation: Communal politics uses religion exclusively and partly supports one group.

activities.prompt: What can political power do when it regulates religion?
options: To support one religion only
To remove every religious need
To stop discrimination or oppression
To choose the best religion
activities.explanation: Political power can regulate religion and prevent discrimination or oppression.

activities.prompt: Match each idea with its matching idea from the lesson.
pairs: Can state their needs and demands
activities.explanation: Each pair connects a clear lesson idea with its matching statement.

activities.prompt: A political leader uses fear and religious symbols to unite followers. What is this called?
options: Equal political action
Religious mobilisation
Community religious demands
Fair religious treatment
activities.explanation: Using religious symbols, leaders, emotions and fear to unite followers is religious mobilisation.

activities.prompt: Which group includes the ugliest forms of communal politics?
options: Equal rights and fair laws
Shared needs and demands
Religious symbols and leaders
Violence, riots and massacres
activities.explanation: The lesson names communal violence, riots and massacres as the ugliest forms.

activities.prompt: A city gives equal support to all religious communities. Is this political use of religion acceptable?
options: Yes, because every religion is treated equally.
No, because political power must never touch religion.
Yes, because one religion receives more support.
No, because only one religion may guide decisions.

why.No, because political power must never t: This wrongly thinks political power cannot be used for religion.
why.Yes, because one religion receives more: This wrongly treats equal support as giving one religion more.
why.No, because only one religion may guide: This wrongly accepts one religion guiding all decisions.

activities.explanation: This is correct because political acts must treat every religion equally.

activities.prompt: One speaker says their religion is superior. Soon, other groups face threats and riots. What best explains this change?
options: Communal prejudice can grow into riots and violence.
Equal treatment caused the threats and riots.
Community voices made groups attack each other.
Shared needs made every group feel safe.

why.Equal treatment caused the threats and r: This wrongly blames equal treatment for communal conflict.
why.Community voices made groups attack each: This wrongly links fair expression with attacks.
This wrongly assumes shared needs always create safety.

activities.explanation: This is correct because communal prejudice can develop into riots and violence.

activities.prompt: At a public meeting, Place A lets communities state needs. Place B uses sacred symbols and fear. Which place shows exclusive political use?
options: Place B, because it unites followers through religion in a partisan way.
Place A, because equal community expression is exclusive.
Place B, because every voice there is heard equally.
Place A, because sacred symbols decide community needs.

why.Place A, because equal community express: This wrongly calls fair community expression exclusive politics.
why.Place B, because every voice there is he: This wrongly claims exclusive mobilisation includes every voice.
why.Place A, because sacred symbols decide c: This wrongly gives sacred symbols the power to decide needs.

activities.explanation: This is correct because exclusive partisan politics uses religion to unite followers.

activities.prompt: During a political meeting, a leader uses sacred symbols, emotions, and fear. Why is this religious mobilisation?
options: It uses religion to gather support for political action.
It lets every community voice shape the meeting.
It treats all religions equally during the meeting.
It asks each follower to state different needs.

why.It lets every community voice shape the: This wrongly treats mobilisation as equal community expression.
why.It treats all religions equally during t: This wrongly assumes political mobilisation treats religions equally.
why.It asks each follower to state different: This wrongly assumes followers are asking for different needs.

activities.explanation: This is correct because mobilisation uses religion to unite followers politically.

lessons.title: The secular state and religious equality

activities.prompt: How can a diverse nation protect religious equality and strengthen democracy?
activities.explanation: Now read on to find out.

activities.title: India as a secular state
activities.body: India is a secular state. This means it has no official religion. The Constitution gives no religion special status. Every individual may follow, practise, spread or reject any religion. The Constitution also stops discrimination based on religion. Secularism is a foundation of India. It must work in everyday life and politics.
keyPoints: India has no official religion.
Every individual may choose any religion or reject religion.
The Constitution prohibits religious discrimination.
activities.explanation: A secular state treats religions equally and protects every individual.

activities.prompt: An election poster attacks one religion to win votes. A friend repeats it. What should they do?
steps: They should challenge the poster because it uses religion for political mobilisation.
They should answer the friend because communal prejudice must be challenged daily.
They should act together because a secular Constitution cannot defeat communalism alone.
This protects India's secular idea because communalism threatens that idea.
activities.explanation: Think it through with Hooty.

activities.prompt: India has an official religion.
activities.explanation: India has no official religion. No religion receives special status.

activities.prompt: What does India's secular state mean?
options: One religion leads all state work.
Religious groups receive special status.
It has no official religion.
Only one faith may be practised.
activities.explanation: India has no official religion. The Constitution gives no religion special status.

activities.prompt: Match each idea with its lesson meaning.
activities.explanation: These pairs show India's secular rules and the daily effort needed to protect equality.

activities.prompt: The Constitution makers chose India to be a ______ state.
activities.hint: Look for the word meaning that no religion has special status.
activities.explanation: The Constitution makers chose a secular state. No religion receives special status.

activities.prompt: Which action supports constitutional equality?
options: Giving one religion special status
Allowing religion-based discrimination
Banning untouchability
Rejecting the equality rule
activities.explanation: The constitutional ban on untouchability is an example of action against discrimination.

activities.prompt: What else is needed to defeat communalism?
options: Challenges must continue every day and in politics.
One religion should get special legal protection.
Challenges should stop when local elections are finished.
Only political leaders should challenge all propaganda.
activities.explanation: Communal prejudices and propaganda must be challenged in everyday life. Religion-based political mobilisation must also be challenged in politics.

activities.prompt: Secularism is only the idea of one political party.
activities.explanation: Secularism is a foundation of India. It is not tied to one party or person.

activities.prompt: A child is called untouchable at school. The Constitution bans this. What should teachers do?
options: Challenge the insult, because a secular law alone cannot defeat communalism.
Remove the ban, because daily insults show the Constitution failed.
Wait for the law alone, because legal rules stop daily prejudice.
Join the insult, because stronger groups should decide who matters.

why.Remove the ban, because daily insults sh: This wrongly treats daily prejudice as a reason to remove the ban.
why.Wait for the law alone, because legal ru: This mistakes legal rules for enough to change daily behaviour.
why.Join the insult, because stronger groups: This accepts the very prejudice the Constitution and secularism oppose.

activities.explanation: The ban matters, but everyday action is also needed against communalism.

activities.prompt: Children begin calling one faith superior. What does this show, and how should adults respond?
options: Communalism threatens India's idea, so adults should challenge prejudice.
Religious difference helps democracy, so adults should leave it alone.
India needs one official faith, so adults should choose the strongest group.
Only political leaders can fix this, so ordinary people should stay quiet.

why.Religious difference helps democracy, so: This wrongly treats religious difference as helpful to democracy.
why.India needs one official faith, so adult: This mistakes secularism for giving one faith official priority.
why.Only political leaders can fix this, so: This wrongly makes political leaders more important than everyday action.

activities.explanation: Communalism threatens India's idea, and prejudice must be challenged daily.

lessons.title: Caste inequalities and change

activities.prompt: Why can a family’s background shape how people are treated in society?
activities.explanation: Now read on to find out.

activities.title: Understanding the caste system
activities.body: Caste division was special to India and was an extreme form of social division. Its hereditary occupational division was supported by rituals. Caste members were expected to share an occupation and marry within the caste. The system excluded and discriminated against outcaste groups. Jotiba Phule, Gandhiji, B.R. Ambedkar and Periyar worked against these inequalities.
keyPoints: Caste division involved hereditary occupations.
Outcaste groups faced exclusion and discrimination.
Many people worked against caste inequalities.
activities.explanation: The lesson explains how caste inequalities operated and who opposed them.

activities.prompt: A student asks why people today can take different jobs. The old system fixed jobs by birth.
steps: The old system made occupations hereditary, so jobs stayed within castes.
Rituals supported this rule, so it became a strong social duty.
Economic change, urbanisation, education and job mobility weakened old caste ideas.
Thus, new job choices are possible, but caste still affects life.
activities.explanation: Think it through with Hooty.

activities.title: Change and continuing inequality
activities.body: Change has weakened old caste ideas. Economic development, urbanisation, education and occupational mobility have helped bring this change. The Constitution now prohibits caste-based discrimination. Yet caste has not completely disappeared. Groups denied education in the old system have continued to lag behind. Caste also remains closely connected with economic status.
keyPoints: Several changes have weakened old caste ideas.
Caste-based discrimination is prohibited by the Constitution.
Caste still affects social and economic life.
activities.explanation: The lesson shows both progress against caste inequalities and their continuing presence.

activities.prompt: Caste division is special to India.
activities.explanation: The lesson describes caste division as special to India.

activities.prompt: What were caste members expected to do?
options: Work and marry within the caste
Work and marry outside the caste
Only work and avoid marriage
Reject work and change castes
activities.explanation: They were expected to share an occupation and marry within the caste.

activities.prompt: Hereditary occupational division was supported by ______.
activities.hint: Think about the beliefs that backed this division.
activities.explanation: Rituals supported the hereditary occupational division.

activities.prompt: Match each caste feature to its meaning.
activities.explanation: Each pair links a feature of the caste system to its meaning.

activities.prompt: Only economic development has weakened old caste ideas.
activities.explanation: Urbanisation, education and occupational mobility also helped weaken old caste ideas.

activities.prompt: Which statement does the lesson support?
options: Census counts exclude both Scheduled Castes and Tribes.
The Constitution permits caste-based discrimination in India.
Census counts include Scheduled Castes and Scheduled Tribes.
Education denial has ended for all caste groups.
activities.explanation: The Census counts Scheduled Castes and Scheduled Tribes as broad social groups.

activities.prompt: Economic change, education and job mobility have weakened old caste ideas. What shows this?
options: People choose new jobs and leave old caste duties behind.
People keep fixed jobs and follow old caste duties more strictly.
Children stop attending school when their cities grow larger.
People marry only inside their caste and reject all change.

why.People keep fixed jobs and follow old ca: This assumes old caste duties have become stronger, not weaker.
why.Children stop attending school when thei: This wrongly connects city growth with stopping education.
why.People marry only inside their caste and: This mistakes an old expectation for the direction of change.

activities.explanation: This fits because job mobility and economic change weaken old caste ideas.

activities.prompt: The Constitution bans caste-based discrimination. A school refuses one caste group entry. Which rule applies?
options: The school is breaking the constitutional rule against caste discrimination.
The school may refuse entry because caste decides social status.
The rule allows schools to separate children by caste.
The rule begins only after the Census records each group.

why.The school may refuse entry because cast: This wrongly treats caste-based exclusion as a valid school rule.
why.The rule allows schools to separate chil: This reverses the rule that prohibits caste-based discrimination.
why.The rule begins only after the Census re: This wrongly adds a Census condition that the fact does not state.

activities.explanation: This is right because caste-based refusal is banned by the Constitution.

activities.prompt: Jotiba Phule, Gandhiji, B.R. Ambedkar and Periyar opposed caste inequalities. Why did they act?
options: They opposed exclusion and discrimination against outcaste groups.
They wanted every person to keep one fixed occupation forever.
They believed rituals should decide each person's daily work.
They wanted outcaste groups to control all other groups.

why.They wanted every person to keep one fix: This wrongly makes their aim the preservation of fixed work.
why.They believed rituals should decide each: This mistakes the rituals they opposed for their goal.
why.They wanted outcaste groups to control a: This wrongly turns fighting discrimination into controlling other groups.

activities.explanation: This is right because caste inequality depended on exclusion and discrimination.

activities.prompt: One family was denied education under the old system. Another gained education and job mobility. What may happen?
options: The denied family may still lag behind the educated family.
The denied family will now have exactly the same position.
Education and mobility always remove every effect of old denial.
The denied family will move ahead because occupations have changed.

why.The denied family will now have exactly: This wrongly assumes past denial has no lasting effect.
why.Education and mobility always remove eve: This wrongly treats education and mobility as erasing every effect.
why.The denied family will move ahead becaus: This wrongly assumes occupational change guarantees the same advantage.

activities.explanation: This is right because denied groups have continued to lag behind.

lessons.sceneCaption: A statue shows Jotiba Phule teaching Indian feminist and educationist Savitribai Phule at Phulewada in Pune.

lessons.title: Caste and electoral politics

activities.prompt: How does caste shape the way people vote and choose leaders?
activities.explanation: Now read on to find out.

activities.title: Caste and electoral politics
activities.body: Casteism treats caste as the only basis of a social community. Political parties consider the caste composition of the electorate when choosing candidates. Sometimes they appeal to caste feelings to gain support. No parliamentary constituency has a clear majority from a single caste. Caste groups can join coalitions with other castes and communities.
keyPoints: Casteism treats caste as the only basis of a social community.
Parties consider caste composition when choosing candidates.
Caste groups can join coalitions with other communities.
activities.explanation: These points show how caste shapes electoral politics.

activities.prompt: A party has voters from several castes. How should it choose candidates and build support?
steps: Parties look at voters’ caste groups, so this affects candidate choices.
Caste feelings may bring support, but voters may also feel loyal to a party.
No constituency has a clear single-caste majority, so support must come from several castes.
Parties may form coalitions, while caste-only politics can hide poverty, development and corruption.
activities.explanation: Think it through with Hooty.

activities.prompt: What does casteism treat as the only basis of a social community?
options: Caste
Wealth
Education
Age
activities.explanation: Casteism treats caste as the only basis of a social community. This is its central idea.

activities.prompt: What may parties and candidates do to gain support?
options: Appeal to caste feelings
Ignore voters' choices
Avoid choosing candidates
Stop organising politically
activities.explanation: Sometimes parties and candidates appeal to caste feelings to gain support.

activities.prompt: A caste vote bank means many voters from that caste support one ______.
activities.hint: This is the group that receives their support.
activities.explanation: A caste vote bank means that many voters from that caste support one party.

activities.prompt: What is true about a clear majority from one caste?
options: Every constituency has one.
Some castes have one everywhere.
No parliamentary constituency has one.
Only one caste votes in each constituency.
activities.explanation: No parliamentary constituency has a clear majority from a single caste. Parties therefore need support from different groups.

activities.prompt: Match each electoral idea with its meaning.
activities.explanation: Parties consider caste composition, voters can support one party, and caste groups can join coalitions.

activities.prompt: Which communities have gained better access to decision-making through caste politics?
options: Rich and poor people
Dalit and OBC communities
Men and women from one caste
Single-caste majorities
activities.explanation: Caste politics has helped Dalit and OBC communities gain better access to decision-making.

activities.prompt: A voter supports the same party even when people of their caste support another party. What does this show?
options: The voter feels more attached to the party than to the caste.
The voter has stopped noticing the party’s caste choices.
Caste feelings are the only reason people join a party.
The voter believes one caste can win every constituency alone.

why.The voter has stopped noticing the party: This wrongly says party choices do not matter to voters.
why.Caste feelings are the only reason peopl: This wrongly treats caste feelings as the only cause of party support.
why.The voter believes one caste can win eve: This wrongly assumes that one caste can always win alone.

activities.explanation: Voters can feel more strongly attached to a party than to their caste.

activities.prompt: Every adult can vote, and each person has one vote. What result can this have for castes?
options: Castes may organise politically to use their votes.
Castes may stop organising because votes no longer matter.
Each caste will control every constituency by itself.
Party loyalty will disappear because every adult can vote.

why.Castes may stop organising because votes: This wrongly assumes that voting makes political organisation unnecessary.
why.Each caste will control every constituen: This wrongly assumes that every constituency has one caste majority.
why.Party loyalty will disappear because eve: This wrongly assumes that voting removes feelings for political parties.

activities.explanation: Universal adult franchise and one-person-one-vote encourage castes to organise politically.

activities.prompt: A constituency contains many castes, but no one caste has a clear majority. What must a party do to win support?
options: It must seek support from several castes or communities.
It must ask only one caste to support its candidates.
It must treat one caste as the whole social community.
It must ignore caste groups because voters have no links.

why.It must ask only one caste to support it: This wrongly assumes one caste can provide enough support alone.
why.It must treat one caste as the whole soc: This wrongly treats one caste as the only social community.
why.It must ignore caste groups because vote: This wrongly assumes voters have no connections to caste groups.

activities.explanation: Without a single-caste majority, a party needs support from several groups.

activities.prompt: Poor and rich people from one caste vote for different parties. What does this show about caste votes?
options: People in one caste do not always vote in the same way.
One party always controls every group within a caste.
Caste is always the strongest bond among all voters.
A caste vote bank requires every member to support one party.

why.One party always controls every group wi: This wrongly assumes one party controls every group in a caste.
why.Caste is always the strongest bond among: This wrongly treats caste as the strongest bond for all voters.
why.A caste vote bank requires every member: This wrongly assumes a vote bank needs every member to support one party.

activities.explanation: Poor and rich people, or men and women, can vote differently within one caste.

activities.prompt: A party wins support by using caste feelings and ignoring poverty, development and corruption. What concern does this create?
options: Caste-only politics may distract people from other public problems.
Caste politics always prevents Dalit and OBC communities gaining access.
A party with caste support cannot form links with other groups.
Caste voting makes every poor and rich voter think alike.

why.Caste politics always prevents Dalit and: This wrongly ignores the help caste politics gives Dalit and OBC communities.
why.A party with caste support cannot form l: This wrongly assumes caste groups never form coalitions.
why.Caste voting makes every poor and rich v: This wrongly assumes all people within a caste vote alike.

activities.explanation: Caste-only politics can distract attention from poverty, development and corruption.
