activities.context: In a village, a woman fetches water, collects fuel and works in fields. She also cooks and cleans the home. A man in the same community earns outside the home, while housework is treated as women’s duty. When a household pays a man to cook and clean, he accepts the work. The woman says her contribution is never noticed, even though she also does paid work.
activities.prompt: If the woman in the case also takes up regular paid work, what is the most likely outcome?
options: She will do both paid work and housework, and much of her contribution may remain unrecognised.
She will stop doing housework because paid work takes most of her time.
Her housework will become paid and therefore be fully recognised.
She will move into public life because paid work gives her the same role as men.

why.She will stop doing housework because pa: Their contributions may still go unrecognised.
why.Her housework will become paid and there: Paid work does not remove domestic responsibilities.
why.She will move into public life because p: Women’s public role remains minimal in most societies.

activities.explanation: Women often combine paid and domestic work.

activities.context: In a village, a woman fetches water, collects fuel and works in fields. She also cooks and cleans the home. A man in the same community earns outside the home, while housework is treated as women’s duty. When a household pays a man to cook and clean, he accepts the work. The woman says her contribution is never noticed, even though she also does paid work.
activities.prompt: Why is the man in the case willing to cook and clean when the household pays him?
options: The payment changes housework from a gendered duty into a job.
He has become physically unable to do work outside the home.
Paid work proves that housework is naturally suited to men.
Cooking and cleaning are not part of everyday work.

why.He has become physically unable to do wo: Men are not physically unable to do housework.
why.Paid work proves that housework is natur: Gender division rests on expectations, not biology.
why.Cooking and cleaning are not part of eve: Housework is clearly part of everyday work.

activities.explanation: Men accept housework when it is paid for.

activities.context: In a village, a woman fetches water, collects fuel and works in fields. She also cooks and cleans the home. A man in the same community earns outside the home, while housework is treated as women’s duty. When a household pays a man to cook and clean, he accepts the work. The woman says her contribution is never noticed, even though she also does paid work.
activities.prompt: Which change would most directly challenge the hierarchy described in the case?
options: Recognising both women’s and men’s paid and domestic contributions as work.
Allowing women to do all outside work while men continue doing housework.
Paying only the man for housework and continuing to ignore the woman’s contribution.
Leaving household and paid work outside the area of social study.

why.Allowing women to do all outside work wh: The change would not reverse existing work divisions.
why.Paying only the man for housework and co: Ignoring the woman would deepen the hierarchy.
why.Leaving household and paid work outside: Gender division should be studied rather than ignored.

activities.explanation: Recognition would challenge unequal treatment of contributions.

activities.prompt:
Assertion (A): The belief that housework is women’s duty helps explain why gender division is based on social expectations and stereotypes.
Reason (R): Many people think cooking and cleaning are women’s duty, although men are not physically unable to do housework.
options: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true but R is false.
A is false but R is true.
activities.explanation: Both are true, and the belief about women’s duty directly explains the role of social expectations and stereotypes.

activities.prompt:
Assertion (A): Women’s role in public life and politics remains minimal in most societies.
Reason (R): The main social differences discussed are gender, religion and caste.
options: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true but R is false.
A is false but R is true.
activities.explanation: Both are true, but listing the main social differences does not explain women’s minimal role in public life and politics.

activities.prompt: Explain how social expectations and stereotypes shape the gender division of everyday work.
activities.answer: Gender division of everyday work is shaped by expectations and stereotypes rather than biology. People believe cooking, cleaning and other housework are women’s duty, while men are expected to work outside the home. Men are not physically unable to do housework; they often take it up when it is paid for. This arrangement makes women’s domestic contribution less visible, especially when they also do paid work. In villages, women also fetch water, collect fuel and work in fields, while poor urban women may work as domestic helpers. Such expectations create a hierarchy that can keep women’s public role minimal.
points: Housework is expected of women because of stereotypes.
Men are expected to work outside the home.
Men can do housework and may accept it when paid.
Unequal recognition helps keep women’s public role minimal.
activities.explanation: Compare your answer with the points a marker looks for.

activities.context: A woman and a man do exactly the same work, but the woman is paid less. She points to the Equal Remuneration Act, 1976, which says equal work should receive equal wages. She also does an extra hour of unpaid work each day. In her family, a girl leaves school because parents spend more on their sons’ education. After learning about feminist movements, the woman supports equality in personal and family life and women’s demands for better legal and political status.
activities.prompt: If the employer follows the Equal Remuneration Act, 1976, what should happen next?
options: The woman should receive the same wages as the man for identical work.
The woman should continue receiving less because her unpaid extra work makes her total contribution smaller.
Both should receive different wages because their family responsibilities are different.
Both wages should be doubled because women generally do more work.

why.The woman should continue receiving less: Unpaid work does not justify paying less for identical work.
why.Both should receive different wages beca: Family duties are not stated as a reason for different pay.
why.Both wages should be doubled because wom: The Act requires equal amounts, not doubled amounts.

activities.explanation: The Act requires equal pay for equal work.

activities.context: A woman and a man do exactly the same work, but the woman is paid less. She points to the Equal Remuneration Act, 1976, which says equal work should receive equal wages. She also does an extra hour of unpaid work each day. In her family, a girl leaves school because parents spend more on their sons’ education. After learning about feminist movements, the woman supports equality in personal and family life and women’s demands for better legal and political status.
activities.prompt: Why is the woman’s effort to challenge unequal pay connected with feminist ideas?
options: Her effort is part of securing equal rights and opportunities for women and men.
Only women who work outside the home can be feminists.
Feminist movements aim to preserve unequal roles within families.
Legal and political campaigns alone define every feminist movement.

why.Only women who work outside the home can: Feminism is not restricted to a particular kind of work.
why.Feminist movements aim to preserve unequ: Its aim is equality, not the preservation of unequal roles.
why.Legal and political campaigns alone defi: Feminist movements also concern equality in personal and family life.

activities.explanation: A feminist believes in equal rights and opportunities for women and men.

activities.context: A woman and a man do exactly the same work, but the woman is paid less. She points to the Equal Remuneration Act, 1976, which says equal work should receive equal wages. She also does an extra hour of unpaid work each day. In her family, a girl leaves school because parents spend more on their sons’ education. After learning about feminist movements, the woman supports equality in personal and family life and women’s demands for better legal and political status.
activities.prompt: What is a likely result of the family spending more educational resources on its sons?
options: Some girls may leave school, reducing the proportion who continue to higher studies.
The girls’ literacy rate will rise until it equals that of boys.
More girls will enter higher studies because their brothers receive less attention.
The child sex ratio proves that more girls are leaving school.

why.The girls’ literacy rate will rise until: Less school participation does not automatically raise literacy.
why.More girls will enter higher studies bec: Sons’ greater share of resources does not benefit girls directly.
why.The child sex ratio proves that more gir: The child sex ratio and school participation are different issues.

activities.explanation: Unequal educational resources can cause some girls to leave school.

activities.prompt:
Assertion (A): A feminist movement campaigns for equality in personal and family life.
Reason (R): Agitations for women’s rights demanded better legal and political status for women.
options: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true but R is false.
A is false but R is true.
activities.explanation: Both statements are true, but demands for legal and political status do not explain the movement’s focus on personal and family equality.

activities.prompt:
Assertion (A): The Equal Remuneration Act, 1976 requires every woman to receive the same wage as every man, even when their work is different.
Reason (R): Women are often paid less than men even when they do exactly the same work.
options: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true but R is false.
A is false but R is true.
activities.explanation: The reason is true, but the assertion misstates the Act because it applies equal pay only to equal work.

activities.prompt: Explain how gender inequality affects women’s education and work, and why the Equal Remuneration Act, 1976 is important.
activities.answer: Women’s inequality affects education because some girls leave school when parents spend more resources on sons. This helps explain why women’s literacy is only 54 per cent, compared with 76 per cent for men, and why a smaller proportion of girls enter higher studies. In work, an average Indian woman works one hour longer each day, much of it unpaid and often unvalued. The Equal Remuneration Act, 1976 is important because it requires equal wages for equal work, yet women often receive less even for exactly the same work.
points: Some girls leave school because educational resources favour sons.
Women’s literacy is 54 per cent, compared with 76 per cent for men.
Women work an average of one extra hour each day, much of it unpaid.
The Act requires equal wages for equal work.
activities.explanation: Compare your answer with the points a marker looks for.

activities.context: At a civic meeting, a group reviews women’s political representation. Women hold 14.36 per cent of Lok Sabha seats and less than 5 per cent of state assembly seats, placing India in the bottom group of nations. Although the Nari Shakti Vandan Adhiniyam provides 33 per cent reservation for women and local bodies have reserved seats, cabinets remain largely all-male. The group considers whether legally requiring a fair proportion of women representatives could help.
activities.prompt: If the group supports a legal rule requiring a fair proportion of women to be elected, what is the most likely result?
options: More women could gain elected power, so women’s problems may receive more attention.
Women’s concerns would become less important because elected positions are reserved.
Only panchayat seats would be affected, while national elections would continue unchanged.
Every government cabinet would immediately become equally represented by women.

why.Women’s concerns would become less impor: Making representation legally protected would not reduce the importance of women’s concerns.
why.Only panchayat seats would be affected,: The proposed legal rule concerns women’s representation rather than only panchayat seats.
why.Every government cabinet would immediate: The law provides reservation for seats, but it does not state that cabinets will become equally represented.

activities.explanation: More elected women could help ensure proper attention to women’s problems.

activities.context: At a civic meeting, a group reviews women’s political representation. Women hold 14.36 per cent of Lok Sabha seats and less than 5 per cent of state assembly seats, placing India in the bottom group of nations. Although the Nari Shakti Vandan Adhiniyam provides 33 per cent reservation for women and local bodies have reserved seats, cabinets remain largely all-male. The group considers whether legally requiring a fair proportion of women representatives could help.
activities.prompt: In a local body, an elected woman raises an issue affecting disadvantaged groups. What benefit may follow from this action?
options: The social division may become a political issue, allowing disadvantaged groups to benefit.
Disadvantaged groups will benefit only if the elected woman removes all reserved seats.
The issue will disappear because reserved representatives cannot discuss social divisions.
Women from disadvantaged groups will be the only people allowed to contest reserved seats.

why.Disadvantaged groups will benefit only i: Removing reserved seats would reduce women’s opportunities for elected representation.
why.The issue will disappear because reserve: Making an issue political can help those affected by it.
why.Women from disadvantaged groups will be: Reserved seats are not stated to be limited to women from advantaged groups.

activities.explanation: Disadvantaged groups benefit when social divisions become political issues.

activities.prompt:
Assertion (A): The Nari Shakti Vandan Adhiniyam, or Women’s Reservation Act, was passed in 2023.
Reason (R): The new law provides 33 per cent reservation of seats for women.
options: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true but R is false.
A is false but R is true.
activities.explanation: Both statements are true, but the reservation provision does not explain why the law was passed in 2023.

activities.prompt:
Assertion (A): Government cabinets remain largely all-male even when the leader is a woman.
Reason (R): The 33 per cent reservation law guarantees equal representation in every government cabinet.
options: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true but R is false.
A is false but R is true.
activities.explanation: The statement about cabinets is true, but the stated guarantee about cabinet representation is false.

activities.prompt: Explain the difference between women’s representation in national legislatures and their representation in local bodies.
activities.answer: Women’s representation in national legislatures is much lower than in local bodies. In the Lok Sabha, elected women make up 14.36 per cent of total strength, while their share in state assemblies is below 5 per cent. India is therefore in the bottom group of nations for women’s representation in legislatures. By contrast, seats in panchayats and municipalities are reserved for women, and more than 10 lakh elected women representatives serve in rural and urban local bodies. The Women’s Reservation Act, passed in 2023, also provides 33 per cent reservation of seats for women.
points: Lok Sabha representation is stated as 14.36 per cent.
Women’s share in state assemblies is below 5 per cent.
Panchayat and municipal seats are reserved for women.
More than 10 lakh elected women representatives are in rural and urban local bodies.
activities.explanation: Compare your answer with the points a marker looks for.

activities.context: A local party is preparing a political rally. Its campaign uses a sacred symbol, religious leaders, emotional speeches and fear of outsiders to build support. It claims one religion is superior and says only members of that religion should decide community needs. Other residents object because every community has many voices. One councillor argues that religious differences can enter politics only when every religion is treated equally and political power should be used to prevent oppression.
activities.prompt: If the councillor acts on the residents’ concerns, what should they do?
options: Hear all community voices and judge political demands without treating one religion as superior.
Make one religion’s beliefs the standard for deciding the community’s needs.
Allow only members of one religion to present their demands.
Use political power to enforce the superior religion’s rules over others.

why.Make one religion’s beliefs the standard: This makes one religion the basis of community decisions.
why.Allow only members of one religion to pr: This excludes other communities from expressing their needs.
why.Use political power to enforce the super: This turns political power into religious domination.

activities.explanation: This respects different voices and equal treatment.

boss.title: Chapter challenge: Gender, Religion and Caste

activities.prompt: Which are the main social differences discussed in this chapter?
options: Gender, religion and caste
Class, income and occupation
Region, language and age
Gender, language and class
activities.explanation: The lesson identifies gender, religion and caste as the main social differences. It also says social diversity does not threaten democracy.

activities.prompt: Gender division is based on biology rather than social expectations.
activities.explanation: Gender division comes from social expectations and stereotypes, not biology.

activities.prompt: According to the gender division, who does all the work inside the home?
options: Women do all home work
Men do all home work
Women do all outside work
Men do all village work
activities.explanation: This division assigns all home work to women and all outside work to men.

activities.prompt: A feminist believes in ______ rights and opportunities for women and men.
activities.hint: Think about fair chances for both women and men.
activities.explanation: A feminist believes women and men should have equal rights and opportunities.

activities.prompt: What does the Equal Remuneration Act, 1976 say?
options: Equal work receives equal wages
Equal work receives different wages
Paid work receives no wages
Unpaid work receives equal wages
activities.explanation: The Act says that equal work should receive equal wages.

activities.prompt: Match each law or place with the measure described in the lesson.
pairs: 33 per cent reservation of seats for women
More than 10 lakh elected women representatives
Equal work should receive equal wages
activities.explanation: Each pair connects a law or institution with the measure described in the lesson.

activities.prompt: Put these steps towards women’s political representation in order.
items: Demand better legal and political status
Make a fair proportion of women legally binding
Pass the Women’s Reservation Act in 2023
Provide 33 per cent reservation of seats for women
activities.explanation: The steps move from demands for equality towards legal reservations for women.

activities.prompt: Which action describes communal politics?
options: Using religion in an exclusive way
Treating every religion equally
Letting people choose any religion
Stopping religious discrimination
activities.explanation: Communal politics uses religion in an exclusive and partisan way.

activities.prompt: Caste groups can form coalitions with other castes and communities.
activities.explanation: Caste groups enter into coalitions with other castes and communities.

activities.prompt: What can caste-only politics distract attention from?
options: Poverty, development and corruption
Literacy, health and travel
Caste equality, voting and laws
Women’s rights, secularism and democracy
activities.explanation: Caste-only politics can distract attention from poverty, development and corruption.

chapters.title: Political Parties
chapters.summary: In this chapter: what is a political party?; what do political parties do?; how many parties should a democracy have?; national and state parties.

lessons.title: What is a political party?

activities.prompt: What makes a political party different from other groups?
activities.explanation: Now read on to find out.

activities.title: Political parties in democracy
activities.body: Political parties are visible parts of democracy. Many people see democracy and political parties as almost the same thing. A party is a group that contests elections and holds government power. Its members agree on some policies and programmes. Parties try to persuade people and gain support through elections. Visibility does not mean people like or trust the party.
keyPoints: Political parties contest elections and hold government power.
Members agree on some policies and programmes.
Parties seek support through elections.
activities.explanation: This card explains the main features of a political party.

activities.prompt: A party is visible everywhere, but people still do not trust it. Why?
steps: Political parties contest elections and hold power in government.
This public role makes them among democracy's most visible institutions.
However, being visible does not mean that people like or trust them.
Therefore, people can notice a party while still doubting its policies.
activities.explanation: Think it through with Hooty.

activities.title: What is one key job of a political party?
activities.prompt: What is one key job of a political party?
options: Contest elections and hold power
Agree on every policy
Protect every interest
Gain complete trust
activities.explanation: A political party is a group that contests elections and holds power in government.

activities.title: Visibility and trust
activities.prompt: A party's visibility proves that people trust it.
activities.explanation: A party can be visible in democracy without people liking or trusting it.

activities.title: What do members agree on?
activities.prompt: Members of a party agree on some ______ and programmes.
activities.hint: These are the party's plans and guiding ideas.
activities.explanation: Members of a political party agree on some policies and programmes.

activities.title: Understanding a partisan
activities.prompt: What does a partisan do?
options: Strongly supports a party
Shows both sides equally
Avoids all party views
Trusts every party
activities.explanation: A partisan strongly supports a party and shows a one-sided view.

activities.title: How parties seek to implement policies
activities.prompt: How do parties seek to implement their policies?
options: By winning support at elections
By avoiding support at elections
By rejecting all party policies
By trusting every party's policies
activities.explanation: Parties seek to implement their policies by winning support through elections.

activities.title: The path of a political party
activities.prompt: Put these actions in order.
activities.explanation: Members agree on policies, persuade people, seek electoral support, and then implement policies.

activities.prompt: A party is visible, but people still doubt its policies. Why?
options: Visibility does not make people like or trust the party.
Visibility makes people trust every policy promised by the party.
Public trust makes a party almost invisible in democracy.
A party becomes trusted only when nobody can see it.

why.Visibility makes people trust every poli: This mistake assumes that being seen makes a party trusted.
why.Public trust makes a party almost invisi: This mistake reverses the link between public trust and visibility.
why.A party becomes trusted only when nobody: This mistake assumes that a hidden party must be trusted.

activities.explanation: This is right because visibility does not create liking or trust.

activities.prompt: A poster says a party protects shopkeepers and supports policies. What does this show?
options: It is known for its group, policies, and protected interests.
It is known only for being visible, not for its policies.
It has no policies, so it can protect only one group.
It represents every group, so it protects all their interests.

why.It is known only for being visible, not: This mistake believes visibility is a party's only important feature.
why.It has no policies, so it can protect on: This mistake thinks protecting one group means having no policies.
why.It represents every group, so it protect: This mistake assumes one group's interests represent every group.

activities.explanation: This is right because these show its group, policies, and interests.

activities.prompt: A party has fewer supporters. It says its policies are best. What should it do?
options: Win support through elections so it can implement its policies.
Declare the policies better, because saying so should be enough.
Avoid elections, because winning support is not needed for power.
Change the policies without seeking support from other people.

why.Declare the policies better, because say: This mistake thinks claiming superiority is enough to gain power.
why.Avoid elections, because winning support: This mistake believes elections and public support are unnecessary.
why.Change the policies without seeking supp: This mistake thinks policies can change without anyone's support.

activities.explanation: This is right because winning support through elections helps implement policies.

activities.prompt: Someone supports one party and ignores other views. What does this show?
options: They are partisan because they strongly support one party.
They are neutral because they support no political party.
They are partisan because they support every political party.
They are unbiased because they ignore all other political parties.

why.They are neutral because they support no: This mistake confuses one-sided support with having no party support.
why.They are partisan because they support e: This mistake thinks a partisan supports every party instead of one.
why.They are unbiased because they ignore al: This mistake thinks ignoring other parties shows an unbiased view.

activities.explanation: This is right because they strongly support one party and ignore other views.

activities.prompt: Two party members disagree about one issue. What must still be true?
options: They agree on at least some policies and programmes.
They agree on every policy and every programme.
They must support a different party to remain members.
They must have no policy or programme in common.

why.They agree on every policy and every pro: This mistake changes some agreement into agreement on everything.
why.They must support a different party to r: This mistake assumes party members must support different parties.
why.They must have no policy or programme in: This mistake thinks one disagreement removes all shared agreement.

activities.explanation: This is right because party members agree on some policies and programmes.

lessons.title: What do political parties do?

activities.prompt: How do political parties help people shape the country they live in?
activities.explanation: Now read on to find out.

activities.title: The work of political parties
activities.body: Political parties contest elections and select candidates in different ways. They offer policies and programmes for voters to choose from. Parties group similar opinions, form and run governments, and become opposition after losing. They also shape public opinion, launch movements, help people reach government schemes, and must respond to people’s needs. This work helps democracy work properly.
keyPoints: Parties contest elections and offer choices.
Winning parties form and run governments.
Parties help democracy work properly.
activities.explanation: Political parties connect voters, governments, and people’s needs.

activities.prompt: People with similar opinions group together before an election. What should each party do after people vote?
steps: The winning party forms the government, because parties form and run governments.
The losing party becomes the opposition, because it lost the election.
Similar opinions stay grouped, so government receives a clear direction.
Thus, both parties answer people's needs, because parties must respond to demands.
activities.explanation: Think it through with Hooty.

activities.prompt: What do political parties do during elections?
options: They contest elections.
They choose all voters.
They change every law.
They select every candidate.
activities.explanation: Political parties contest elections. Parties may select their own candidates in different ways.

activities.prompt: Political parties offer different policies and programmes for voters to choose from.
activities.explanation: Yes. Different policies and programmes give voters choices to consider.

activities.prompt: Political parties form and run ______.
activities.hint: Parties help lead the country after winning an election.
activities.explanation: Political parties form and run governments.

activities.prompt: Match each party task with its meaning.
activities.explanation: These tasks show how parties organise choices, opinions, and public issues.

activities.prompt: What happens when a party loses an election?
options: It leads the government.
It acts as the opposition.
It stops all its work.
It forms a movement.
activities.explanation: A party that loses an election acts as opposition to the party in power.

activities.prompt: How can political parties help ordinary people?
options: By helping them reach government schemes.
By stopping all government work.
By choosing their policies alone.
By avoiding people’s demands.
activities.explanation: Parties help ordinary people reach government machinery and welfare schemes.

activities.prompt: Why are political parties necessary for democracy?
options: They help democracy work properly.
They replace every government office.
They make elections unnecessary.
They remove people’s needs.
activities.explanation: Political parties are necessary for a democracy to work properly.

activities.prompt: Political parties only act after they have won an election.
activities.explanation: No. Parties also contest elections, shape public opinion, launch movements, and help people reach government schemes.

activities.prompt: A party keeps raising an issue that many people face. What effect can this have on public opinion?
options: It can shape how people think about the issue.
It can choose all candidates for the coming election.
It can turn the party into the government party.
It can end the party's work on public issues.

why.It can choose all candidates for the com: This mistake mixes shaping opinion with selecting candidates.
why.It can turn the party into the governmen: This mistake assumes that raising issues wins power.
why.It can end the party's work on public is: This mistake assumes parties stop raising issues.

activities.explanation: Raising and highlighting issues can shape public opinion.

activities.prompt: Parties launch movements, respond to demands, and help people reach welfare schemes. Why are they needed in democracy?
options: They help people and make democracy work properly.
They choose voters and remove candidate selection.
They stop movements and ignore public demands.
They replace the government and remove elections.

why.They choose voters and remove candidate: This wrongly assumes parties replace elections and candidate selection.
why.They stop movements and ignore public de: This wrongly believes parties avoid movements and ignore demands.
why.They replace the government and remove e: This wrongly treats parties as replacements for government and elections.

activities.explanation: These public roles show why parties are necessary for democracy.

lessons.title: How many parties should a democracy have?

activities.prompt: How many parties should a democracy have, and why?
activities.explanation: Now read on to find out.

activities.title: Democracy and Political Parties
activities.body: In a democracy, any group of citizens can form a political party. India has a multiparty system, where different parties join together to form a government. This system can appear messy and may cause political instability. However, it allows many interests and opinions to receive political representation. A country's party system develops over time and cannot simply be chosen.
keyPoints: Citizens can form political parties.
India has a multiparty system.
Parties come together to form a government.
Many interests can receive representation.
Party systems develop over time.
activities.explanation: Different parties can represent different interests, even when forming a government together.

activities.prompt: Students want a simpler two-party system because India's multiparty system looks messy. Is a simple switch the answer?
steps: Messiness matters because a multiparty system may cause political instability.
Representation is a benefit, because many interests and opinions can gain it.
A two-party system is narrower: only two main parties can seriously win.
So a simple switch is not justified, because party systems develop over time.
activities.explanation: Think it through with Hooty.

activities.prompt: Who can form a political party in a democracy?
options: Any group of citizens
Only elected officials
Only wealthy business owners
Only Election Commission staff
activities.explanation: Any group of citizens is free to form a political party in a democracy.

activities.prompt: More than ______ parties are registered with the Election Commission of India.
activities.hint: Think of the registered party total.
activities.explanation: More than 750 parties are registered with the Election Commission of India.

activities.prompt: When do various parties form a government in a multiparty system?
options: When they come together
After all parties reject a plan
After citizens stop taking part
When the Election Commission selects them
activities.explanation: A government is formed when various parties come together in a multiparty system.

activities.prompt: Match each idea with its meaning.
pairs: Any group of citizens may form one
Parties come together to form a government
Only two main parties have a serious winning chance
activities.explanation: Citizens can form parties. In a multiparty system, parties join together. In a two-party system, only the main parties have serious chances.

activities.prompt: Put these steps in order, from citizens forming a party to government formation.
activities.explanation: Citizens can form parties, and various parties can come together to form a government.

activities.prompt: Which statement best describes India's multiparty system?
options: It limits opinions but gives parties more trust
It represents many interests but can cause instability
It develops quickly but removes citizen choice
It has two parties but blocks representation
activities.explanation: A multiparty system allows many interests and opinions to receive representation. It can also appear messy and cause political instability.

activities.prompt: A country has a two-party system. A new party forms. What is likely?
options: It has a serious chance of winning.
It has little chance of winning.
It must join the government.
It must become a main party.

Right: only the two main parties have a serious chance of winning.
This mistake assumes joining government follows from forming a party.
This mistake assumes every new party must become a main party.

activities.explanation: This mistake gives a new party the same chance as the two main parties.

activities.prompt: One country has a two-party system. India has a multiparty system. What difference follows?
options: More interests can gain representation in India.
More interests can gain representation in the other country.
Only one interest can gain representation in India.
Only two main parties can seriously win in India.

why.More interests can gain representation i: This mistake reverses the two countries' party systems.
why.Only one interest can gain representatio: This mistake wrongly says only one interest can gain representation.
why.Only two main parties can seriously win: This mistake swaps the systems, because the two-party limit applies to a two-party system.

activities.explanation: Right: India's multiparty system allows many interests and opinions to gain representation.

activities.prompt: India's party membership has risen steadily. Party participation was fairly high. A leader wants two parties. What should the leader remember?
options: Party systems develop over time and cannot simply be chosen.
Two parties can replace all others with one order.
A public vote can choose any party system.
Fewer parties prove the current system has failed.

why.Two parties can replace all others with: This mistake treats the party system as a simple choice.
why.A public vote can choose any party syste: This mistake assumes any party system can be chosen by voting.
why.Fewer parties prove the current system h: This mistake treats fewer parties as proof of failure.

activities.explanation: Right: party systems develop over time, so they cannot simply be chosen.

activities.prompt: An Election Commission list shows over 750 registered parties. What does this suggest about party choice?
options: Citizens can choose among many registered parties.
Citizens can choose among only two main parties.
Citizens can form only parties already on the list.
Citizens have only one registered party to choose.

why.Citizens can choose among only two main: This mistake treats India's multiparty system as a two-party system.
why.Citizens can form only parties already o: This mistake confuses current registration with freedom to form new parties.
why.Citizens have only one registered party: This mistake ignores the many parties shown by the list.

activities.explanation: Right: the long list shows that many registered parties exist.

activities.prompt: Political parties have low trust in South Asia. In a democracy there, what remains possible?
options: Citizens can still form new political parties.
Citizens can form only two political parties.
Citizens can form no new political party.
Citizens must trust parties before forming one.

why.Citizens can form only two political par: This mistake limits party formation to two choices.
why.Citizens can form no new political party: This mistake assumes low trust removes the freedom to form.
why.Citizens must trust parties before formi: This mistake adds a trust rule that is not given.

activities.explanation: Right: low trust does not remove the freedom to form political parties.

lessons.title: National and State parties

activities.prompt: How does a political party become national or State?
activities.explanation: Now read on to find out.

activities.title: National and State parties
activities.body: Political parties in India register with the Election Commission. State parties meet the vote rule and win at least two seats. National parties meet the vote rule and win at least four Lok Sabha seats. Countries with federal systems usually have parties at national and State levels. National party units follow policies, programmes and strategies decided nationally.
keyPoints: All parties register with the Election Commission.
State parties need at least two seats.
National parties need at least four Lok Sabha seats.
activities.explanation: This card introduces how national and State parties differ.

activities.prompt: Two parties met the vote rule. One won four Lok Sabha seats, while the other won two State seats. Which labels should they get?
steps: Labels follow separate rules, because each party type has its own test.
Party A is national: it met the vote rule and four-seat rule.
Party B is State: it met the vote rule and two-seat rule.
Their labels differ because their seats meet different rules.
activities.explanation: Think it through with Hooty.

activities.title: State party seats
activities.prompt: A State party must win at least ______ seats.
activities.hint: Check the State party rule.
activities.explanation: A State party must meet the vote rule and win at least two seats.

activities.title: National party seats
activities.prompt: A national party must win at least how many Lok Sabha seats?
options: Two
Four
Six
activities.explanation: A national party must meet the vote rule and win at least four Lok Sabha seats.

activities.title: Party connections
activities.prompt: Match each party term to its description.
pairs: Follow policies, programmes and strategies decided nationally
Have formed alliances with State parties
activities.explanation: National units follow national decisions, while State parties are also called regional parties.

activities.title: Recognised national parties
activities.prompt: How many recognised national parties were there in 2023?
activities.explanation: There were six recognised national parties in 2023.

activities.title: Aam Aadmi Party
activities.prompt: The Aam Aadmi Party was formed in ______.
activities.hint: It formed after the anti-corruption movement.
activities.explanation: The Aam Aadmi Party was formed in 2012 after the anti-corruption movement.

activities.title: Parties and their ideas
activities.prompt: Match each party to its important idea.
pairs: Seeks to represent dalits, adivasis, Other Backward Classes and religious minorities
Treats cultural nationalism as an important political idea
activities.explanation: Each party is linked to an important idea from the lesson.

activities.prompt: A country has a federal system. A new party plans to contest elections in India. What must the party do, and what party levels are usual there?
options: Register with the Election Commission; national and State levels are usual.
Register with State government; only national-level parties are usual.
Win four seats before registration; only State-level parties are usual.
Join an alliance; every party stays at just one level.

why.Register with State government; only nat: This confuses Election Commission registration with State government approval.
why.Win four seats before registration; only: It confuses later seat recognition with first registration.
why.Join an alliance; every party stays at j: It thinks an alliance can replace required registration.

activities.explanation: Every political party in India must register with the Election Commission.

activities.prompt: Party A met the vote rule and won four Lok Sabha seats. Party B met it and won exactly two State seats only. What status can each get?
options: A is national; B is State.
A is State; B is national.
Both can be national parties.
Both can be State parties.

This swaps the national and State seat rules.
Party B's two State seats do not meet the national rule.
Four Lok Sabha seats do not show two State seats.

activities.explanation: Party A meets the national rule; Party B meets the State rule.

activities.prompt: A national party has units in two States. One unit wants a different policy. What should the party do?
options: Keep one policy decided at the national level.
Let each State unit choose its own policy.
Ask the State government to choose the policy.
Make each State unit a separate State party.

why.Let each State unit choose its own polic: This treats a national party like separate State parties.
why.Ask the State government to choose the p: This gives State governments a role not stated for party units.
why.Make each State unit a separate State pa: This confuses policy differences with changing party status.

activities.explanation: State units follow policies decided at the national level.

activities.prompt: A State party supports an all-India aim. It also joins a national party's alliance. What do these facts show?
options: State parties can have wider aims and form alliances.
State parties always have regional aims and avoid alliances.
An alliance turns every State party into a national party.
Only national parties can support wider political aims.

why.State parties always have regional aims: This assumes State parties always have regional aims and avoid alliances.
why.An alliance turns every State party into: It mistakes an alliance for a change in party status.
why.Only national parties can support wider: It confuses party level with the aims a party may hold.

activities.explanation: State parties need not have regional aims, and national-State alliances occur.

activities.prompt: A source says India had six recognised national parties in 2023. A new party meets the vote rule. It wins four Lok Sabha seats. Can it get national status?
options: Yes, because it meets both national party rules.
No, because only six parties may become national.
No, because State parties need only two seats.
Yes, but only because six parties already existed.

why.No, because only six parties may become: The 2023 number describes that year, not a permanent limit.
why.No, because State parties need only two: It mixes the State two-seat rule with the national rule.
why.Yes, but only because six parties alread: It uses the old number instead of checking the party's own rule.

activities.explanation: It meets both the vote rule and the four-seat national rule.

activities.prompt: Student A wants dalits, adivasis, Other Backward Classes and minorities represented. Student B wants cultural nationalism to guide a party. Student C wants a party formed after anti-corruption. Which set of parties is correct?
options: A: Bahujan Samaj Party. B: Bharatiya Janata Party. C: Aam Aadmi Party.
A: Bharatiya Janata Party. B: Bahujan Samaj Party. C: Aam Aadmi Party.
A: Bahujan Samaj Party. B: Aam Aadmi Party. C: Bharatiya Janata Party.
A: Aam Aadmi Party. B: Bahujan Samaj Party. C: Bharatiya Janata Party.

why.A: Bharatiya Janata Party. B: Bahujan Sa: This swaps the first two parties, reversing the first two wishes.
why.A: Bahujan Samaj Party. B: Aam Aadmi Par: This swaps the last two parties, reversing the last two wishes.
why.A: Aam Aadmi Party. B: Bahujan Samaj Par: This gives all three students the wrong party.

activities.explanation: The names match A, B, and C in the correct order.

lessons.title: Challenges faced by political parties

activities.prompt: What makes political parties weaker, and how can we make them better?
activities.explanation: Now read on to find out.

activities.title: Challenges Facing Political Parties
activities.body: Political parties face several challenges. The first is a lack of internal democracy. Power can become concentrated in a few leaders at the top. Many parties lack membership registers and regular meetings. Dynastic succession can let one family control important positions. Money and muscle power can gain influence, especially during elections. Some parties support criminals. These problems can reduce meaningful choices for voters and blur ideological differences.
keyPoints: Internal democracy is lacking in many parties.
One family can control important positions.
Money and muscle power influence parties.
Voters may not receive meaningful choices.
activities.explanation: These are the main challenges described in this lesson.

activities.prompt: A party has no membership register and rarely holds organisational meetings. What may happen?
steps: Without a register or regular meetings, members have little say.
Leaders gain more power to decide because members check them less often.
Power becomes concentrated in a few leaders at the top.
Thus, the party lacks internal democracy.
activities.explanation: Think it through with Hooty.

activities.prompt: Which challenge is described as the first one for political parties?
options: Dynastic succession
Internal democracy
Money and muscle power
Ideological differences
activities.explanation: The lesson identifies a lack of internal democracy as the first challenge.

activities.prompt: Many parties keep membership registers and hold regular organisational meetings.
activities.explanation: Many parties do not keep these records or hold these meetings.

activities.prompt: Match each challenge with its description.
pairs: Voters often receive no meaningful choice
activities.explanation: Each pairing links a challenge with its description in the lesson.

activities.prompt: Important positions are controlled by members of a ______ family.
activities.hint: This word shows the number of families involved.
activities.explanation: In dynastic succession, members of one family control important positions in many parties.

activities.prompt: Why do party leaders gain greater power to make decisions?
options: Because money and muscle power are declining.
Because voters receive meaningful choices.
Because many parties lack regular meetings.
Because every party supports criminals.
activities.explanation: Many parties do not keep membership registers or hold regular organisational meetings.

activities.prompt: Which pair describes two challenges faced by political parties?
options: Some support criminals; every party holds regular meetings.
Some support criminals; dynastic succession affects every family.
Some support criminals; internal democracy is strong in every party.
Some support criminals; voters often lack meaningful choice.
activities.explanation: Some parties support criminals. Parties also often fail to give voters a meaningful choice.

activities.prompt: A party keeps no membership register and holds no regular meetings. What is likely to happen?
options: Leaders at the top gain more decision-making power.
Every member gains more power over party decisions.
Party meetings become more regular and stronger.
Members begin choosing leaders more often.

why.Every member gains more power over party: This wrongly suggests that weak organisation gives members more power.
why.Party meetings become more regular and s: More regular meetings would show better internal organisation.
why.Members begin choosing leaders more ofte: Choosing leaders more often would show stronger internal democracy.

activities.explanation: Top leaders gain more power when members cannot check them.

activities.prompt: A party gives voters almost the same choices as other parties. Which problem does this create?
options: Voters have little meaningful choice.
Party members have more internal democracy.
One family controls important positions.
Top leaders make fewer important decisions.

why.Party members have more internal democra: Voter choices and members’ internal democracy are different issues.
Family control is another challenge, not the effect of similar choices.
why.Top leaders make fewer important decisio: Fewer decisions by leaders is not shown by similar voter choices.

activities.explanation: Similar choices leave voters without a meaningful choice.

activities.prompt: During an election, a party supports a criminal who can help it win. Why might voters still support it?
options: They believe the criminal's help can win elections.
They want more regular internal party meetings.
They want one family to control important posts.
They hope all parties will offer similar choices.

why.They want more regular internal party me: Wanting regular meetings is about internal democracy, not election success.
why.They want one family to control importan: Family control is a separate challenge faced by some parties.
why.They hope all parties will offer similar: Similar choices between parties do not explain this election support.

activities.explanation: The criminal can help the party win, so this explains their support.

lessons.title: How can political parties be reformed?

activities.prompt: What reforms could make political parties more democratic and accountable?
activities.explanation: Now read on to find out.

activities.title: Ideas for reforming political parties
activities.body: The Constitution was amended to stop elected MLAs and MPs changing parties. An elected member who changes loses the seat. Candidates must file affidavits about property and pending criminal cases. Parties should hold organisational elections, file income tax returns and follow laws for internal affairs. They should give about one-third of tickets to women and receive state funding for election expenses. Citizens can pressure them through petitions, publicity and agitations.
keyPoints: Changing party can cost an elected MLA or MP their seat.
Party reforms include candidate affidavits, internal elections and tax returns.
Citizens can pressure parties and take an active part in democracy.
activities.explanation: These ideas cover party rules, money, candidates, women and citizen action.

activities.prompt: What happens if an elected MLA changes parties after the election?
steps: The Constitution was amended to prevent elected MLAs and MPs changing parties.
This protection applies after voters have elected them.
An elected MLA who changes parties loses their seat in the legislature.
So, changing parties means losing the elected seat.
activities.explanation: Think it through with Hooty.

activities.prompt: What happens to an elected MLA or MP who changes parties?
options: Keeps their seat
Loses their seat
Gets a new ticket
Becomes a candidate again
activities.explanation: The anti-defection law makes the elected member lose their seat.

activities.prompt: Every election candidate must file an affidavit about property and pending criminal cases.
activities.explanation: The law requires this affidavit. There is still no system to check whether its information is true.

activities.prompt: Candidates must file an ______ giving details of property and pending criminal cases.
activities.hint: This document gives details about a candidate’s property and cases.
activities.explanation: Every election candidate must file an affidavit with these details.

activities.prompt: Match each person or group with its result or duty.
pairs: Loses their seat after changing party
activities.explanation: Each pair shows a rule or duty from the lesson.

activities.prompt: What is suggested to regulate political parties’ internal affairs?
options: An internal affairs law
An election result law
A candidate age law
A citizen funding law
activities.explanation: A law should regulate the internal affairs of political parties.

activities.prompt: Political parties have already accepted all the suggested reforms.
activities.explanation: These suggested reforms have not yet been accepted by political parties.

activities.prompt: Political parties should give about ______ of their tickets to women candidates.
activities.hint: The lesson suggests a fixed fraction of tickets for women candidates.
activities.explanation: Political parties should give about one-third of their tickets to women candidates.

activities.prompt: What should citizens do to improve democracy?
options: Join party activities actively
Stop using public pressure methods
Keep away from party activities
Accept party decisions silently
activities.explanation: Democracy improves when ordinary citizens take an active part in political parties.

activities.prompt: A law is made to control how parties choose internal leaders. What must parties do?
options: They must follow the law for their internal affairs.
They must stop choosing any internal leaders.
They must allow every citizen to choose their leaders.
They must give one-third of their tickets to women.

why.They must stop choosing any internal lea: Regulation does not mean ending the choice of leaders.
why.They must allow every citizen to choose: It confuses party regulation with direct citizen control.
why.They must give one-third of their ticket: It mixes internal affairs with a separate ticket reform.

activities.explanation: The law should regulate political parties' internal affairs.

activities.prompt: Ordinary residents want a stronger democracy. What is the best way to help?
options: Take an active part in parties and pressure them when needed.
Wait quietly because citizens cannot change political parties.
Only discuss parties without joining any party work.
Ask every party member to change parties.

why.Wait quietly because citizens cannot cha: It wrongly treats citizens as unable to act.
why.Only discuss parties without joining any: It avoids the active party work that can improve democracy.
why.Ask every party member to change parties: It confuses active participation with party switching.

activities.explanation: Active citizens can improve democracy and pressure parties.

lessons.title: Test practice
lessons.sceneAlt: Samajwadi Party activists march through Mumbai’s streets during an election campaign.
lessons.sceneCaption: Samajwadi Party activists march through Mumbai during an election campaign.

activities.context: In an election, a political party asks people to support its policies. Its members agree on some policies and programmes, and the party is known for the part of society it represents, the policies it supports and the interests it protects. The party wins support at the election and holds power in government. Some citizens still say they do not trust the party, while one enthusiastic member speaks only in its favour.
activities.prompt: After winning support in the election, what should the political party do next?
options: Work to put its policies into effect through the elected government
Keep persuading citizens because winning support does not help it implement policies
Focus only on becoming more visible, because visibility is the same as implementation
Ask members to drop the party's policies because some citizens do not trust it

why.Keep persuading citizens because winning: The party's aim is not simply to remain visible.
why.Ask members to drop the party's policies: Some distrust does not mean members should abandon their policies.

activities.explanation: Winning support helps a party seek to implement its policies.

activities.context: In an election, a political party asks people to support its policies. Its members agree on some policies and programmes, and the party is known for the part of society it represents, the policies it supports and the interests it protects. The party wins support at the election and holds power in government. Some citizens still say they do not trust the party, while one enthusiastic member speaks only in its favour.
activities.prompt: The enthusiastic member supports the party and presents only its point of view. What does this show?
options: The member is acting as a partisan and showing a one-sided view
The member is representing every part of society equally
The member no longer agrees with the party's policies
The member is directly implementing the party's policies through elections

why.The member is representing every part of: A party represents a part of society, not every part equally.
why.The member no longer agrees with the par: One-sided support does not show disagreement with the party.
why.The member is directly implementing the: Persuading people is different from implementing policies through elections.

activities.explanation: Strong support combined with one-sidedness shows partisan behaviour.

activities.prompt:
Assertion (A): A political party is a group of people who contest elections and hold power in government.
Reason (R): The members of the party agree on some policies and programmes.
options: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true but R is false.
A is false but R is true.
activities.explanation: Both statements are true, but agreement on policies does not explain the party's role in elections and government.

activities.prompt:
Assertion (A): Political parties seek to implement their policies by winning support through elections.
Reason (R): Parties try to persuade people that their policies are better than those of other parties.
options: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true but R is false.
A is false but R is true.
activities.explanation: Persuading people to prefer a party's policies helps it win the support needed to seek their implementation.

activities.prompt: Explain the difference between a political party and a partisan.
activities.answer: A political party is a group of people who contest elections and hold power in government. Its members agree on some policies and programmes. The party is known for the part of society it represents, the policies it supports and the interests it protects. A partisan, on the other hand, strongly supports a party and shows a one-sided view. Thus, a party is an organisation that takes part in elections and government, while a partisan is a person who strongly supports that organisation in a one-sided way.
points: Defines a political party
Includes contesting elections and holding government power
Mentions agreement on some policies and programmes
Explains that a partisan strongly supports a party and shows a one-sided view
activities.explanation: Compare your answer with the points a marker looks for.

activities.prompt:
Assertion (A): Political parties contest elections.
Reason (R): Contesting elections is one of the activities that political parties perform.
options: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true but R is false.
A is false but R is true.
activities.explanation: The reason directly explains that election contesting is a political party's activity.

activities.prompt:
Assertion (A): Political parties are necessary for a democracy to work properly.
Reason (R): Political parties contest elections.
options: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true but R is false.
A is false but R is true.
activities.explanation: Both statements are true, but contesting elections alone does not explain why parties are necessary for democracy.

activities.prompt: Explain why political parties are important for a democracy to work properly.
activities.answer: Political parties are important because they contest elections, select candidates, and offer different policies and programmes for voters to choose from. They group similar opinions so that governments receive a clear direction. Parties also form and run governments, while parties that lose elections act as opposition. In this way, different viewpoints are represented and people have choices. Political parties also shape public opinion, launch movements, help people reach government machinery and welfare schemes, and must respond to people's needs and demands.
points: Explains their role in elections and offering choices
Shows how parties give direction to government
Explains government, opposition, and public opinion roles
Explains their responsibility to people
activities.explanation: Compare your answer with the points a marker looks for.

activities.context: A student in India notices that more than 750 parties are registered with the Election Commission of India, although India has a multiparty system. The student learns that a government is formed when various parties come together, and that this arrangement can appear messy and may cause political instability. Yet, the student also sees that many interests and opinions can receive political representation. The student wonders whether India would be better off with only two parties.
activities.prompt: If India changed to a two-party system, which outcome would most directly follow?
options: Only the two main parties would have a serious chance of winning.
Every registered party would have a serious chance of winning.
The number of registered parties would no longer matter.
A multiparty government would still be the only possible result.

why.Every registered party would have a seri: The lesson says only the two main parties have a serious chance.
why.The number of registered parties would n: In a two-party system, other parties do not have the same serious chance.
why.A multiparty government would still be t: A two-party system would not normally produce a multiparty government.

activities.explanation: This is the defining feature of a two-party system.

activities.context: A student in India notices that more than 750 parties are registered with the Election Commission of India, although India has a multiparty system. The student learns that a government is formed when various parties come together, and that this arrangement can appear messy and may cause political instability. Yet, the student also sees that many interests and opinions can receive political representation. The student wonders whether India would be better off with only two parties.
activities.prompt: The student thinks the multiparty system is messy. Which response best balances the lesson's ideas?
options: It may cause political instability, but it also allows broad political representation.
It is automatically better because it guarantees a stable government.
It should be replaced because every registered party can form the government.
It has no value because it does not represent different interests.

why.It is automatically better because it gu: The lesson does not say that a multiparty system guarantees stability.
why.It should be replaced because every regi: It says various parties come together, not that every registered party can form the government.
why.It has no value because it does not repr: A multiparty system allows many interests and opinions to receive political representation.

activities.explanation: This recognizes both possible instability and the benefit of representation.

activities.prompt:
Assertion (A): India has a multiparty system.
Reason (R): A multiparty system allows many interests and opinions to receive political representation.
options: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true but R is false.
A is false but R is true.
activities.explanation: Both statements are true, but the reason explains the benefits of multiparty systems rather than why India has one.

activities.prompt:
Assertion (A): A country's party system cannot simply be chosen.
Reason (R): A country's party system develops over time.
options: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true but R is false.
A is false but R is true.
activities.explanation: The reason explains the assertion because a system that develops over time cannot simply be chosen.

activities.prompt: Explain how India's multiparty system works and what advantages and difficulties it can involve.
activities.answer: India has a multiparty system, and more than 750 parties are registered with the Election Commission of India. In this system, a government is formed when various parties come together. This arrangement can make politics look messy and may cause political instability. At the same time, it allows many interests and opinions to receive political representation. Therefore, a multiparty system has both possible difficulties and an advantage: different groups can have their interests represented in government.
points: India has a multiparty system.
More than 750 parties are registered with the Election Commission of India.
Various parties come together to form a government.
It can appear messy and may cause instability, but it allows broad representation.
activities.explanation: Compare your answer with the points a marker looks for.

activities.prompt:
Assertion (A): The units of a national party follow the policies, programmes and strategies decided at the national level.
Reason (R): The policies, programmes and strategies of a national party are decided at the national level.
options: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true but R is false.
A is false but R is true.
activities.explanation: The reason directly explains why the units of a national party follow its nationally decided policies, programmes and strategies.

activities.prompt:
Assertion (A): A national party must meet the vote rule and win at least four Lok Sabha seats.
Reason (R): A State party must win at least four Lok Sabha seats.
options: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true but R is false.
A is false but R is true.
activities.explanation: The assertion is correct, but the reason gives the wrong seat requirement for State parties.

activities.prompt: What is the difference between a national party and a State party?
activities.answer: A national party and a State party both have to satisfy the vote rule. The main stated difference in seats is that a national party must win at least four Lok Sabha seats, while a State party must win at least two seats. A State party is also called a regional party, but this label does not mean that every State party has regional ideas or aims. In contrast, the units of a national party follow policies, programmes and strategies decided at the national level.
points: Both must meet the vote rule.
A national party needs at least four Lok Sabha seats.
A State party needs at least two seats.
State parties do not always have regional ideas or aims.
activities.explanation: Compare your answer with the points a marker looks for.

activities.context: In a political party, membership records are rarely updated and regular meetings are not held. A family controls several important positions, while the top leadership increasingly relies on money and muscle power during elections. The party also backs criminals because they can help it win. Meanwhile, voters have little meaningful choice, and the party's differences from other parties are becoming harder to identify.
activities.prompt: If the party began keeping an accurate membership register and holding regular meetings, what would most likely happen next?
options: Decision-making would be shared more widely and top leaders would face regular scrutiny.
The party would become more dynastic because families would lose control of key posts.
Election money and muscle power would immediately lose all influence over the party.
Voters would gain more meaningful choice because all ideological differences would return.

why.The party would become more dynastic bec: Losing family control would reduce, not increase, dynastic succession.
why.Election money and muscle power would im: Internal reform would not automatically remove external election pressure.
why.Voters would gain more meaningful choice: Voting and party differences are separate issues from internal organisation.

activities.explanation: Regular meetings and records would strengthen internal checks on leaders.

activities.context: In a political party, membership records are rarely updated and regular meetings are not held. A family controls several important positions, while the top leadership increasingly relies on money and muscle power during elections. The party also backs criminals because they can help it win. Meanwhile, voters have little meaningful choice, and the party's differences from other parties are becoming harder to identify.
activities.prompt: If the family stopped controlling important positions in the party, what would be the most reasonable expectation?
options: The dynastic-succession challenge would weaken, while money-and-muscle influence could remain.
The party would automatically become internally democratic because one family had left.
Money and muscle power would disappear simply because important posts changed hands.
Meaningful voter choice would be restored in every election.

why.The party would automatically become int: Ending family control does not create membership records or meetings.
why.Money and muscle power would disappear s: Money and muscle power can influence elections independently of family positions.
why.Meaningful voter choice would be restore: Greater party competition does not automatically restore meaningful choice.

activities.explanation: Family control is the basis of the dynastic-succession problem.

boss.title: Chapter challenge: Political Parties

activities.title: What is a political party?
activities.prompt: What is a political party?
options: A group that only supports social movements.
A group that contests elections and holds power.
A group that only checks government spending.
A group that only registers election candidates.
activities.explanation: A political party contests elections and holds power in government.

activities.prompt: A party is visible in democracy, so people must like and trust it.
activities.explanation: Visibility does not mean that people like or trust a party.

activities.title: Match party features
activities.prompt: Match each party feature with its description.
pairs: Members agree on policies and programmes.
Parties shape opinion by raising issues.
activities.explanation: Parties select candidates, contest elections and influence public opinion.

activities.title: From persuasion to action
activities.prompt: Put the party's path from persuasion to action in order.
items: Persuade voters their policies are better.
activities.explanation: Parties persuade voters, win support, and then implement their policies.

activities.title: Forming a multiparty government
activities.prompt: How is a government formed in India's multiparty system?
options: When one party rejects elections.
When citizens stop joining parties.
When various parties come together.
When State parties merge into one.
activities.explanation: India has a multiparty system. A government is formed when various parties come together.

activities.prompt: An elected MLA or MP keeps their seat after changing parties.
activities.explanation: An elected MLA or MP who changes parties loses their seat in the legislature.

activities.title: A major party challenge
activities.prompt: Many parties lack internal ______.
activities.hint: Think about how members choose their leaders.
activities.explanation: The first challenge is the lack of internal democracy within parties.

activities.title: Suggested reforms
activities.prompt: Which pair matches two suggested reforms for political parties?
options: Allow criminal support and avoid organisational elections.
Check candidate affidavits and allow party switching.
Regulate internal affairs and give women one-third of tickets.
Fund all parties and remove women's ticket shares.
activities.explanation: A law should regulate parties. Parties should also give about one-third of tickets to women.
